How to use this guide

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Find your way around the guide and its interactive parts
  • Follow a study routine that makes new knowledge stick
  • Know what to do when you get stuck

Welcome. This guide teaches you Rust, a modern programming language, starting from nothing. You do not need to know any other language, any maths beyond arithmetic, or any computer science. You need a computer, a web browser, and the patience to type things out and see what happens.

What you will be able to do

Finish every chapter, exercise and project and you will be able to build real software in Rust: command-line tools, web services backed by a database, programs that do many things at once. You will also understand ideas that apply to every programming language: how memory works, how to organise a large program, how to handle errors, and how to test that your code is right.

This guide is intentionally scoped to the core Rust language, its tooling, the most important crates and ecosystem patterns, and the practical projects in this book. It does not pretend to cover every niche branch of the ecosystem: blockchain, kernel programming, robotics and other specialised domains are outside the main path of a from-zero guide. The point is to give you a solid foundation before you choose a deeper specialism.

Choose a learning route

You do not have to study every topic before building useful software. If you are new to Rust, follow the chapters in order through chapter 26, then use the short tool commands from chapter 2 and consult the deeper guides in chapters 39–41 as your projects need them. After that, choose a goal-specific route in chapter 54. The advanced language and ecosystem chapters are there when your work calls for them.

Learning to program is like learning to cook or to play an instrument. Reading alone does not work. Each chapter gives you something to do, and the doing is where the learning happens.

What is in this guide

It is worth knowing the size of what you are starting, so that you can plan.

Chapters55, of which 8 are complete projects you build file by file
Appendices4: a glossary, a reference, a catalogue of compiler errors, and Rust for people who know other languages
Rust examples913 across 1,163 code listings, with real compiled output and diagnostics
Exercises190, each with a hint and a worked solution
Quiz questions238, each with an explanation

Nothing here is a mock-up. When the guide shows a compiler error, that is the message the compiler really printed, on the line number it really pointed at. When it shows program output, the program really produced it. This is checked automatically, for every example, on every change to the guide.

What this guide covers, and what it does not

“Everything about Rust” is an endless subject, so this guide has a written rule. Each part of the Rust world is handled in one of three ways, and it says which:

  • Taught. At least one section with a compiled example, plus an exercise or a quiz question.
  • Named with advice. A table row or short paragraph that names the mainstream crates, says how mature they are, and says when to choose them. You are not left guessing, and you are not misled into thinking a passing name is a lesson.
  • Out of scope, on purpose. Declared in chapter 54 with a reason and somewhere else to read.

A few areas are deliberately outside this guide: blockchain and Web3, operating-system and kernel development, robotics, high-frequency trading, and cloud-provider SDKs beyond one example. They are real and interesting ecosystems, and each has its own books. A guide that starts from zero cannot teach them honestly, so it names them and steps aside rather than pretending.

Everything else in the ecosystem chapter follows the first two rules. If you find a crate that is named once and never explained, that is a mistake worth reporting.

How a chapter is built

Every chapter follows the same rhythm:

  1. The idea in plain words, usually with a comparison to everyday life.
  2. A small example you can run, with an explanation of each part.
  3. Exercises, so you use the idea yourself right away.
  4. A quick quiz, so you find out what did not stick before you move on.

Along the way you will meet the coloured boxes below. Each colour always means the same thing.

How code is shown

Code appears in boxes like this one:

The grey box below the code shows the output: what appears on the screen when the program runs. Do not worry about what the code means yet. That starts in chapter 2.

Each code box has buttons in its top-right corner:

  • Copy puts the code on your clipboard so you can paste it somewhere else.
  • Run appears on complete programs. It opens the code in the Rust Playground, a free website that runs Rust for you, so you can try things without installing anything. It needs an internet connection.

Some examples are meant to be wrong, because the error teaches something. They have a red label:

Good to know
Tested examples and reference code

Standard-library examples and core crate examples marked for verification are compiled against the Rust compiler (edition 2024, targeting Rust 1.100) by tools/check.py, and failing examples fail in the way the text describes. Larger multi-file snippets or examples that talk to external services (such as databases, message brokers, or telemetry collectors) are shown as complete reference code.

Exercises, hints and solutions

Exercises come in three kinds:

PracticeYou apply the idea on your ownTry for at least ten minutes before opening the hint

Each exercise has a hint and a full solution with an explanation. Here is a small one to try the buttons:

Need a hint?

A hint nudges you in the right direction without giving the answer away.

Show solution and explanation

A solution shows working code and explains why it works. Your own solution does not have to look the same. If it does the job and you understand it, it is a good solution.

One rule: try before you look. A solution you worked for stays in your head. A solution you only read is gone by tomorrow.

Quizzes give you an answer straight away. Try this one:

Try a quiz question
1

What is the best way to use the examples in this guide?

Typing code yourself trains your fingers and your eyes. Guessing the result first turns each example into a small experiment, and you learn the most when your guess turns out to be wrong.

A study routine that works

  • Little and often. Forty minutes a day beats five hours on Sunday. At that pace the whole guide takes about three to five months.
  • Type the code. Do not copy and paste while you are learning. Typing makes you notice every bracket and semicolon.
  • Predict, then run. Before you run a program, say out loud what you think it will print.
  • Break things on purpose. Remove a line or change a number and see what the compiler says. You cannot damage anything.
  • Read error messages slowly. Rust’s error messages are among the most helpful of any language. They usually tell you exactly what is wrong, and often how to fix it. Learning to read them is a skill this guide teaches on purpose.
  • Do the projects. They join the small ideas into something real.
Tip
Already know another programming language?

You can read Part 1 quickly, but do not skip it: Rust does some basic things differently. Slow down at Part 2 (ownership). It is the part that is new for everybody.

When you get stuck

Being stuck is a normal part of programming. Professionals are stuck several times a day. This order of steps usually works:

  1. Read the error message again, slowly, from the top. Read the line it points to.
  2. Make the problem smaller. Delete code until the error goes away. The last thing you deleted is the cause.
  3. Explain the problem out loud, to a friend or to a rubber duck on your desk. Saying it in words often shows you the answer.
  4. Look it up. Use the search box in this guide, the glossary, and the list of common compiler errors.
  5. Ask people. The Rust community is known for being kind to beginners. The official forum at users.rust-lang.org is a good place to ask.
  6. Take a break. Many problems are solved on a walk.

Your progress

At the end of each chapter there is a Mark as complete button. Completed chapters get a tick in the table of contents, and the bar at the top of the list fills up. Your progress, quiz answers and ticked exercises are saved in your browser on this device. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Recap
  • Each chapter goes: idea, example, exercise, quiz.
  • Type the code, predict the result, then run it.
  • Try each exercise before opening the hint or the solution.
  • Error messages are there to help you. Read them slowly.
  • Being stuck is normal. Make the problem smaller, look it up, ask, rest.

01

Programs, languages, and why Rust exists

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what a program, a programming language and a compiler are
  • Describe the problem Rust was created to solve
  • Compare Rust with Python, JavaScript, C, C++, Go and Java in plain terms
  • Decide what you would like to build with Rust

Before you write any code, it helps to know what code is, what happens to it after you write it, and why the world needed one more programming language. This chapter has no code to type. It gives you the map for everything that follows.

What is a program?

A computer is a machine that follows instructions. It is very fast and it never gets bored, but it understands nothing. It does exactly what it is told, in exactly the order it is told, including the mistakes.

A program is a list of instructions for a computer. The app you use to send messages, the website you are reading, and the software inside a washing machine are all programs.

Real-world analogy
A program is a recipe

A recipe lists exact steps: take 200 g of flour, add two eggs, stir for one minute. A cook follows the steps and gets a cake. A program lists exact steps too, and the computer is the cook.

There is one difference. A human cook fills gaps with common sense. If the recipe forgets to say “take the cake out of the oven”, a person will take it out anyway. A computer will let it burn. Programming is the skill of writing instructions so complete and so exact that even a machine with no common sense gets the right result.

Programming (also called coding) is writing those instructions. The text you write is called source code, or just code.

What is a programming language?

Deep down, a computer understands only numbers. Its real instructions, called machine code, look like this to a human: 10110000 01100001. Writing programs that way is slow and painful, so people invented programming languages: ways of writing instructions with words and symbols that humans can read. For example, this line of Rust tells the computer to show a message on the screen:

A programming language has strict rules about how instructions must be written. These rules are called its syntax, the same way English has grammar. Forget one bracket and the computer cannot understand you. That feels harsh at first. It becomes normal quickly.

There are thousands of programming languages. You may have heard of Python, JavaScript, Java, C or C++. They all describe instructions for a computer, but they make different choices, the way a sports car, a bus and a tractor are all vehicles built for different jobs.

From your text to a running program

Your computer cannot run source code directly. Something must translate it into machine code. There are two main ways to do that.

Real-world analogy
Translating a book or interpreting a speech

Imagine you wrote a speech in English and the audience speaks only Japanese.

  • You can hire a translator to turn the whole speech into Japanese before the event. This takes time up front, but then the speech can be read aloud at full speed, as often as you like. The translator also has time to spot sentences that make no sense and send them back to you.
  • Or you can hire an interpreter who stands next to you and translates each sentence as you say it. You can start at once, but the speech is slower every time, and a nonsense sentence is only noticed when you reach it, in front of everyone.
  • A compiler is the translator. It reads all your source code, checks it for mistakes, and produces a finished program (a file your computer can run directly). Rust, C, C++ and Go work this way.
  • An interpreter is the live interpreter. It reads your code and carries it out line by line, every time the program runs. Python and JavaScript mostly work this way.
In plain English
Compiler, compile, compile time, run time

The compiler is the tool that turns your source code into a program the computer can run. For Rust this tool is called rustc. To compile is to do that translation. Compile time is the moment when the compiler is working. Run time (also written runtime) is the moment when the finished program is running. A mistake caught at compile time never reaches the people who use your program. That idea is central to Rust.

Bugs, and the kind Rust was built to stop

A mistake in a program is called a bug. Some bugs are small, like a button in the wrong colour. Some are serious: a program that crashes (stops suddenly), loses your data, or lets a criminal break in.

One family of bugs has caused huge damage for decades: memory bugs. A program keeps the data it is working with in the computer’s memory. In older languages such as C and C++, the programmer must manage that memory by hand: ask for it, use it, give it back, and never touch it afterwards. A person who does this thousands of times will get it wrong sometimes. The results are crashes and security holes. Microsoft and Google have both reported that about 70% of the serious security bugs in their large C and C++ products were memory bugs.

Languages such as Java, Python, JavaScript and Go avoid most of these bugs with a garbage collector: a helper that runs inside your program, watches the memory, and cleans up what is no longer used. That is safe, but it has a cost. The helper uses time and memory, and now and then it makes the program pause for a moment.

So for a long time programmers had to choose:

Fast and in full controlSafe from memory bugs
C, C++YesNo. Safety depends on the programmer never making a mistake
Java, Python, JavaScript, GoLess. The garbage collector costs time and memoryYes
RustYesYes

Rust gets both by using a new idea called ownership. The Rust compiler follows a small set of rules about who is responsible for each piece of data. With those rules it can prove, before the program ever runs, that the memory will be used correctly. No garbage collector is needed, so the program stays fast. You will learn ownership in Part 2. It is the heart of Rust.

Key idea
Rust’s promise

Rust moves whole families of mistakes from “found by your users at run time” to “found by the compiler on your own computer”. If a Rust program compiles, a large class of bugs simply cannot be in it.

A short history of Rust

  • 2006: Graydon Hoare, a programmer at Mozilla (the makers of the Firefox browser), starts Rust as a personal project. He wanted a language that made software more reliable.
  • 2009: Mozilla begins to pay for its development.
  • 2015: Rust 1.0 is released. From here on the language promises stability: code that compiles today keeps compiling with newer versions.
  • 2021: The Rust Foundation is created, backed by companies such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Huawei and Mozilla, to look after the language.
  • Today: Rust is used inside Windows, Android and the Linux kernel, and by companies such as Amazon, Cloudflare, Discord and Dropbox. A new version comes out every six weeks. This guide was written for version 1.100.

Rust is developed in the open by volunteers and paid engineers from many organisations. People who write Rust call themselves Rustaceans, and the unofficial mascot is a friendly orange crab called Ferris.

What people build with Rust

  • Command-line tools: small, fast programs you run by typing a command. You will build several.
  • Web servers and services: the programs behind websites and apps. See Part 10.
  • Programs that run inside a web page, through a technology called WebAssembly.
  • Desktop and mobile apps, and games.
  • Embedded software: the code inside small devices such as sensors, watches and robots.
  • Operating systems, browsers and databases: the foundations other software stands on.

Rust compared with other languages

You do not need to know these languages. The table shows where Rust sits among them.

LanguageHow it runsMemory safetyTypical speedKnown for
RustCompiledChecked by the compiler, no garbage collectorVery fastSafety and speed together
CCompiledUp to the programmerVery fastOperating systems, small devices
C++CompiledMostly up to the programmerVery fastGames, browsers, large systems
GoCompiledGarbage collectorFastSimple network services
Java, C#Compiled to an in-between form, then run by a helper programGarbage collectorFastBusiness software, Android apps
PythonInterpretedGarbage collectorSlowData science, scripts, beginners
JavaScriptInterpretedGarbage collectorMediumWeb pages
How other languages do it
What you gain and what you pay

Rust is honest about its price. The compiler is strict: it refuses programs that other languages would accept, and beginners sometimes feel they are “fighting the compiler”. Compiling also takes longer than in some languages. In return you get programs that are fast, use little memory, and rarely crash in surprising ways. Many people find that once their Rust program compiles, it simply works.

There is another benefit that is easy to miss. Rust makes you think clearly about things every program has to deal with, in any language: who owns this data, who may change it, what can go wrong. People who learn Rust often say it made them better at other languages too.

Is Rust a good first language?

Yes, with the right guide. Rust asks you to learn a few ideas early that other languages hide. That is more work in the first weeks. But the compiler acts like a patient tutor: it catches your mistakes, explains them in full sentences, and often shows the fix. You also learn how computers really work, which pays off for the rest of your programming life.

Recap
  • A program is a list of exact instructions. Source code is the text you write.
  • A compiler translates all your code into a runnable program before it runs, and checks it for mistakes.
  • Memory bugs are a major cause of crashes and security holes in C and C++ programs.
  • Garbage-collected languages avoid them at a cost in speed. Rust avoids them at compile time, with no such cost, through ownership.
  • The price is a strict compiler and a steeper start. The reward is fast, reliable software.
Check your understanding
1

What does a compiler do?

A compiler translates the whole program ahead of time. Running code line by line is what an interpreter does, and cleaning up memory during the run is the job of a garbage collector.

2

Why can a mistake caught at compile time be called a “cheap” mistake?

The earlier a bug is found, the less harm it does. A compile-time error never reaches your users. Rust is designed to move as many mistakes as possible to compile time.

3

How does Rust avoid memory bugs without a garbage collector?

Ownership rules are checked at compile time, so the finished program needs no helper to watch its memory. You will learn these rules in Part 2.

4

Which statement about Rust is true?

Rust trades a steeper learning curve for speed and reliability. It is used for many kinds of software and is developed by an open community, supported by the Rust Foundation.

Guided exerciseWrite instructions for a machine

Programming starts with exact thinking, not with typing. On paper, write step-by-step instructions for making a cup of tea, for a robot that has no common sense. The robot knows only these actions: pick up, put down, fill, pour, switch on, wait until, and it can check whether something is true.

Then read your steps again and look for gaps. What happens if the kettle is already full? What if there is no tea bag left?

Need a hint?

Go slower than feels natural. “Boil water” is not one step for this robot. It has to pick up the kettle, fill it, put it down, switch it on, and wait until the water boils.

Show solution and explanation

One possible answer:

  1. Check whether the kettle contains water. If it does not, pick up the kettle, fill it with water, and put it down on its base.
  2. Switch on the kettle.
  3. Wait until the water boils.
  4. Check whether there is a tea bag in the box. If there is none, stop and report “no tea”.
  5. Pick up a tea bag and put it down in the cup.
  6. Pick up the kettle, pour water into the cup until the cup is nearly full, and put the kettle down.
  7. Wait until three minutes have passed.
  8. Pick up the tea bag and put it down in the bin.

You have just used the three building blocks of every program, in any language:

  • Sequence: steps that run in order.
  • Decision: “check whether … if …” picks between paths. You will write these with if in chapter 6.
  • Repetition: “wait until” and “pour until” repeat something until a condition is met. These are loops.

You also thought about what could go wrong (no tea bag). That is error handling, and Rust takes it very seriously.

PracticePick your goal

Write down one thing you would like to build once you know Rust. It can be small: a tool that renames your photo files, a simple game, a website that tracks your reading. Keep the note. A concrete goal makes it much easier to keep going.

Need a hint?

Choose a project you already care about. A personal problem is easier to motivate than a generic toy project.

Show solution and explanation

There is no wrong answer. If you cannot think of anything yet, borrow one of these: a quiz game in the terminal, a tool that counts the words in a file, a personal expense tracker, or a small website for a club. You will build something similar to each of them in this guide.

PracticeChoose the first kind of Rust program you want to build

Pick a category for your first project: command-line tool, web service, terminal game, desktop app, or small library. Write one sentence explaining why that category fits your goal.

Need a hint?

Think about what you want to do with the program, not about the syntax. A CLI is easier to start with if you want a tool for files and folders.

Show solution and explanation

A good answer is specific and connected to a real task. For example: “I want a command-line tool that renames my photos by date, because I have many files and I want a quicker way to organise them.” The purpose of the exercise is to turn a vague wish into a project you can finish and learn from.

Setting up and running your first program

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Run Rust code in the browser without installing anything
  • Use a terminal for basic tasks
  • Install Rust and a code editor on your own computer
  • Create, run and change a Rust project with Cargo
  • Read a compiler error message without fear

Time to write a real program. First you will run Rust in your web browser with nothing to install. Then you will set up Rust on your own computer, create a project, and learn what every character of your first program means.

Two ways to run Rust

Real-world analogy
A kitchen you can borrow, and a kitchen you own

A borrowed kitchen lets you try a recipe quickly, but a real kitchen is what you need when you are cooking for a week. The Rust Playground is the borrowed kitchen: perfect for a first try. A real Rust install is the kitchen you keep: the place where you build larger projects and keep your files.

1. In the browser: the Rust Playground. Open play.rust-lang.org. You see an editor with a small program in it. Press the Run button and the result appears below. That is all. The Playground is perfect for the first chapters and for quick experiments. The Run button on examples in this guide opens the example there for you.

2. On your own computer. You need this for real projects: programs made of several files, programs that read your files, and everything from the first mini-project onwards. Installing takes about ten minutes and is explained below.

If you cannot install software right now, use the Playground and come back to the installation later.

Real-world analogy
Setting up a workshop before building anything

A carpenter spends the first day hanging tools on the wall. Nothing is built that day, yet every later hour is faster. Setting up Rust, a terminal and an editor is that day: dull while it lasts, paid back every day after.

A five-minute tour of the terminal

Programmers often control the computer by typing commands instead of clicking. The window where you type them is called the terminal (also command line, console or shell). It looks old-fashioned, but it is quick and exact, and Rust’s tools are used through it.

How to open it:

  • Windows: press the Windows key, type terminal, press Enter. (On older systems, search for PowerShell.)
  • macOS: press Cmd + Space, type terminal, press Enter.
  • Linux: press Ctrl + Alt + T on most systems.

The terminal is always “inside” one folder, called the current folder or working directory. These few commands are enough for this guide:

CommandWhat it does
pwdShows which folder you are in (“print working directory”)
lsLists the files in the current folder (on old Windows consoles: dir)
cd projectsMoves into the folder called projects (“change directory”)
cd ..Moves up to the folder that contains the current one
mkdir projectsCreates a new folder called projects (“make directory”)

Three keys save a lot of typing. The up arrow brings back your previous command. The Tab key completes a name you have started to type. Ctrl + C stops a program that is running.

Good to know
How commands are written in this guide

Commands are shown with a $ in front, like this:

The $ only marks “type this line”. Do not type the $ itself. Lines without a $ are what the computer answers. The Copy button copies only the commands.

Installing Rust

Rust is installed with a small tool called rustup. It downloads the compiler, keeps it up to date, and can remove it again cleanly.

On Windows

  1. Go to rustup.rs and download rustup-init.exe. Run it.
  2. If the installer says that the Visual Studio C++ Build Tools are missing, choose the option to install them (the first option). Rust needs them to produce finished programs.
  3. When it asks how to proceed, press Enter to accept the standard installation.
  4. Close the terminal and open a new one, so that it notices the new tools.

On macOS and Linux

Paste this command into the terminal and press Enter:

When it asks, press Enter to accept the standard installation. Then close the terminal and open a new one.

Rust also needs a few standard build tools from your system. On macOS, run xcode-select --install if you have never installed Apple’s developer tools. On Ubuntu or Debian Linux, run sudo apt install build-essential.

Check that it worked

Your version numbers may be higher. That is fine. If the terminal says the command was not found, close it, open a new one, and try again.

You now have these tools:

ToolWhat it is
rustcThe Rust compiler. It turns source code into a program
cargoRust’s project manager. It creates projects, runs the compiler for you, downloads code written by other people, and runs your tests. You will use cargo every day and almost never call rustc yourself
rustupThe installer. rustup update gets the newest Rust. A new version appears every six weeks
How other languages do it
One tool instead of many

In many languages you must choose and combine separate tools: one to build, one to download libraries, one to run tests, one to format code. Rust ships a single official tool, Cargo, that does all of it, and almost every Rust project uses it in the same way. Once you know how one Rust project works, you know how they all work.

A code editor

You write code in a code editor: a text editor that understands programming. A word processor such as Microsoft Word will not work, because it stores hidden formatting in the file.

A good free choice is Visual Studio Code (code.visualstudio.com). After installing it, open the Extensions panel, search for rust-analyzer, and install it. rust-analyzer is the official helper that makes an editor understand Rust. It underlines mistakes while you type, completes names for you, and shows explanations when you point at something. Other good editors with Rust support are RustRover, Zed, Helix and Neovim.

Your first project

In the terminal, go to a folder where you want to keep your projects, then type:

cargo new created a folder called hello_rust with a complete, working project inside:

Cargo.toml describes the project:

The name and version are your project’s name and version number. The edition says which set of language rules to use: 2024 is the newest. Under [dependencies] you will later list code from other people that your project uses. It is empty for now.

Real-world analogy
Cargo.toml is a project recipe card

Imagine handing a friend a kit to assemble a shelf. You do not hand them a sack of random screws and hope for the best: you include a card saying which board, which screws, and which instructions to follow. Cargo.toml is that card for your program. Anyone with Cargo and that file can reproduce the exact same build on Windows, macOS or Linux.

Rust source files end in .rs. Cargo already wrote a small program into src/main.rs:

Run it:

Cargo did three things, and reported each one: it compiled your code into a program, it finished without errors, and it ran the program, which printed Hello, world!. You are now a programmer.

What every part of the program means

  • fn is short for function. A function is a named group of instructions. You will write your own in chapter 5.
  • main is the function’s name. This name is special: every Rust program starts by running the function called main.
  • () would hold the inputs of the function. main has none, so the brackets are empty.
  • { and } mark where the function’s instructions begin and end. Everything between them is called the function’s body.
  • println! means “print a line”: show some text on the screen, then move to the next line. The ! tells you that println! is a macro, a special kind of instruction that writes some code for you. For now, just remember that printing needs the !.
  • "Hello, world!" is the text to print. Text inside double quotes is called a string.
  • ; ends the instruction, like a full stop ends a sentence.

The line inside the function is pushed four spaces to the right. This indentation is not required by the compiler, but it shows humans what is inside what, and all Rust programmers use it. You do not have to do it by hand: the command cargo fmt tidies the layout of your whole project.

Printing more

Change src/main.rs to this and run it again with cargo run:

What is new here:

  • {} is a placeholder. Each {} in the text is replaced by the next value after the comma. Values can be calculated: 2 + 3 becomes 5.
  • print! prints without moving to a new line. An empty println!() just ends the line.
  • A backslash gives the next character a special meaning. \" is a quote mark inside a string, \n starts a new line, and \\ is a real backslash. To print a real curly bracket, write it twice: {{ or }}.

The computer runs the lines from top to bottom, one after the other. This order is the most basic rule of programming.

Comments: notes for humans

Text after // is a comment. The compiler ignores it. Comments explain to people (including yourself, next month) why the code does something.

Putting // in front of a line of code switches it off without deleting it. Programmers call this commenting out a line.

The Cargo commands you need every day

CommandWhat it doesWhen to use it
cargo new nameCreates a new project in a folder called nameOnce per project
cargo runCompiles the project and runs itAll the time
cargo checkOnly checks the code for errors. Much faster than a full compileWhile writing, to find mistakes quickly
cargo buildCompiles without runningWhen you only want the finished program
cargo build --releaseCompiles a slower-to-build but much faster-running versionWhen you give the program to others
cargo fmtTidies the layout of your codeBefore you save your work
cargo testRuns the project’s testsWhenever you change behavior
cargo clippyReports common mistakes and improvementsBefore sharing your code

The finished program is an ordinary file. cargo build puts it in the target/debug folder (named hello_rust, or hello_rust.exe on Windows). You could copy that one file to a friend with the same kind of computer and they could run it without installing Rust.

For a quick project check, run cargo fmt --check, cargo test and cargo clippy. The first checks formatting without changing files; the others check behavior and flag common pitfalls. The later quality tools chapter explains how to use these checks in a team.

In plain English
Debug and release

A debug build (the default) compiles quickly but runs slowly, and it contains extra information that helps you find bugs. A release build (--release) takes longer to compile because the compiler works hard to make the program fast. Use debug while you develop and release for the final program. The speed difference can be ten times or more.

When something goes wrong

Sooner or later you will make a typing mistake. Let us make one on purpose. Remove the ! after println:

Run cargo run. The program is not started. The compiler stops and explains:

This looks like a lot, but every part helps you. Read it from the top:

  1. error[E0423]: cannot find function ... says what is wrong, in one sentence. E0423 is the number of this kind of error.
  2. --> src/main.rs:2:5 says where: the file, then line 2, then character 5 on that line.
  3. The code with ^^^^^^^ under it shows the exact place.
  4. help: suggests a fix, and even shows the corrected line with a + under the character to add.
  5. rustc --explain E0423 is a command you can type to get a longer explanation of this kind of error.

Another classic is the forgotten semicolon:

Key idea
The compiler is on your side

A compiler error is not a failure. It is the compiler doing its job: catching a mistake now, on your computer, before the program runs. When you see several errors, fix the first one and compile again. Later errors are often just consequences of the first.

Recap
  • The Rust Playground runs code in your browser. For real projects, install Rust with rustup.
  • cargo new creates a project, cargo run compiles and runs it, cargo check quickly looks for errors.
  • Every program starts in fn main() { ... }. Instructions end with ; and run from top to bottom.
  • println!("...") prints a line. {} is a placeholder for a value.
  • // starts a comment.
  • Error messages tell you what is wrong, where, and often how to fix it.
Check your understanding
1

Where does a Rust program start running?

Every Rust program begins with the main function, wherever it appears in the file.

2

What does cargo run do?

cargo run builds and runs in one step. cargo check only checks, and cargo new creates a project.

3

What does this line print? println!("{} apples and {} pears", 3, 5);

Each {} is replaced by the next value, in order: the first by 3, the second by 5.

4

The compiler reports an error at src/main.rs:7:12. Where should you look?

The format is file, then line, then column (the character position on that line).

Guided exerciseMake it yours
  1. In src/main.rs, change the message so that the program greets you by name.
  2. Add a second println! that prints your city.
  3. Add a third line that uses a placeholder to print the result of 365 * 24, with the words “hours in a year” after it.
  4. Run the program with cargo run.
Need a hint?

For step 3 the pattern is println!("{} some words", calculation);. The star * means “multiplied by”.

Show solution and explanation

The computer worked out 365 * 24 and put the result where the {} was. Notice that the calculation is not inside the quotes. Anything inside the quotes is plain text and is printed exactly as written.

PracticeA name badge

Write a program that prints this badge, with your own name in it:

Need a hint?

Use one println! for each line. Spaces inside the quotes are printed too.

Show solution and explanation

Five instructions, run from top to bottom. Later you will learn to draw a box of any size with a loop, without typing every line yourself.

PracticeBug hunt

This program has three mistakes. Find and fix them. Try to find them by reading first. Then check with the compiler: fix the first error it reports, run again, and repeat.

Need a hint?

Compare each line with a working println! line, one character at a time: the !, the two quote marks, the semicolon.

Show solution and explanation
  1. Line 2 was missing the ; at the end.
  2. Line 3 was missing the ! after println.
  3. Line 4 was missing the closing " of the string. Without it, the compiler thinks the rest of the file is still text.

Finding small mistakes like these is a normal part of programming. It gets much faster with practice.

ChallengeA recipe card

Print a recipe card for pancakes for 3 people. One person needs 50 g of flour, 1 egg and 100 ml of milk. Do not work out the amounts in your head: let the program calculate them from the number 3, using *. The output should look like this:

Need a hint?

You can put a calculation after the comma: println!("- {} g flour", 50 * 3);

Show solution and explanation

It works, but the number 3 is written four times. To cook for 5 people you would have to change it in four places, and it is easy to miss one. The next chapter fixes that with variables: you give the value a name once and use the name everywhere.

03

Variables: giving names to values

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Store a value under a name with let and use it
  • Explain why Rust variables cannot change unless you write mut
  • Use shadowing, scopes and constants correctly
  • Read the compiler errors that variables cause

In the last exercise the number 3 appeared in four places. Real programs are full of values that are used again and again: a player’s score, a price, a name. A variable lets you store a value once, give it a name, and use the name wherever you need the value.

Your first variable

The line let people = 3; reads: “let people be 3”. From that line on, the name people stands for the value 3. To cook for 5, you change one number in one place.

Real-world analogy
A labelled jar

A variable is like a jar with a label on it. let people = 3; puts the value 3 in a jar and writes “people” on the label. Later, when the program reads people, it looks in the jar with that label and uses what it finds.

There are two ways to put a variable into printed text:

  • {people} puts the name directly inside the curly brackets. This works for a simple name only.
  • {} with the value after the comma works for anything, including a calculation such as 50 * people.
In plain English
Declare, initialise, assign, statement

To declare a variable is to create it (with let). To initialise it is to give it its first value. To assign is to give a variable a value with =. In Rust, = does not mean “is equal to” as in maths. It means “store the value on the right under the name on the left”. A complete instruction such as let people = 3; is called a statement.

Variables do not change, unless you say so

Here is the first place where Rust surprises people who know other languages. Try to change a variable:

In Rust a variable is immutable by default: once it has a value, the value cannot change. (Immutable means “cannot be changed”. The opposite is mutable.) The compiler even tells you the fix: add the word mut.

let mut creates a variable that may change. The line score = score + 5; looks strange if you read = as “equals”. Read it as an instruction instead: “work out score + 5, then store the result in score”. Because this is so common, there is a short form: score += 5;.

Short formMeans the same asIn words
x += 5;x = x + 5;add 5 to x
x -= 5;x = x - 5;subtract 5 from x
x *= 5;x = x * 5;multiply x by 5
x /= 5;x = x / 5;divide x by 5

Why immutable by default?

It can feel like the language is being difficult. It is being careful, for three good reasons:

  1. Fewer surprises. When you see let tax_rate = 15;, you know that tax_rate is 15 everywhere below that line. You do not have to read 200 lines to check that nothing changed it.
  2. mut is a signal. The word tells every reader “watch this one, it changes”.
  3. It makes Rust’s safety rules possible. In Part 2 you will see that data which cannot change can be shared freely, and that this is the key to safe programs that do many things at once.

Most variables in real programs never need to change. In Rust you will write plain let far more often than let mut.

How other languages do it
Other languages start from the other side

In Python, JavaScript (with let), Java and C, a variable can be changed unless you take a special step to forbid it (const in JavaScript and C++, final in Java). Rust turns this around: nothing changes unless you allow it with mut. The careful choice is the default, and the risky choice needs an extra word.

Rules for names

  • A name may contain letters, digits and the underscore _. It cannot start with a digit and cannot contain spaces.
  • Upper and lower case are different: total and Total are two different names.
  • Rust programmers write variable names in snake_case: all lower case, with words joined by underscores, like player_score or items_in_cart. The compiler warns you if you use another style.
  • Some words belong to the language and cannot be used as names, for example let, fn, mut and if. They are called keywords. The full list is in the reference appendix.
  • Choose names that say what the value means. price_per_kg is better than p or x2.

If you create a variable and never use it, the program still compiles, but the compiler gives a warning. A warning does not stop the program. It points at something that is probably a mistake.

Take warnings seriously. A good habit is to keep your program free of them.

A first look at types

Every value in Rust has a type: what kind of value it is. 3 is a whole number, "red" is text. The compiler works out the type by itself from the value you write. This is called type inference. You can also write the type yourself after a colon:

u32 is one of Rust’s whole-number types and &str is a type for text. The next chapter explains types properly. For now, know that the type of a variable is fixed: a variable that holds a number cannot later hold text.

Shadowing: reusing a name

You may declare a new variable with the same name as an old one. The new one shadows the old one: from that line on, the name means the new variable.

Each let creates a fresh variable. This is different from mut in two ways:

  • Without let, the compiler still protects you. The value cannot be changed by accident later, because the variable is still immutable.
  • The new variable can have a different type. This is handy when you turn a value from one form into another and do not want to invent two names:

(.len() asks the text for its length. You will see many such methods later.) With mut the same idea is rejected, because a variable can never change its type:

Scope: where a variable lives

Curly brackets { } create a block. A variable exists from the line where it is declared to the end of the block that contains it. That stretch of code is the variable’s scope. When the block ends, the variable is gone.

Code inside a block can see the variables of the blocks around it. The reverse is not true:

Real-world analogy
Scope is like a room

A block is a room. Things you bring into the room stay in the room, and when you leave, they are cleared away. From inside you can look out through the window and see what is in the bigger room around you. From outside you cannot see in.

Shadowing inside a block lasts only until the block ends. Predict the output before you read it:

Scope will become very important in Part 2, because Rust frees memory at the moment a variable goes out of scope.

A variable always has a value before you read it

You may declare a variable first and give it a value later. What Rust never allows is reading a variable that has no value yet:

How other languages do it
Why this matters

In C, reading a variable before giving it a value is allowed and gives you whatever happened to be in that spot of memory: a random-looking number, different on every run. Bugs like that can hide for years. In Java or JavaScript you would get a special “nothing” value (null or undefined) that often causes a crash later. Rust refuses to compile the program, so this whole kind of bug cannot happen.

Constants: values that are fixed forever

Some values never change at all: the number of seconds in a minute, the maximum number of players in a game. For these, use a constant:

let variableconst constant
Can it change?Only with mutNever
TypeUsually worked out by the compilerMust always be written
ValueCan be calculated while the program runsMust be known when the program is compiled
WhereInside functionsAnywhere, including outside all functions
Name stylesnake_caseSCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE

Constants give a meaning to “magic numbers”. price * VAT_RATE explains itself. price * 15 does not.

Recap
  • let name = value; creates a variable. It is immutable: it cannot change.
  • let mut creates a variable that can change. x += 1 is short for x = x + 1.
  • Every variable has one fixed type. The compiler usually works it out.
  • A second let with the same name shadows the first, and may even change the type.
  • A variable lives until the end of the block { } it was declared in. That is its scope.
  • Rust never lets you read a variable that has no value.
  • const NAME: Type = value; defines a value that is fixed for the whole program.
Check your understanding
1

What is wrong with this code?

Variables are immutable unless declared with let mut. The compiler reports error E0384 and suggests adding mut.

2

What does this program print?

The second let shadows n with 2 × 2 = 4. The let inside the block creates another n (104), but that one disappears when the block ends. Outside, n is still 4. (The compiler will warn that the inner n is never used.)

3

Which name follows Rust’s style for a normal variable?

Variables use snake_case. SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE is for constants, and the capitalised styles are used for other things you will meet later.

4

When should you use const instead of let?

A constant is for a value that is the same in every run, such as a conversion factor or a limit. An immutable let variable can still get a different value each time the program runs, for example from user input.

Guided exerciseA greeting with variables

Write a program with two variables: name holding your name as text, and age holding your age as a number. Print two lines, like this:

The program must work out the second number from age.

Need a hint?

Text goes in double quotes: let name = "Sara";. For the second line you need {} and a calculation after the comma, because {age + 1} is not allowed inside the brackets.

Show solution and explanation

Neither variable needs mut: we never change age, we only calculate a new value from it. Change the two values at the top and every line of output follows.

PracticeRepair the program

This program should print count is 1, then count is 2, then total is 20. It has two mistakes. Find them and fix them.

Need a hint?

One mistake is about changing a variable. The other is about upper and lower case letters.

Show solution and explanation
  1. count is changed on line 4, so it must be declared with let mut.
  2. The variable was declared as Total but used as total. Names are case-sensitive, so the compiler could not find total. The lower-case spelling is the right one, because variables use snake_case.
PracticeTemperature converter

To convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 9, divide by 5, and add 32. Store 25 in a variable called celsius, calculate fahrenheit from it, and print:

Then change celsius to 100 and check that you get 212.

Need a hint?

* multiplies and / divides. let fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32;

Show solution and explanation

The calculation follows the usual rules of arithmetic: multiplication and division happen before addition. With whole numbers, division drops anything after the decimal point, so this version is exact only for some temperatures. The next chapter introduces numbers with decimals.

ChallengeSwap two values

Start with this program. Add code where the comment is so that the program prints a = 2, b = 1. You may not type the digits 1 or 2 again.

Need a hint?

If you write a = b; first, the old value of a is lost. Where could you keep it safe for a moment?

Show solution and explanation

A third variable holds the old value of a while a is overwritten. This is like swapping the contents of two glasses: you need a third glass. Swapping is so common that Rust has a ready-made tool for it, std::mem::swap, which you will be able to read after the chapter on references.

Part 1 · First stepsBeginnerabout 35 min
04

Basic data types: numbers, truth values, characters and groups

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Choose the right number type and explain what the names like i32 and u8 mean
  • Calculate with whole numbers and decimals, and convert between them
  • Work with true/false values and single characters
  • Group several values in a tuple or an array
  • Explain what Rust does when a number gets too big or an index is out of range

Every value in a program is of some type: a whole number, a number with decimals, a piece of text, a yes-or-no answer. The type decides how much memory the value needs and what you are allowed to do with it. You can multiply two numbers, but you cannot multiply two names.

Why types matter

Real-world analogy
Types are like containers

A kitchen has egg boxes, milk cartons and spice jars. Each is built for one kind of thing. Nobody pours milk into an egg box. A type is the same idea for data: it says what kind of thing is stored and how big the container is.

Rust is statically typed: the compiler must know the type of every value before the program runs. That sounds like extra work, but you have already seen that the compiler usually works the type out by itself (type inference). The benefit is large: mistakes such as “add a number to a name” are found at compile time, not by your users.

How other languages do it
Static and dynamic typing

Python and JavaScript are dynamically typed: a variable may hold a number now and text later, and type mistakes show up only when the faulty line actually runs, maybe months after you wrote it. Rust, like C, C++, Java and Go, checks all types during compilation. Rust’s type inference gives you most of the comfort of a dynamic language with the safety of a static one.

Bits and bytes in one minute

A computer stores everything as bits. A bit is a tiny switch that is either off (0) or on (1). Eight bits make a byte. With 8 switches there are 256 possible on/off patterns, so one byte can stand for 256 different values, for example the numbers 0 to 255. More bits give more patterns: 16 bits give 65,536, and 32 bits give over 4 billion. That is all you need to know to understand Rust’s number types.

Whole numbers: integers

A whole number is called an integer. Rust has several integer types. The name tells you two things:

  • i or u: i types are signed: they can be negative or positive. u types are unsigned: zero or positive only.
  • A number: how many bits the value uses. More bits mean a larger range and more memory.
TypeSmallest valueLargest value
i8−128127
u80255
i16−32,76832,767
u16065,535
i32−2,147,483,6482,147,483,647
u3204,294,967,295
i64about −9.2 quintillionabout 9.2 quintillion
u640about 18.4 quintillion
i128, u128astronomically smallastronomically large
isize, usizeas big as your computer’s “natural” size: 64 bits on most machines today

You do not have to remember the limits. The program can tell you:

Which one should you use?

  • If you are not sure, use i32. It is what Rust picks when you write let x = 5;.
  • For counting things and for positions in a list, Rust uses usize.
  • Use u8 for raw bytes, and i64 or u64 when numbers can get very large.

Ways to write a number

Arithmetic

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
+add7 + 29
-subtract7 - 25
*multiply7 * 214
/divide7 / 23
%remainder after division7 % 21
Watch out
Dividing integers throws away the decimals

7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. When both numbers are integers, the result is an integer, and anything after the decimal point is cut off. This is not rounding: 99 / 100 is 0. The remainder operator % gives you the part that was left over. Together they are very useful, as you will see in the exercises.

When a number gets too big: overflow

A u8 can hold at most 255. What is 255 + 1 in a u8? There is no room for 256. This situation is called overflow.

Real-world analogy
A car’s mileage counter

An old mileage counter with five digits shows 99999, and after one more kilometre it shows 00000. The number did not get smaller. The counter simply ran out of digits. Integer overflow is the same thing.

Overflow is almost always a bug, so Rust takes it seriously. When the compiler can see the problem in advance, it refuses to compile:

When the numbers are only known while the program runs, Rust does this:

  • In a debug build (the normal cargo run), the program stops at once with a clear error message. Rust calls such a controlled stop a panic.
  • In a release build, the check is left out for speed, and the number wraps around like the mileage counter.

If overflow can really happen in your program, say what you want with one of these methods:

wrapping_add wraps around on purpose. saturating_add stops at the largest value. checked_add gives None (“no valid answer”) on overflow and Some(result) otherwise. You will learn about Some and None in chapter 13. The {:?} placeholder is explained at the end of this chapter.

How other languages do it
What other languages do

In C and C++, overflowing a signed integer is “undefined behaviour”: the program may do anything, and compilers use that freedom in ways that have caused real security holes. Java silently wraps around. Python switches to bigger numbers automatically, which is safe but slow. Rust makes you notice the problem while you develop, and lets you choose the behaviour.

Numbers with decimals: floats

Numbers with a decimal point are called floating-point numbers, or floats. Rust has two: f32 (32 bits) and f64 (64 bits, more exact). Use f64 unless you have a reason not to. It is the type Rust picks for let x = 2.5;.

{:.2} prints a float rounded to two decimal places. (With a variable name it is written {total:.2}.)

Watch out
Floats are approximate

Look at the last line: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. A float stores a number in a fixed number of bits, and most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly, just as 1/3 cannot be written exactly as a decimal. This is true in every programming language. Two rules follow:

  • Never test floats for exact equality. Check that the difference is very small instead.
  • Do not use floats for money. Store the amount in the smallest unit (cents) as an integer.

Rust never converts numbers behind your back

An integer and a float are different types, and Rust will not mix them silently. You must convert one of them yourself with the keyword as:

Converting to a bigger type is always safe. Converting to a smaller type with as can silently change the value, as the last lines show (300 − 256 = 44). Later you will meet safer conversions that report the problem instead (chapter 29).

How other languages do it
Why so strict?

C, Java and JavaScript convert between number types automatically in many places, and the rules are complicated enough to cause real bugs: a large number quietly squeezed into a small type, or decimals quietly dropped. In Rust every conversion is visible in the code. You type a little more, and you can always see what happens.

True or false: bool

A Boolean (bool) has only two possible values: true and false. Comparisons produce Booleans, and decisions in your program are based on them.

OperatorMeaningOperatorMeaning
==is equal to&&and: true if both sides are true
!=is not equal to||or: true if at least one side is true
< >less than, greater than!not: turns true into false and back
<= >=less or equal, greater or equal
Watch out
One equals sign or two

= stores a value: age = 20. == asks a question: age == 20 (“is age equal to 20?”) and gives true or false. Mixing them up is a classic beginner mistake. Rust’s compiler catches it.

A single character: char

A char holds exactly one character, written in single quotes. Rust’s char can hold any character from any writing system, including emoji, because it is based on the worldwide Unicode standard.

Single quotes mean one character ('a', a char). Double quotes mean text of any length ("a", a string). They are different types. Strings get their own chapter (chapter 11), because text is more complicated than it looks.

Groups of values: tuples

A tuple groups a fixed number of values into one. The values may have different types.

  • You reach one part with a dot and its position: person.0 is the first part. Counting starts at 0.
  • let (name, age, is_member) = person; unpacks the tuple into three variables in one step. This is called destructuring.
  • The type of this tuple is written (&str, i32, bool).

Tuples are good for small groups, such as a pair of coordinates (x, y). For anything bigger you will use a struct, which gives each part a name (chapter 12).

The empty tuple () is called the unit type. It means “nothing useful here”, and you will meet it in the next chapter.

Lists of the same type: arrays

An array is a row of values that all have the same type. Its length is fixed when you write the program.

  • The position of an element is called its index. The first element has index 0, so an array of 5 elements has indexes 0 to 4.
  • [0; 3] is short for “the value 0, three times”.
  • The type of scores is [i32; 3]: three i32 values. The length is part of the type.
  • To change an element, the array must be mut.
Real-world analogy
Why counting starts at zero

Think of the index as “how many steps from the start”. The first element is zero steps away. Floors in many countries are numbered the same way: ground floor, then first floor.

Reaching past the end

What if you ask for an element that does not exist?

The program panics: it stops immediately and says exactly what went wrong and where. (The number is produced from text here so that the compiler cannot know it in advance. If you write days[7] directly, the compiler already refuses to build the program.)

Good to know
A small difference you may notice

On your computer the first line has a number in parentheses after the name, for example thread 'main' (48213) panicked at …. It identifies the running thread and changes from run to run, so this guide leaves it out of the printed outputs.

How other languages do it
A crash that protects you

In C, reading days[7] would not stop the program. It would read whatever lies in memory after the array and carry on with garbage, or leak secret data. Many famous security holes are exactly this mistake. Rust checks every index while the program runs. A clean stop with a clear message is far better than a program that silently works with wrong data.

An array cannot grow or shrink. For a list that can, Rust has the vector (Vec), which you will use all the time from chapter 15 on.

Printing for programmers: {:?}

{} prints a value in a form meant for the users of your program. Some types, such as tuples and arrays, have no single obvious way to be shown to users, so {} does not work for them. {:?} prints a value in a form meant for programmers, called the debug form. It works for almost everything and is perfect for looking inside your data while you develop.

The basic types at a glance

TypeHoldsExample
i32, u8, usize …whole numbers42, -7, 1_000
f64, f32numbers with decimals3.14, -0.5
booltrue or falsetrue
charone character'a', '🦀'
(i32, bool)tuple: a fixed group of mixed types(5, true)
[i32; 3]array: a fixed row of one type[1, 2, 3]
&strtext"hello"
Recap
  • Every value has a type, and the compiler knows it before the program runs.
  • Integers: i types can be negative, u types cannot, and the number is the size in bits. Use i32 by default.
  • Integer division cuts off the decimals. % gives the remainder.
  • Overflow is treated as a bug: a compile error when it can be seen in advance, a panic in debug builds.
  • Floats (f64) hold decimals but are approximate. Do not use them for money.
  • Rust never mixes number types silently. Convert with as.
  • bool is true or false. char is one character in single quotes.
  • Tuples group mixed types, arrays hold one type. Both have a fixed size, and indexes start at 0.
  • An index that is out of range causes a panic, not a silent error.
Check your understanding
1

Which of these values fits in a u8?

A u8 holds whole numbers from 0 to 255. It cannot be negative (the u means unsigned), 256 is one too big, and 3.5 is not a whole number.

2

What does println!("{}", 9 / 2); print?

Both numbers are integers, so the result is an integer and the decimals are cut off. For 4.5 you would write 9.0 / 2.0.

3

Which line compiles?

Rust never mixes integers and floats silently. 5 as f64 converts the integer first. The other lines try to mix types or put a value into a type that cannot hold it.

4

An array has 4 elements. What is the index of the last one?

Indexes start at 0, so four elements have the indexes 0, 1, 2 and 3. The last index is always the length minus one.

5

What is the difference between 'x' and "x"?

Single quotes make a char, which is always exactly one character. Double quotes make a string, which can hold any number of characters.

Guided exerciseSeconds to hours, minutes and seconds

A video is 7384 seconds long. Write a program that prints its length as hours, minutes and seconds:

Work it out in steps. How many whole hours fit into the total? How many seconds remain after that? How many whole minutes fit into the rest?

Need a hint?

An hour has 3600 seconds. total / 3600 gives the whole hours and total % 3600 gives the seconds that remain. Do the same again with 60.

Show solution and explanation

Integer division and remainder work as a pair: / tells you how many whole units fit, and % tells you what is left. The same pattern converts cents to dollars and cents, days to weeks and days, and many other things.

PracticeAn average with decimals

Three test scores are 71, 86 and 90. Store them in three integer variables. Print their sum, and their average with two decimal places:

Need a hint?

sum / 3 gives 82, because both are integers. Convert the sum to a float first: sum as f64 / 3.0. Print with {:.2}.

Show solution and explanation

The conversion must happen before the division. (sum / 3) as f64 would divide the integers first, giving 82, and only then convert, giving 82.0. The lost decimals do not come back.

PracticeSplit the bill

A restaurant bill of 100.00 is shared by 3 friends. Following the advice in this chapter, store the bill in cents as an integer (10000). Calculate what each person pays and how many cents are left over, and print:

Need a hint?

each / 100 gives the whole part of the amount and each % 100 the cents. The placeholder {:02} prints a number with at least two digits, adding a zero in front if needed (so 5 becomes 05).

Show solution and explanation

With integers, no cent can appear or vanish through rounding: 3 × 3333 + 1 = 10000 exactly. With floats, 100.0 / 3.0 is 33.333333…, and you would have to decide how to round and who pays the missing cent. Real banking software works in whole units for this reason.

ChallengeType detective

For each expression, write down the value you expect before running anything. Then run the program and compare.

Need a hint?

Integer division cuts off decimals. as i32 on a float also cuts off decimals (it moves towards zero). Characters are stored as numbers inside the computer.

Show solution and explanation
  • (7 / 2) as f64 is 3: the integer division already happened inside the brackets. (A float with no decimal part is printed without .0.)
  • 2.9 as i32 is 2 and -2.9 as i32 is −2: the decimals are cut off, never rounded.
  • 'A' as u8 is 65: every character has a number in the Unicode standard, and A is number 65. Going the other way, 97 is a.
  • true as i32 is 1, and false would be 0.

Part 1 · First stepsBeginnerabout 25 min
05

Functions: naming a piece of work

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Write your own functions and call them
  • Pass values into a function and get a result back
  • Explain the difference between a statement and an expression
  • Document a function with comments that tools can read

So far all your code lived inside main. That stops working as programs grow. A function is a group of instructions with a name. You write the instructions once and then run them from anywhere by using the name. Functions are the main tool for keeping a program readable.

Real-world analogy
A function is a machine with a slot and a tray

Think of a coffee machine. You put something in (water, beans), press the button, and something comes out (coffee). You do not need to know what happens inside. A function is the same: values go in, work happens, a result comes out. Once it exists, you only need its name and what to put in.

Defining and calling a function

  • fn greet() { ... } defines a function called greet. A definition does not run anything by itself.
  • greet(); calls the function: the program jumps into greet, runs its lines, and then comes back to continue after the call.
  • The order of definitions in the file does not matter. greet is written below main and still found.

Parameters: giving a function its inputs

A function becomes much more useful when it can work with different values each time.

The names in the brackets of the definition (name, width, height) are parameters: variables that receive their value when the function is called. The values you pass in the call ("Sara", 4, 3) are arguments. They are matched by position: the first argument goes to the first parameter.

Every parameter must have its type written out. Inside a function the compiler works types out for you, but at the border of a function it wants a clear promise. That promise also makes error messages short and local: if you call print_area("four", 3), the error points at exactly that call.

Return values: getting a result back

Printing a result is fine for a person, but often the program needs the result to continue working with it. A function can return a value to whoever called it.

  • -> u32 after the brackets says: this function gives back a u32.
  • The call area(4, 3) is replaced by the returned value, so you can store it or calculate with it.
  • Look closely at the body: width * height has no semicolon. In Rust, the value of the last line of a function is its return value, if that line has no semicolon.

The first line of a function, such as fn area(width: u32, height: u32) -> u32, is called its signature. It tells you everything you need in order to use the function: its name, what goes in, and what comes out.

Statements and expressions

To understand that missing semicolon you need two words. They are worth learning well, because Rust is built around them.

  • An expression is code that produces a value. 5, width * height, area(4, 3) and x > 10 are expressions.
  • A statement is code that does something and produces no value. let x = 5; is a statement.

Putting a semicolon after an expression turns it into a statement: the value is thrown away. That is why the last line of area has none.

Even a block in curly brackets is an expression. Its value is the value of its last line:

Here is what happens if you add the semicolon by habit:

The function promised a u32 but, because of the semicolon, produces nothing. “Nothing” has a type in Rust: the empty tuple (), called unit. A function without -> returns (). The compiler even points at the semicolon to remove. You will see this error often in your first weeks. Now you know what it means.

Leaving early with return

You can also return with the keyword return. It is used to leave a function before its last line:

(if runs its block only when the condition is true. It is the subject of the next chapter.) By convention, return is used only for early exits. The normal result is the last expression without a semicolon.

How other languages do it
Other languages

In C, Java, JavaScript and Python, you must write return to give back a value. Forgetting it is a common bug: in JavaScript and Python the function then quietly returns “nothing”. In Rust the compiler checks that every path through a function produces a value of the promised type.

A function works on its own copies

add_ten received a copy of the number 5 in its own variable n. Changing n does not touch number in main. Parameters and all variables declared inside a function are local: they exist only while that function runs. This keeps functions independent of each other. For simple values such as numbers, passing means copying. For bigger data the story is more interesting, and it is the subject of Part 2.

Documenting a function

A comment that starts with three slashes, ///, is a documentation comment. It describes the thing that follows it. Rust’s tools collect these comments and build a website from them: run cargo doc --open in a project to see it. Your editor also shows them when you point at a function name.

What makes a good function

  • It does one thing, and its name says what: calculate_tax, print_report, is_valid. Function names use snake_case, like variables.
  • It is short. If you cannot see all of it on the screen, think about splitting it.
  • It prefers returning a value over printing. A function that returns its result can be reused anywhere. One that prints can only print.
Recap
  • fn name(parameter: Type) -> ReturnType { body } defines a function. name(argument) calls it.
  • Parameter types and the return type must always be written.
  • The last expression of the body, without a semicolon, is the return value. return leaves early.
  • Expressions produce values. Statements do not. A semicolon turns an expression into a statement.
  • A function with no return value returns the unit type ().
  • /// comments document the item below them.
Check your understanding
1

What does this function return?

The value of the final expression is returned automatically. With a = 5 the result is 11.

2

Which one is a statement, not an expression?

A let line does something (it creates a variable) but produces no value. The other three all produce a value.

3

Why must parameter types be written in a function signature?

The compiler infers types inside function bodies, but signatures are fixed contracts. You can understand how to use a function from its signature alone.

4

Why does returning a value usually make a function easier to reuse?

A function that returns a value can be used in expressions, assigned to variables, or tested. That makes it composable.

Guided exerciseYour first function with a result

Write a function square that takes one i32 and returns that number multiplied by itself. Call it from main to print the squares of 4 and of −9.

Need a hint?

The signature is fn square(n: i32) -> i32. The body is a single expression without a semicolon.

Show solution and explanation

The call square(4) is itself an expression with the value 16, so it can be placed directly inside println!.

PracticeTwo small tools

Write two functions and test them from main:

  1. celsius_to_fahrenheit takes an f64 and returns an f64 (multiply by 9.0, divide by 5.0, add 32.0).
  2. is_even takes an i32 and returns a bool.

Expected output for 36.6 degrees and for the numbers 10 and 7:

Need a hint?

n % 2 == 0 is an expression of type bool. It can be the whole body of is_even. Print the temperature with {:.2}.

Show solution and explanation

A comparison is an expression like any other, so is_even needs no if. Beginners often write “if it is even return true, else return false”. Returning the comparison directly says the same thing in one line.

ChallengeReturn three values at once

In the last chapter you converted seconds to hours, minutes and seconds. Turn that into a function to_clock that takes the total seconds (u32) and returns all three numbers as a tuple. In main, unpack the tuple and print 2 h 3 min 4 s for 7384.

Need a hint?

The return type is (u32, u32, u32). The last line of the body builds the tuple: (hours, minutes, seconds). In main, write let (h, m, s) = to_clock(7384);.

Show solution and explanation

A function returns exactly one value, but that value can be a tuple, which is how Rust functions give back several results. The caller destructures the tuple into separate variables.
