Part 1 · First stepsBeginnerabout 35 min
06

Control flow: decisions and repetition

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Make a program choose between paths with if, else and match
  • Repeat work with loop, while and for
  • Stop or skip rounds of a loop with break and continue
  • Pick the right kind of loop for a task

A program that always runs the same lines in the same order cannot do much. Real programs decide (if the password is right, let the user in) and repeat (do this for every item in the list). Together these are called control flow: they control which line runs next. With sequence, decision and repetition you can express any computation.

Real-world analogy
A crossroads with signs

When you reach a junction, a sign tells you which road to take. A program is the same. It reaches a condition and chooses one path, not several. The road signs are the if, else if, and else branches.

Decisions with if

Real-world analogy
if is a railway switch

A train approaches a fork in the track. The signal box checks a single yes-or-no question: is the switch thrown? Depending on the answer, the train takes the left branch or the right branch—never both. if / else if / else works the same way: your program tests each condition in order and runs only the first matching branch.

  • After if comes a condition: an expression that is true or false. No brackets are needed around it.
  • If the condition is true, the block after it runs, and the rest of the chain is skipped.
  • else if tests another condition, only when all the ones before were false.
  • else runs when nothing above was true. Both else if and else are optional.

The conditions are tested from top to bottom and only the first true one runs. With temperature = 31 both > 30 and > 15 are true, but only “It is hot.” is printed.

The condition must be a bool

How other languages do it
No “truthy” values

In C, Python and JavaScript, a number or a piece of text can be used as a condition: zero and empty count as false, everything else as true. That is short to write, and a well-known source of bugs. Rust wants you to say what you mean: if items > 0 or if items != 0.

if is an expression

In Rust if produces a value, so you can use it on the right side of let:

The value of each block is its last expression (no semicolon, as in functions). Both blocks must produce the same type, and the else part is required, because kind needs a value in every case.

Many choices with match

When one value is compared against many possibilities, a chain of else if gets long. match is clearer:

Each line inside is called an arm: a pattern, then =>, then the result for that case. 3..=5 means “3 up to and including 5”, 6 | 7 means “6 or 7”, and _ means “anything else”. The compiler checks that every possible value is covered. Remove the _ arm and the program does not compile. match is one of Rust’s most loved features, and chapter 13 shows its full power.

Repeating with loop

loop repeats its block forever, until the code says break.

A loop is also an expression. break can carry a value out of it:

Tip
If your program never stops

A loop without a reachable break runs forever. This is called an infinite loop, and everyone writes one by accident sooner or later. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop the program.

Repeating while a condition holds: while

The condition is checked before each round. When it is false, the loop ends. If it is false at the start, the block never runs.

Repeating for each item: for

The for loop is the one you will use most. It runs its block once for every item in a collection or a range of numbers.

RangeMeansNumbers produced
1..4from 1 up to, but not including, 41, 2, 3
1..=4from 1 up to and including 41, 2, 3, 4
(1..=4).rev()the same, reversed4, 3, 2, 1
(0..10).step_by(5)every fifth number0, 5

Going through an array works the same way:

.iter().enumerate() hands you each item together with its position, as a tuple that the loop unpacks into index and fruit. You will learn how this works in chapter 25.

How other languages do it
Why Rust has no C-style for

C, Java and JavaScript write for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++): three parts that you must get exactly right. A wrong < or <= there is the famous “off-by-one” error, and with an array it reads past the end. Rust’s for item in collection cannot go out of range, because you never handle the index yourself.

A common pattern: collecting a result in a loop

A variable created before the loop (here sum) is updated in every round and holds the answer afterwards. This variable is often called an accumulator.

break, continue and labels

break leaves the loop completely. continue skips the rest of the current round and starts the next one.

Loops can be placed inside loops. break and continue then act on the innermost one. To control an outer loop, give it a label (a name that starts with a single quote):

Which loop should I use?

SituationUse
“Do this for every item” or “do this N times”for
“Keep going as long as this is true”while
“Keep going until something inside decides to stop”loop with break

When in doubt, try for first. It is the safest and usually the clearest.

Recap
  • if condition { } else if other { } else { } chooses a path. Conditions must be bool.
  • if and match are expressions: they produce a value.
  • match compares one value against several patterns and must cover every case.
  • loop repeats until break, while repeats while a condition is true, and for goes through a range or a collection.
  • 1..4 excludes the end, 1..=4 includes it.
  • break leaves a loop, continue jumps to the next round, and labels choose which loop.
Check your understanding
1

How many lines does this print?

0..5 produces 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: five numbers. The end of a .. range is not included.

2

What is printed?

Only the first true condition runs. x > 5 is also true, but it is never tested, because the branch above it already matched.

3

What does continue do inside a loop?

continue jumps to the next round. break is the one that ends the loop.

4

Why does let size = if n > 100 { "large" }; not compile?

When if is used as a value, every case must produce a value of the same type. Without else, the “false” case produces nothing.

Guided exerciseFizzBuzz

This is the most famous beginner exercise in programming. Print the numbers from 1 to 15, one per line, but:

  • for numbers divisible by 3, print Fizz instead,
  • for numbers divisible by 5, print Buzz instead,
  • for numbers divisible by both, print FizzBuzz.
Need a hint?

A number is divisible by 3 when n % 3 == 0. The order of the tests matters: check the “both” case first. Otherwise 15 is caught by the test for 3 and you never reach it.

Show solution and explanation

A number divisible by both 3 and 5 is divisible by 15, so n % 15 == 0 tests the “both” case. It must come first because an if chain stops at the first true condition.

PracticeA triangle of stars

Write a program that prints this triangle. The number of rows (here 4) should be stored in one variable, so that changing it changes the triangle.

Need a hint?

Use a loop inside a loop. The outer loop goes through the rows 1 to 4. The inner loop prints as many stars as the row number, with print!. After the inner loop, println!() ends the line.

Show solution and explanation

For each row, the inner loop runs row times. The name _ is used for the inner loop variable because its value is never needed: we only want “do this row times”. The underscore tells the compiler, and the reader, that this is on purpose.

ChallengePrime numbers

A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that can be divided only by 1 and by itself. Write a function is_prime(n: u32) -> bool, and use it to print all primes up to 30 on one line:

Need a hint?

To test n, try every possible divisor from 2 up to n - 1. If n % divisor == 0 for any of them, return false at once. If the loop finishes without finding one, n is prime.

Show solution and explanation

return false inside the loop leaves the whole function as soon as one divisor is found. If the loop ends normally, no divisor exists, and the last expression true is returned. For n = 2 the range 2..2 is empty, so the loop body never runs and 2 is correctly reported as prime.

This solution combines everything from Part 1: a function, a loop, a decision, an early return, and the remainder operator.

Part 1 · First stepsProjectBeginnerabout 60 min
07

Project: a number guessing game

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Plan a program in plain words before writing code
  • Read what the user types and turn it into a number
  • Use code written by other people (a crate) through Cargo
  • Combine variables, loops, decisions and functions in one working program

You now know enough to build a complete program that someone can use. In this project the computer picks a secret number between 1 and 100, and the player guesses until they find it. After each guess the program says “too small” or “too big”.

This project needs Rust installed on your computer, because it reads from the keyboard and uses a library from the internet. If you skipped the installation, go back to chapter 2 first.

A session will look like this:

Step 0: plan in plain words

Experienced programmers do not start by typing. They first describe the program in everyday language. A plan written this way is called pseudocode (“almost code”).

  1. Pick a secret number between 1 and 100.
  2. Repeat:
    1. Ask the player for a guess.
    2. Read what the player typed.
    3. Turn the text into a number. If it is not a number, say so and ask again.
    4. Compare the guess with the secret number.
    5. If it is too small or too big, say so. If it is right, congratulate the player and stop.

Each line will become a few lines of Rust. You will build the program in small steps, and run it after every step. Working in small steps is the most important habit in programming: when something breaks, you know it was the last thing you added.

Create the project:

Step 1: read what the player types

Replace the contents of src/main.rs with this:

Run it with cargo run, type something, and press Enter. Several things here are new. You will study each of them properly later. For now, this is what they do:

  • use std::io; Rust comes with a large collection of ready-made code called the standard library, or std. Its part called io (for input/output) handles reading and writing. This line makes the name io available in your file.
  • String::new() creates a new, empty piece of text that can grow. The variable is mut because reading will put characters into it.
  • io::stdin() gives access to the keyboard input of the terminal (“standard input”).
  • .read_line(&mut input) waits until the player presses Enter and adds everything they typed to input. The &mut in front means “you may change my variable”. Why that is needed is the subject of chapter 10.
  • .expect("...") Reading can fail, for example if the terminal is closed. read_line therefore does not just “work”: it reports whether it worked. .expect says “if it failed, stop the program and show this message”. Chapter 18 covers this in depth.

The call is written over three lines only to keep it readable. io::stdin().read_line(&mut input).expect("...") is one instruction, ending in one semicolon.

Step 2: pick a secret number

Rust’s standard library is kept small on purpose. It has no random number generator. For that you use a crate: a package of Rust code that someone has published for others to use. Crates are shared on the website crates.io, and Cargo downloads them for you. A crate that your project uses is called a dependency.

The crate for random numbers is called rand. Add it to your project:

Open Cargo.toml. Cargo has added a line under [dependencies]:

The next time you run cargo run, Cargo downloads rand and compiles it together with your code. It also creates a file called Cargo.lock, which records the exact version of everything that was downloaded. Thanks to that file, the project builds the same way on every computer. You never edit Cargo.lock by hand.

How other languages do it
Sharing code in other languages

Every modern language has a place for shared code: Python has PyPI and the pip tool, JavaScript has npm. C and C++ have no single standard way, which is one reason why using libraries there is harder. In Rust, Cargo and crates.io were part of the language from the start, so adding a library is always one command.

Now use the crate:

rand::random_range(1..=100) means: from the crate rand, call the function random_range with the range 1 to 100 (both included). Run it a few times. You get a different number each time.

Tip
Reading the manual of a crate

How would you know that rand has a function called random_range? Every crate has documentation at docs.rs. For this one it is docs.rs/rand. You can also run cargo doc --open in your project to see the documentation of all your dependencies in the browser, without internet.

Step 3: turn the text into a number

The player’s input is text, such as "50". The secret is a number. Rust does not compare text with numbers, so the text must be converted.

  • When the player presses Enter, a “new line” character (\n) ends up at the end of the input. .trim() removes spaces and new-line characters from both ends of a text.
  • .parse() tries to turn text into another type. Which type? The one you asked for with let guess: u32.
  • Turning text into a number can fail: "twenty" is not a number. So parse also reports success or failure.

Using .expect here would stop the whole program on a typing mistake. That is unfriendly. It is better to handle the problem: tell the player and ask again. For that you use match, which you met in the last chapter:

The result of parse is one of two things: Ok with the number inside, or Err with a description of the problem inside. The first arm takes the number out of Ok and makes it the value of the whole match. The second arm runs when the conversion failed. (Inside the game loop you will write continue there instead of return, to jump to the next round.)

Key idea
Errors are ordinary values

In many languages a failed conversion “throws an exception” that flies through the program until something catches it, or crashes the program if nothing does. In Rust, a function that can fail returns a value that says “it worked, here is the result” or “it failed, here is why”. The compiler makes sure you look at it. You cannot forget to handle the failure.

Step 4: compare the guess with the secret

guess.cmp(&secret) compares two values and answers with one of exactly three possibilities: Ordering::Less, Ordering::Greater or Ordering::Equal. The match has one arm for each. If you forget one, the program does not compile, so no case can be missed. (The & means “look at this value without taking it”. It is explained in chapter 10.)

You could write the same with if guess < secret { ... } else if guess > secret { ... } else { ... }. Both are correct. The match version lets the compiler check that all cases are covered.

Step 5: put it together in a loop

Now join the steps with a loop, and count the guesses:

Run it and play. Read the program once more from top to bottom and match every part with a line of the plan from Step 0.

Three details are worth a second look:

  • input is created inside the loop, so every round starts with fresh, empty text. read_line adds to the text. If input were created once before the loop, the second guess would be glued to the first.
  • continue in the Err arm jumps back to the top of the loop, so a typing mistake does not count as an attempt.
  • break in the Equal arm ends the loop, and with it the program.
Tip
A strategy for the player

Always guess the middle of what is still possible: 50, then 25 or 75, and so on. Each guess removes half of the remaining numbers, so you never need more than 7 guesses for 1 to 100. This method is called binary search, and it is one of the most important ideas in computer science.

Make it better

A project is never really finished. These tasks let you practise changing a program that already works, which is what programmers do most of the time.

PracticeA limit on guesses

Give the player only 7 guesses. If they have not found the number by then, print Out of guesses. The number was 37. (with the real number) and end the game.

Need a hint?

Store the limit in a constant such as const MAX_ATTEMPTS: u32 = 7;. After a wrong guess, check whether attempts has reached the limit.

Show solution and explanation

The new check sits after the comparison. If the seventh guess is right, the Equal arm has already left the loop with break, so the “out of guesses” message is never reached. The limit is a constant with a name, so it appears only once and explains itself.

PracticeMove the reading into a function

The loop is getting long. Move the code that asks for and reads a line into a function read_guess that returns the typed text as a String. The loop should then start with let input = read_guess();.

Need a hint?

The return type is String. Create the String inside the function, fill it with read_line, and make it the last expression of the function.

Show solution and explanation

In the game, replace the four lines that create and fill input with let input = read_guess();. The loop now reads almost like the plan: read a guess, convert it, compare it. Giving a name to a group of lines is the main purpose of functions.

ChallengeWarm and cold

Make the hints more helpful. If the guess is wrong but within 5 of the secret number, add You are very close!.

Need a hint?

You need the distance between two numbers, whichever one is bigger. For unsigned numbers, guess - secret panics when secret is larger, because the result would be negative. Use guess.abs_diff(secret), which gives the difference as a positive number.

Show solution and explanation

Add these lines after the conversion and before the match:

abs_diff avoids the overflow problem you met in chapter 4: with u32 values, 3 - 5 cannot be stored, because a u32 cannot be negative. In a debug build that subtraction would panic. Whenever you subtract unsigned numbers, ask yourself which one is bigger.

What you have learned

Recap
  • Plan in plain words first, then build in small steps and run after each step.
  • use std::io; brings part of the standard library into your file. read_line reads keyboard input into a String.
  • A crate is a package of code. cargo add name adds one to your project as a dependency.
  • .trim() removes surrounding spaces and line ends. .parse() turns text into a number.
  • Operations that can fail return Ok(value) or Err(problem). Handle both with match, or stop the program with .expect("message").
  • match forces you to cover every case.

You have finished Part 1. You can now write small programs with variables, types, functions, decisions and loops. Part 2 covers the idea that sets Rust apart from every other language: ownership.

08

How a program uses memory: the stack and the heap

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Describe what memory is and what a pointer is
  • Explain the difference between the stack and the heap
  • Name the classic memory bugs and how they happen
  • Compare the three ways languages manage memory

Part 2 is about ownership, the idea that makes Rust different. Ownership is a set of rules about memory. They only make sense when you have a picture of what memory is and what can go wrong with it. This chapter gives you that picture. It has very little Rust in it, and what you learn here is true for every programming language.

What memory is

While a program runs, it keeps its data in the computer’s memory (also called RAM). Memory is fast, and it is temporary: when the program ends, its memory is given back to the computer.

Real-world analogy
A very long street of letterboxes

Picture a street with billions of small letterboxes in a row. Each box holds one byte, and each has a house number. That number is called its address. To store a value, the program puts it in some boxes and remembers the address. To read it back, it goes to that address.

A program uses its memory in two different ways, in two different areas: the stack and the heap.

How other languages do it
Memory management in other languages

A garbage-collected language such as Java or Python also hides many memory details from you, but it keeps a helper running in the background. C and C++ let the programmer manage memory by hand, which is fast but easy to get wrong. Rust gives a middle path: many rules are checked by the compiler, and the memory is freed when ownership ends, without a garbage collector.

The stack: fast and automatic

Real-world analogy
A pile of trays

In a canteen, clean trays are piled up. You always put a tray on the top and take a tray from the top. You never pull one out from the middle. This “last in, first out” order is simple, and that makes it very fast.

The stack works like that pile. Every time a function is called, it gets a fresh tray on top of the pile for its parameters and local variables. This tray is called a stack frame. When the function ends, its whole frame is taken off the pile in one step, and all its variables are gone.

Step through this program and watch the stack:

Step through it: Function calls and the stack
  1. fn main() {
  2. let a = 5;
  3. let b = double(a);
  4. println!("{b}");
  5. }
  7. fn double(n: i32) -> i32 {
  8. let result = n * 2;
  9. result
  10. }

The stack has two great strengths. It is fast, because storing a value is just “put it on top”. And it is automatic: nobody has to remember to clean up, because the frame disappears when the function ends.

It also has two limits:

  1. The size of everything on the stack must be known when the program is compiled. An i32 is always 4 bytes, so it can live on the stack. A text typed by the user could have 3 characters or 3 million. The compiler cannot reserve the right amount of stack space for it in advance.
  2. Data on the stack dies with its function. Sometimes data must live longer than the function that created it.

For both cases there is the heap.

Recursion and stack overflow

A function may call itself. This is called recursion. Every call gets its own stack frame, with its own copies of the variables.

factorial(5) calls factorial(4), which calls factorial(3), and so on down to factorial(1), which returns 1 without another call. Then the calls finish one by one, from the top of the stack down. The case that stops the chain (n <= 1) is called the base case. Every recursive function needs one.

The stack is small, usually a few megabytes. A recursion that never stops, or goes millions of calls deep, fills it up. This is called a stack overflow. Rust detects it and stops the program with a clear message instead of letting it write over other memory.

The heap: flexible, but someone must tidy up

Real-world analogy
A self-storage warehouse

You go to the front desk of a storage warehouse and say: “I need room for 20 boxes.” The staff find a free unit that is big enough and give you a slip with the unit’s number. Later you use that number to find your things. When you no longer need the unit, you must hand it back. If you do not, it stays reserved for ever, even though nobody uses it.

The heap is that warehouse:

  • The program asks for a certain number of bytes. This is called allocating memory.
  • It gets back the address of a free area. A value that holds an address is called a pointer, because it points to where the data is.
  • When the data is no longer needed, the memory must be given back. This is called freeing or deallocating it.

The heap can hold data of any size, the size may be decided while the program runs, and the data stays alive until it is freed, no matter which functions start or end in the meantime. The price: allocating is slower than using the stack, reaching the data takes an extra step (follow the pointer), and someone has to free the memory at the right time.

How the stack and the heap work together

Most interesting data uses both. Rust’s growable text type, String, is a good example. The characters live on the heap, because nobody knows in advance how many there will be. On the stack there is a small record of fixed size that says where the characters are and how many there are.

Step through it: A String uses the stack and the heap
  1. fn main() {
  2. let n = 42;
  3. let mut s = String::from("hi");
  4. s.push_str(" there");
  5. println!("{n} {s}");
  6. }

You can check this picture with a small program. size_of_val reports how many bytes a value takes up directly (for a String, that is the record on the stack, not the characters on the heap):

Both strings take 24 bytes on the stack on a normal 64-bit computer, however long their text is. The record has three parts of 8 bytes each: the pointer, the length, and the capacity (how much room is reserved on the heap).

StackHeap
SpeedVery fastSlower
Size of dataFixed, known at compile timeAny size, decided while running
How long data livesUntil its function endsUntil it is freed
Cleaning upAutomaticSomebody must do it
Typical contentsNumbers, booleans, characters, small fixed groups, pointersText, lists that grow, large data

What goes wrong when memory is managed by hand

In C, the programmer asks for heap memory with a function called malloc and must give it back with free. In a large program this is done in thousands of places, and people make mistakes. There are four classic ones.

Real-world analogy
Hotel rooms and key cards

Think of heap memory as hotel rooms and of pointers as key cards.

  • Memory leak: you leave the hotel but never check out. The room stays blocked, and if this keeps happening the hotel runs out of rooms. In a program: memory is never freed, the program uses more and more, and at some point it slows down or crashes.
  • Use after free: you check out but keep a copy of the key card. Later you walk back into the room. By now another guest lives there. You read their papers or move their things. In a program: data is used after its memory was freed and given to something else.
  • Double free: you check out of the same room twice. The second time, the hotel’s records get mixed up and they cancel the booking of the new guest. In a program: freeing memory twice damages the bookkeeping of the heap.
  • Out-of-bounds access (buffer overflow): you booked room 12 but also walk into rooms 13 and 14. In a program: reading or writing past the end of an array.

A pointer that still holds the address of memory that has been freed is called a dangling pointer. It is the “key card you kept”.

These bugs are dangerous because the program often keeps running with wrong data. They may show up only sometimes, on some machines. Attackers look for them on purpose: a use-after-free or a buffer overflow can often be turned into a way to take control of a program. As you read in chapter 1, around 70% of the serious security bugs in large C and C++ products are memory bugs of this kind.

Three ways to manage memory

How other languages do it
Where your language sits

If you come from Python, Java, JavaScript, Go or C#, you have been relying on a garbage collector and have never had to free anything by hand. If you come from C or C++, you have written free and delete yourself, and you have probably met a crash caused by calling them at the wrong moment. Rust takes a third path: the compiler proves where the clean-up belongs, so the code runs at C speed while the bugs of hand-written memory management fail to compile.

ApproachWho frees the memory?LanguagesAdvantagesDisadvantages
ManualThe programmer, by handC, older C++Full control, top speedEvery mistake is a possible crash or security hole
Garbage collectionA helper that runs inside your program, finds data that is no longer reachable, and frees itJava, C#, Go, Python, JavaScriptSafe and easy for the programmerUses extra time and memory, can pause the program, less control
OwnershipThe compiler works out where each value is no longer needed and inserts the clean-up code thereRustSafe and fast, no pauses, no helper neededYou must learn the rules, and the compiler is strict
In plain English
Garbage collector

A garbage collector (GC) is a part of a language’s runtime that looks for data the program can no longer reach and frees it automatically. It is convenient, and it removes use-after-free and double-free bugs. It costs processor time and memory, and the program has little control over when the cleaning happens. That is a problem for software that must react without delay, such as games, audio, or the brakes of a car.

How other languages do it
Ownership vs manual freeing vs garbage collection
  • C and older C++ give you raw speed, at the cost of checking every malloc and free in your own head.
  • Python, JavaScript, Go and Java give you memory safety automatically, at the cost of a garbage collector running alongside your code.
  • Rust moves the bookkeeping to compile time: the compiler inserts the clean-up at the exact line an owner goes out of scope, so you get C-like speed with no garbage-collector pauses.

Rust’s approach is built on one simple thought: if every piece of heap data has exactly one clear owner, the right moment to free it is obvious. It is the moment when the owner goes away. No one has to remember to free, so there are no leaks by forgetfulness. Nothing is freed twice, because there is only one owner. And the compiler makes sure nobody still uses the data afterwards.

How that works is the subject of the next chapter.

Recap
  • Memory is a long row of numbered bytes. The number of a byte is its address. A pointer is a value that holds an address.
  • The stack holds the local variables of running functions. It is fast and cleans itself up, but everything on it needs a fixed, known size.
  • The heap holds data of any size for as long as needed. It must be freed by someone.
  • A String is a small fixed-size record on the stack that points to its characters on the heap.
  • Manual memory management leads to leaks, use after free, double free and out-of-bounds access.
  • Garbage collectors avoid most of these bugs at a cost in speed and control. Rust avoids them at compile time through ownership.
Check your understanding
1

Why can the characters of a text typed by the user not simply be stored on the stack?

Everything on the stack has a size that the compiler knows. Data whose size is decided while the program runs goes to the heap, and the stack keeps a fixed-size pointer to it.

2

What happens to a function’s local variables when the function returns?

The whole frame is removed in a single step. That is what makes the stack fast and automatic.

3

A program frees a block of memory and later reads from it through an old pointer. What is this bug called?

The pointer is “dangling”: it holds the address of memory that no longer belongs to that data. A leak is memory that is never freed, and a double free is freeing the same block twice.

4

What is the main cost of a garbage collector?

A garbage collector trades some speed and control for safety and convenience. Rust gets the safety without that cost by doing the checking at compile time.

Guided exerciseTrace the stack on paper

Draw the stack for this program, the way the first stepper did. Make one drawing for the moment when the program is on the line marked // here. Which frames exist, and what do they contain?

Need a hint?

At that moment two functions are active: main has called area, and area has not finished yet. The variable size does not have a value yet, because the call has not returned.

Show solution and explanation

At the marked line the stack looks like this, from top to bottom:

FrameVariables
area (top)w = 3, h = 4, result = 12
mainwidth = 3, height = 4

w and h are separate copies of the values from main. size has no value yet. When area returns, its frame is removed and the 12 is stored in size. The heap is not used at all: every value in this program is a number with a fixed size.

PracticeStack or heap?

For each piece of data, decide whether its contents can live on the stack or need the heap. Give the reason.

  1. A player’s score, as an i32.
  2. The text of an email that the user is writing.
  3. The three numbers of a colour, as (u8, u8, u8).
  4. A list of all files in a folder.
  5. The days of the week, as an array of 7 values.
Need a hint?

Ask one question each time: is the size known when the program is compiled, and does it stay the same?

Show solution and explanation
  1. Stack. An i32 is always 4 bytes.
  2. Heap. The length is unknown and changes while the user types. A small record on the stack points to it.
  3. Stack. A tuple of three u8 values is always 3 bytes.
  4. Heap. The number of files is known only while the program runs.
  5. Stack. An array has a fixed length that is part of its type.

The rule of thumb: a fixed, known size can go on the stack. A size that is unknown or changing needs the heap.

ChallengeMeasure it

Use size_of_val to print the size in bytes of each of these values: true, 'x', 3.5, [0u8; 100] and String::from("x"). Predict each number before you run the program.

Need a hint?

A bool needs one byte. A char can hold any Unicode character, so it needs more than one byte. A float written without a type is an f64.

Show solution and explanation

A char is always 4 bytes, because that is enough for every character in Unicode. An array of 100 bytes takes exactly 100 bytes, directly on the stack. The String takes 24 bytes on the stack plus one byte on the heap for the letter x.

Part 2 · Ownership: Rust's big ideaBeginnerabout 40 min
09

Ownership: one owner for every value

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • State the three rules of ownership
  • Explain what a move is and why the old variable can no longer be used
  • Decide when to move, when to clone, and which types are copied automatically
  • Follow ownership as values go into functions and come back out

This is the most important chapter in the guide. Ownership is the idea that lets Rust manage memory safely without a garbage collector. The rules are short. They feel strict for a week or two, and then they start to feel like common sense.

The three rules

Key idea
The rules of ownership
  1. Every value has an owner: the variable that holds it.
  2. A value has only one owner at a time.
  3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped: its memory is given back.
Real-world analogy
Owning a car

A car has one name on its ownership papers. You can sell or give the car to someone else. Then the papers change, and you can no longer drive it. When the owner sends the car to the scrapyard, it is gone. Nobody argues about who has to scrap it, and nobody can scrap it twice, because there is exactly one owner.

The rest of this chapter shows what these rules mean in code.

Rule 3 in action: the value is dropped with its owner

You already know scopes from chapter 3: a variable lives until the closing } of its block. Ownership adds one thing. When a variable goes out of scope, Rust also cleans up everything the variable owns. Rust calls this dropping the value.

String::from("hello") creates a String: a growable text whose characters are stored on the heap, as you saw in the last chapter. At the closing bracket of the inner block the compiler inserts the code that frees those characters. You did not write that code, and you could not forget it.

How other languages do it
The same idea in C++

C++ programmers know this pattern under the awkward name RAII (“resource acquisition is initialisation”): an object cleans up after itself when it goes out of scope. Rust uses the same mechanism, and builds its ownership rules on top so that the compiler can check them.

Rule 2 in action: a move

What happens when you assign a String to a second variable?

The compiler says the value was moved. Step through what happens in memory:

Step through it: What let s2 = s1; does
  1. fn main() {
  2. let s1 = String::from("hello");
  3. let s2 = s1;
  4. println!("{s2}");
  5. }

Why does Rust do this, instead of letting both variables use the text? Think about the end of main. If s1 and s2 were both owners, both would try to free the same heap memory. That is the double free bug from the last chapter. Rust could also copy the heap data on every assignment, but for a large text that would be slow, and you would not see it in the code.

So Rust picks the cheap and safe option: an assignment moves ownership. The old variable becomes unusable, and the compiler enforces that.

Real-world analogy
Giving away your only copy

You have one printed copy of a report and you hand it to a colleague. Now they have it and you do not. You cannot read from it or write on it any more, and it would be absurd for both of you to shred it. If you both need one, somebody has to make a photocopy first.

How other languages do it
What other languages do on assignment
  • Python, Java, JavaScript: b = a makes b a second name for the same object. Both stay usable, and a change made through one is visible through the other, which is a common source of surprises. A garbage collector is needed to work out when nobody uses the object any more.
  • C++: b = a makes a full copy of the object, including its heap data. That is safe, but it can be expensive, and you cannot see the cost in the code. C++ also has moves (std::move), but the compiler does not stop you from using the old object afterwards.
  • Rust: b = a moves. It is always cheap, and using a afterwards is a compile error.

Making a real copy: clone

When you do want two independent copies of heap data, ask for it with .clone():

Step through it: What .clone() does
  1. fn main() {
  2. let s1 = String::from("hello");
  3. let s2 = s1.clone();
  4. println!("{s1} {s2}");
  5. }

.clone() is visible in the code on purpose. When you read Rust code, the word clone tells you: “here something may be copied that costs time and memory”.

Tip
Do not be afraid of clone while learning

Beginners often worry that clone is “bad style”. It is not wrong. It is a trade: simpler code for some extra work at run time. While you are learning, use clone whenever ownership blocks you. As you learn about borrowing in the next chapter, you will need it less and less.

Simple values are copied automatically

Now a surprise. This compiles:

Why is x still usable? An integer lives entirely on the stack. Copying it means copying 4 bytes, which is as cheap as a move, and there is no heap data that could be freed twice. For such types a move would have no benefit, so Rust simply copies them. These types are called Copy types.

Copy types: assignment copiesNot Copy: assignment moves
All integers (i32, u8, usize …)String
Floats (f64, f32)Vec and other collections
bool and charAnything that owns heap data or another resource, such as an open file
Tuples and arrays that contain only Copy types, such as (i32, f64) or [u8; 4]Tuples and arrays that contain a non-Copy type, such as (i32, String)

A rule of thumb: if a value is small, lives only on the stack, and needs no clean-up, it is Copy. In chapter 12 you will see how to make your own types Copy.

Ownership and functions

Passing a value to a function works exactly like assigning it to a variable: Copy types are copied, everything else is moved into the function.

Step through it: Passing a String to a function
  1. fn main() {
  2. let s = String::from("hello");
  3. print_text(s);
  4. println!("done");
  5. }
  7. fn print_text(text: String) {
  8. println!("{text}");
  9. }

So after print_text(s), the variable s is gone for main:

Read the compiler’s notes: it tells you where the value was moved, why (the type is not Copy), and it suggests two fixes. One is clone. The other, changing the function so that it borrows the value, is the subject of the next chapter.

Getting a value back

Return values move too: a function can give ownership to its caller.

make_greeting creates a String and moves it out to the caller, so the text lives on after the function has ended. This is the answer to a problem from the last chapter: data on the heap can outlive the function that created it, because ownership can be handed on.

add_exclamation takes ownership of a String, changes it, and hands it back. That works, but it is clumsy: if a function only wants to look at a value, taking it away and returning it again is a lot of ceremony. The next chapter introduces borrowing, which solves this neatly.

More details that are good to know

Assigning a new value drops the old one

When you assign a new value to a mut variable, the value it held before is dropped at once:

A moved-out variable can be filled again

After a move, a variable is empty, but it still exists. If it is mut, you can give it a new value and use it again:

Dropping a value early

A value is normally dropped at the end of its scope. To drop it sooner, pass it to the function drop. It takes ownership of its argument and does nothing else, so the value’s life ends right there.

Why this is worth the trouble

  • No garbage collector. The compiler knows exactly where each value’s life ends, and puts the clean-up there. The program does not pause, and it uses no extra memory for bookkeeping.
  • No double free and no use after free. There is one owner, so memory is freed once. A moved-out variable cannot be used, so freed data cannot be touched.
  • No hidden costs. Moves are always cheap. An expensive copy is always written as .clone().
  • Not only memory. The same rules close files, release network connections and unlock locks at the right moment. Anything that needs cleaning up can be tied to an owner.
Recap
  • Every value has one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory freed.
  • Assigning or passing a non-Copy value moves it. The old variable can no longer be used.
  • .clone() makes an explicit, complete copy.
  • Small stack-only types (numbers, bool, char, and tuples or arrays of them) are Copy: they are copied instead of moved.
  • A function parameter takes ownership of what is passed in. A return value hands ownership to the caller.
Check your understanding
1

What happens at let b = a; when a is a String?

Assigning a String moves it. Only the small record on the stack is copied, and the compiler forbids any later use of a. Nothing is checked at run time.

2

Why does this compile, although the same code with String values would not?

Copy types are duplicated on assignment. There is no heap data, so nothing could be freed twice.

3

When is the heap memory of the String in this program freed?

The call moves the String into text. consume is now the owner, and the value is dropped when text goes out of scope at the end of that function.

4

What does .clone() do for a String?

After a clone there are two separate texts, each with its own owner. Changing or dropping one does not affect the other.

Guided exerciseFollow the owner

Without running it, decide which of the three println! lines the compiler accepts. Then check by compiling. Remove the lines that fail.

Need a hint?

Follow the text step by step. After line 3, who owns “apple”? Does line 4 move anything?

Show solution and explanation
  • Line 3 moves the text from a to b. From then on a cannot be used, so println!("{a}") is rejected.
  • Line 4 clones: c gets its own copy, and b stays the owner of the original. Both b and c can be printed.
PracticeRepair it in two ways

This program does not compile. Fix it in two different ways: first with clone, then by changing only the order of two lines.

(format! works like println!, but instead of printing, it returns the text as a new String.)

Need a hint?

The problem is that name is moved into make_greeting and used afterwards. For the second fix: is name still valid before the call?

Show solution and explanation

Way 1: clone. The function gets its own copy, and name stays valid.

Way 2: use the value before you give it away.

The second way needs no extra memory, but it changes the order of the output. The best fix is a third one: let the function borrow the name instead of taking it. You will be able to write that after the next chapter.

PracticeMove or copy?

For each snippet, say whether the last line compiles, and why.

Need a hint?

A tuple is Copy only if every part of it is Copy.

Show solution and explanation
  1. Compiles. f64 is Copy.
  2. Compiles. A tuple of two integers contains only Copy types, so the tuple is Copy.
  3. Does not compile. The tuple contains a String, which is not Copy. So the whole tuple is moved into b, and a can no longer be used.
  4. Compiles. char is Copy.

The general rule: one part that owns heap data makes the whole value movable instead of copyable.

ChallengeA function that builds and returns

Write a function repeat_word(word: String, times: u32) -> String that returns the word repeated that many times, separated by spaces. For ("hey", 3) it returns hey hey hey. Use a loop and push_str, which adds text to the end of a String. To pass a String to push_str you write &word, which means “look at this without taking it”.

Need a hint?

Start with let mut result = String::new();. In each round, add a space first unless it is the first round, then add the word.

Show solution and explanation

result is created inside the function and moved out to the caller by the last line, so it lives on in shout. The parameter word is owned by the function and dropped when the function ends. Inside the loop, &word only lends the word to push_str. If the loop moved word in the first round, there would be nothing left for the second round. That & is called a reference, and the next chapter is about it.

Part 2 · Ownership: Rust's big ideaBeginnerabout 45 min
10

References and borrowing

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Let a function use a value without taking ownership of it
  • Tell shared references (&) from mutable references (&mut) and use each
  • State the borrowing rules and explain which bugs they prevent
  • Read and fix the borrow checker’s most common error messages

At the end of the last chapter, a function had to take ownership of a String and then hand it back. That is like giving your car to a mechanic by signing the ownership papers over, and signing them back afterwards. In real life you just lend the car. Rust has the same idea, and calls it borrowing.

Borrowing with &

Two small symbols changed everything:

  • In the call, &name creates a reference to name. A reference lets the function reach the value without owning it.
  • In the signature, text: &String says: this parameter is a reference to a String.

name is still valid after the call, because ownership never moved. Creating a reference is called borrowing. When the function ends, the reference goes away. The text stays, because the reference never owned it.

Real-world analogy
Lending a book

You lend a book to a friend. They can read it, but it is still yours, and they give it back when they are done. They may not sell it or throw it away, because it is not theirs.

Step through it: A reference in memory
  1. fn main() {
  2. let name = String::from("Ferris");
  3. let length = count_letters(&name);
  4. println!("{name} has {length} letters.");
  5. }
  7. fn count_letters(text: &String) -> usize {
  8. text.len()
  9. }

In plain English
Reference

A reference is a pointer that Rust guarantees to be valid: it always points to a living value of the right type. You create one with &. In the last chapter you read that a pointer is an address. A reference is an address plus a promise checked by the compiler.

A shared reference cannot change the value

Like variables, references are immutable by default. Through a plain & you may look, but not change:

Mutable references with &mut

To let a function change a value it does not own, lend the value mutably:

Three things must all say “mutable”:

  1. The variable itself: let mut text.
  2. The reference you create: &mut text.
  3. The type of the parameter: t: &mut String.

This is deliberate. Anyone who reads the call shout(&mut text) can see that text may be changed by it. In many other languages you have to read the function to find that out.

Reaching the value behind a reference: *

For method calls such as t.push_str(...), Rust follows the reference for you. When you want to read or replace the value itself, write * in front of the reference. This is called dereferencing: “go to what this points at”.

In chapter 5, a function could not change the caller’s number, because it got a copy. With &mut it can, and the caller can see it in the call.

The borrowing rules

Key idea
The two rules of borrowing
  1. At any moment you can have either any number of shared references (&T) or exactly one mutable reference (&mut T) to a value. Never both.
  2. A reference must never outlive the value it points to.
Real-world analogy
A shared document

Any number of people can read a document at the same time. Nothing can go wrong, because nobody changes anything. But if one person is rewriting it, nobody else should be reading it at that moment. They might read a half-finished sentence. And two people editing the same paragraph at once would destroy each other’s work. So: many readers, or one writer.

That is why &T is called a shared reference and &mut T an exclusive (mutable) reference. The part of the compiler that checks these rules is called the borrow checker.

Rule 1 forbids this:

The message tells the whole story: where the shared borrow starts, where the mutable borrow is attempted, and where the shared borrow is used later.

And this, two writers at once:

A borrow ends at its last use

The rules are less strict than they first look. A reference counts as “active” only from its creation to the last place where it is used. After that, the borrow is over, even if the variable is still in scope.

Why the rules exist: a real bug they prevent

The rules can feel like bureaucracy until you see what they stop. A Vec is a list that can grow. You will study it in chapter 15. For now: vec![1, 2, 3] creates one, and .push(4) adds an element at the end.

Why would that be dangerous? A Vec stores its elements in one block on the heap. When the block is full and another element is pushed, the Vec asks for a bigger block, moves all the elements there, and frees the old block. The reference first would still point into the old, freed block. It would be a dangling pointer, and reading it would be a use after free.

How other languages do it
The same code in other languages

In C++ the equivalent code compiles without complaint, and the program then reads freed memory. The bug even has a name there: iterator invalidation. It may seem to work in testing and crash, or silently produce garbage, in production. Java and Python avoid the crash with a garbage collector, but have a related problem: changing a list while looping over it gives an error at run time or wrong results. Rust rejects the program at compile time.

The “many readers or one writer” rule also prevents data races: two parts of a program changing the same data at the same time. You will see in Part 7 that this makes programs that run on several processor cores far safer in Rust than in other languages.

A second way to see the rules: what each name may do

Here is another way to think like the borrow checker. For every name in your program, ask what it is allowed to do with its value on this line. An owner can have up to three abilities:

  • read the value,
  • change it (only if it was declared with mut),
  • give it away: move it to another owner, or let it be dropped.

A reference takes some of these abilities away from the owner for as long as the reference is in use. The owner gets them back after the last use of the reference.

While this is in use …the owner maythe reference may
no referenceread, change, give away
a shared reference (&)readread
a mutable reference (&mut)nothing at allread, change

Follow the abilities through the program from the last section, with the lines in the order that compiles:

Linenumbers mayfirst may
let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];read, change, give away
let first = &numbers[0];readread
println!("{first}"); (the last use of first)read, change, give away
numbers.push(4);read, change, give away

push needs the ability to change. In the order that failed, push came while first was still in use, and on that line numbers could only be read.

The table also explains two errors that the two rules do not mention directly. First, a value cannot be given away while it is borrowed:

Second, while a mutable reference is in use, the owner cannot even read:

When several names lead to the same value, programmers call it aliasing. Every memory bug in this chapter has the same shape: one name changes or frees the data while another name still looks at it.

Key idea
One sentence to remember

A value may be reachable through several names, or it may be changed. Never both at the same moment.

References must not outlive the value

The second rule prevents references to data that no longer exists:

value is dropped at the end of the inner block, but reference would still be used after that. The compiler compares how long the reference is used with how long the value lives, and refuses the program.

The same mistake often appears in a function that tries to return a reference to one of its own local variables:

s is dropped when the function ends, so the returned reference would point at freed memory. The error message talks about a “lifetime”, which is Rust’s word for how long a reference stays valid. Chapter 21 explains lifetimes in full. The fix here is simple: return the String itself and move ownership to the caller.

Owned, shared or mutable: which should a function ask for?

Parameter typeThe function …The caller writesAfterwards the caller …
text: &Stringonly reads the valuef(&s)still owns s, unchanged
text: &mut Stringchanges the value in placef(&mut s)still owns s, possibly changed
text: Stringtakes the value over: keeps it, or uses it upf(s)can no longer use s

Ask for the least you need. Most functions only read, so most parameters are shared references.

Fighting the borrow checker, and winning

When the borrow checker rejects your code, it has usually found a real problem, or a way of writing things that it cannot prove to be safe. These moves solve most cases:

  1. Read the whole message. It shows where the first borrow starts, where the conflict is, and where the first borrow is used later.
  2. Shorten the borrow. Finish using a reference before you change the value. Often it is enough to move one line.
  3. Copy out what you need. If you only need a number from inside the data, store the number, not a reference to it: let first = numbers[0]; copies the integer.
  4. Clone. It costs some time and memory, but it is always correct.
  5. Ask what would go wrong. Suppose the compiler accepted your code: which name would be left looking at freed or half-changed data? If you can point at it, the compiler has found a real bug and the design has to change. If you cannot, the code is probably safe, but written in a way the compiler cannot follow, and a small rearrangement is enough. Chapter 15 walks through the cases that come up most often with lists.
Recap
  • &value borrows: it creates a reference without moving ownership.
  • A shared reference &T can only read. A mutable reference &mut T can change the value, and needs a mut variable.
  • *reference reaches the value behind a reference.
  • At any moment: many shared references, or one mutable reference. Never both.
  • A borrow lasts from its creation to its last use.
  • A reference can never outlive its value, so dangling pointers cannot exist in safe Rust.
Check your understanding
1

What does &name do?

& borrows. The owner stays the owner, and the reference only allows access for a while.

2

Which combination is allowed at the same moment for one value?

Any number of readers may exist together. A writer must be alone.

3

Why is this rejected?

The shared reference is used after the push, so both borrows would be active together. Growing the vector can move its data to a new place in memory.

4

A function only needs to read a large String. What is the best parameter type?

Ask for the least power you need. A shared reference lets the caller keep the value and promises not to change it. (In the next chapter you will see that &str is even better for text.)

Guided exerciseBorrow instead of move

In the last chapter you fixed this program with clone or by reordering lines. Now fix it properly: change make_greeting so that it borrows the name.

Need a hint?

Two places need a &: the type of the parameter, and the argument in the call.

Show solution and explanation

The function only reads the name, so a shared reference is all it needs. Nothing is copied, and name stays usable. The returned greeting is a new String that the function creates and hands to the caller.

PracticeChange it in place

Write a function double_it that doubles a number in the caller’s variable. This main should print 42:

Need a hint?

The parameter type is &mut i32. To change the number behind the reference, dereference it with *.

Show solution and explanation

number is a reference, and *number is the integer it points at. *number *= 2 reads as “multiply the value behind number by 2”. The first * dereferences, and *= is the multiply-and-assign operator.

PracticeCalm the borrow checker

This program is rejected. Explain why in one sentence. Then fix it without using clone, so that it prints Longest so far: 5 and then hello world.

Need a hint?

Is view really needed after the change? What is the smallest piece of information the program wants from the old text?

Show solution and explanation

The shared borrow view is still used after push_str, which needs a mutable borrow, so a reader and a writer would be active at the same time.

The program only needs the old length, which is a plain number. Copying that number out ends the borrow immediately. This is the most common fix of all: keep the small piece of data you need, not a reference into the big thing.

ChallengeWhich ones compile?

Decide for each program whether the borrow checker accepts it. Give a reason. Then test your answers.

Need a hint?

For each reference, find the last line where it is used. Two borrows conflict only if both are active on the same stretch of lines.

Show solution and explanation
  • A compiles. Two shared references at once are fine. (The compiler warns that s does not need to be mut.)
  • B compiles. r1 is last used at r1.push('b'). The mutable borrow ends there, so creating the shared reference r2 afterwards is allowed.
  • C does not compile. r1 is used after r2 is created, and r2 is used after that. A mutable and a shared borrow are active together, so the compiler reports error E0502.

B and C contain the same lines in a different order. What matters to the borrow checker is where each reference is last used.

Part 2 · Ownership: Rust's big ideaBeginnerabout 45 min
11

Strings and slices

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain the difference between String and &str and choose the right one
  • Build, grow and combine text
  • Borrow a part of a text or a list with a slice
  • Work correctly with text in any language of the world
  • Use the most common text methods

Text is everywhere in programs: names, messages, file contents. It looks simple, and it is one of the trickiest kinds of data. Rust has two main text types, and beginners often ask why. The answer comes straight from ownership: one type owns its text, the other borrows it.

Two kinds of text

String&str (say “string slice”)
Relationship to the textOwns itBorrows it: a view of text that lives somewhere else
Can it grow or change?Yes, if mutNo
Where the characters areOn the heapWherever the owner put them
What it is made ofPointer, length, capacityPointer, length
Typical useText you build, keep or returnText you only read, and function parameters
Real-world analogy
A notebook and a highlighted passage

A String is your own notebook. You can add pages, cross things out, or throw it away. A &str is a passage you marked with a highlighter in someone else’s book: you can read exactly that passage, but the book is not yours, and the passage is only there as long as the book is.

Text written in double quotes in your code, such as "hello", is called a string literal. Its type is &str. The characters are stored inside the program file itself, so they are available for as long as the program runs.

Building and growing a String

  • push_str adds a &str, and push adds one char.
  • format! works like println! but returns the result as a new String. It is the most readable way to combine values into text, and it does not move any of them.
  • + glues text onto a String. The left side must be a String and is moved into the result. Everything added must be a &str, so a String on the right needs a &. After this line first cannot be used any more, but second can. When this feels confusing, use format!.

Slices: borrowing a part

A slice is a reference to a connected part of a sequence. For text you write the range of bytes you want inside square brackets:

Step through it: A string slice in memory
  1. fn main() {
  2. let text = String::from("hello world");
  3. let first = &text[0..5];
  4. let second = &text[6..];
  5. println!("{first} / {second}");
  6. }

SliceMeans
&text[0..5]bytes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (the end is not included, as with ranges in loops)
&text[..5]the same: a missing start means “from the beginning”
&text[6..]from byte 6 to the end
&text[..]the whole text

A slice is a normal shared borrow, so the borrowing rules protect it. This function returns the first word of a text as a slice:

char_indices gives each character together with the position where it starts. At the first space, the function returns the part before it. If there is no space, the whole text is one word.

Now try to empty the sentence while the slice is still in use:

word is a view into sentence. If clear were allowed, word would point at text that no longer exists. The compiler knows that the returned slice borrows from the argument, and rejects the program. In many languages this would be a bug that shows up later, somewhere else.

Prefer &str for parameters

A function that takes &str can be called with a string literal, with a slice, and with a reference to a String. Rust turns &String into &str automatically.

Key idea
Which text type where?
  • Function parameter that only reads text: &str.
  • Text that a struct or a variable should own, or that you build yourself: String.
  • Function that creates new text: return String.
  • From &str to String: .to_string() or String::from(...). From String to &str: put & in front.

Text is more than English letters

Computers store text as numbers. The worldwide standard Unicode gives every character of every writing system a number, and UTF-8 is the usual way to store those numbers as bytes. In UTF-8, characters take a different number of bytes:

CharacterBytes in UTF-8
a, Z, 7, ? (English letters, digits, basic signs)1
é, ñ, ж (most European and Middle Eastern letters)2
ሰ, 中, あ (Ethiopic, Chinese, Japanese and many others)3
🦀, 😀 (emoji and rare signs)4

A Rust String is always valid UTF-8. This has consequences that surprise people:

.len() counts bytes, not characters. To count characters, use .chars().count().

For the same reason, Rust does not let you pick a character by number:

What should word[0] be? The first byte is only a third of the first letter. Finding the first character means reading the text from the start, which gets slower the longer the text is. Rust refuses to hide that. You say what you mean instead:

.chars() walks through the text character by character, and .bytes() byte by byte. nth(1) answers Some('ላ') because a text might be too short to have a character there, in which case the answer would be None. .collect() gathers the characters into a new String. Both ideas return in later chapters.

Slices of text use byte positions, and a slice must not cut a character in half. If it does, the program panics:

Watch out
Be careful with byte ranges

Slicing with fixed numbers such as &text[0..3] is only safe when you know what the text contains. In real programs, get positions from methods such as find or char_indices, which always return valid positions, or use methods that work with whole characters, such as chars, split and trim.

How other languages do it
Text in other languages
  • C: a string is a row of bytes that ends with a zero byte. It does not know its own length. Forgetting the final zero, or writing past the end, causes the buffer overflows described in chapter 8.
  • Java and JavaScript: strings are stored as 16-bit units. "🦀".length is 2 in JavaScript, although it is one character, and taking “the first character” can give half an emoji.
  • Python 3: indexing by character works, at the price of a storage format that can use up to 4 bytes for every character.
  • Go: strings are byte sequences like in Rust, and indexing gives a byte without warning.
  • Rust: the text is compact UTF-8, always valid, and you must say whether you mean bytes or characters.
What looks like one character may be several

Some things that look like one character on screen are built from several chars. The letter é can be stored as one char, or as e followed by a separate accent mark. A flag emoji is two chars. A “character as a human sees it” is called a grapheme cluster. The standard library does not split text into those. When you need it, for example to cut a text for display, use the crate unicode-segmentation.

A toolbox of text methods

MethodWhat it gives you
.len() / .is_empty()length in bytes / whether the text is empty
.trim(), .trim_start(), .trim_end()the text without spaces and line ends around it
.to_uppercase(), .to_lowercase()a new String in upper or lower case
.contains(x), .starts_with(x), .ends_with(x)true or false
.find(x)the byte position of the first match, as Some(position), or None
.replace(a, b)a new String with every a replaced by b
.split(x), .split_whitespace(), .lines()the parts of the text, one after another
.chars(), .bytes(), .char_indices()the characters, the bytes, or characters with their positions
.parse::<Type>()the text converted to a number or another type, as Ok or Err
.repeat(n)the text n times in a row
==, <, >comparison, letter by letter (upper and lower case are different)

Most of these work on &str, and because a &String turns into a &str automatically, they work on String too. Methods that produce changed text, such as to_uppercase and replace, return a new String and leave the original untouched.

Slices of arrays and lists

Slices are not only for text. A slice of an array or a Vec has the type &[T], where T is the type of the elements: &[i32] is “a borrowed row of i32 values”.

A function that takes &[i32] works with arrays of any length, with vectors, and with parts of both. It is to lists what &str is to text. A mutable slice, &mut [T], lets a function change the elements in place:

Formatting text precisely

println! and format! can control how a value is shown. The instructions go after a colon inside the brackets.

The full list is in the reference appendix.

Recap
  • String owns text on the heap and can grow. &str is a borrowed view of text.
  • String literals are &str. .to_string() makes an owned String, and & turns a String into a &str.
  • Use &str for parameters and String for text you own or return.
  • A slice (&text[a..b], &array[a..b]) borrows a part without copying. The borrow checker keeps it valid.
  • Text is UTF-8: .len() counts bytes, characters can take 1 to 4 bytes, and you cannot index by number. Use .chars().
  • format! builds a String the way println! prints one.
Check your understanding
1

What is the type of "hello" written directly in the code?

A string literal is a string slice, &str. Its characters are stored in the program itself. To get an owned String, call .to_string() or String::from.

2

What does "ሰላም".len() return, and why?

.len() is the number of bytes. For the number of characters, use .chars().count().

3

Which signature is the most flexible for a function that only reads a text?

&str accepts string literals, slices, and references to String values. &String works only with a String, and String would take ownership.

4

Why does Rust not allow text[0] on a string?

Indexing would have to return either a byte, which is often not a character, or do a slow search for the right character. Rust makes you choose with .bytes() or .chars().

5

After let c = a + &b; where a and b are Strings, which variables can still be used?

+ moves the left operand a into the result and only borrows b. To keep everything, write format!("{a}{b}").

Guided exerciseCount the vowels

Write a function count_vowels(text: &str) -> usize that counts the letters a, e, i, o and u in a text, in upper or lower case. For "Rust is Awesome" the answer is 6.

Need a hint?

Loop over text.to_lowercase().chars(). A match with the pattern 'a' | 'e' | 'i' | 'o' | 'u' recognises a vowel.

Show solution and explanation

Converting to lower case first means only five characters need checking. The arm _ => {} says “for anything else, do nothing”: the empty block {} is how you write “no action” in a match.

PracticeReverse a text

Write a function reverse(text: &str) -> String that returns the text backwards, and test it with "stressed" and with "ሰላም". Use a loop and push.

Need a hint?

text.chars().rev() gives the characters from last to first. Start with an empty String and push each character.

Show solution and explanation

Because the loop goes through chars and not bytes, it works for every writing system. Reversing the bytes of the Amharic word would produce invalid text. The short form you saw earlier, text.chars().rev().collect(), does the same thing in one line.

PracticeThe longest word

Write longest_word(text: &str) -> &str, which returns the longest word of a sentence. For "the quick brown fox" it returns quick (the first one, if several are equally long).

Need a hint?

Keep a variable let mut longest = "";. For each word from split_whitespace(), compare word.chars().count() with the count of longest.

Show solution and explanation

The function returns a slice of the original sentence. No text is copied: split_whitespace hands out slices into text, and one of them is returned. Using > instead of >= keeps the first of several equally long words.

ChallengeTitle case

Write title_case(text: &str) -> String that makes the first letter of every word a capital: "the rust programming language" becomes "The Rust Programming Language". Words in the result are separated by single spaces.

Need a hint?

Go through the words with split_whitespace(). For each word, go through its characters with .chars().enumerate() to know which one is the first. c.to_uppercase() can produce more than one character (the German ß becomes SS), so turn it into text with .to_string() and add it with push_str.

Show solution and explanation

The outer loop handles words and puts a space before every word except the first. The inner loop handles characters, treating position 0 specially. The detail about to_uppercase shows how much care Rust’s standard library takes with text: in some languages one letter turns into two when capitalised, and Rust’s API does not pretend otherwise.
