Part 3 · Modelling dataBeginnerabout 40 min
12

Structs: building your own types

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Define a struct that groups related values under one name
  • Create, read and change struct values
  • Give a struct behaviour with methods and associated functions
  • Print structs for debugging and add common abilities with derive
  • Explain how structs differ from classes in other languages

So far you have used types that Rust provides: numbers, text, tuples, arrays. Real programs are about things: a user, an order, a rectangle, a song. A struct (short for structure) lets you define your own type that describes such a thing by grouping its parts under one name.

The problem structs solve

Suppose a program handles users. Without structs, each user is several loose variables:

Nothing says these three belong together. Passing a user to a function means passing three arguments in the right order, and with ten users you would need thirty variables. A tuple (String, String, u32) keeps them together, but user.0 and user.1 do not tell you which one is the email.

Real-world analogy
A form with labelled fields

A struct is like a printed form: “Name: ____, Email: ____, Age: ____”. The form defines which fields exist and what kind of answer goes in each. Every filled-in copy of the form is one concrete user.

Defining and creating a struct

  • The struct User { ... } block defines a new type called User. Each line inside is a field: a name and a type. Type names are written in CamelCase: every word starts with a capital letter and there are no underscores.
  • User { name: ..., ... } creates a value of that type. Such a value is called an instance. Every field must get a value. The order does not matter.
  • You read a field with a dot: user.name.

A struct definition is written outside of functions, usually near the top of the file.

Changing fields

To change a field, the whole instance must be mut. Rust does not let you mark single fields as mutable.

Two shortcuts

  • Field init shorthand: when a variable has the same name as the field, write the name once.
  • Struct update syntax: ..first fills every field you did not list with the value from first.
Watch out
Struct update moves fields

..first moves or copies each remaining field, following the normal ownership rules. Here email is a String, so it is moved out of first. Afterwards first.email can no longer be used, but first.age and first.active can, because they are Copy types.

A struct owns its fields

The User struct holds String fields, not &str. That is a choice: each User owns its name and email. When the user is dropped, its strings are dropped with it. A user can be moved around or returned from a function freely, because it depends on nothing outside itself.

A struct can also hold references, but then the compiler must be sure that the borrowed data lives at least as long as the struct. That needs lifetimes, the subject of chapter 21. Until then, let your structs own their data.

Fields are borrowed and moved one at a time

The compiler looks at every field separately. You can hold a mutable reference to one field and still read another:

The same holds for moves. Moving one field out of a struct is called a partial move. The fields that stayed can still be used, but the struct as a whole cannot:

If you need the struct afterwards, borrow the field (&player.name) or clone it. If you want to take the struct apart for good, say so with a pattern, let Player { name, score } = player;, which chapter 14 explains.

Printing a struct

println!("{}", user) does not compile. Rust cannot know how you would like a User to look in a message for users. For debugging, ask the compiler to generate a debug representation by writing #[derive(Debug)] above the struct:

  • {:?} prints the struct on one line. {:#?} prints it “pretty”, over several lines, which helps with big structs.
  • dbg! is a macro made for quick debugging. It prints the file name, the line number, the expression and its value, to the error output of the terminal. That is why you do not see it in the output box above. In your terminal it shows [src/main.rs:11:5] &p = Point { x: 3, y: -7, } spread over a few lines.
Good to know
A warning you may see

When you run small examples like this one, the compiler may warn that the fields x and y are “never read”. It is right: the program only prints the struct for debugging and never uses the fields one by one. In a small example you can ignore that warning.

In plain English
Attribute and derive

A line such as #[derive(Debug)] is an attribute: extra information for the compiler about the item that follows it. derive asks the compiler to write some standard code for your type automatically. Debug is the ability to be printed with {:?}. You will meet more of these abilities below. They are called traits, and chapter 20 explains them.

Methods: giving a struct behaviour

A method is a function that belongs to a type. Methods are written in an impl block (“implementation”) and are called with a dot.

The first parameter of a method is always some form of self: the instance the method is called on. In big.area(), self is big. The form of self tells you what the method does with the instance, with exactly the meanings you learned in the borrowing chapter:

First parameterThe method …Example
&selfonly reads the instancearea, is_square
&mut selfchanges the instancea method that resizes the rectangle
selftakes ownership and uses the instance upa method that turns it into something else

When you call big.area(), Rust borrows big in the right way automatically. You do not write (&big).area().

What the dot does for you

A method is an ordinary function whose first parameter is called self. A call with a dot is a short way to write a call with the full name of that function:

The compiler compares the type in front of the dot with what the method asks for, and adds &, &mut or * until the two fit. It does this only for the value in front of the dot, never for the other arguments. That is why you write big.can_hold(&small): a & for small, and none for big.

Watch out
A method borrows the whole struct

Inside one function, the compiler can see that two fields are different. Across a method call it cannot:

The borrow checker reads only the signature of add_points, and &mut self means “I may change anything in this player”. So no reference into the player may be in use during the call. The repair is usually to change the order: call add_points first, and borrow the name afterwards.

Associated functions: making new instances

A function inside an impl block that has no self parameter is called an associated function. It belongs to the type, not to one instance, and is called with ::. You have used one many times: String::from. The most common use is a function that builds a new instance, by convention called new.

Inside an impl block, Self (with a capital S) is another name for the type itself, here Rectangle.

How other languages do it
Structs and classes

If you know Java, Python, C# or C++, a struct with an impl block looks like a class. There are important differences:

  • Data and behaviour are written separately: fields in struct, methods in impl.
  • No inheritance. A struct cannot extend another struct. Rust shares behaviour between types through traits (chapter 20) and builds bigger things by putting structs inside structs.
  • No special constructors. new is an ordinary function with a conventional name. A struct can have several such functions with descriptive names.
  • No half-built objects and no null. Every field must be given a value when the instance is created.
  • self is explicit, and its form (&self, &mut self, self) tells you whether the method reads, changes or consumes the instance. In most languages you must read the method body to find that out.

Tuple structs and unit structs

A tuple struct has a name, but its fields do not. It is useful when names for the fields would add nothing:

Meters and Seconds both wrap an f64, yet they are different types. A function that expects Meters will not accept Seconds. Wrapping a simple value in its own type so that it cannot be mixed up with other values is called the newtype pattern. It turns “I passed the arguments in the wrong order” from a hidden bug into a compile error.

A famous bug that newtypes prevent

In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter, a spacecraft worth hundreds of millions of dollars. One piece of software produced numbers in pound-force seconds and another expected newton seconds. Both were plain numbers, so nothing complained. With distinct types for the two units, the compiler would have refused to build the program.

A struct with no fields at all is a unit struct: struct Marker;. It carries no data. It becomes useful together with traits, later in the guide.

More abilities with derive

Debug is one of several abilities the compiler can write for you:

DeriveWhat you getCondition
Debugprinting with {:?}all fields are Debug
Clonean explicit copy with .clone()all fields are Clone
Copyautomatic copying instead of movingall fields are Copy. Needs Clone too
PartialEqcomparison with == and !=all fields can be compared
DefaultType::default() with zero, false, empty text and so onall fields have a default

A struct with a String field cannot be Copy, because a String is not Copy. It can still be Clone.

Structs in memory

A struct’s fields are stored side by side as one block. A Point with two i32 fields takes 8 bytes, and it lives wherever the variable lives, usually on the stack. Fields that are Strings keep their small record inside the struct and their characters on the heap, as always. Making a struct costs nothing extra compared with using its fields as separate variables. Rust calls this kind of feature a zero-cost abstraction: it makes the code clearer and adds no cost when the program runs.

Recap
  • A struct groups named fields into a new type. An instance is one concrete value of it.
  • Fields are read and changed with a dot. Changing needs a mut instance.
  • A struct normally owns its fields.
  • #[derive(Debug)] lets you print it with {:?} and {:#?}.
  • Methods live in impl blocks. &self reads, &mut self changes, self consumes.
  • Associated functions have no self and are called with Type::name(). new is the usual constructor.
  • Tuple structs give a name to a group of unnamed fields. Wrapping one value in its own type is the newtype pattern.
Check your understanding
1

What does &self in a method signature mean?

&self is a shared borrow of the instance. To change it, a method needs &mut self. To take ownership, it uses self.

2

How do you call the associated function new of the struct Rectangle?

Associated functions are called on the type with ::. Methods are called on an instance with a dot.

3

Why does this not compile?

Rust has no half-initialised values. All fields need a value, either written out or taken from another instance with ..other.

4

What is the newtype pattern good for?

struct Meters(f64); and struct Seconds(f64); are different types although both hold an f64, so they cannot be confused.

Guided exerciseA Book type

Define a struct Book with the fields title (String), pages (u32) and finished (bool). Add:

  • an associated function new(title: &str, pages: u32) that creates an unfinished book,
  • a method is_long that returns true when the book has more than 300 pages,
  • a method finish that marks the book as finished.

Derive Debug, and test all of it from main.

Need a hint?

new takes a &str and must store a String: use title.to_string(). is_long only reads, so it takes &self. finish changes a field, so it takes &mut self, and the variable in main must be mut.

Show solution and explanation

new accepts a &str so that callers can pass a plain string literal, and converts it into an owned String for the struct. The two methods show the difference between &self (look) and &mut self (change).

PracticeGrow a rectangle

Add two methods to Rectangle (with width and height as u32):

  • scale(&mut self, factor: u32) multiplies both sides by factor,
  • perimeter(&self) -> u32 returns the total length of all four sides.

A 3 × 4 rectangle scaled by 2 should have the perimeter 28.

Need a hint?

The perimeter is 2 * (width + height). Inside scale, write self.width *= factor;.

Show solution and explanation

scale needs &mut self because it changes the fields, so r must be declared with let mut. perimeter only reads, so &self is enough.

ChallengeA bank account

Write a struct Account with an owner (String) and a balance in cents (u64). Give it:

  • Account::new(owner: &str) with a balance of 0,
  • deposit(&mut self, amount: u64),
  • withdraw(&mut self, amount: u64) -> bool, which takes the money out and returns true only if the balance is large enough. Otherwise it changes nothing and returns false.

Test it: deposit 5000, withdraw 2000 (works), then withdraw 9999 (fails). The balance at the end is 3000.

Need a hint?

In withdraw, check amount > self.balance first and return false early. Remember from chapter 4 that subtracting below zero would overflow a u64.

Show solution and explanation

The check before the subtraction keeps the account in a valid state: the balance can never go below zero. Because code outside the type must go through withdraw, the rule is enforced in one place. In chapter 17 you will learn to make fields private, so that nothing can change balance directly. And in chapter 18 you will replace the bool with a result that also says why a withdrawal failed.

13

Enums, Option and match

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Define a type whose value is one of several named possibilities
  • Attach different data to each possibility
  • Handle every case safely with match, if let and let … else
  • Use Option instead of null, and explain why that prevents a whole class of crashes

A struct says “a user has a name and an email and an age”. Many things are better described with or: a traffic light is red or yellow or green. A payment is by cash or by card or by bank transfer. A search finds something or finds nothing. For “one of several possibilities” Rust has the enum (short for enumeration).

A simple enum

  • enum Direction { ... } defines a new type. The possibilities inside are called variants.
  • A value of type Direction is always exactly one of the four variants. You write a variant with the enum’s name in front: Direction::North.
  • match looks at the value and runs the arm of the matching variant.
Real-world analogy
A multiple-choice question

An enum is like a question on a form with tick boxes where exactly one box must be ticked. You cannot tick two, you cannot tick none, and you cannot write in your own answer.

Without enums, people use numbers (0 for north, 1 for east …) or text ("north"). Both allow nonsense values such as 7 or "nroth", and the mistake shows up only when the program runs. With an enum, an invalid direction cannot even be written down.

match must cover everything

Remove one arm, and the program no longer compiles:

The compiler names the forgotten case. This is called exhaustiveness checking, and it matters most months later: when you add a fifth variant to an enum, the compiler shows you every match in the program that needs a new arm. In most languages you would have to find those places by searching, and you would learn about the ones you missed from bug reports.

When several variants should be treated alike, join them with |, or catch all the rest with _:

Use _ with care. It also swallows variants that are added later, so the compiler can no longer remind you about them.

Variants that carry data

Each variant of an enum can hold its own data, and different variants can hold different kinds of data. This is what makes Rust’s enums far more powerful than those of most languages.

The patterns in the match do two jobs at once: they check which variant the value is, and they take the data out and give it names (radius, width, height) that the arm can use. You can only reach the radius inside the arm for Circle. There is no way to ask a rectangle for its radius by mistake.

In plain English
Why this is a big deal

A circle has a radius. A rectangle has a width and a height. In a language without such enums you would write one struct with all three fields and a “kind” field, and hope that nobody reads radius on a rectangle. Rust’s enum stores exactly the data that belongs to the current variant, and match makes sure you only touch data that is really there. The idea is known as a sum type or tagged union.

Like structs, enums can have methods:

The _ inside Circle(_) means “there is a value here, but I do not need it”.

Option: a value that may be missing

Often a value may or may not be there. A search may find nothing. A list may be empty, so it has no first element. A user may not have given a phone number.

How other languages do it
The billion-dollar mistake

Most languages solve this with a special value called null (None in Python, nil in Go, undefined in JavaScript). Any variable might secretly hold null instead of a real value. If the program uses it without checking, it crashes: NullPointerException in Java, “undefined is not a function” in JavaScript, a segmentation fault in C. Tony Hoare, who invented null references in 1965, later called them his “billion-dollar mistake” because of the countless crashes and security holes they have caused.

Rust has no null. A value of type String is always a real string. If something may be missing, the type has to say so.

The way to say so is an enum from the standard library, Option:

The <T> means “this works for any type”: Option<i32> is “maybe an integer”, Option<String> is “maybe a string”. (Chapter 19 explains this notation.) Option is used so often that you can write Some and None without Option:: in front.

The important part: an Option<usize> is not a usize. You cannot calculate with it until you have dealt with the possibility that it is None.

The compiler will not let you forget the “nothing” case. A crash from an unexpected null cannot happen, because the type system makes “may be missing” visible and forces a decision.

Ways to get at the value inside

map applies a small function to the value inside a Some and leaves a None alone. The |n| n * 2 is a closure, a function written in place. Chapter 24 covers closures. For now read it as “take n, give back n * 2”.

There are also two blunt tools:

.unwrap() says “give me the value, and if there is none, panic”. .expect("message") does the same with your own message. They are fine in experiments, in tests, and where a None would mean a bug in your own program. In real code, prefer one of the gentler ways above. Each unwrap marks a place where your program can crash.

Shorter forms of match: if let and let … else

Often you care about one case only. A full match is then a lot of writing:

Read if let Some(colour) = favourite as: “if favourite matches the pattern Some(colour), run the block, with colour holding the value inside”. The else part is optional.

let … else turns it around. It takes the value out, or leaves the function when the pattern does not match. This keeps the main path of a function free of nesting:

The else block must leave the current function or loop, with return, break, continue or a panic. (parse::<u32>() is another way of telling parse which type you want.)

while let repeats as long as a pattern matches. Here pop removes the last element of a list and returns it as Some(value), or returns None when the list is empty:

Result: success or failure

Option says “a value or nothing”. Its sibling Result says “a value or an error”. You met it in the guessing game:

Everything you learned in this chapter (match, if let, let … else, unwrap_or) works for Result too. Error handling with Result gets its own chapter: chapter 18.

How an enum is stored

An enum value stores a small number, called the tag or discriminant, that says which variant it currently is, plus enough room for the data of the largest variant. A value of an enum with no data in any variant is just the tag, usually one byte.

Option often costs nothing

You might expect Option<T> to need extra memory for its tag. Often it does not. A reference can never be zero, so the compiler uses the “impossible” value zero to mean None. Option<&T> is therefore exactly as big as &T. You get the safety of an explicit “maybe missing” type at the price of a plain pointer.

How other languages do it
Enums in other languages

In C, C++ and Java (in its basic form), an enum is a list of named constants. It cannot carry different data per variant, and in C you can even put a number in it that matches no variant. Languages such as Swift, Kotlin (sealed classes), TypeScript (union types), Haskell and OCaml have features similar to Rust’s enums. The idea came from that last family of languages, where it has been used for decades.

Recap
  • An enum is a type whose value is exactly one of several variants.
  • Variants can carry data, and each variant can carry different data.
  • match checks the variant and takes out the data. It must cover every variant.
  • Option<T> is Some(value) or None. Rust has no null, so “may be missing” is always visible in the type.
  • Get the value with match, if let, let … else, unwrap_or, or map. unwrap and expect panic on None.
  • Result<T, E> is Ok(value) or Err(error).
Check your understanding
1

What is special about Rust’s enums compared with enums in C or Java?

A Rust enum variant can hold values, and different variants can hold different types and numbers of values.

2

What happens if a match on an enum does not cover one of the variants?

match must be exhaustive. The compiler reports error E0004 and names the missing variant.

3

A function returns Option<String>. What does that tell you?

An Option<String> is not a String. The compiler makes the caller deal with the None case.

4

What does value.unwrap_or(10) do for value: Option<i32>?

unwrap_or supplies a fallback. Unlike unwrap, it never panics.

5

When is if let a better choice than match?

if let is a shorter way to write a match that cares about one pattern. For several cases, match is clearer and keeps the exhaustiveness check.

Guided exerciseCoins

Define an enum Coin with the variants Penny, Nickel, Dime and Quarter (US coins worth 1, 5, 10 and 25 cents). Write a function value_in_cents(coin: &Coin) -> u32 and use it to add up an array of coins.

Need a hint?

match coin { Coin::Penny => 1, ... } can be the whole body of the function. For the sum, loop over a reference to the array and add to a mut total.

Show solution and explanation

match is an expression, so its value (the number of the matching arm) is the return value of the function. If a new coin is added to the enum later, this function stops compiling until an arm for it is written.

PracticeSafe division

Dividing an integer by zero makes a program panic. Write safe_divide(a: i32, b: i32) -> Option<i32> that returns None when b is zero. In main, print the results of 10 ÷ 2 and 10 ÷ 0 as Result: 5 and Cannot divide by zero.

Need a hint?

Return None early when b == 0, and otherwise Some(a / b). Use match or if let … else to print.

Show solution and explanation

The signature tells every caller that this operation may have no answer. Compare that with chapter 5, where safe_divide returned 0 for a division by zero. That hid the problem, because 0 is also a perfectly normal result.

PracticeDescribe a message

A chat program has this enum. Write describe(msg: &Message) -> String that returns a readable text for each variant, for example Text: hello, Image 800x600, and User left.

Need a hint?

The patterns are Message::Text(content), Message::Image { width, height } and Message::Left. Build each text with format!.

Show solution and explanation

Each arm sees only the data of its own variant. Because describe takes &Message, the names content, width and height are references into the message, so nothing is moved out of it.

ChallengeA traffic light

Model a traffic light as an enum with the variants Red, Green and Yellow. Add two methods: next(&self) -> TrafficLight (red → green → yellow → red) and seconds(&self) -> u32 (red 30, green 25, yellow 5). Starting at red, print the light and its duration for 4 steps.

Need a hint?

Derive Debug so that you can print the variant. In the loop, replace the current light with light = light.next();, which needs a mut variable.

Show solution and explanation

This is a small state machine: a thing that is always in exactly one of a fixed set of states and moves between them by fixed rules. Enums and match are a natural fit for state machines, and the compiler guarantees that every state has a next state and a duration.

14

Pattern matching in depth

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Recognise every place where Rust uses patterns
  • Take apart tuples, structs, enums, arrays and references with one pattern
  • Use ranges, alternatives, guards and bindings in match
  • Combine conditions with if let chains
  • Avoid accidentally moving values out while matching

You have already used patterns many times: in match arms, in if let, and in let (a, b) = pair;. A pattern describes the shape of a value. Rust compares a value with the pattern, and if the shape fits, it can pull out the parts and give them names. This chapter collects everything patterns can do. You do not need to memorise it all. Read it once, do the exercises, and come back when you need a particular form.

Real-world analogy
Sorting a desk drawer

Patterns are like sorting a mixed drawer of tools by shape. You look for a handle with a square end, a plug that matches a socket, or a narrow blade. The pattern is the shape you are asking for, and the matching value is the item you pull out.

Patterns are everywhere

Even the plain let x = 5; uses a pattern: the name x is a pattern that fits any value and gives it that name.

Real-world analogy
A pattern is a coin sorter

Think of a mechanical coin sorter at a bank: a tray with shaped cutouts of exact widths. Pour mixed coins in, and each coin drops only through the slot whose shape matches it, landing in a labelled tube. A Rust pattern is that cutout: it tests whether a value has the right shape and simultaneously unpacks its inner pieces into variables.

Patterns that can fail and patterns that cannot

  • A pattern that fits every possible value is called irrefutable. x, (a, b) and Point { x, y } are examples. let, for and function parameters need this kind, because there is no “else” to go to.
  • A pattern that fits only some values is called refutable. Some(n) does not fit None. match arms, if let, while let and let … else are made for this kind.

The compiler suggests the fix: let … else, which says what to do when the pattern does not fit.

A catalogue of patterns

Literals, ranges and alternatives

| means “or”. 4..=9 is a range that includes both ends, and 10.. means “10 and above”. Ranges work for numbers and characters. The four arms together cover every u32, so no _ arm is needed, and the compiler has checked that. (&'static str is the type of a string literal that lives for the whole program. The 'static part is explained in chapter 21.)

Names, _ and ..

  • A name fits anything and binds the value to that name.
  • _ fits anything and binds nothing. Use it for parts you do not need.
  • .. stands for “all the remaining parts”.

Structs

Point { x, y, z } is short for Point { x: x, y: y, z: z }: the field name, then the pattern for that field. Writing a literal there, as in y: 0, means “this field must be 0”.

Enums and nesting

Patterns can be nested as deeply as the data:

Guards: an extra condition on an arm

The if width == height after a pattern is a match guard. The arm is taken only if the pattern fits and the condition is true. Arms are tried from top to bottom, so put the more specific arm first.

Watch out
Guards and exhaustiveness

The compiler does not analyse guard conditions. If every arm of a match has a guard, the compiler assumes that all of them could be false, and asks for an arm without a guard.

Binding a name to a tested value: @

Sometimes you want to test a value against a pattern and keep it under a name. name @ pattern does both:

Arrays and slices

[first, .., last] fits any slice with at least two elements. rest @ .. gives a name to “all the other elements” as a slice. The sum function uses it to add up a list by recursion: the sum of a list is its first element plus the sum of the rest.

Matching without moving

Patterns follow the ownership rules. If you match on an owned value and bind a part that is not Copy, that part is moved out of the value:

The String moved into n, so name is no longer complete. The compiler suggests the keyword ref, which is explained in the box below. The more common fix today is to match on a reference. Then the names in the pattern become references too, and nothing moves:

The same works for changing a value in place, by matching on &mut:

The older spelling: ref and ref mut

In older code and in some special situations you will see the keyword ref inside a pattern: Some(ref n) binds n as a reference instead of moving the value, and Some(ref mut n) binds a mutable reference. Matching on &value or &mut value, as above, does the same job and is what most code uses today.

Option also has two methods that do the conversion for you: .as_ref() turns an &Option<T> into an Option<&T>, and .as_mut() gives an Option<&mut T>.

A & in a pattern does the opposite of & in an expression: it takes a reference apart. This is common when looping over references to Copy values:

Combining conditions: if let chains

In the 2024 edition, an if or while can join several conditions and several let patterns with &&. Each part can use the names bound by the parts before it:

Without a chain you would write an if let with a second if nested inside it. The same idea works inside match: a guard may contain a let.

matches!: a pattern as a yes-or-no question

The macro matches!(value, pattern) gives true if the value fits the pattern. It saves a match with two arms:

The pattern cheat sheet

PatternFitsExample
5, 'a', "hi", trueexactly that value0 => ...
nameanything, and binds itn => ...
_anything, binds nothing_ => ...
a | beither pattern1 | 2 => ...
1..=5, 10..a range of numbers or characters'a'..='z' => ...
(a, b), (first, ..)a tuplelet (x, y) = pair;
[a, b], [first, .., last], [head, rest @ ..]an array or slice[] => ...
Point { x, y }, Point { x, .. }a structlet Point { x, .. } = p;
Some(x), Shape::Circle { radius }an enum variantSome(n) => ...
&xa reference, binding what it points tofor &n in &list
name @ patternthe pattern, and binds the whole valuen @ 1..=9 => ...
pattern if conditionthe pattern, when the condition holdsSome(n) if n > 0 => ...
How other languages do it
Pattern matching elsewhere

Older mainstream languages have only a switch statement, which compares a value with constants. It cannot take data apart, and in C and Java it runs on into the next case if you forget break. Pattern matching in Rust’s style comes from functional languages such as ML and Haskell. It has proved so useful that Python (match, since 3.10), Java, C# and Swift have added their own versions. Rust’s stands out because the compiler checks that all cases are covered.

Recap
  • A pattern describes the shape of a value and can bind its parts to names.
  • Patterns appear in let, function parameters, for, match, if let, while let and let … else.
  • Irrefutable patterns always fit. Refutable patterns may not, and need a construct that has an “otherwise”.
  • Useful forms: literals, _, .., |, ranges, tuples, structs, enums, slices, name @ pattern, and guards with if.
  • Matching on an owned value can move parts out of it. Match on &value or &mut value to borrow instead.
  • if let … && … chains several patterns and conditions. matches! turns a pattern into a bool.
Check your understanding
1

Which pattern can be used in a plain let statement without else?

A plain let needs a pattern that always fits. A tuple pattern fits every tuple of that size. The others can fail to fit, so they need if let, match or let … else.

2

What does this print?

7 is not in the range 1 to 5, so the first arm does not fit. The second arm fits any value and its guard is true for 7.

3

Why does match &name { Some(n) => ... } leave name usable afterwards, when name is an Option<String>?

Matching through &name only borrows. The bound names become references to the parts.

4

What does the pattern [first, .., last] fit?

first and last each need an element, and .. stands for zero or more elements in between.

Guided exerciseClassify a point

Write a function quadrant(point: (i32, i32)) -> &'static str that returns "origin" for (0, 0), "on an axis" if exactly one coordinate is 0, and otherwise "top right", "top left", "bottom left" or "bottom right" depending on the signs of x and y.

Need a hint?

Match on the tuple. Use literal patterns for the zero cases first: (0, 0), then (0, _) | (_, 0). For the rest, bind (x, y) and add guards such as if x > 0 && y > 0.

Show solution and explanation

The order of the arms matters. (0, 0) must come before the axis arm, because (0, _) would fit it too. The last arm is a plain _, because the compiler cannot work out from the guards that every case is covered.

PracticeCommands for a robot

A robot understands these commands:

Write run(cmd: &Command, position: &mut (i32, i32)). For Move it changes the position, with one extra rule: a move where both dx and dy are 0 prints Not moving. For Say it prints the text, and for Stop it prints Stopping at (x, y).

Need a hint?

Put the special case Command::Move { dx: 0, dy: 0 } before the general Command::Move { dx, dy }. Change the position with position.0 += dx;.

Show solution and explanation

Because cmd is a reference, dx and dy are &i32 values. position.0 += dx still works, because adding a &i32 to an i32 is allowed. The literal pattern dx: 0, dy: 0 handles the special case without an if.

ChallengeThe middle of a list

Write middle(list: &[i32]) -> Option<&[i32]> that returns the list without its first and last element, or None if the list has fewer than two elements. So [1, 2, 3, 4] gives Some([2, 3]), [1, 2] gives Some([]), and [1] gives None.

Need a hint?

One slice pattern does all the work: [_, inner @ .., _].

Show solution and explanation

The pattern needs one element at each end and names everything in between. For a list of exactly two elements, “everything in between” is an empty slice, which is a valid result and is different from None. No index is calculated by hand, so an off-by-one mistake is impossible.

15

Collections: lists, maps and sets

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Store any number of values in a Vec and work with them safely
  • Look things up by a key with HashMap
  • Keep unique values in a HashSet
  • Choose the right collection for a task
  • Handle ownership of the values inside a collection

An array has a fixed length, decided when you write the program. Real data is rarely like that: a shopping cart, the lines of a file and the players in a game all grow and shrink. A collection is a type that holds a changing number of values on the heap. The standard library has several. Three of them cover almost everything: Vec, HashMap and HashSet.

Vec: a list that grows

A Vec<T> (say “vector”) is a growable list of values that all have the same type T. It is by far the most used collection in Rust.

Vec::new() creates an empty vector. The macro vec![...] creates one with values in it. pop returns an Option, because the vector might be empty.

Reading elements

Use v[i] when an index that is out of range would be a bug in your program. Use v.get(i) when it is a normal situation that you want to handle, for example when the index comes from the user.

Going through all elements

There are three ways to loop over a vector, and they correspond to the three ways of using a value that you know from ownership:

LoopEach item isThe vector afterwards
for x in &v&T, a shared referencestill usable
for x in &mut v&mut T, change it with *x = ...still usable, maybe changed
for x in vT, the element itselfmoved, no longer usable

Most of the time you want the first one.

Changing a vector

insert and remove in the middle must shift all later elements by one place, so they get slow on very long vectors. push and pop at the end are always fast.

Everything you learned about slices in chapter 11 applies: &v turns into a slice &[T] automatically, so a function that takes &[i32] accepts a vector, and &v[1..3] borrows a part of it.

How a vector grows

A vector keeps its elements in one block of heap memory. It usually reserves a little more room than it needs. The number of elements is its length, and the room it has reserved is its capacity.

When the block is full, the vector asks for a bigger block (usually twice the size), moves all elements there, and frees the old one. That is the moment that made the borrow checker reject numbers.push(4) while a reference to an element existed, in chapter 10. Because the size doubles each time, moving happens rarely, and push is fast on average. If you know roughly how many elements are coming, Vec::with_capacity(n) reserves the room at once.

Ownership of the elements

A vector owns its elements. When the vector is dropped, all its elements are dropped. With Copy types such as numbers you will hardly notice. With Strings and other owned values you will:

Taking the String out by index would leave a hole in the vector, so Rust refuses. You have several choices, and the right one depends on what you want:

When the borrow checker objects to a list

Three situations cause most of the borrow errors with lists. For each one, ask the question from chapter 10: what would go wrong if this compiled?

1. A reference kept across a change. This is the bug from chapter 10: let first = &numbers[0];, then numbers.push(4);, then first is used. The push may move all the elements, and first would point at freed memory. Keep the position (let first = 0;) and write numbers[first] when you need the element, or clone the element.

2. Changing the list inside a loop over it.

The loop holds a reference into the list from its first round to its last. A push in the middle may move the elements away under the loop. Other languages accept this code and then fail or misbehave while the program runs. In Rust you choose one of these:

3. Two elements at the same time.

This case is different: nothing would go wrong, because the two elements are different. But the compiler does not follow which position you ask for. To it, &mut scores[0] borrows the whole list. The code is safe, and the compiler cannot prove it. So you write it in a way that it can follow:

split_at_mut(1) returns the elements before position 1 and the elements from position 1 on, as two mutable slices. get_disjoint_mut checks while the program runs that the positions are different and inside the list.

A list of different kinds of things

All elements of a vector have the same type. To store different kinds of things, wrap them in an enum:

HashMap: looking things up by a key

A HashMap<K, V> stores pairs: a key of type K and a value of type V. You put a value in under a key, and later get it back by giving the key.

Real-world analogy
A phone book

A phone book stores pairs: a name and a number. You do not read it from the first page to the last. You jump to the name and find the number at once. The name is the key and the number is the value. Each name appears once.

  • HashMap is not available automatically. The line use std::collections::HashMap; brings it in.
  • get returns an Option<&V>, because the key may be missing. .copied() turns the Option<&u32> into an Option<u32>, and .unwrap_or(0) supplies a value for the “missing” case.
  • Each key exists once. Inserting with an existing key replaces the value.
  • Like a vector, a map owns its keys and values. A String that you insert is moved into the map.

Update a value, or insert it if it is missing

A very common task: “add one to the counter for this key, and if there is no counter yet, start at zero”. The entry method does this in one step:

Read the line from the inside out. counts.entry(word) looks at the place for this key. .or_insert(0) puts a 0 there if the place is empty, and in both cases returns a mutable reference to the value. *... += 1 adds one through that reference. (counts["the"] reads a value by key and panics if the key is missing, like indexing a vector.)

Going through a map

You can also write for (name, age) in &ages. The example collects and sorts the keys first for an important reason:

Watch out
A HashMap has no order

The pairs of a HashMap come out in an order that looks random, and it can be different each time the program runs. Never rely on it. If you need a stable order, sort the keys as above, or use a BTreeMap, described below.

How a hash map finds things so fast

A HashMap runs the key through a hash function, a calculation that turns any key into a number. That number decides in which “bucket” the pair is stored. To look up a key, the map calculates the same number and goes straight to that bucket, without looking at the other pairs. It works like a cloakroom: your ticket number tells the attendant exactly which hook to go to.

Two consequences:

  • A key type must be hashable and comparable for equality. Integers, bool, char, String, &str, and tuples of these all work. Floats do not, because of their odd equality rules.
  • Rust’s default hash function is designed to resist attacks in which someone sends specially chosen keys to make a server slow. It is a little slower than the fastest possible hash. Programs that need more speed and do not handle untrusted input can use a faster one from a crate such as rustc-hash or ahash.

HashSet: a collection of unique values

A HashSet<T> stores values with no repeats and no order. It answers one question very quickly: “is this value in the set?”

insert returns false when the value was already present, which makes “have I seen this before?” a one-liner. The set operations give the values that are in both sets (intersection), only in the first (difference), or in at least one (union). (Vec<_> asks the compiler to work out the element type itself.)

The rest of the family

CollectionWhat it isUse it when
Vec<T>a growable listalmost always. It is the default choice
VecDeque<T>a list that is fast at both endsyou need a queue: add at the back, take from the front
HashMap<K, V>key–value pairs, no orderyou look things up by key
BTreeMap<K, V>key–value pairs, always sorted by keyyou need the keys in order, or all keys in a range
HashSet<T>unique values, no orderyou test membership or remove duplicates
BTreeSet<T>unique values, sortedyou need unique values in order
BinaryHeap<T>a pile from which you always get the largest elementa priority queue: “what is the most urgent task?”
LinkedList<T>a chain of separately stored elementsalmost never. A Vec or VecDeque is nearly always faster

All of them live in std::collections, except Vec, which is always available.

How to talk about speed: “Big O” in plain words

Programmers describe how the work of an operation grows as the collection gets bigger. They write it with a capital O:

  • O(1), “constant”: the work is the same whether there are ten elements or ten million. Examples: push on a Vec, reading v[i], get on a HashMap.
  • O(log n), “logarithmic”: the work grows very slowly. Doubling the data adds one step. Examples: lookups in a BTreeMap, and binary search (your strategy from the guessing game).
  • O(n), “linear”: the work grows in step with the size. Twice the data takes twice as long. Examples: contains on a Vec, insert at the front of a Vec.
  • O(n log n): a little more than linear. Example: sorting.
  • O(n²), “quadratic”: twice the data takes four times as long. A loop inside a loop over the same data does this. It is fine for 100 elements and painful for a million.

This is why HashSet::contains (constant) beats Vec::contains (linear) for big collections, and why choosing the right collection can matter more than any other speed trick.

How other languages do it
Collections in other languages
RustPythonJavaScriptJavaC++
Vec<T>listArrayArrayList<T>std::vector<T>
HashMap<K, V>dictMapHashMap<K, V>std::unordered_map
HashSet<T>setSetHashSet<T>std::unordered_set
BTreeMap<K, V>(none built in)(none built in)TreeMap<K, V>std::map

The ideas are the same everywhere. Rust’s versions differ in three ways: every element has the same, known type; a missing element gives an Option, never a null or an exception; and the borrow checker stops you from changing a collection while you are still holding references into it or looping over it.

Recap
  • Vec<T> is a growable list: push, pop, v[i], v.get(i), for x in &v.
  • Indexing panics when out of range. get returns an Option.
  • A collection owns its elements. You cannot move a non-Copy element out by index: borrow it, clone it, or remove it.
  • HashMap<K, V> stores values under keys. get returns an Option, entry(key).or_insert(v) updates or inserts, and the order is arbitrary.
  • HashSet<T> stores unique values and tests membership quickly.
  • BTreeMap and BTreeSet keep their contents sorted. VecDeque is a queue.
Check your understanding
1

What is the difference between v[10] and v.get(10) on a vector with 3 elements?

Indexing is for cases where an invalid index is a bug. get returns an Option, so the program can handle a missing element.

2

Which loop lets you change the elements of v in place?

&mut v gives a mutable reference to each element, which you change with *x = .... &v only reads, and v consumes the vector.

3

What does *map.entry(key).or_insert(0) += 1; do?

entry finds the place for the key, or_insert(0) fills it if it is empty and returns a mutable reference to the value, and += 1 increments it.

4

You need to print names in alphabetical order with a number for each. Which collection gives you that order without sorting?

A BTreeMap always keeps its keys sorted. A HashMap returns its pairs in an arbitrary order.

5

Why does let s = names[0]; not compile for a Vec<String>?

Moving out by index is forbidden for non-Copy types. Borrow with &names[0], copy with .clone(), or take the element out with remove or pop.

Guided exerciseStatistics

Write a function stats(numbers: &[i32]) -> Option<(i32, i32, f64)> that returns the smallest value, the largest value and the average. For an empty list it returns None. Test it with vec![4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42] and with an empty vector.

Need a hint?

Return None first if numbers.is_empty(). Then start min and max with numbers[0], loop over &numbers, and keep a running sum. Each n in the loop is a &i32, so write *n to get the number.

Show solution and explanation

An empty list has no smallest element and no average (it would be a division by zero), so the honest answer is None. The function takes a slice, so it works for vectors and arrays. Later you will write the same in three short lines with iterator methods: iter().min(), iter().max() and iter().sum().

PracticeWord frequency

Count how often each word appears in a text, ignoring upper and lower case, and print the words in alphabetical order with their counts. For "The cat saw the other cat" the output is:

Need a hint?

Use a BTreeMap<String, u32>, so that the output is sorted without extra work. Convert each word with .to_lowercase(), which gives a String, and count with entry(...).or_insert(0).

Show solution and explanation

to_lowercase creates a new String, which the map takes ownership of as the key. That is why the key type is String here and not &str: the lower-case text does not exist anywhere else that a reference could point to. A BTreeMap has the same entry method as a HashMap.

PracticeRemove duplicates, keep the order

Write unique(items: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32> that returns the values without repeats, in the order of their first appearance. [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] gives [3, 1, 2].

Need a hint?

Keep a HashSet of the values you have already seen. seen.insert(x) returns true only the first time. Push the value onto the result in that case.

Show solution and explanation

The set answers “have I seen this?” quickly, and the vector remembers the order. Two collections work together, each doing what it is good at. The pattern for &item in items takes each &i32 apart, so item is a plain i32.

ChallengeGroup by first letter

Write group_by_initial(names: &[&str]) -> BTreeMap<char, Vec<String>> that groups names by their first letter. For ["Sara", "Tomas", "Selam", "Lena", "Teddy"], printing the result with {:?} gives:

Skip empty names.

Need a hint?

name.chars().next() gives the first character as an Option<char>. Use let Some(initial) = ... else { continue; };. Then groups.entry(initial).or_insert_with(Vec::new).push(...) adds the name to the right list, creating the list if needed.

Show solution and explanation

The value type of the map is itself a collection. entry(initial).or_default() returns a mutable reference to the list for that letter, creating an empty one first if the letter is new (or_default is short for or_insert_with(Vec::new): it inserts the type’s default value, which for a Vec is an empty vector). let … else deals with empty names in one line. A map of lists is one of the most common ways to organise data.

Project: a to-do list for the terminal

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Design the data of a program with structs and enums before writing logic
  • Keep a list of structs in a Vec and change it through methods
  • Turn a line of text into a command with match
  • Separate “understanding the input” from “doing the work”

In this project you build a to-do list that runs in the terminal. You type commands, and the program keeps a list of tasks in memory. It uses everything from Part 3: a struct for a task, a Vec for the list, an enum for the commands, and pattern matching to connect them.

A session will look like this:

Create the project with cargo new todo, open src/main.rs, and build it step by step. Run the program after every step.

Step 0: plan the data first

In the guessing game you planned the steps. For a bigger program, experienced Rust programmers start with a different question: what data does the program work with? Once the types are right, much of the code writes itself, and the compiler can check a lot more.

Ask three questions:

  1. What things exist? Tasks. A task has a number (so the user can refer to it), a title, and a state: done or not done. That is a struct.
  2. What holds them? A list of tasks that grows and shrinks: a Vec<Task>. The list also has to remember which number the next task gets.
  3. What can the user ask for? One of a fixed set of commands: add, list, done, remove, help, quit. Some carry data (the title, or a task number). “One of several possibilities, each with its own data” is an enum.

Step 1: the task and the list

Three decisions are worth a comment:

  • add takes a String, not a &str. The task will own its title, so the list needs an owned string in the end. By asking for a String, the function lets the caller hand over one it already has, with no copy.
  • add returns the new id, so the caller can tell the user which number the task got.
  • Why an id, and not the position in the list? Positions change when a task is removed: after removing the first task, the second one would become “task 1”. An id that is given once and never reused always means the same task.

Try it with a temporary main:

{:#?} earns its place here: with one derive you can see the complete state of your program at any moment.

Step 2: the rest of the list’s behaviour

Add three more methods inside the same impl TodoList block:

  • mark_done loops over &mut self.tasks, so that it can change the task it finds. It returns true if a task with that id exists. The caller needs to know, in order to print the right message.
  • remove uses retain, which keeps only the tasks for which the condition is true: all tasks whose id is not the one to delete. Comparing the length before and after tells whether something was removed.
  • print only reads, so it takes &self. The format {:>2} prints the id right-aligned in two columns, so that the titles line up.

Each method’s first parameter tells you whether it changes the list. That is useful documentation, and the compiler checks it.

Step 3: the commands

This small enum is the heart of the design. The user types text, which can be anything. A Command can only be one of six well-formed requests. If the program manages to build a Command, the input was valid: Done always has a number, and Add always has a title. The rest of the program never has to check the input again.

Key idea
Make invalid states impossible to represent

This is a guiding idea of Rust design. Check untidy input once, at the edge of the program, and turn it into a precise type. Everything behind that edge works with values that cannot be wrong. People call it “parse, don’t validate”.

Step 4: from text to command

Now the function that sits at that edge. It can fail, so it returns a Result: Ok(command) or Err(message for the user).

Go through it slowly:

  1. split_once(' ') cuts the line at the first space and gives Some((before, after)), or None if there is no space. The match turns both cases into a pair: the command word and the rest of the line.
  2. The second match looks at both parts at once, as a tuple. ("add", "") is “the word add with nothing after it”, an error. ("add", title) is “the word add with anything else after it”. The order matters: the more specific arm comes first.
  3. For done and remove, the rest must be a number. text.parse() returns a Result, and an inner match turns it into a command or an error message. Rust works out that the number must be a u32, because it goes into Command::Done(u32).
  4. The last arm catches every other word and puts it into the error message.

Notice what the function does not do. It does not print anything, and it does not touch the list. It only translates. That makes it easy to understand and, as you will see in chapter 22, easy to test.

Step 5: the main loop

Add use std::io; as the first line of the file.

  • read_line returns the number of bytes it read. Zero means the input has ended (for example, the user pressed Ctrl+D, or Ctrl+Z on Windows), so the loop stops.
  • The match uses nested patterns: Ok(Command::Add(title)) checks that parsing worked, that the command is Add, and takes out the title, all at once.
  • list.add(title) moves the title from the command into the list. The text typed by the user is copied exactly once, in parse.
  • If you add a seventh command to the enum later, this match will not compile until you handle it.

The complete program

Tip
Keep the Debug derive

The finished program no longer prints a task with {:?}. Keep the derive anyway. The moment something goes wrong, a quick dbg!(&list.tasks); shows you what is inside.

The program has three clearly separated layers, and each could be changed without touching the others:

LayerCodeKnows about
Data and rulesTask, TodoList and its methodstasks. Nothing about text commands or the keyboard
TranslationCommand, parsethe command language. Nothing about how tasks are stored
Conversationmain, print_helpreading lines and printing answers

The tasks disappear when the program ends. Saving them to a file is the natural next step, and you will be able to do it after chapter 18, which covers files and errors.

Make it better

PracticeUndo a tick

Add a command undo <number> that marks a finished task as not done.

Need a hint?

You need four small changes: a new variant Undo(u32), a new arm in parse, a new method on TodoList (very similar to mark_done), and a new arm in the match in main. The compiler will remind you of the last one.

Show solution and explanation

The new parts:

In parse, the new arm is ("undo", text) => parse_undo(text), and in main it is:

Instead of a copy of mark_done, the solution has one method set_done(id, done) that covers both directions, and mark_done(id) can now simply call self.set_done(id, true). The three number commands also share the same parsing shape, so a small helper function for it is a good idea. Removing repetition like this is called refactoring: improving the structure of code without changing what it does.

PracticeA summary line

After the list, print a summary such as 2 of 5 done. If all tasks are done, print All done! instead.

Need a hint?

Count in the loop that prints the tasks, with a mut counter, or write a separate method count_done(&self) -> usize.

Show solution and explanation

A separate count_done method keeps print short and can be reused. The check total > 0 avoids announcing “All done!” for an empty list. With iterators (chapter 25) the counting becomes one line: self.tasks.iter().filter(|t| t.done).count().

ChallengePriorities

Give each task a priority: low, normal or high. add creates tasks with normal priority. A new command priority <number> <low|normal|high> changes it. list shows high-priority tasks first, then normal, then low.

Need a hint?

Make an enum Priority and derive Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord. With Ord derived, variants compare in the order they are written, so write High first. Then sort before printing with self.tasks.sort_by_key(|task| task.priority);. The sort keeps tasks with equal priority in their existing order. print must then take &mut self, or you sort a list of references instead.

Show solution and explanation

The central pieces:

The priority is an enum, not a number or a string, so an invalid priority cannot exist inside the program. parse_priority is again the single place where text becomes a precise type. Deriving PartialOrd and Ord makes the variants comparable in the order they are listed, which is all that sort_by_key needs. The solution sorts a separate vector of references to the tasks, so the list itself keeps its order and printing can stay a &self method.

For the command, parse has to split the rest of the line once more: rest.split_once(' ') gives the number and the priority word.

What you have learned

Recap
  • Start with the data: which things exist, what holds them, and what requests are possible.
  • A struct with methods keeps data and the rules for changing it in one place.
  • An enum describes all valid commands. Turning text into that enum once, at the edge, frees the rest of the program from checking input.
  • match on a tuple looks at several values at once. Nested patterns take apart Result and enum in one step.
  • Functions that only translate or only calculate, and do no input or output, are easy to reuse and test.

You have finished Part 3. You can now model real things with your own types and store them in collections. Part 4 is about growing programs: splitting code into modules, handling errors properly, writing code that works for many types, and testing it.

Organising code: packages, crates and modules

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what packages, crates and modules are
  • Group code into modules and control what is visible from outside
  • Refer to items with paths and shorten them with use
  • Split a program into several files
  • Build a library and a program in the same package

Your programs so far lived in one file. That works up to a few hundred lines. After that, you scroll a lot, names start to collide, and it gets hard to see which parts depend on which. Rust has a system for dividing code into named, nested groups, and for deciding which parts of a group the rest of the program is allowed to use.

Real-world analogy
A company with departments

A company puts people into departments: sales, accounting, the workshop. Each department has a front desk that the rest of the company may talk to, and internal procedures that are nobody else’s business. If accounting changes how it files its papers, nobody outside notices, as long as the front desk still answers the same questions. Modules are departments for code.

Three words: package, crate, module

WordWhat it isYou know it as
PackageA folder with a Cargo.toml file. It is what cargo new creates, and what you build, test and sharethe hello_rust folder
CrateOne unit that the compiler translates as a whole. It is either a binary crate (a program with fn main) or a library crate (code for other programs to use)src/main.rs and everything it pulls in
ModuleA named group of items (functions, structs, enums, constants, other modules) inside a cratenew in this chapter

A package contains one or more crates. Most contain one. A crate contains a tree of modules. The file where the compiler starts (src/main.rs for a program, src/lib.rs for a library) is called the crate root.

Modules and privacy

A module is declared with mod. Start with modules written inside one file:

  • mod kitchen { ... } creates a module. Its contents are reached from outside with a path: kitchen::make_pizza.
  • pub (for “public”) makes an item usable from outside its module.
  • prepare_dough has no pub. It is private: only code inside kitchen (and inside modules nested in it) can use it.

Everything in Rust is private unless you write pub. Trying to reach a private item from outside is a compile error:

Key idea
Why private by default?

Whatever is public is a promise: other code may depend on it, so changing it can break that code. Whatever is private can be rewritten freely. By making privacy the default, Rust keeps your promises few and deliberate. The set of public items of a module or crate is called its API (application programming interface): the “front desk” that others talk to.

Privacy for structs and enums

pub on a struct makes the type public. Its fields stay private unless each one is marked pub too. That is how a type protects its own rules:

Code outside bank can read the balance through the method balance(), but it cannot set it. It also cannot build an Account with Account { owner: ..., balance: 1_000_000 }, because that would need access to the private field. The only way in is Account::new. The module is now the single place that decides how a balance can change.

A method that only returns a private field, like balance(), is called a getter. Rust names it after the field, without a get_ in front.

For an enum, pub makes all its variants public. An enum is only useful if you can name its variants, so they are not hidden one by one.

Finer levels of visibility

Written asVisible to
(nothing)the current module and the modules inside it
pubeveryone who can reach the parent module
pub(crate)the whole current crate, but not other crates that use it as a library
pub(super)the parent module

pub(crate) is very useful in libraries: it shares a helper between your own modules without making it part of the promise to the outside world.

Paths: saying where something is

A path names an item by its location in the module tree, with :: between the steps, like / in a file path.

  • crate:: starts at the root of the current crate. It is like a path that begins with /.
  • super:: goes one level up, like .. in a file path.
  • self:: means the current module. It is rarely needed.
  • A path that starts with a plain name is looked up from the current module, as shop::report::print() in main.

Note that the inner modules are declared pub mod. A module is an item like any other, and private unless marked.

use: shorter names

Writing a full path every time is tiring. use brings a name into the current scope, so you can write it without the path:

A few conventions make code easier to read. They are habits, not rules of the language:

  • For types (structs, enums), bring in the type itself: use std::collections::HashMap; and then write HashMap.
  • For functions, bring in the parent module and keep one step of the path: shapes::area_of_square(3.0). The reader sees at once that the function is not defined in this file.
  • use lines go at the top of the file.

More forms of use:

Use the glob form * sparingly. It hides where names come from. It is common in two places: in tests (use super::*;, see chapter 22) and for a library’s prelude, a module that collects the names nearly every user needs.

In plain English
Why String, Vec and Option need no use

Rust automatically brings a small set of names from the standard library into every file. It is called the prelude. It contains String, Vec, Option, Result, Some, None, Ok, Err, Box, and the most common traits. Everything else, such as HashMap, needs a use line.

Re-exporting with pub use

pub use brings a name into a module and at the same time makes it public from there. Library authors use it to offer a simple public structure that differs from the internal file structure:

Modules in separate files

Modules really pay off when each one lives in its own file. The rule is simple:

mod list; (with a semicolon, and no braces) tells the compiler: “the contents of the module list are in another file”. The compiler looks for src/list.rs.

Here is the to-do program from chapter 16, split into three files:

What changed compared with the single file:

  1. main.rs declares the two modules with mod command; and mod list;. Without these lines the compiler would not even look at the other files.
  2. Everything that main.rs uses from the modules got a pub.
  3. Task did not get a pub. Nothing outside list.rs ever names it. It has become an internal detail of the list, and you could change it completely without touching the other files.
Watch out
mod is not import

In Python or JavaScript, every file that needs another file imports it. In Rust, a module is declared with mod name; exactly once, in its parent module (for a top-level module, that is the crate root). Every other place refers to it with a path or use. Writing mod list; in two files would create two different modules.

If command.rs needed something from list.rs, it would write use crate::list::TodoList;.

Modules inside modules

A module can have child modules. Their files go into a folder named after the parent:

The older layout: mod.rs

You will meet projects that use src/shop/mod.rs in place of src/shop.rs. Both mean the same, and both still work. The newer style (shop.rs next to the folder shop/) avoids having many files that are all called mod.rs open in your editor.

A library and a program in one package

A package can contain a library crate (src/lib.rs) and a binary crate (src/main.rs) at once. This is a very common structure for real programs:

The modules now belong to the library. The program in main.rs is a separate crate that uses the library through its name, todo, exactly as it would use a crate from the internet. It can only see what the library made pub.

Why bother?

  • Tests. Code in a library is much easier to test (chapter 22).
  • Reuse. Another program, such as a web version of the to-do list, could use the same library.
  • Discipline. main.rs stays small: read the input, call the library, print the result.

Create a library-only package with cargo new --lib name.

Crates from other people

You already used an external crate in the guessing game. The mechanism is the same module system:

After cargo add rand has written that line into Cargo.toml, the crate’s name is available as the first step of a path: rand::random_range(1..=100). The standard library is also a crate, called std, that is always available. Chapter 39 covers Cargo in depth, and chapter 42 shows how to find and judge crates.

How other languages do it
Module systems in other languages
  • Python and JavaScript: every file is automatically a module, and the files import each other. Rust is different: files become part of the crate only through mod declarations, which form one tree from the crate root.
  • Java and C#: package or namespace lines at the top of each file group classes, and public/private control visibility per class and per member. Rust’s privacy boundary is the module, not the type: all code in the same module can see each other’s private items.
  • C and C++: the public face of a file is written a second time in a header file, which is copied into every file that uses it. Rust needs no headers. The pub keyword in the one and only source file says what is public.
Recap
  • A package is a folder with Cargo.toml. It contains crates. A crate is a tree of modules, starting at the crate root (main.rs or lib.rs).
  • mod name { ... } defines a module in place. mod name; loads it from name.rs.
  • Everything is private by default. pub opens an item to the outside. Struct fields need their own pub.
  • Paths use ::. crate:: starts at the root, and super:: goes up one level.
  • use shortens paths. pub use re-exports a name.
  • A package can hold a library (lib.rs) and a program (main.rs) that uses it.
Check your understanding
1

What is the visibility of a function declared without pub inside a module?

Private is the default. Code in the same module, and in child modules, can use the item. Code outside cannot.

2

A struct is declared pub struct User { name: String } in a module. What can code outside that module do?

pub on the struct makes only the type public. The field has no pub, so it is private. Outside code needs public functions such as User::new and getters.

3

What does the line mod network; in src/main.rs do?

mod name; with a semicolon tells the compiler to load the module from a file with that name.

4

In a module crate::shop::report, what does super::stock::count() refer to?

super is the parent module of the current one. The parent of shop::report is shop, so the path is shop::stock::count.

5

Why would you put most of a program’s code into src/lib.rs and keep src/main.rs small?

A library crate has a clear public API, can be tested directly, and can serve several programs. main.rs then only connects it to the outside world.

Guided exerciseA geometry module

In one file, write a module geometry with two public functions, rectangle_area(w: f64, h: f64) -> f64 and circle_area(r: f64) -> f64, and one private constant PI with the value 3.14159. Call both functions from main. Then try to print geometry::PI from main and read the error.

Need a hint?

Inside the module: const PI: f64 = 3.14159; without pub. The functions inside the module can use PI directly. Call them as geometry::circle_area(1.0).

Show solution and explanation

PI is an internal detail. Printing geometry::PI from main gives error E0603, “constant PI is private”. If the module later switched to the more precise std::f64::consts::PI, no code outside would have to change, because no code outside could ever depend on the private constant.

PracticeRepair the visibility

This program has three visibility mistakes. Fix it by adding pub in the right places, and nothing else. It should print Lena (admin: false).

Need a hint?

main names the type users::User, calls User::new, and reads the field name. Each of the three needs to be public. The field admin does not: it is only read through the method.

Show solution and explanation

The type, the constructor and the name field are part of the public face. The admin field stays private. That is a real protection: no code outside users can turn a user into an administrator by writing user.admin = true.

ChallengeA temperature that is always valid

Write a module thermo with a struct Celsius that can never hold a temperature below absolute zero (−273.15 °C).

  • Celsius::new(value: f64) -> Option<Celsius> returns None for impossible values.
  • value(&self) -> f64 returns the number.
  • to_fahrenheit(&self) -> f64 converts it (multiply by 9/5 and add 32).

Make sure that code outside the module cannot create an invalid Celsius in any way.

Need a hint?

Use a tuple struct with a private field: pub struct Celsius(f64);. Because the field is private, thermo::Celsius(-500.0) does not compile outside the module, and new is the only way to get a value.

Show solution and explanation

This combines three ideas: the newtype pattern from chapter 12, Option for a constructor that can refuse, and a private field. Together they give a guarantee: if a Celsius exists, it is valid. Every function that receives a Celsius can rely on that and needs no check of its own. The condition value >= ABSOLUTE_ZERO also rejects the special float value NaN, because every comparison with NaN is false.
