18

Error handling

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Tell apart errors a program should recover from and bugs that should stop it
  • Return, handle and pass on errors with Result and the ? operator
  • Read and write files
  • Define your own error type
  • Choose between panic!, Option and Result, and compare anyhow, thiserror, eyre and miette

Things go wrong. A file is missing, the user types letters where a number belongs, the network is down. A good program expects this and reacts sensibly. Rust takes an unusual and very deliberate approach: errors are ordinary values that functions return, and the compiler makes sure you do not ignore them.

Two kinds of problems

Real-world analogy
A restaurant

A guest orders a dish that is sold out. That is a normal situation: the waiter says so, and the guest picks something else. Now imagine the kitchen is on fire. Nobody carries on taking orders. Everything stops.

Rust separates these two cases:

Recoverable errorUnrecoverable error
Examplefile not found, invalid input, no networkan index outside a list, a broken assumption: a bug
Whose fault?the outside worldthe programmer
Toolreturn a Resultpanic!
What happensthe caller decides what to dothe program (or the current thread) stops

panic!: stop, something is badly wrong

A panic prints a message with the file and line, cleans up (the values on the stack are dropped in order), and ends the program. You can cause one yourself with the panic! macro:

When a panic comes from deep inside a program, set the environment variable RUST_BACKTRACE=1 when running (RUST_BACKTRACE=1 cargo run). Rust then prints the backtrace: the chain of function calls that led to the panic.

Other macros that panic, useful while a program is under construction:

  • todo!() marks code you have not written yet. The program compiles, and panics if it reaches that point.
  • unreachable!() marks a place that, by your reasoning, can never be reached.
  • assert!(condition) panics if the condition is false. You will use it a lot in tests.

Result: an error as a value

A function that can fail in a normal way returns Result<T, E>: either Ok(value) with a value of type T, or Err(error) with an error of type E.

fs::read_to_string reads a whole file into a String. Its return type is Result<String, std::io::Error>. The file does not exist here, so the result is the Err variant, and the program goes on in an orderly way. (On Windows the text of the message is a little different.)

The compiler helps in two ways. You cannot use the String without dealing with the Result first, exactly as with Option. And if you call a function that returns a Result and throw the result away, you get a warning:

Shortcuts for handling a Result

.unwrap() and .expect("message") exist for Result too. They return the Ok value or panic with the error. In other words, they turn a recoverable error into a crash:

Passing errors on: the ? operator

Very often a function cannot deal with an error itself. The right thing to do is to stop and hand the error to its caller, which may know better what to do. Written out with match, that looks like this:

This pattern is so common that Rust has an operator for it, a single question mark:

Key idea
What ? does

Put ? after an expression of type Result:

  • If it is Ok(value), the ? unwraps it. The expression becomes value, and the function carries on.
  • If it is Err(error), the function returns that error to its caller at once.

Read ? as “…or else give up and report the error”.

? makes the normal path of a function read from top to bottom without interruptions, and the error path is still visible: every place that can fail carries a ?. You can chain it:

? only works in a function whose return type can carry the error. Using it in a function that returns nothing is an error:

The compiler suggests the usual fix: let main itself return a Result.

If main returns an Err, Rust prints the error and the program ends with an exit code that is not zero. The exit code is a number that a program hands back to whatever started it. Zero means “all went well”, and anything else means “something failed”. Other programs and scripts rely on it.

? also works on Option in a function that returns an Option: a None is returned at once.

Working with files

You now have the tools to use files properly. The module std::fs has functions for the common cases, and all of them return a Result:

For big files, or to add to the end of a file, you open the file and work with it piece by piece:

  • File::create and File::open give a File. It is closed automatically when the variable goes out of scope. This is ownership at work again: you cannot forget to close a file.
  • BufReader wraps a file and reads it in large chunks, which is much faster than asking the operating system for every small piece. “Buf” is short for buffer, a temporary storage area.
  • use std::io::Write and use std::io::BufRead bring in the methods writeln! relies on and the .lines() method. They are traits, the topic of chapter 20.

Your own error type

count_lines could only fail in one way, so io::Error was a fine error type. Real functions can fail in several ways. Take a function that reads a volume setting, a number from 0 to 100, from a file. The file may be missing, the content may not be a number, or the number may be too big.

A function has exactly one error type, so you define one that covers all cases. An enum is the natural fit:

There is a fair amount of new syntax here. Take it as a recipe for now. The blocks that begin with impl … for ConfigError are trait implementations, which the next chapters explain. What each part is for:

  1. The enum lists everything that can go wrong. Callers can match on it and react differently to each case.
  2. Display gives the text for people. It is what {} prints.
  3. Error marks the type as an error.
  4. From teaches ? a conversion. When a function returns Result<_, ConfigError> and a ? meets an io::Error, Rust calls ConfigError::from(error) automatically. That is why the two ? lines in read_volume work although the functions they call return different error types.

Less typing with thiserror

Steps 2 to 4 are routine, and the popular crate thiserror writes them for you. This is the same error type:

The #[error("…")] attribute gives the text for Display, and #[from] creates the From conversion. Add the crate with cargo add thiserror.

When you do not care which error it was

A program (as opposed to a library) often does not need to tell errors apart. It only wants to report them and stop. For that there is a type that can hold any error: Box<dyn Error>.

Read Box<dyn Error> as “some error, I do not say which”. ? converts every error type into it, and even a plain text becomes an error with .into(). (Chapter 27 explains Box and dyn.) The price is that the caller can no longer easily match on the kind of error.

The crate anyhow is a more comfortable version of the same idea, and is what most applications use. It adds context, which attaches a description of what the program was trying to do:

anyhow::Result<T> is short for Result<T, anyhow::Error>. bail! returns an error built from a message. The output shows the chain: what the program tried to do, and the underlying cause.

Rich reports for applications: eyre and miette

anyhow is enough for most applications. Two related crates solve slightly different problems.

eyre is anyhow’s close sibling. It adds WrapErr, which attaches context while keeping the cause, and it works with color-eyre: a hook that prints coloured error reports with source locations, much like a compiler error message. An application or CLI tool that uses eyre shows the user what went wrong, without you writing formatting code.

miette is different. An error can carry a diagnostic: a severity, a help text, a link, and even a snippet of the offending source with the offending part underlined. miette is the choice for developer tools — linters, code generators, compilers — whose users appreciate compiler-style reports.

eyre in an application. wrap_err adds context; wrap_err_with builds the context lazily, only when there is an error. The program below is written deliberately without a settings.toml, so that you can see what the user would see:

Nothing in main formats an error: returning Err from main makes the runtime print the report, context first, and exit with a non-zero code. That is why an application’s main returns Result and almost never calls unwrap.

color-eyre installs itself once, at the start of main:

After that, every error and every panic prints in colour, with the file and line where it happened. Pick one application-report ecosystem for a program and stay in it; converting between anyhow, eyre and Box<dyn Error> at every layer adds code and loses causes.

miette in a library. The #[derive(Diagnostic)] attribute turns an error into a diagnostic:

With miette’s own report handler the same error also prints its help line and its error code; the handler is what gives you compiler-style reports, including source snippets when you add #[label] spans.

Best forWhat it adds
thiserrorlibrariesprecise error enums callers can match on
anyhowapplicationsone error type, context and bail!
eyreapplications, especially CLIscoloured reports and source locations via color-eyre
miettedeveloper toolscompiler-style diagnostics: codes, help text, source snippets
How other languages do it
Which error crate today?
  • Writing a library: thiserror, so callers can react to each case.
  • Writing an application: anyhow, quick context for every error.
  • Writing a CLI tool that people run: eyre; add color-eyre for coloured reports.
  • Writing a tool that parses or generates code or config: miette.

The chain of causes: source

Where does anyhow get the “Caused by” lines from? Every error type can name the error that led to it, through the method source of the Error trait. The standard answer is “none”. An error that wraps another one overrides the method:

Read Option<&(dyn Error + 'static)> as “perhaps a reference to some other error”. The loop in report follows the chain from the error the user sees down to the first cause. Each level says one thing: what it was trying to do.

You rarely write source by hand:

  • With thiserror, a field marked #[from] or #[source] becomes the source. (#[source] does the same as #[from] without creating the From conversion.)
  • With anyhow, every .context(…) adds a level on top of the chain. Printing an anyhow::Error with {} shows the top level only, {:#} shows all levels on one line, and {:?} shows the “Caused by” list from above.
Watch out
Say each thing once

There are two styles. Either the message of an error includes the message of its cause, as ConfigError does above with {e}: good when errors are printed with {} and nothing else. Or the message describes its own level only, and the cause is found through source, as in SettingError: good when the report walks the chain. Choose one style for a program. If you mix them, a chain report prints every cause twice.

Tip
The usual division of labour
  • In a library: define precise error enums (with thiserror), so that users of the library can react to each case.
  • In an application: use anyhow (or Box<dyn Error>) and add context, so that the person in front of the program gets a helpful message.

Which tool when?

SituationUse
A value may be absent, and that is normal (search found nothing)Option<T>
An operation can fail, and the caller should be able to react (file, network, user input)Result<T, E>
The situation “cannot happen” unless the code has a bugpanic!, unreachable!, expect("why this cannot fail")
Quick experiments, examples and testsunwrap() and expect() are fine

A useful habit: when you write expect, let the message say why you believe it cannot fail, for example .expect("the pattern is a valid regular expression"). Whoever sees the panic later learns which assumption was wrong.

Watch out
Do not hide errors

Avoid patterns that throw an error away without a decision: let _ = risky();, .ok(); or .unwrap_or_default() used only to make the compiler quiet. If ignoring an error is truly right, write a comment that says why.

How other languages do it
Errors in other languages
  • Exceptions (Java, Python, C#, JavaScript, C++): a function “throws” an error, and it travels up through the callers until some try/catch block catches it. Any call may throw, and usually nothing in the code or the types shows it. Errors that nobody thought of are common. In Rust, the possibility of failure is part of the function’s type, and every place where an error can leave a function is marked with a visible ?.
  • Error codes (C): a function returns a special number such as -1, and the caller is supposed to check it. Nothing forces the check, and forgetting it is a classic source of bugs.
  • Go: functions return a value and an error side by side, and nearly every call is followed by if err != nil { return err }. Rust’s ? does the same in one character, and the compiler will not let you use the value without looking at the error.
Recap
  • Bugs and impossible situations: panic!. Expected failures: return a Result.
  • Result<T, E> is Ok(value) or Err(error). Handle it with match, if let, unwrap_or, or pass it on.
  • ? unwraps an Ok or returns the Err to the caller. The function must return a Result (or Option) itself. main may return a Result.
  • std::fs reads and writes files. Every operation returns a Result.
  • A custom error enum lists the ways a function can fail. Display gives the message, and From lets ? convert other errors into it. thiserror generates this code.
  • Box<dyn Error> and anyhow hold any error, which is convenient in applications.
  • eyre is another flexible application report with customizable handlers; miette is useful when a command-line user benefits from structured diagnostics and source snippets.
Check your understanding
1

What does the ? operator do when the value before it is an Err?

? unwraps an Ok, and on an Err it returns early with that error, converting it with From if needed.

2

Which of these situations calls for a Result and not a panic?

A missing file is a normal event that the program should handle. The other three are bugs: the code is wrong, and stopping is the honest reaction.

3

Why does this not compile?

? may return an error from the function, so the function’s return type must be able to hold one. Declare fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> and end with Ok(()).

4

What is the job of impl From<io::Error> for MyError?

? calls From::from on the error before returning it. With this implementation, a function returning Result<_, MyError> can use ? on I/O operations.

5

You are writing a library that other programmers will use. Which error style suits it best?

A library should not decide for its users how to react. A precise error type gives them all the information and leaves the decision to them.

Guided exerciseAdd the numbers in a text

Write sum_of(text: &str) -> Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> that takes numbers separated by commas, such as "4, 8, 15", and returns their sum. If any part is not a number, it returns the error. Use ?.

Need a hint?

Loop over text.split(','). For each part, part.trim().parse::<i32>()? gives the number or leaves the function with the error.

Show solution and explanation

The ? ends the loop and the function at the first part that is not a number. The success value must be wrapped: the last line is Ok(total), not total, because the function returns a Result.

PracticeA withdrawal that explains itself

In chapter 12, withdraw returned a bool. Improve it. Define an enum WithdrawError with two variants: ZeroAmount and InsufficientFunds { missing: u64 }. Change withdraw to return Result<u64, WithdrawError>, where the Ok value is the new balance. In main, print a suitable sentence for each case.

Need a hint?

Check amount == 0 first, then amount > self.balance. The missing sum is amount - self.balance. In main, use a match with three arms: Ok(balance), Err(WithdrawError::ZeroAmount) and Err(WithdrawError::InsufficientFunds { missing }).

Show solution and explanation

A bool could only say “no”. The error enum says why, and carries data (how much is missing) that the caller can show to the user. Because the caller matches on an enum, adding a third kind of failure later makes the compiler point at every place that has to handle it.

ChallengeSave and load the to-do list

Write two functions for the to-do list of chapter 16:

  • save(path: &str, tasks: &[Task]) -> Result<(), io::Error> writes one task per line in the form 1|buy milk (1 for done, 0 for open, then the title).
  • load(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Task>, Box<dyn Error>> reads such a file. A line without |, or with something other than 0 or 1 in front, is an error.

Use a simplified Task with just title and done.

Need a hint?

For saving, build a String with format! and push_str, then fs::write it. For loading, go through text.lines(), split each with line.split_once('|'), and turn a None into an error with .ok_or("message")?. ok_or converts an Option into a Result.

Show solution and explanation

save ends with fs::write(path, text) without ? or Ok: the call already returns exactly the Result<(), io::Error> that the function must return. In load, three different kinds of problem (an I/O error, a missing separator, a bad flag) all travel through the same Box<dyn Error>. ok_or is the bridge from Option to Result that lets ? work on the result of split_once.

The format breaks if a title contains a line break. Real programs use a standard format such as JSON for this, with the serde crate (chapter 43).

Generics: code that works for many types

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Remove duplicated code by writing a function once for many types
  • Define generic structs, enums and methods
  • Read and write the <T> notation with confidence
  • Explain why generic code in Rust is as fast as hand-written code

You have been using generic types for a while: Vec<i32>, Option<String>, Result<u32, io::Error>, HashMap<String, u32>. The part in angle brackets says what the type holds. One Vec implementation works for every element type. In this chapter you learn to write such code yourself.

The problem: the same code twice

Here is a function that finds the largest number in a list:

It works for i32. For a list of f64 you would copy the function and change two words. For char you would copy it again. Three copies of the same logic mean three places to fix when you find a bug.

Real-world analogy
A recipe with a blank

A recipe for jam says “take 1 kg of fruit and 500 g of sugar”. It does not say which fruit. The steps are the same for strawberries, apricots and plums. “Fruit” is a blank that you fill in when you cook. A generic function is a recipe with such a blank for a type.

A generic function

Read the first line piece by piece:

  • <T> after the function name declares a type parameter: a blank called T. Any name works, but single capital letters are the convention, and T (for “type”) is the usual first choice.
  • list: &[T] says the parameter is a slice of that type, whatever it is.
  • -> T says the function returns a value of that same type.
  • T: PartialOrd + Copy restricts the blank. It is explained next.

When you call largest(&[3, 9, 4]), the compiler sees a slice of i32 and fills in T = i32 by itself.

Why the restriction is needed

Without : PartialOrd + Copy, the function does not compile:

T could be any type, and not every type can be compared with >. What would it mean for one HashMap to be greater than another? Inside a generic function, Rust only lets you do what is certain to work for every allowed type.

So you narrow down the allowed types. T: PartialOrd means “T can be any type that supports comparison with < and >”. PartialOrd is a trait, a named ability, and such a restriction is called a trait bound. + Copy adds a second requirement: values of the type can be copied, which the line let mut largest = list[0]; needs. Traits are the subject of the next chapter. Generics and traits belong together: generics say “any type”, and traits say “…that can do this”.

Tip
A more flexible version

Requiring Copy excludes String. Returning a reference avoids that: fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T. It needs no copying, so it works for any comparable type. One of the exercises asks you to write it.

Generic structs

Point<T> uses the same T for both fields, so Point { x: 5, y: 1.5 } is an error: the two fields would have different types. Labelled<T, U> has two independent blanks.

Methods on generic types

  • impl<T> Point<T> reads: “for every type T, these are methods of Point<T>”. The <T> after impl declares the blank, and the <T> after Point uses it.
  • impl Point<f64> has no blank. Its methods exist only for that one concrete type.

Generic enums

You know the two most important ones. This is how the standard library defines them:

Nothing about them is built into the language. You could have written them yourself.

Telling the compiler which type you mean

Usually the compiler works out the type parameters from the arguments. When it cannot, you say it explicitly. There are two ways:

The form ::<Type> is nicknamed the turbofish, because ::<> looks a little like a fish. It is handy in the middle of a chain of method calls, where there is no variable to annotate.

Generics cost nothing at run time

When you call largest with i32, with f64 and with char, the compiler generates three separate versions of the function, each made for one type, exactly as if you had written largest_i32, largest_f64 and largest_char by hand. This process is called monomorphization (roughly: “making into single forms”).

The result: generic code runs exactly as fast as code written for one specific type. You pay nothing when the program runs. The price is paid at compile time (more code to generate) and in the size of the finished program.

How other languages do it
Generics in other languages
  • Java and C#: also have generics with <T>. Java removes the type information when compiling (“type erasure”) and stores everything as general objects, which costs some speed and memory for simple types like numbers.
  • C++: templates work much like Rust’s generics and are also monomorphized. A C++ template is only checked when it is used with a concrete type, which can give very long error messages. Rust checks a generic function once, against its trait bounds, and reports problems at the definition.
  • Go: added generics in version 1.18 (2022), after ten years without them.
  • Python and JavaScript: have no need for generics at run time, because any variable can hold any type. The type checkers for these languages (mypy, TypeScript) have generics for the same reason as Rust: to describe “the same type in, the same type out”.

Const generics: a number as a parameter

A type parameter stands for a type. A const generic parameter stands for a value that is known at compile time. Its main use is the length of arrays:

[i32; 3] and [i32; 4] are different types. With const N: usize, one function covers arrays of every length. A Grid<3, 2> and a Grid<8, 8> are different types too, so the compiler can check that you do not mix up grids of different sizes.

Recap
  • A type parameter <T> is a blank that stands for a type. It is filled in when the generic item is used.
  • Functions, structs, enums and impl blocks can be generic.
  • A trait bound such as T: PartialOrd limits the blank to types with a certain ability, and allows you to use that ability inside.
  • The compiler usually infers the types. If not, annotate the variable or use the turbofish ::<T>.
  • Monomorphization creates one specialised copy per type used, so generics have no run-time cost.
  • const N: usize makes a value, such as an array length, a parameter.
Check your understanding
1

What does the <T> in fn first<T>(list: &[T]) -> &T declare?

T stands for a type. Each call of first fills it in, for example with i32 or String.

2

Why does this function not compile?

Without a bound, T could be any type, and the compiler only allows operations that every type has. The bound T: std::ops::Add<Output = T> + Copy would make it work.

3

What is monomorphization?

The compiler turns one generic definition into several concrete ones, so the running program has no extra work to do.

4

Which line uses the turbofish correctly?

The type goes after :: and inside angle brackets, between the function name and the parentheses.

Guided exerciseA pair that can swap

Define a generic struct Pair<T> with the fields first and second, both of type T. Give it a method swap(self) -> Pair<T> that returns a new pair with the two values exchanged. Test it with numbers and with strings.

Need a hint?

The method header is fn swap(self) -> Pair<T> inside impl<T> Pair<T>. It takes self by value, so it can move the fields into the new pair without copying.

Show solution and explanation

swap needs no trait bound: moving a value is possible for every type. Because the method takes self, the old pair is used up and its fields move into the new one. Even for Strings, no text is copied.

PracticeLargest without copying

Write largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T that returns a reference to the largest element, so that it also works for String. Test it with a vector of Strings.

Need a hint?

Start with let mut largest = &list[0]; and loop with for item in list. Both item and largest are &T, and references can be compared with > when T can.

Show solution and explanation

Comparing two references compares the values they point to. Strings are compared alphabetically, so “Tomas” is the largest. This version asks less of T (only PartialOrd) and is therefore usable with more types. As a rule, ask for as few abilities as the function really needs.

The function panics on an empty list, because of list[0]. Returning Option<&T> would be the more careful design.

ChallengeA generic stack

Build a struct Stack<T> that wraps a Vec<T> and offers only these operations: new(), push(&mut self, item: T), pop(&mut self) -> Option<T>, peek(&self) -> Option<&T> (look at the top element without removing it), len(&self) and is_empty(&self). Test it with numbers and with strings.

Need a hint?

The struct is struct Stack<T> { items: Vec<T> }. Every method passes its work on to the vector: self.items.push(item), self.items.pop(), self.items.last().

Show solution and explanation

A stack is a pile: you add to the top and take from the top. The wrapper offers less than a Vec, on purpose. Users of Stack cannot insert in the middle or sort it, so the “last in, first out” rule always holds. For numbers, the compiler works out T = i32 from the first push. The types in the signatures follow ownership: pop hands out the value itself, and peek only lends it.

Traits: shared behaviour

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Define a trait and implement it for your own types
  • Write functions that accept any type with a certain ability
  • Use the standard traits (Debug, Display, Clone, PartialEq, Ord, Default, From)
  • Store values of different types together with dyn Trait
  • Explain how traits replace inheritance

A struct describes what a value is. A trait describes what a value can do. Traits are how Rust expresses “these different types share an ability”, and they are behind much of what you have used so far: printing with {}, comparing with ==, cloning, and the bounds on generic functions.

Real-world analogy
A job description

“Driver: can start, steer and stop a vehicle.” The description says nothing about who the driver is: young or old, employee or freelancer. Anyone who has these skills can do the job, and whoever hires a driver can rely on the skills without knowing the person. A trait is a job description for types.

Defining and implementing a trait

  • trait Describe { ... } defines the trait. Inside is a method signature: name, parameters and return type, ending with a semicolon and without a body. It says what a type must be able to do, not how.
  • impl Describe for Dog { ... } implements the trait for a type: it supplies the body. The compiler checks that every required method is there and that the signatures match.

A dog and a car have nothing else in common. They now share one ability.

Default methods

A trait can supply a body. Types then get the method for free, and may replace it with their own version:

The default greet calls name, which has no default. This is a common design: a trait asks for one or two small methods and builds many useful ones on top. The standard Iterator trait asks for a single method, next, and gives you more than seventy others in return.

Traits as parameters

Now the payoff. A function can accept any type that implements a trait:

&impl Describe reads “a reference to some type that implements Describe”. It is a short way of writing a generic function with a trait bound. These three signatures mean the same:

  • The impl Trait form is the shortest. Use it for simple cases.
  • The <T: Trait> form gives the type a name. You need it when two parameters must have the same type: fn pair<T: Describe>(a: &T, b: &T).
  • The where form moves the bounds below the signature. It keeps signatures readable when there are several parameters with several bounds.

Several bounds are joined with +:

Returning impl Trait

A function can also promise “I return some type that implements this trait” without naming the type:

The real type returned here is long and awkward to write. The caller only needs to know that it can be iterated. You will use this form a lot with iterators and closures in Part 5.

What the returned type is allowed to borrow: use<…>

An impl Trait return type is an opaque type, and an opaque type has to say which lifetimes it depends on. Since the 2024 edition the rule is the simple one: the hidden type may capture every lifetime in scope. Before 2024 it captured only the ones it obviously needed, which caused the opposite problem — a returned iterator that did borrow something failed to compile until you added a lifetime nobody could see in the signature.

The new rule is easier to explain and occasionally too generous: capturing a lifetime ties the returned value to a borrow it does not really need. When that happens, say precisely what the return type captures with a use<…> list — an empty use<> means “captures nothing”:

Without use<>, edition 2024 would make the return type depend on the borrow of words, and the program above would not compile: printer would be carrying a lifetime that ended with the block. The error would point at the block, not at the closure, which is why this rule surprises people who upgraded a working 2021 project.

Two rules of thumb:

  • You rarely need to write use<…>. Write it when the compiler complains that a value is borrowed for too long, or when you are returning a closure or iterator that obviously owns everything it uses.
  • List what the type really needs. use<'a> for one lifetime, use<'a, T> when a generic type parameter is also involved. In edition 2024 all type parameters are captured by default, so a use<…> list must mention every type parameter the hidden type uses — the compiler checks this and tells you which one is missing.

The standard traits you meet every day

The standard library defines traits for the common abilities. Many can be derived, as you saw in chapter 12.

TraitAbilityHow you get it
Debugprinting with {:?} for programmers#[derive(Debug)]
Displayprinting with {} for userswrite it yourself
Clonean explicit copy with .clone()derive
Copyimplicit copies instead of movesderive (only if all fields are Copy)
PartialEq, Eq== and !=derive
PartialOrd, Ord<, >, sortingderive (compares field by field, in order)
Hashusable as a key in HashMap and HashSetderive
Defaulta sensible starting value with Type::default()derive or write
From, Intoconversion from another typewrite
Dropcode that runs when the value is destroyedwrite (rarely needed)
Why are there PartialEq and Eq, PartialOrd and Ord?

The “partial” versions allow that some values cannot be compared. The floating-point value NaN (“not a number”) is not equal to anything, not even to itself, and is neither smaller nor larger than any number. So f64 has PartialEq and PartialOrd, but not Eq and Ord. That is the reason a float cannot be a HashMap key, and why sorting floats needs an extra word: v.sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b)).

For your own types: derive all four if every field supports them, and leave out Eq and Ord if a field is a float.

Display: your type in {}

The method fmt receives a “formatter” and writes into it with write!, which works like println! but sends the text to its first argument. Every type with Display gets the method to_string() automatically.

Comparing and sorting

The derived ordering compares the fields from top to bottom: first major, and only if those are equal, minor, and so on. So the order in which you write the fields matters.

Default

..Default::default() fills in “everything I did not mention” from the default value. It is a common way to build a struct with many optional settings.

From and Into: conversions

From defines how to create a type from another type. You have used it from the start: String::from("hello").

When you implement From<A> for B, you get Into<B> for A automatically, so a.into() works wherever the target type is clear. From is also what the ? operator uses to convert errors, as you saw in chapter 18. For conversions that can fail, there are TryFrom and TryInto, which return a Result:

Who may implement what

You can implement:

  • your trait for any type, including types that are not yours, such as i32 or Vec<String>,
  • any trait for your type.

You cannot implement someone else’s trait for someone else’s type. impl Display for Vec<String> is refused, because both Display and Vec belong to the standard library. This is called the orphan rule. It makes sure that two crates can never supply conflicting implementations for the same combination. The usual way around it is a newtype: wrap the foreign type in your own struct, and implement the trait for that.

Adding a method to an existing type with your own trait looks like this:

A trait used this way is called an extension trait. The methods are only available where the trait is in scope. That explains a compiler message you will see sooner or later: “method not found … the trait X is implemented but not in scope”. The cure is the use line that the compiler suggests.

A list of different types: trait objects

Generic code is compiled separately for each concrete type. That fails for one task: a single collection holding different types. A Vec<T> has one element type.

  • dyn Shape means “a value of some type that implements Shape, and which type is only known while the program runs”. Such a value is called a trait object.
  • Different shapes have different sizes, so they cannot sit directly in a vector. Box::new(value) puts each value on the heap and keeps a pointer to it. All the pointers have the same size. Chapter 27 covers Box in detail.
  • When shape.area() is called, the program looks up at run time which area belongs to this value. This is called dynamic dispatch. Generic code decides at compile time (static dispatch).
Generics (impl Trait, <T: Trait>)Trait objects (dyn Trait)
The concrete type is knownat compile timeat run time
Different types in one collectionnoyes
Speedfastest. Calls can be fully optimiseda small cost per call (one lookup)
Program sizeone copy of the code per typeone copy in total

Use generics by default, and dyn Trait when you need to mix types in one place.

Tip
Enum or trait object?

In chapter 13 you put different shapes into one Vec with an enum. When should you use which?

  • An enum, when you know all the variants and the list is closed. Adding a new operation is easy: write one more function with a match.
  • A trait, when others should be able to add new types later, without changing your code.

Traits in place of inheritance

How other languages do it
Traits, interfaces and inheritance
  • Java, C#, Go, TypeScript interfaces are the closest relatives of traits. Three differences: a Rust trait can be implemented for a type after the fact, even for a type from another library. Traits can have default methods and associated constants and types. And with generics, a trait is resolved at compile time, at no run-time cost.
  • Class inheritance (“a Dog is an Animal and gets all its fields and methods”) does not exist in Rust. Deep hierarchies of classes tend to become rigid: a change at the top affects everything below, and a class is forced into exactly one family tree. Rust follows the advice that many object-oriented programmers arrived at themselves: prefer composition over inheritance. Shared behaviour comes from traits, and shared data comes from putting one struct inside another.
  • Python and JavaScript use “duck typing”: if an object has a method describe, you can call it, and if not, the program fails at run time. A trait bound checks the same thing at compile time.
  • Haskell’s type classes are the direct ancestor of Rust’s traits.

A trait can require another trait. Every type that implements Named below must also implement Display:

Display is called a supertrait of Named. This is the nearest thing Rust has to inheritance, and it applies to abilities only, never to data.

Recap
  • A trait is a named set of methods that types can implement. It describes an ability.
  • impl Trait for Type supplies the methods. Traits can provide default methods.
  • &impl Trait or <T: Trait> lets a function accept every type with that ability. -> impl Trait returns one.
  • Common standard traits: Debug, Display, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Default, From/Into.
  • The orphan rule: the trait or the type must be yours.
  • Box<dyn Trait> holds a value whose concrete type is decided at run time. It allows mixed collections.
  • Rust has no inheritance. Share behaviour with traits and data with composition.
Check your understanding
1

What does a trait definition contain?

A trait describes behaviour: method signatures, some of which may come with a default implementation. It never contains fields.

2

What does the parameter item: &impl Summary accept?

impl Trait in a parameter is shorthand for a generic type parameter with that trait bound.

3

You wrote impl From<Meters> for Feet. What else do you get?

The standard library implements Into<B> for A automatically for every From<A> for B. The reverse conversion needs its own impl.

4

Why is impl std::fmt::Display for Vec<i32> not allowed in your crate?

At least one of the two must be local. Otherwise two crates could implement the same trait for the same type differently. Wrap the vector in your own struct to get around it.

5

When do you need Box<dyn Shape> and not a generic T: Shape?

A Vec<T> holds one type. Trait objects let each element be a different concrete type, at the cost of a run-time lookup per call.

Guided exerciseThings with an area

Define a trait HasArea with one method area(&self) -> f64. Implement it for Square { side: f64 } and Triangle { base: f64, height: f64 }. Write a generic function print_area that accepts anything with HasArea.

Need a hint?

The area of a triangle is 0.5 * base * height. The function can be written as fn print_area(shape: &impl HasArea).

Show solution and explanation

print_area knows nothing about squares or triangles. It relies on one promise: the value has an area method. A new shape written next year works with it unchanged, as soon as it implements the trait.

PracticeDisplay for a point

Implement Display for struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 } so that println!("{p}") prints (3, -7). Then use to_string() to check that the text has 7 characters.

Need a hint?

Copy the shape of the Money example: impl fmt::Display for Point with fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result, and inside it write!(f, "({}, {})", self.x, self.y).

Show solution and explanation

write! returns a fmt::Result, which is exactly what fmt must return, so it is the last expression without a semicolon. Debug is for programmers and can be derived. Display is for users, so Rust asks you to decide yourself how the value should look.

PracticeA zoo of sounds

Define a trait Animal with the methods name(&self) -> String and sound(&self) -> String, and a default method speak(&self) -> String that returns, for example, Rex says woof. Implement it for Dog and Cat, put two dogs and a cat into one Vec, and let each one speak.

Need a hint?

The vector’s type is Vec<Box<dyn Animal>>, and each element is created with Box::new(...).

Show solution and explanation

speak is written once, in the trait, and works for every animal, because it only uses the two required methods. The vector holds boxes of dyn Animal, so a Dog and a Cat can sit side by side, and the right name and sound are found at run time.

ChallengeSort people your way

Define struct Person { name: String, age: u32 } and derive what is needed so that a Vec<Person> can be sorted with .sort(), by age first and then by name. Then sort the same list by name only, using sort_by.

Need a hint?

Derived ordering compares fields from top to bottom, so declare age before name. You need PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord. For the second sort: people.sort_by(|a, b| a.name.cmp(&b.name));.

Show solution and explanation

The derived Ord gives the type one “natural” order, which sort() uses. For any other order, sort_by takes a small function that compares two elements. cmp returns an Ordering: Less, Equal or Greater. A shorter form for sorting by one field is people.sort_by_key(|p| p.age).

Lifetimes: how long references stay valid

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what a lifetime is and why the compiler tracks it
  • Read and write lifetime annotations such as 'a
  • Know when annotations are needed and when the compiler fills them in
  • Put references into structs
  • Recognise 'static and avoid misusing it

In chapter 10 you learned the rule that a reference must never outlive the value it points to. The compiler checks this rule by working out, for every reference, the stretch of code in which it is valid. That stretch is the reference’s lifetime.

Most of the time you never see lifetimes: the compiler works them out silently. Occasionally a function or struct is ambiguous, and the compiler asks you to describe how the references relate to each other. That description is a lifetime annotation. It is the part of Rust with the most unfamiliar syntax, but the idea behind it is simple.

Real-world analogy
A library book

You borrow a book from a library. You may lend it to a friend for a while, but your friend must give it back before your own loan ends. A loan that hangs on another loan cannot last longer than the original one. Lifetimes are the due dates, and the compiler is a librarian who checks all of them before anybody leaves the building.

What the borrow checker checks

The comments draw the two lifetimes. r is used on the println! line, so the reference must be valid until there. But it points to x, and x is gone at the closing brace of the inner block. The value lives for a shorter time than the reference to it, so the compiler refuses.

Without this check, r would point to memory that no longer belongs to x: a dangling reference.

The function the compiler cannot work out alone

Here is a function that returns the longer of two string slices:

The body is fine. The problem is the signature. The function returns a reference, and the compiler needs to know how long that reference will be valid, in order to check the code that calls the function. It could point to the data of a or to the data of b. Which one depends on the lengths, which are only known when the program runs.

The compiler checks each function by its signature alone, without looking into the bodies of the functions it calls. So the signature has to say how the returned reference relates to the parameters.

Lifetime annotations

  • 'a is a lifetime parameter. The name starts with an apostrophe and is, by convention, a short lower-case word. It is declared in angle brackets after the function name, like a type parameter.
  • &'a str is “a string slice that is valid for at least the lifetime 'a”.

The signature now says: there is some stretch of code 'a during which both a and b are valid, and the returned reference is valid for that same stretch. In practice: the result must not be used after either of the two inputs has gone away.

Key idea
Annotations describe. They do not change anything

A lifetime annotation never makes a value live longer or shorter. It is a statement about a relationship between references, which the compiler then checks on both sides: inside the function (“does the body really return something that lives that long?”) and at each call (“is the result used only while the inputs are still alive?”).

Watch the compiler use that statement:

You can see that the result will be first, which is still alive. The compiler does not run the program. It goes by the signature, which says the result may point into either argument, and second is gone before the println!. This is the safe side to err on: change the texts so that second is the longer one, and the same code really would read freed memory.

Only tie together what belongs together

If the result always comes from one particular parameter, give only that one the lifetime:

The result is tied to text only. The compiler now knows that it does not matter how long separator lives.

You cannot return a reference to something the function made

No annotation can fix this. greeting is destroyed when the function ends, so every reference to it would dangle. The answer is to return the value itself, and with it the ownership: fn make_greeting(name: &str) -> String.

Tip
A rule of thumb for return types

A function can return a reference only if it points to something that came in through a parameter (or to something that lives for the whole program). Data that is created inside the function must be returned as an owned value.

Why you rarely write annotations: elision

fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str from chapter 11 returns a reference and needed no annotation. The compiler applies three simple rules to fill in lifetimes by itself. This is called lifetime elision (“elision” means leaving something out).

  1. Every reference parameter gets its own lifetime.
  2. If there is exactly one reference parameter, its lifetime is given to all references in the return type.
  3. If one of the parameters is &self or &mut self, the lifetime of self is given to all references in the return type.

If references in the return type are still without a lifetime after these rules, the compiler asks you to write them. That is error E0106.

SignatureWhat the compiler makes of it
fn first_word(text: &str) -> &strrule 2: the result borrows from text
fn name(&self) -> &strrule 3: the result borrows from self
fn find(&self, key: &str) -> &strrule 3: the result borrows from self, not from key
fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &strtwo candidates and no self: you must annotate
fn print(a: &str, b: &str)no reference is returned: nothing to decide

So annotations are needed in one main situation: a function takes several references and returns one.

References inside structs

So far your structs owned all their data. A struct can hold a reference, and then it needs a lifetime parameter, because the struct must not outlive the data it points to:

Read struct Excerpt<'a> { text: &'a str } as: “an Excerpt holds a reference that is valid for 'a, so the Excerpt itself cannot be used for longer than 'a”. The excerpt borrows from book, and the compiler makes sure that book is not dropped or changed while the excerpt is in use. No text was copied.

The impl<'a> Excerpt<'a> line declares the lifetime and then uses it, the same pattern as impl<T> Point<T> for generic types. In recent Rust you may also write impl Excerpt<'_> when the methods do not need to name the lifetime. '_ means “a lifetime that the compiler should fill in”.

Watch out
Start with owned data

A struct that holds references is harder to use: it cannot be returned from the function that owns the data, cannot easily be stored for a long time, and its lifetime parameter spreads to everything that contains it. For most structs, owning the data (String, not &str) is the right first choice. Use references in structs for short-lived views, where avoiding a copy matters, such as an iterator or a parser that walks over a text.

The lifetime 'static

'static is the one lifetime with a fixed name. It means “valid for the entire run of the program”. Every string literal has it, because its text is stored inside the program file itself:

You will also see 'static as a bound on a type: T: 'static. It means “T contains no borrowed data that could expire”, which is true for all owned types such as String, Vec<u8> and i32. A new thread, for instance, requires that of the data you give to it, because the thread might run longer than the function that started it (chapter 30).

Watch out
'static is rarely the fix

When a lifetime error appears, the compiler sometimes mentions 'static, and it is tempting to write it everywhere until the errors stop. This almost never solves the real problem. It demands that the data lives for ever, which you usually cannot provide. Ask instead: who should own this data, and how long does it need to live?

Everything together

Type parameters, trait bounds and lifetimes can appear in the same signature. Lifetimes come first in the angle brackets:

Three things you will meet later

You can write Rust for a long time without this section. Read it now to know the words, and come back when one of them appears in an error message or in the documentation of a library.

1. One lifetime outlives another: 'long: 'short. A bound between lifetimes reads “'long lasts at least as long as 'short”. It lets a function hand out a long-lived reference where a short-lived one was promised:

The same sign works for types: T: 'a means “nothing borrowed inside T expires before 'a”. T: 'static from the last section is the best-known case.

2. For every lifetime: for<'a>. A function that accepts a closure sometimes has to say: this closure must work for any lifetime, not for one that the caller picks. That is written for<'a>:

The caller of apply cannot name the lifetime of text, because text does not exist yet when apply is called. So the bound asks for a closure that accepts a reference of every lifetime. You almost never type for<'a> yourself: F: Fn(&str) -> &str means exactly the same, because elision adds it. You will see it in error messages.

3. Shorter is fine, except behind &mut. A reference that lives long can be used where a shorter life is asked for. That is why a &'static str can be passed to any function that takes a &str. The compiler simply treats it as shorter-lived. Behind a &mut, it refuses to do that:

If the compiler shortened the 'static inside &mut kept to fit the call, overwrite would store a short-lived reference in a variable that promises 'static, and the last line would read freed memory. So the type behind a &mut must match exactly. The rules that decide where a lifetime may be shortened are called variance. You do not need to learn them. It is enough to know why this error exists when you meet it.

When the borrow checker says no

A short guide for lifetime errors, from the simplest remedy to the more involved:

  1. Read the whole message. It shows where the borrow starts, where the value is dropped, and where the reference is used afterwards. Often the fix is to move a declaration to an outer scope, so that the value lives longer.
  2. Return an owned value when the data is created inside the function.
  3. Own the data in structs: String in place of &str.
  4. Clone when the data is small or the code runs rarely. A clone that removes a difficult lifetime problem is a good trade. You can optimise later, when measurements show that it matters.
  5. Store an index or a key, not a reference, when one part of a data structure must refer to another part. For example, keep the position of an element in a Vec, and look it up when needed.
  6. Shared ownership with Rc or Arc when several parts of the program truly need to own the same value (chapter 27).
How other languages do it
Lifetimes in other languages
  • C and C++ have the same problem and leave the checking to the programmer. Returning a pointer to a local variable compiles (perhaps with a warning), and using it is undefined behaviour. A large share of the security holes in C and C++ programs are exactly these “use after free” bugs.
  • Garbage-collected languages (Java, Python, Go, JavaScript, C#) keep every value alive for as long as anything refers to it. The problem cannot occur, at the price of a garbage collector that runs alongside the program.
  • Rust is the first mainstream language to check lifetimes at compile time. The annotations are the small amount of extra information the compiler needs in the cases it cannot decide alone.
Recap
  • A lifetime is the stretch of code in which a reference is valid. The borrow checker makes sure no reference outlives its value.
  • Annotations such as 'a describe how the lifetimes of references relate. They never change how long a value lives.
  • fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str: the result is valid only while both inputs are.
  • Elision rules fill in lifetimes in the common cases: one reference parameter, or a &self method.
  • A struct holding a reference needs a lifetime parameter and cannot outlive the data it borrows.
  • 'static means “for the whole program”. String literals have it.
  • When lifetimes get complicated, prefer owned data.
Check your understanding
1

What does a lifetime annotation like 'a do?

Annotations are descriptions for the borrow checker. They do not exist in the finished program and never change how long anything lives.

2

Why does fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str need annotations, while fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str does not?

The elision rules cover the case of exactly one reference parameter. With two candidates and no self, you must say how the result relates to them.

3

Can this function be fixed by adding lifetime annotations?

A reference to a local value always dangles after the function returns. Return the owned value and let ownership move to the caller.

4

What does struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str } tell you?

The lifetime parameter ties the struct to the data it references. The compiler will not let the struct outlive that data.

5

Which values have the lifetime 'static?

A string literal is part of the program file and is therefore valid for the whole run. A local variable in main is dropped when main ends, which is not quite the same.

Guided exerciseThe shorter one

Write a function shorter that takes two string slices and returns the shorter one (the first one if they have the same length). Add the lifetime annotations it needs, and test it.

Need a hint?

The shape is the same as longest: declare <'a> after the name and use &'a str for both parameters and for the return type.

Show solution and explanation

The result may come from either parameter, so both carry the same lifetime as the result. The compiler will then make sure that callers use the result only while both arguments are alive.

PracticeText after a marker

Write after<'a>(text: &'a str, marker: &str) -> Option<&'a str> that returns the part of text that follows the first appearance of marker, or None if the marker does not appear. Show in main that the result can be used after the marker string has been dropped.

Need a hint?

text.split_once(marker) returns Option<(&str, &str)>. Take the second part. Only text needs the lifetime 'a, because the result never points into marker.

Show solution and explanation

Because marker has its own, unrelated lifetime, the borrow checker accepts that it is dropped before the result is printed. If you gave marker the lifetime 'a too, this main would be rejected, although the function body would be exactly the same. A precise signature gives the callers more freedom.

PracticeA struct that borrows

Define struct Highlight<'a> { line: &'a str, word: &'a str } and a function find_highlight<'a>(text: &'a str, word: &'a str) -> Option<Highlight<'a>> that returns the first line of text containing word. Print the result for a text of three lines.

Need a hint?

Loop over text.lines(). When line.contains(word) is true, return Some(Highlight { line, word }). After the loop, return None. Derive Debug to print the struct.

Show solution and explanation

The struct holds two references and copies no text. Its lifetime parameter says that a Highlight is only usable while both the text and the word are alive. Here both are string literals, so they live for the whole program.

ChallengeA word reader

Write a struct Words<'a> that holds the remaining text (rest: &'a str) and a method next_word(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str>. Each call returns the next word and removes it from rest. When no word is left, it returns None. The returned words must stay usable after the Words value itself has been dropped.

Need a hint?

Trim the start of rest first with trim_start(). If it is empty, return None. Otherwise find the end of the word with rest.find(' '), which returns an Option<usize>, and use split_at. The return type must be Option<&'a str>, not Option<&str>. Without the 'a, rule 3 of elision would tie the word to the borrow of self.

Show solution and explanation

The key is the return type Option<&'a str>. It says that each word borrows from the original text, which lives for 'a, and not from the Words value. That is why first can be used after words has been dropped, and why next_word can be called again while earlier words are still held. With the elided form Option<&str>, each word would be tied to the &mut self borrow. The compiler would then reject a second call of next_word while first is still in use, and it would reject the use of first after words is gone.

You have just written a small iterator by hand. Chapter 25 shows the standard way to do this with the Iterator trait.

Testing your code

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Write tests and run them with cargo test
  • Check results with assert!, assert_eq! and assert_ne!, and read a failure report
  • Test that code panics or returns errors as intended
  • Organise unit tests, integration tests and documentation tests
  • Choose good test cases

The compiler proves a lot about a Rust program: no dangling references, no missing cases, no mixed-up types. It cannot know what your program is supposed to do. A function that should add two numbers and subtracts them instead compiles perfectly. Tests close that gap: they are small pieces of code that run your code and check that the result is what you expect.

Real-world analogy
A pilot’s checklist

Before every flight, pilots go through a checklist: flaps, fuel, instruments. They do it even after ten thousand flights, because the list catches the one mistake that experience overlooks. A test suite is a checklist that the computer runs for you in a second, every time you change something.

Why it is worth the effort:

  • You find mistakes early, minutes after making them, not weeks later through a user.
  • You can change code without fear. If the tests still pass after a rewrite, the behaviour is unchanged.
  • Tests are examples of how the code is meant to be used, and they never go out of date, because they fail if they do.

Testing needs no extra installation. The test runner is built into Cargo.

A first test

Create a library package with cargo new --lib textkit, and put this into src/lib.rs:

Run cargo test:

What the parts mean:

  • #[test] marks a function as a test. cargo test finds all such functions, runs each one, and reports ok or FAILED. A test passes if it finishes without panicking.
  • assert_eq!(a, b) checks that two values are equal, and panics if they are not.
  • mod tests is an ordinary module that holds the tests. The name is a convention.
  • #[cfg(test)] tells the compiler to include this module only when testing. In a normal cargo build the tests are left out, so they add nothing to your finished program.
  • use super::*; brings everything from the parent module into the test module. Because tests is a child module, it can also use private functions of its parent.

A test’s name should say what is being checked. When it fails, the name is the first thing you read.

The assertion macros

MacroPasses whenTypical use
assert!(condition)the condition is trueassert!(list.is_empty())
assert_eq!(left, right)the values are equalassert_eq!(add(2, 3), 5)
assert_ne!(left, right)the values are differentassert_ne!(new_id, old_id)

Prefer assert_eq! to assert!(a == b), because on failure it prints both values. All three accept an extra message with format arguments, which is printed when the check fails. The compared values must implement PartialEq and Debug, so for your own types add #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)].

Reading a failure

Here is a test that is wrong about what the function does:

The report names the failing test, the file and line of the failed check, your message, and the two values: left is the first argument (what the code produced), and right is the second (what the test expected). Here the code is right and the test is wrong: the text has two words. That happens too. A failing test tells you that the code and the test disagree, and you decide which one to fix.

A bug caught by a test

Add a second function to the library, with two tests:

A palindrome is a text that reads the same in both directions. The function keeps only letters and digits, and compares them with their reverse.

The second test found a real bug: the capital “N” at the start is not equal to the small “n” at the end. The fix is to convert every character to lower case before comparing:

Now all tests pass, and they will keep guarding this behaviour. If someone removes the lower-casing next year, the test fails at once. A test that is written because of a bug, and stays to make sure the bug never returns, is called a regression test.

Testing panics and errors

Sometimes the correct behaviour is a panic. The attribute #[should_panic] turns the logic around: the test passes only if the code panics.

expected = "no words" also checks that the panic message contains that text. Without it, the test would pass for any panic, including one caused by an unrelated bug.

A test can also return a Result. Then you can use ? inside it, and the test fails if an Err comes back:

To check that a function returns an error, assert on the result itself:

map_err changes the error inside a Result and leaves an Ok alone. Here it replaces the standard parsing error with our own.

Three places for tests

1. Unit tests: next to the code

Everything so far was a unit test: a test of one small piece (a “unit”) in isolation. Unit tests live in the same file as the code, in a #[cfg(test)] mod tests block at the bottom. They can test private functions.

2. Integration tests: from the outside

An integration test uses your library the way another crate would: only through its public API. Integration tests live in a folder called tests next to src. Each file there is compiled as its own small crate.

No #[cfg(test)] and no mod tests are needed here, because Cargo only compiles this folder when testing. Integration tests need a library crate. That is one more reason to keep the logic of a program in src/lib.rs and only a thin main.rs on top, as described in chapter 17.

3. Documentation tests: examples that cannot rot

A comment that starts with /// is a documentation comment. It describes the item that follows, and cargo doc turns these comments into a website. Code blocks inside them are compiled and run by cargo test:

If the function changes and the example no longer works, the test fails. The documentation can never promise something the code does not do. This is why examples in the documentation of Rust crates are so dependable.

With all three kinds in place, cargo test reports three sections:

Controlling what runs

CommandEffect
cargo testrun all tests
cargo test palindromerun only tests whose name contains “palindrome”
cargo test --libonly unit tests
cargo test --test public_apionly the integration test file tests/public_api.rs
cargo test --doconly documentation tests
cargo test -- --nocapturealso show what passing tests print with println!
cargo test -- --test-threads=1run the tests one after another
cargo test -- --ignoredrun only the tests marked #[ignore]

Two things to know:

  • Output is hidden. What a test prints is shown only if the test fails. --nocapture shows everything.
  • Tests run in parallel, several at a time, and in no fixed order. Each test must therefore stand alone: it must not depend on another test having run, and two tests should not write to the same file.

A slow test can be marked so that it is skipped in normal runs:

What makes a good test

One behaviour per test. A test called it_works that checks ten things tells you little when it fails. Ten tests with clear names tell you exactly what broke.

Arrange, act, assert. Most tests have three steps: set up the input, call the code, check the result.

Think about the edges. Bugs gather at boundaries. For each function, ask:

  • What about nothing? An empty text, an empty list, zero.
  • What about exactly one?
  • What about the limits? The largest allowed value, and one more than that.
  • What about strange input? Extra spaces, capital letters, non-English characters, negative numbers.
  • What about the error cases? Each way of failing deserves a test.

Test behaviour, not details. Check what a function returns for given inputs, not how it works inside. Then you can rewrite the inside freely.

Keep the logic separate from input and output. A function that takes a &str and returns a value is trivial to test. A function that reads the keyboard and prints to the screen is not. This is the reason parse in the to-do project returned a value and printed nothing. Its tests are short:

(To compare commands with assert_eq!, the enum needs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)].)

Writing the test first

Some programmers write the test before the code. The method is called test-driven development (TDD) and goes in a short cycle:

  1. Red: write a small test for behaviour that does not exist yet. Run it and watch it fail. Now you know the test can fail.
  2. Green: write the simplest code that makes the test pass.
  3. Refactor: tidy up the code. The tests tell you if you broke something.

You do not have to work this way all the time. It is especially useful when you fix a bug: first write a test that shows the bug, then fix it. The test proves the fix and stays as a guard.

How other languages do it
Testing in other languages

In most languages you choose and install a test framework first: JUnit for Java, pytest for Python, Jest or Vitest for JavaScript, GoogleTest or Catch2 for C++. In Rust (as in Go) testing is part of the standard tools. Every Rust project is tested the same way, with cargo test, and documentation examples that are run as tests are a feature that few other languages have.

Tip
More tools for later

Chapter 41 goes further: tests that generate hundreds of random inputs (property testing), snapshot tests, measuring speed (benchmarks), replacing parts of a system with stand-ins (mocking), and running tests automatically on every change (continuous integration).

Recap
  • A test is a function marked #[test]. It passes if it does not panic. cargo test runs all tests.
  • assert!, assert_eq! and assert_ne! check results. assert_eq! shows both values on failure.
  • #[should_panic(expected = "…")] tests for a panic. A test may return a Result and use ?.
  • Unit tests sit in #[cfg(test)] mod tests next to the code and can test private items. Integration tests sit in tests/ and use only the public API. Code in /// comments is tested too.
  • Tests run in parallel and must be independent. Output is shown only for failing tests.
  • Test the edges: empty, one, limits, strange input, every error case.
Check your understanding
1

When does a test function pass?

The test runner treats a panic as a failure. The assertion macros panic when their check fails.

2

What does #[cfg(test)] on the tests module do?

cfg is short for “configuration”. The module is included only under cargo test, so tests cost nothing in the finished binary.

3

Why prefer assert_eq!(result, 5) to assert!(result == 5)?

Both check the same thing. assert_eq! gives the more useful failure message, with left and right.

4

Where do integration tests live, and what can they use?

Each file in tests/ is its own crate that depends on your library like any outside user would.

5

A test passes when run alone, and sometimes fails when all tests run together. What is the most likely reason?

Tests run at the same time and in no fixed order. Tests that share state can disturb each other. Make each test independent, for example by giving each its own file name.

Guided exerciseTest a temperature converter

Here is a function. Write a test module with three tests: freezing point (0 °C is 32 °F), boiling point (100 °C is 212 °F), and −40, where both scales show the same number.

Need a hint?

Start with #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; ... }. Each test is a function marked #[test] with one assert_eq!.

Show solution and explanation

Three well-known reference points make good test cases, and each test’s name says what it checks. One caution for floats: results of calculations are often off by a tiny amount (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3), so comparing with assert_eq! can fail unexpectedly. These three values happen to be exact. In general, compare floats with a tolerance: assert!((result - expected).abs() < 1e-9);.

PracticeFind the bug with a test

This function should return the middle value of a sorted list (the median). For a list with an even number of elements, it should return the average of the two middle values. Write tests for a list of three elements, a list of four elements, and a list of one element. One of them will fail. Fix the function.

Need a hint?

For [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] the median is 2.5. The function returns sorted[2], which is 3.0. For an even length, take the average of sorted[middle - 1] and sorted[middle].

Show solution and explanation

The test with four elements exposed the bug: the original code ignored the even case. The fourth test documents what happens for an empty list. Here it panics, because middle - 1 on a usize of 0 overflows. Returning Option<f64> would be the friendlier design, and writing the test first makes you think about that case.

ChallengeTest-drive a password check

Use test-driven development to write check_password(password: &str) -> Result<(), PasswordError>. The rules: at least 8 characters, at least one digit, and at least one upper-case letter. Define the enum PasswordError with one variant per rule. Write one test per rule first, plus one for a valid password, and then write the function.

Need a hint?

The enum needs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)] for assert_eq!. Useful methods: password.chars().count(), and password.chars().any(|c| c.is_ascii_digit()), which is true if at least one character passes the check. Decide in which order the rules are checked, and let a test fix that order.

Show solution and explanation

Each rule has a test, the boundary (exactly 8 characters) has its own test, and one test pins down which error wins when several rules are broken. The function uses chars().count() and not len(), so that a password with non-English letters is measured in characters, not bytes. Because the function returns an enum, the tests can check exactly which rule was broken, which a bool could not express.
