Project: a file search tool

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read command-line arguments
  • Structure a program as a library with a thin main
  • Return borrowed results with a lifetime
  • Report errors on the error stream and through exit codes
  • Develop a function test-first

In this project you build finder, a small version of the classic command-line tool grep. It searches files for a text and prints every line that contains it:

The project uses everything from Part 4: modules and a library crate, error handling with Result and ?, a struct with a lifetime, traits through derive, and tests.

Step 0: plan

What does the user give us? A text to search for, one or more file names, and two optional switches: -i to ignore upper and lower case, and -n to show line numbers.

What are the parts?

  1. Understand the command line and turn it into a precise value (a Config), or explain what is wrong.
  2. Search one text for the pattern and return the matching lines. This is the core, and it needs no files and no printing, so it is easy to test.
  3. Tie it together: read each file, search it, print the matches.

Where does the code go? Parts 1 to 3 go into a library, src/lib.rs. The file src/main.rs only connects the library to the outside world: it gets the arguments, calls the library, and turns errors into messages and exit codes.

Create the package with cargo new finder. Then create the file src/lib.rs next to src/main.rs. Also create two text files in the project folder to try the program on:

Step 1: read the command line

When you start a program as finder rust poem.txt, the words after the program’s name are its command-line arguments. std::env::args() gives them to the program, one String per word. The first item is the program’s own name, so we skip it. Put this into src/main.rs for a first experiment:

With Cargo, the program’s own arguments go after a double dash, which separates them from Cargo’s arguments:

Step 2: from arguments to a Config

A Vec<String> could contain anything. As in the to-do project, we turn the untidy input into a precise type at the edge of the program. Put this into src/lib.rs:

How it works:

  • The loop sorts every argument into one of three groups: a known switch, an unknown switch (an error), or an ordinary word. The match uses alternatives (|), a guard (if flag.starts_with('-')) and a catch-all name, all from chapter 14. arg.as_str() turns the &String into a &str, so that it can be compared with string literals.
  • Switches may appear anywhere, before or after the other words, as users expect from command-line tools.
  • After the loop, the first word is the pattern and all the others are file names. words.into_iter() gives the words one at a time, with ownership. .next() takes the first, and let … else handles the case that there is none. .collect() gathers the rest into a new vector.
  • The error type is a plain String. Whoever calls the function only wants to show the message.

Both the struct and its fields are pub, because main.rs is a different crate and must be able to use them.

Step 3: the search, test first

The core function takes a pattern and a text, and returns the lines that match. Before writing it, decide what a result looks like, and write a test that describes the behaviour. This is the “red” step of test-driven development from chapter 22.

A Match does not copy the line. It holds a &str that points into the text being searched. That is why the struct has a lifetime parameter: a Match must not outlive that text. For a tool that may search very large files, avoiding one allocation per matching line is a real saving.

The tests, at the bottom of src/lib.rs:

cargo test fails to compile at this point, because search does not exist. Now write it:

The signature is worth reading closely:

The function takes two references and returns data that contains references, so the compiler cannot guess the relationship, and you must annotate it (chapter 21). The annotation says that the matches borrow from text, and not from pattern. A caller may throw the pattern away and keep the matches.

Other details:

  • text.lines() gives each line as a &str slice of the original text, without the line ending. enumerate() adds a counter that starts at 0, and people count lines from 1, so the line number is index + 1.
  • For the case-insensitive search, both sides are converted to lower case. The pattern is converted once, before the loop, and not once per line.

Run cargo test. All three tests pass: “green”.

Step 4: put the pieces together

Add use std::error::Error; and use std::fs; at the top of src/lib.rs.

  • The function returns Result<usize, Box<dyn Error>>: the number of matches, or any kind of error.
  • fs::read_to_string(path) can fail. Its error message says “No such file or directory”, but not which file. map_err replaces the error with a text that includes the path, and the ? passes it on. A String is turned into a Box<dyn Error> automatically.
  • When several files are searched, each line is prefixed with the file name, as grep does.
  • Look at how the lifetimes work out. text owns the content of one file. The matches borrow from it and are used up inside the inner loop. When the outer loop moves on to the next file, the old text is dropped, and by then nothing refers to it any more. The compiler has checked that.

Step 5: a thin main

Replace the contents of src/main.rs:

main contains no logic of its own. It does three things that only the outermost layer of a program should do: it reads the arguments, prints error messages, and chooses the exit code.

Two new tools appear here.

eprintln! works like println!, but writes to a different channel. Every program has two output channels:

ChannelNameWritten withMeant for
standard outputstdoutprintln!the results of the program
standard errorstderreprintln!error messages and diagnostics

In the terminal both appear on the screen. The difference shows when the output is sent somewhere else. finder rust poem.txt > result.txt writes the results into a file. An error message should still reach the user’s screen and must not end up inside that file. With eprintln!, it does not.

process::exit(code) ends the program at once with the given exit code. By convention, 0 means success. This program follows the convention of grep: 0 if something was found, 1 if nothing was found, and 2 if an error occurred. Scripts use these codes to decide what to do next.

Try it

Check that errors really go to the error stream. Send the standard output into a file, and the error still appears on the screen while the file stays empty:

Tip
Install your tool

cargo install --path . builds the program in release mode and copies it into Cargo’s bin folder, which is on your search path. After that you can type finder rust poem.txt in any folder, like any other command. cargo uninstall finder removes it again.

The complete library

The tests for Config::from_args use a small helper, args, that turns a list of string literals into the Vec<String> the function expects. Helper functions inside the test module keep the tests short and readable.

Make it better

PracticeCount only

Add a switch -c (or --count). With it, the program prints only the number of matching lines per file, for example poem.txt:2, and not the lines themselves.

Need a hint?

Add a field count_only: bool to Config and an arm to the match in from_args. In run, get the matches for a file into a variable first. If count_only is set, print path and matches.len(), otherwise print the lines as before. Update the test that builds a Config by hand: the compiler will tell you that a field is missing.

Show solution and explanation

The changed part of run:

In from_args, the new arm is "-c" | "--count" => count_only = true, with a let mut count_only = false; before the loop, and the field is added to the Config at the end.

search did not change at all. Because it returns data and prints nothing, a new way of presenting the results needs no change in the core. Adding a field to Config made the compiler point to every place that builds one, including the test.

PracticeWhole words only

Add a switch -w that matches whole words only: with -w, the pattern rust matches the line learn rust today but not Trust the compiler.

Need a hint?

Write a helper fn contains_word(line: &str, word: &str) -> bool. Split the line into words with line.split(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()) and check whether any piece equals the word. Write tests for the helper first: a match in the middle, at the start and at the end of a line, next to punctuation, and no match inside a longer word.

Show solution and explanation

split accepts a closure that decides where to cut: here, at every character that is not a letter or a digit. any is true as soon as one piece equals the word. In search, the line line.contains(pattern) becomes a choice between contains_word(line, pattern) and line.contains(pattern).

search now has two bool parameters, and a call like search("rust", text, true, false) is hard to read. A better design passes one small struct of options, or the whole &Config. Noticing this kind of thing and improving it is a normal part of growing a program.

ChallengeSearch folders

Let finder accept folders as well as files. For a folder, it searches every file inside it, and inside all its subfolders. Files that cannot be read as text are skipped with a note on the error stream.

Need a hint?

std::fs::read_dir(path)? gives the entries of a folder. Each entry is a Result, so write let entry = entry?;, and entry.path() is the full path as a PathBuf. path.is_dir() tells folders from files. Write a function collect_files(path: &Path, files: &mut Vec<PathBuf>) -> io::Result<()> that calls itself for subfolders.

Show solution and explanation

Path and PathBuf are to file paths what str and String are to text: a borrowed view and an owned value. They exist because paths are not always valid UTF-8, and because the separator differs between systems (/ or \). file.display() turns a path into something printable.

The function is recursive: for a folder it calls itself on every entry. The results are collected in a vector that is passed along as &mut, which avoids creating and joining many small vectors. The list is sorted, because read_dir promises no particular order.

In run, call collect_files for each path from the command line, then loop over the collected files. For a file that is not valid text, fs::read_to_string returns an error. Print it with eprintln! and continue with the next file, so that one unreadable file does not stop the whole search.

What you have learned

Recap
  • std::env::args() gives the command-line arguments. Turn them into a Config struct once, with clear error messages.
  • Logic in src/lib.rs, a thin src/main.rs: the library can be tested, and main only handles arguments, messages and exit codes.
  • A function can return views into its input with a lifetime (Vec<Match<'a>>), and avoid copying.
  • Results go to standard output with println!, errors to standard error with eprintln!. The exit code tells other programs whether it worked.
  • map_err adds missing information to an error before ? passes it on.
  • Writing the test first makes you decide what a function should return before you write it.

You have finished Part 4. You can now organise a program into modules, handle errors, write generic code, define shared behaviour with traits, reason about lifetimes, and test your work. These are the tools of everyday Rust programming. Part 5 shows a style that Rust programmers use all the time: working with closures and iterators.

Closures: functions you can carry around

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Write closures and pass them to functions
  • Explain how a closure captures values from its surroundings
  • Tell Fn, FnMut and FnOnce apart and know when move is needed
  • Return closures from functions and store them in structs

You have already written closures without much explanation: v.retain(|x| *x > 2), some.map(|n| n * 2), people.sort_by_key(|p| p.age). The part between the bars and after them is a closure: a small function without a name, written right where it is needed.

Closures matter because they let you pass behaviour to a function, in the same way that you pass data. sort_by_key knows how to sort. What to sort by is your decision, and you hand it over as a closure.

Real-world analogy
A note for the babysitter

You leave a note: “If Lena wakes up, read her the book on the kitchen table.” The note is a set of instructions to be carried out later, by someone else. And it refers to something from your surroundings, the book on your kitchen table. A closure is such a note: instructions, plus the things from its surroundings that the instructions need.

The syntax

  • Parameters go between vertical bars: |x|, |a, b|, ||.
  • The body is one expression, or a block in braces.
  • Types are usually left out. The compiler works them out from how the closure is used.

Compare a function and a closure that do the same:

One limit: the compiler fixes the types of a closure at its first use. A closure that was called with an i32 cannot be called with a String afterwards.

Capturing: what makes a closure special

A function can only use its parameters. A closure can also use variables from the place where it is written. It captures them:

A normal function could not do this. Try it, and the compiler says “can’t capture dynamic environment in a fn item”. Capturing is why the name is closure: it “closes over” its surroundings.

Three ways to capture

A closure captures each variable in the least demanding way that its body allows. These are the three ways of using a value that you know from ownership:

Notice let mut increment: a closure that changes a captured variable must itself be declared mut.

The borrow rules apply as always. While increment is alive, it holds a mutable borrow of count, so nothing else may touch count:

move: take everything along

Sometimes a closure must own what it captures, because it will live longer than the place where it was created. The keyword move before the bars makes the closure take ownership of every variable it uses:

The closure borrows n, but n is a parameter of make_adder and disappears when that function returns. The closure would be left with a dangling reference. The compiler’s suggestion is the fix:

make_adder is a function that builds functions. Each closure it returns carries its own n. move is needed in two typical places: when a closure is returned from a function, and when it is handed to a new thread (chapter 30).

In plain English
What a closure really is

There is no magic. For each closure, the compiler creates a hidden struct with one field per captured variable, and one method that contains the body. make_adder(5) returns a struct holding the number 5. Calling the closure calls the method. That is why closures are exactly as fast as ordinary functions, and why each closure has its own unique type that has no name you can write.

Fn, FnMut and FnOnce

To accept a closure as a parameter, a function needs a type for it. Each closure has its own unnameable type, so you describe it by a trait. There are three, and they differ in what the closure does with its captured values:

TraitThe closure …It can be calledExample body
Fnonly reads what it capturedany number of times, even from several places at once|x| x + n
FnMutchanges what it capturedany number of times, one call at a time|| count += 1
FnOnceuses up what it capturedonce|| drop(text)

They form a ladder. Every Fn closure can also be used where an FnMut or FnOnce is asked for, and every FnMut where an FnOnce is asked for. So when you write a function that takes a closure, ask for the least you need, to accept the most:

  • If you call it once: FnOnce.
  • If you call it several times: FnMut.
  • If you must call it from several places at the same time, or through a shared reference: Fn.

The trait is written with the parameter types in parentheses and the return type after an arrow:

The standard library follows the same reasoning. Option::map calls its closure at most once, so it asks for FnOnce. Iterator::map calls it for every item, so it asks for FnMut. thread::spawn runs it once, in another thread, and asks for FnOnce.

Ordinary functions work too

Wherever a closure is expected, you can pass the name of a normal function, as long as the parameters and return type fit:

map(ToString::to_string) passes a method by its path, and map(Some) passes an enum variant, which is a function too: it takes a value and returns an Option.

There is also a plain type for functions that capture nothing, the function pointer fn(i32) -> i32, written with a small f. You need it rarely, mostly when talking to C code or when storing functions in a table:

Storing closures

A struct field can hold a closure. Either make the struct generic over the closure’s type, or box it as a trait object:

  • Box<dyn Fn() -> String> is “some closure that takes nothing and returns a String, stored on the heap”. Because both buttons have this same type, they fit into one vector, although the two closures are of different hidden types.
  • A closure stored in a field is called with extra parentheses: (self.on_click)(). Without them, Rust would look for a method named on_click.
  • A closure that is handed over to be called later, when something happens, is known as a callback. Buttons, timers and network events all work this way.
How other languages do it
Closures in other languages
  • JavaScript (x => x + 1) and Python (lambda x: x + 1) have closures that capture variables by reference, and a garbage collector keeps the captured variables alive. Captured variables that change later are a classic source of surprises there.
  • Java lambdas may only capture variables that never change.
  • C++ lambdas make you list the captures by hand, as in [&total, limit](int x) { ... }, and capturing a reference to a variable that dies too early is undefined behaviour.
  • Rust decides the capture mode automatically, and the borrow checker verifies that every captured reference stays valid. When it cannot be valid, you get an error and the hint to use move.
Recap
  • A closure is an anonymous function: |parameters| body. The types are usually inferred.
  • A closure can capture variables from its surroundings: by shared borrow, by mutable borrow, or by taking ownership.
  • move forces the closure to own what it captures. It is needed when the closure outlives its birthplace: returned closures and threads.
  • Fn reads its captures, FnMut changes them, FnOnce uses them up. A function parameter should ask for the weakest one that is enough.
  • Named functions can be passed where closures are expected.
  • impl Fn(…) returns a closure. Box<dyn Fn(…)> stores closures of different types in one place.
Check your understanding
1

What can a closure do that an ordinary function cannot?

Capturing its environment is the defining feature of a closure. An fn item can only use its parameters and global items.

2

What does move do in move |x| x + n?

Without move, the closure would borrow n. With it, the closure owns its own copy and can live longer than the scope where n was defined.

3

A function calls the closure it receives several times, and the closure adds to a counter outside. Which bound must the parameter have?

The closure changes a captured variable, so it is not Fn. It is called more than once, so FnOnce is not enough. FnMut fits.

4

Why can the closures || 1 and || 2 not be stored in a Vec directly, without Box<dyn Fn() -> i32>?

Even closures that look alike have distinct, unnameable types. A trait object gives them a common type.

5

Why does this not compile?

The closure borrows total mutably from its creation to its last call. Reading total in that stretch breaks the borrowing rules. Move the println! after the last call.

Guided exerciseApply a function three ways

Write a function transform(numbers: &[i32], f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32) -> Vec<i32> that returns a new vector in which f has been applied to every number. Call it with a closure that doubles, with a closure that adds a captured variable offset, and with a named function square.

Need a hint?

Inside transform, create an empty vector, loop with for &n in numbers, and push f(n). For the third call, pass just the name: transform(&data, square).

Show solution and explanation

transform knows how to walk over a list and build a new one. What happens to each number is decided by the caller. The second closure captures offset by reference, which is fine because it is only used during the call. This function is a hand-made version of the iterator method map, which you will meet in the next chapter.

PracticeA counter factory

Write make_counter() -> impl FnMut() -> u32 that returns a closure. Each call of the closure returns the next number: 1, 2, 3, … Two counters made by two calls of make_counter must count independently.

Need a hint?

Inside make_counter, declare let mut count = 0;, and return move || { count += 1; count }. The variable that holds the returned closure must be mut.

Show solution and explanation

move gives each closure its own count, which lives inside the closure for as long as the closure exists. The closure changes its captured value, so its type is FnMut, and calling it needs a mut binding. This is a tiny example of state hidden inside a function: from outside, nobody can reach count except by calling the closure.

PracticeSort in three orders

Given a vector of (String, u32) pairs, name and score, print the list sorted (a) by score from high to low, (b) by name, and (c) by the length of the name, shortest first. Use sort_by or sort_by_key with closures.

Need a hint?

sort_by_key(|p| p.1) sorts by score from low to high. For the reverse order, use sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1)), with a and b swapped, or wrap the key in std::cmp::Reverse. For names, sort_by(|a, b| a.0.cmp(&b.0)) avoids cloning the strings.

Show solution and explanation

One sorting routine, three orders, each chosen by a small closure. Reverse is a wrapper that turns the order of its content around. sort_by_key is the shortest form when the key is cheap to produce. For the names, sort_by compares the strings in place without creating copies. (The first two lines are the same by coincidence: in this data, the order by score happens to equal the alphabetical order.)

ChallengeRemember results

Some calculations are slow. Write a struct Cache<F> that wraps a function F: Fn(u64) -> u64 and remembers every result in a HashMap, so that the function is run only once per input. Give it a method get(&mut self, input: u64) -> u64. Prove that it works by counting how often the wrapped function really runs.

Need a hint?

The struct has two fields: function: F and results: HashMap<u64, u64>. In get, look in the map first. If the input is not there, call (self.function)(input), store the result and return it. To count the calls from outside, the wrapped closure cannot change a plain counter, because the bound is Fn. Use a std::cell::Cell<u32>, which allows changing a value through a shared reference (more about it in chapter 27).

Show solution and explanation

Four requests, but the function ran only twice: once for 12 and once for 7. Remembering results like this is called memoization. The struct is generic over F, so the closure is stored directly in the struct, with no boxing and no run-time lookup. (self.function)(input) needs the parentheses because function is a field, not a method.

Cell lets the closure count its calls although it only holds a shared reference to calls, which keeps the closure an Fn.

Iterators: processing data step by step

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what an iterator is and how for uses it
  • Build processing pipelines with map, filter and other adapters
  • Finish a pipeline with collect, sum, fold, find and friends
  • Understand laziness and why iterator chains are as fast as loops
  • Write your own iterator

A great deal of programming is “go through a collection and do something with each element”: keep some, change them, add them up, find one. You can do all of that with for loops and mut variables. Rust offers a second style that is shorter, harder to get wrong, and just as fast: iterators.

Here is the same task in both styles. Add up the squares of all even numbers in a list:

The second version reads like a description of the result: take the numbers, keep the even ones, square each, sum them. There is no variable that changes, no index, and nothing to get off by one.

Real-world analogy
An assembly line

Items travel along a conveyor belt past a row of stations. One station throws out the damaged items. The next one paints each item. At the end, a worker packs them into a box. Each station does one small job on one item at a time. An iterator chain is such an assembly line for data.

What an iterator is

An iterator is a value that hands out a sequence of items, one at a time. The whole idea is one trait with one required method:

Each call to next returns Some(item), or None when nothing is left. You can call it by hand:

A for loop does exactly this for you. for colour in &colours { ... } creates an iterator, calls next until it gets None, and runs the body for every item.

Three ways to iterate over a collection

MethodItemsThe collection afterwardsThe for shorthand
.iter()&T, shared referencesuntouchedfor x in &v
.iter_mut()&mut T, mutable referencesstill there, maybe changedfor x in &mut v
.into_iter()T, the values themselvesused upfor x in v

The three parts of a pipeline

Every iterator chain has the same shape:

  1. A source creates the iterator: v.iter(), 1..=10, text.chars(), text.lines(), map.keys().
  2. Zero or more adapters each turn the iterator into another iterator: filter, map, take, …
  3. One consumer at the end drives the whole thing and produces a result: collect, sum, count, find, or a for loop.

Adapters: reshaping the stream

map and filter

map changes every item. filter keeps the items for which its closure returns true.

Watch out
The stars in filter

prices.iter() yields &i32. map hands each item to its closure as it is, so p is a &i32. filter only lends each item to its closure, so there p is a &&i32, a reference to a reference, and comparing it with a number needs **p. Three ways to keep this tidy:

  • take the reference apart in the pattern: .filter(|&&p| p > 100),
  • or turn the items into plain values first: prices.iter().copied().filter(|p| *p > 100),
  • or iterate over values from the start: prices.into_iter().

More adapters

Adapters that change the number of items

s.parse().ok() turns the Result into an Option: Some(number) or None. filter_map keeps what is inside the Somes and drops the rest. “Parse what can be parsed, skip the rest” is one line.

Consumers: getting a result

Numbers out of a sequence

max and min return an Option, because an empty sequence has no largest element. For sum and product you must state the result type, as in let total: i32.

To find the largest item by some property, use max_by_key and min_by_key:

Questions about a sequence

any, all, find and position stop as soon as the answer is known. They do not look at the remaining items.

collect: build a collection

collect gathers the items into a collection. It can build many kinds, so you tell it which one you want, by a type annotation or with the turbofish:

An iterator of pairs collects into a map. An iterator of characters or string slices collects into a String.

A particularly useful case: an iterator of Results can be collected into one Result that holds a collection. It is Ok with all the values if every item was Ok, and otherwise it is the first error.

Compare this with filter_map above. filter_map(|s| s.parse().ok()) silently skips bad input. Collecting into a Result refuses the whole batch. Which one is right depends on the task. The same works with Option.

There is a third answer to bad input: keep both piles. partition builds two collections in one pass, by a yes-or-no question. Its relatives are unzip, which turns a sequence of pairs into two collections, and find_map, which returns the first item for which the closure gives Some:

fold: the general tool

fold reduces a sequence to one value. It takes a starting value and a closure that combines the result so far with the next item. sum, count, max and many others can be written with it:

Read fold(0, |total, n| total + n) as: start with 0, and for every item replace the total with total + n. Use fold when no ready-made consumer fits.

for_each runs a closure for every item. It is a for loop written at the end of a chain: names.iter().for_each(|n| println!("{n}"));. For anything longer than one short call, a normal for loop is clearer.

Iterators are lazy

Adapters do nothing by themselves. They only build a description of the work. The work happens when a consumer asks for items:

This program prints nothing, and the compiler says why. map was never asked for an item, so its closure never ran.

Laziness also means that items travel through the whole chain one at a time. No intermediate lists are created. inspect lets you watch it happen:

Follow the order. Item 1 goes in and is thrown out by filter. Item 2 goes all the way through. After the second kept item, take(2) is satisfied, and the items 5 and 6 are never looked at.

Because of laziness, an iterator may even be endless, as long as something downstream stops:

(1..) counts upwards without end. successors builds a sequence in which each item is calculated from the one before.

As fast as a loop

You might expect that all these closures and adapters cost time. They do not. The compiler knows the exact types of the whole chain, merges the closures into one piece of code, and produces the same machine code as a hand-written loop. Iterators are one of Rust’s zero-cost abstractions. Sometimes a chain is even faster than an indexed loop, because v[i] checks on every access that i is in range, and an iterator does not need that check.

So choose between a loop and a chain by which one is easier to read. A good rule: a chain for “turn this collection into that result”, and a for loop when the body has side effects (printing, writing files) or complicated control flow.

Writing your own iterator

To make a type an iterator, implement Iterator for it: say what the items are, and write next.

type Item = u32; is an associated type: a type that belongs to the trait implementation. It says what this iterator yields. You wrote one method, and received filter, map, sum, collect and some seventy more for free, because they are default methods of the trait that build on next.

For a quick one-off iterator, std::iter::from_fn turns a closure into an iterator without a new struct:

To make your own collection usable in a for loop, implement the trait IntoIterator for it. That is what Vec does, and why for x in &v works.

More tools for slices and text

Slices and strings offer iterators for common ways of cutting data into pieces:

A map of the most used methods

I want to …Use
change every itemmap
keep some itemsfilter
change and keep in one stepfilter_map
number the itemsenumerate
take the first n, or skip themtake(n), skip(n)
walk two sequences togetherzip
join two sequenceschain
go backwardsrev
turn each item into severalflat_map, flatten
build a collectioncollect
build two collections at oncepartition, unzip
add up or multiplysum, product
countcount
find the largest or smallestmax, min, max_by_key, min_by_key
find the first that fitsfind, position, find_map
ask yes or noany, all
combine into one valuefold, reduce
look at the next item without taking itpeekable() and then peek()

The crate itertools adds many more, such as sorted, group_by, join, unique and tuple_windows. You will meet it in chapter 42.

How other languages do it
Iterators in other languages
  • Python has the same idea in generators and comprehensions: sum(n*n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0). They are lazy too, but each step costs interpreter time.
  • JavaScript array methods (numbers.filter(...).map(...)) are eager: each step builds a complete new array before the next step begins.
  • Java streams and C# LINQ are lazy pipelines like Rust’s, with some run-time overhead for the objects involved.
  • C++ has had iterators for decades, and “ranges” with the pipeline style since C++20.

Rust’s version combines the pleasant pipeline style with the speed of a hand-written loop, and the borrow checker makes sure that the collection is not changed while you iterate over it. In Java, that mistake is the ConcurrentModificationException. In C++, it is undefined behaviour.

Recap
  • An iterator yields items one at a time through next, which returns Some(item) or None.
  • iter() borrows, iter_mut() borrows mutably, into_iter() takes ownership.
  • A pipeline is a source, some adapters (map, filter, enumerate, zip, take, …) and one consumer (collect, sum, count, find, fold, …).
  • Adapters are lazy: nothing happens until a consumer pulls items through, one at a time.
  • collect builds any collection, and can turn many Results into one.
  • Iterator chains compile to the same code as loops.
  • Implement Iterator (just next) to get all the adapters for your own type.
Check your understanding
1

What does this line print?

Adapters only describe work. Without a consumer such as collect, count or a for loop, no item is ever produced. The compiler warns about the unused iterator.

2

Which call gives ownership of the elements of a Vec<String>?

into_iter consumes the vector and yields each String by value. iter yields &String and iter_mut yields &mut String.

3

What is the result of (1..=4).filter(|n| n % 2 == 0).map(|n| n * 10).collect::<Vec<i32>>()?

filter keeps 2 and 4. map multiplies each by 10.

4

What does collecting an iterator of Result<i32, E> into Result<Vec<i32>, E> do when one item is an Err?

Collecting into a Result succeeds only if every item is Ok. Otherwise it stops and returns the first error.

5

You implement Iterator for your own struct. Which method must you write?

next is the only required method. All adapters and consumers are default methods built on it.

Guided exerciseClean up a list of names

Given [" sara ", "TOMAS", "", " lena", " "], produce a Vec<String> of the non-empty names, trimmed and with the first letter in upper case and the rest in lower case: ["Sara", "Tomas", "Lena"]. Use one iterator chain.

Need a hint?

The chain is: .iter(), then .map(|s| s.trim()), then .filter(|s| !s.is_empty()), then a .map that builds the capitalised String, then .collect(). Write a small helper function capitalise(word: &str) -> String for the last step.

Show solution and explanation

Each step of the chain does one thing, and the order matters: trimming must come before the emptiness test, or " " would slip through. capitalise takes the first character with chars.next(), and chars.as_str() gives the rest of the text. The helper is passed to map by name.

PracticeStatistics in three lines

Rewrite the stats function from chapter 15 with iterators. It takes &[i32] and returns Option<(i32, i32, f64)>: the smallest value, the largest value and the average, or None for an empty slice.

Need a hint?

numbers.iter().min() returns Option<&i32>. Use ? to leave the function with None when the slice is empty, and * to get the number. The sum needs a type: numbers.iter().sum::<i32>().

Show solution and explanation

The fifteen lines with three mut variables have become three lines with none. min() returns None for an empty slice, and ? passes that on as the function’s result, so the division by zero can never be reached.

PracticeWord lengths

For the text "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", build a BTreeMap<usize, Vec<&str>> that groups the words by their length, and print it. Then find the longest word with one iterator call.

Need a hint?

Loop over text.split_whitespace() and use map.entry(word.len()).or_default().push(word). For the longest word, max_by_key(|w| w.len()).

Show solution and explanation

The grouping uses a for loop, because filling a map of lists is a side effect and reads more clearly that way. Finding the longest word is a pure question about the data, so a single consumer fits. When several items share the largest key, max_by_key returns the last of them, which is why the answer is “jumps” and not “quick”.

ChallengeA Fibonacci iterator

Write a struct Fibonacci that implements Iterator<Item = u64> and yields 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … Use it to compute (a) the first 10 numbers, (b) the sum of all even Fibonacci numbers below 4 million, and (c) the first Fibonacci number with more than 10 digits.

Need a hint?

The struct holds the current and the next number. In next, remember the current value, then update both fields: the new current is the old next, and the new next is the sum. Always return Some, because the sequence never ends. For (b), take_while(|n| *n < 4_000_000) cuts the endless stream.

Show solution and explanation

The iterator is endless, and that is fine, because every use contains something that stops it: take, take_while or find. The struct holds only two numbers, however far you go. Each of the three questions is answered by combining the same small building blocks in a different way, which is the main strength of iterators.

One limit: a u64 overflows at the 94th Fibonacci number, and the program would panic there in a debug build. A careful version uses checked_add and returns None when the numbers no longer fit.

Project: a sales report from raw data

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Turn raw text into typed data, and report bad rows without stopping
  • Summarise data with iterator pipelines
  • Write one generic function that groups by any key, using a closure
  • Handle money correctly
  • Print aligned tables

Programs that read data, clean it, summarise it and print a report are among the most common programs in the world. In this project you write one. It reads sales records in CSV form (“comma-separated values”: one record per line, with commas between the fields) and prints this:

The project is a workout for closures and iterators, and it brings back structs, error handling, collections, lifetimes and tests.

Step 0: plan the pipeline

Data flows through the program in one direction:

Each arrow is one small function. Three decisions before writing code:

  1. Bad rows must not stop the program. Real data is never clean. One broken line among ten thousand should be reported, and the rest should still be processed.
  2. Money is stored as whole cents, not as a floating-point number. You saw in chapter 4 that 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in floating point. Small errors like that add up over thousands of sales, and in money they are unacceptable. An integer number of cents is always exact.
  3. Functions that calculate do not print. Then they can be tested.

Create the project with cargo new report. Everything goes into src/main.rs this time, so that the finished program can also run in the online playground.

Step 1: the data

The sample data lives in the program as a constant. Two of its rows are broken on purpose.

(The complete data, with 14 rows, is in the full program at the end of the chapter.)

  • The backslash right after the opening quote makes the string start on the next line without a blank first line.
  • The first line of the data is a header: it names the columns and is not a record.
  • revenue is the amount of money a sale brought in: quantity times price.
  • month returns the first seven characters of the date, such as 2026-01. It returns a slice of the sale’s own date, with no copy. The elision rules from chapter 21 tie the result to &self.

Step 2: read a price

"12.50" must become 1250 cents. Write the tests first. They fix what should happen for the awkward inputs:

  • split_once('.') separates the part before and after the point. If there is no point, unwrap_or supplies the whole text and "0".
  • .parse().ok()? appears three times. parse gives a Result, .ok() turns it into an Option, and ? leaves the function with None if the text was not a number.
  • One digit after the point means tenths (7.8 is 780 cents), so it is multiplied by 10. More than two digits are refused.
  • Parsing into u64 rejects negative prices for free, because "-3" is not a valid u64.

Step 3: read one line

The first two statements do a lot:

  • line.split(',').map(|field| field.trim()).collect() is a small pipeline: cut at the commas, trim each piece, gather the pieces in a vector.
  • let [date, product, category, quantity, price] = fields[..] else { ... } is a slice pattern in a let … else. It fits only if the vector has exactly five elements, and gives each of them a name in the same step. With four or six fields, the else block reports the problem.

Each conversion that can fail gets its own message. map_err replaces the standard error of parse with a sentence that includes the offending text. ok_or turns the Option from parse_price into a Result. In both cases ? ends the function early if something is wrong.

Watch out
Real CSV is harder

Splitting at commas is enough for this data. Real CSV files may contain commas inside quoted fields ("Smith, John"), quotes inside quotes, and line breaks inside fields. For real work, use the csv crate together with serde (chapter 43). It handles all of that and fills your structs directly.

Step 4: read everything, and keep track of problems

The order of the adapters matters:

  1. lines() yields each line.
  2. enumerate() numbers them from 0. It comes before any skipping or filtering, so that the numbers are the true line numbers of the file.
  3. skip(1) drops the header.
  4. filter(...) drops empty lines. The closure receives a reference to a pair, and the pattern (_, line) takes the pair apart.

The loop then sorts each result into one of two vectors. The function returns both as a tuple. The caller gets all the good data and a complete list of what was wrong and where.

Tip
Two ways to deal with bad rows

In the last chapter you saw that an iterator of Results can be collected into one Result<Vec<_>, _>, which gives up at the first error. That is right when one bad row makes the whole input worthless, for example a configuration file. For a report over many rows, collecting the problems and carrying on is more useful. Decide this consciously for each program.

Step 5: summaries with iterators

Totals are one line each:

map(Sale::revenue) passes the method by name. It means the same as map(|s| s.revenue()).

Now the interesting part. The report needs the revenue per category, per month and per product. These are three versions of the same calculation: “put the sales into groups and add up each group”. Only the meaning of “group” differs. So write the calculation once, and let a closure say what the group of a sale is:

It is used like this:

Three reports from one function, and a fourth (by date, by first letter, anything) costs one more line.

The signature combines what you learned in Part 4 and Part 5:

  • F: Fn(&'a Sale) -> &'a str says that key is a closure that takes a reference to a sale and returns a string slice borrowed from that sale.
  • The result, Vec<(&'a str, u64)>, contains those same borrowed names. The lifetime 'a ties them to the sales slice. No name is copied, however many sales there are.
  • Inside, the map counts with the entry pattern from chapter 15. Then the pairs are moved into a vector, which is sorted with a closure that compares the amounts in reverse (b before a), so the largest comes first.

A BTreeMap is used so that groups with equal revenue come out in alphabetical order, always the same. With a HashMap, their order could change from run to run.

Step 6: make it readable

Two small functions turn numbers into a tidy table:

  • money splits the cents into whole units and the remainder. It walks over the digits of the whole part and puts a comma wherever the number of digits still to come is a multiple of three. {:02} prints the cents with two digits, so 5 cents show as 05.
  • In print_table, the format specifiers from chapter 11 create the columns: {name:<16} is left-aligned in 16 characters, {:>14} is right-aligned in 14, and {share:>12.1} is right-aligned with one decimal place.
  • The share in percent is only for display, so a float is fine there.

The complete program

And the tests, to add at the end of the file:

The last lines of main use three more consumers: max_by_key finds the largest sale, filter(...).count() counts the sales above the average, and .max(1) on the length guards against a division by zero when there are no sales at all.

Look at main once more. It contains no loops except for printing the problems. Every calculation is a short pipeline that says what is wanted.

Make it better

PracticeRead a real file

Let the program take a file name as its first command-line argument. If one is given, read that file. Without an argument, use the built-in sample. A file that cannot be read should produce a message on the error stream and exit code 1.

Need a hint?

std::env::args().nth(1) gives Some(file_name) or None. Read with std::fs::read_to_string. Store the text in a String variable that lives until the end of main, because the sales are built from it. Use match on the argument: Some(path) reads the file, None gives SAMPLE.to_string().

Show solution and explanation

Only the source of the text changed. Everything after parse_all(&text) is untouched, because all the functions take a &str or a slice of sales and do not care where the data came from. That is the payoff of keeping input, calculation and output apart.

process::exit never returns, so the compiler accepts that this match arm does not produce a String. Its type is the never type !, which fits anywhere.

PracticeA bar chart

Add a function print_chart(title: &str, rows: &[(&str, u64)]) that prints one line per row with a bar made of # characters. The largest value gets a bar of 30 characters, and the others are scaled in proportion:

Need a hint?

Find the largest amount with rows.iter().map(|(_, amount)| *amount).max(). The length of a bar is amount * 30 / largest, in integer arithmetic. "#".repeat(length as usize) builds the bar. Guard against an empty list and against a largest value of 0.

Show solution and explanation

max() returns None for an empty list, and let … else turns that into an early return. The scaling multiplies before it divides (amount * 30 / largest), which keeps the precision in integer arithmetic. Dividing first would give 0 for every row but the largest.

Because revenue_by returns plain data, the same rows can be shown as a table or as a chart. Neither display function knows how the numbers were produced.

ChallengeFilters from the command line

Let the user restrict the report with options such as --category Food and --month 2026-02, in any combination. Build a list of filter closures from the arguments, and keep only the sales that pass all of them.

Need a hint?

The list has the type Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&Sale) -> bool>>. For --category X, push Box::new(move |s: &Sale| s.category == x). The move matters, because each closure must own the text it compares with. Then: sales.into_iter().filter(|sale| filters.iter().all(|f| f(sale))).collect().

Show solution and explanation

Each option becomes a closure that owns its own value (move). The closures are of three different hidden types, so they are boxed as dyn Fn(&Sale) -> bool to live in one vector. type Filter = … gives that long type a short name: a type alias.

The selection itself is one line: a sale is kept if all filters say yes. With an empty list of filters, all is true, and every sale is kept, which is exactly the right behaviour for “no options given”. Adding a new kind of filter needs one new match arm and nothing else.

What you have learned

Recap
  • A data program is a pipeline: raw text, typed values, summaries, output. Each stage is a small function.
  • Parse at the edge into a precise struct. Collect the problems with their line numbers, and carry on.
  • Store money as integer cents. Use floats only for display values such as percentages.
  • map, filter, sum, max_by_key, count and enumerate replace most hand-written loops.
  • A closure parameter turns three similar functions into one general function (revenue_by).
  • Lifetimes let the summaries borrow names from the data, with no copies.
  • Functions that return data, and do not print, can be tested and reused for different displays.

You have finished Part 5. Closures and iterators are now part of your everyday toolbox. Part 6 looks under the surface again: smart pointers, the deeper features of traits, and the finer points of Rust’s type system.

Smart pointers: Box, Rc, RefCell and friends

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Put data on the heap with Box and build recursive types
  • Explain what Deref and Drop do
  • Share ownership with Rc and break cycles with Weak
  • Change data behind a shared reference with Cell and RefCell
  • Pick the right pointer type for a task

A reference (&T) borrows a value and does nothing else. A smart pointer is a type that also points to data, but in addition owns it and adds some extra ability. You already know two: String and Vec<T> own a block of heap memory and manage it for you. This chapter introduces the smart pointers that are about ownership itself.

Real-world analogy
A smart keycard

A smart pointer is like a keycard that both opens a room and keeps track of who is allowed to use it. It points to the right place and carries extra rules about ownership, borrowing and cleanup.

TypeIn one sentence
Box<T>one owner, data on the heap
Rc<T>several owners, read-only, one thread
RefCell<T>borrowing rules checked while the program runs, not at compile time
Arc<T>, Mutex<T>the same ideas, safe to use from several threads (chapter 31)
Real-world analogy
A visitor badge vs a shared locker key

A normal reference (&T) is a visitor badge: it lets you read what is in a room, but it cannot keep the building open after the owner locks up and leaves. A smart pointer like Box<T> or Rc<T> is a deed or shared key card that actually keeps the data alive until the last holder steps out and closes the door.

Box<T>: a value on the heap

Box::new(value) moves a value to the heap and gives you a pointer to it. The box is the single owner. When the box goes out of scope, the heap memory is freed.

Step through it: A Box in memory
  1. fn main() {
  2. let a = 42;
  3. let b = Box::new(42);
  4. let c = b;
  5. println!("{a} {c}");
  6. }

Putting a single number in a box is pointless. A Box is needed in three situations.

1. Types that contain themselves

A list can be described as “an element, followed by a (shorter) list”. A direct translation does not compile:

The compiler must know the size of every type. A List would contain a List, which contains a List, without end: “infinite size”. The compiler’s hint is the solution. A Box is a pointer, and a pointer has a fixed, known size, whatever it points to:

Each node owns the next one through a box. The same trick builds trees, which appear everywhere in programming: folders that contain folders, the nested structure of a web page, the parts of a mathematical expression.

This is, in miniature, how compilers and calculators represent what you type.

Good to know
Do not build linked lists for everyday work

The linked list above is a teaching example. For a real sequence of values, a Vec is nearly always faster and simpler, because its elements sit side by side in memory.

2. Trait objects

You met Box<dyn Shape> in chapter 20. Values of different types have different sizes, so a collection of “anything that implements Shape” stores boxes, which all have the same size.

3. Large values

Moving a value copies its bytes. For a struct of several thousand bytes, moving a Box (one pointer) is cheaper than moving the struct itself.

Deref: why a box feels like its content

You can call methods of the inner value directly on a box, and pass a &Box<String> where a &str is wanted. The trait Deref makes this possible. It defines what the * operator returns for a type. When the types of a reference do not fit, the compiler inserts as many * steps as needed. That is called deref coercion.

You have relied on this since chapter 11: &String turns into &str, and &Vec<T> into &[T], by the same mechanism. String implements Deref with the target str.

Drop: code that runs at the end

When a value goes out of scope, Rust runs its destructor and then frees its memory. With the trait Drop you supply your own clean-up code:

  • Values are dropped at the end of their scope, in the reverse order of their creation.
  • drop(value) is an ordinary function that takes ownership of its argument and lets it go out of scope immediately.

You will rarely write Drop yourself. You benefit from it all the time: it is how a File closes itself, how a Vec frees its memory, and how a lock releases itself (chapter 31).

How other languages do it
RAII

Tying a resource (memory, a file, a lock, a network connection) to a value, so that the resource is released when the value dies, is a technique from C++ with the awkward name RAII (“resource acquisition is initialization”). In Java, Python or Go you write try … finally, with or defer each time, and can forget it. In Rust the clean-up is attached to the type once, and then it cannot be forgotten.

Rc<T>: several owners

Ownership has one owner per value. Sometimes that does not describe reality. Imagine a city map in which several routes pass through the same stations. No route is “the” owner of a station. The station should exist as long as any route uses it.

Rc<T> (for “reference counted”) allows several owners. It keeps a counter next to the value. Each Rc::clone adds one, each drop of an Rc subtracts one, and when the counter reaches zero, the value is freed.

Step through it: Shared ownership with Rc
  1. use std::rc::Rc;
  3. fn main() {
  4. let a = Rc::new(String::from("shared"));
  5. let b = Rc::clone(&a);
  6. drop(a);
  7. println!("{b}");
  8. }

Three things to remember:

  • Rc::clone(&a) is cheap. It copies a pointer and adds one to a number. By convention it is written as Rc::clone(&a) and not a.clone(), so that readers see at once that no data is copied.
  • The value is read-only. An Rc<T> gives out only shared references. With several owners, a &mut would break the borrowing rules.
  • One thread only. The counter is not protected against simultaneous changes. The compiler refuses to send an Rc to another thread. Arc is the thread-safe version.
How other languages do it
Rc is a small garbage collector

Reference counting is how Python and Swift manage all their objects, and what std::shared_ptr does in C++. In Rust it is something you choose for the few values that need it. Everything else keeps the cheaper single-owner model.

Interior mutability: Cell and RefCell

The borrowing rules say: either many readers, or one writer. The compiler enforces this before the program runs. Occasionally the rule is too strict. You know a change is safe, but the structure of the program hides that from the compiler. For such cases there are types that let you change a value through a shared reference. This is called interior mutability.

Cell<T>: for small Copy values

A Cell never hands out a reference to its content. You can only put a value in (set) or copy the value out (get). Nothing can be left dangling, so this is always safe:

Showing a page does not change it in any way its users care about, so show takes &self. The view counter is a detail on the inside.

RefCell<T>: the borrow checker at run time

A RefCell works for any type. You ask it for a borrow, and it checks the borrowing rules while the program runs:

  • .borrow() gives a shared borrow. Any number of them may exist together.
  • .borrow_mut() gives a mutable borrow. It must be the only borrow at that moment.

log is not declared mut, and yet its content changes. If you break the rules, the compiler does not catch it. The program panics:

Watch out
A trade, not a free lunch

RefCell moves a compile-time guarantee to run time. You gain flexibility. You lose the certainty that the program cannot fail that way, and you pay a tiny cost for each check. Use it when you have a clear reason, keep each borrow short, and prefer ordinary &mut wherever it works. To test without a panic, use try_borrow_mut(), which returns a Result.

The combination: Rc<RefCell<T>>

Rc gives several owners, but read-only access. RefCell gives changes through a shared reference. Together they give data with several owners that can be changed:

Two people share one account, and both can change it. Read the type from the outside in: Rc (shared ownership) of a RefCell (changeable inside) of an Account. You will see this shape in graphical user interfaces, in games, and in graph-like data structures, where many parts refer to the same object.

Cycles and Weak<T>

Reference counting has one weakness. If two values own each other through Rc, their counters can never reach zero, even when nothing else refers to them. The memory is never freed. This is a reference cycle, and it is a memory leak.

Think of a tree. A parent owns its children. A child should also be able to find its parent. If the child held an Rc to its parent, parent and child would own each other: a cycle.

The answer is a second kind of pointer, Weak<T>. A weak pointer refers to the value but does not own it, and does not keep it alive. Because the value may be gone, you must ask for access with .upgrade(), which returns an Option<Rc<T>>.

Rc::downgrade(&parent) creates a weak pointer. Ownership runs in one direction only, from parents down to children. The pointers upwards are weak. When root is dropped, the whole tree is freed.

Key idea
The rule for cycles

Decide which direction owns. Use Rc (or Box) in that direction, and Weak in the other. Parents own children. Children know their parents weakly.

Cow: copy only if you must

One more type from the standard library is worth knowing. Cow<str> (“clone on write”) holds either a borrowed &str or an owned String. It lets a function return its input unchanged, without copying, in the common case, and a new String only when a change was needed:

A Cow<str> can be used like a &str through Deref. The '_ in the return type is the placeholder lifetime from chapter 21: it shows the reader that the result may borrow from the argument. Cow is a tool for making code faster, and you can ignore it until you need it.

Choosing a pointer

You needUse
to look at a value for a while&T
to change a value for a while&mut T
one owner, on the heap (recursive type, trait object, big value)Box<T>
several owners, read-onlyRc<T>
several owners that can change the valueRc<RefCell<T>>
a pointer back to an owner, without owningWeak<T>
to change a small Copy field through &selfCell<T>
the same across threadsArc<T>, Arc<Mutex<T>> (chapter 31)

The order of this table is also the order of preference. Plain references and single ownership are the simplest and the fastest, and the compiler checks them completely. Reach for Rc and RefCell when the shape of your data truly demands shared ownership.

Recap
  • A smart pointer owns the data it points to and adds behaviour.
  • Box<T> puts a value on the heap with one owner. It makes recursive types and trait objects possible.
  • Deref lets a pointer be used like its content. Drop runs clean-up code when a value dies.
  • Rc<T> counts its owners and frees the value when the last one goes. It is read-only and for one thread.
  • Cell<T> and RefCell<T> allow changes through a shared reference. RefCell checks the borrowing rules at run time and panics if they are broken.
  • Rc<RefCell<T>> is shared, changeable data.
  • Rc cycles leak memory. Weak<T> points without owning and breaks the cycle.
Check your understanding
1

Why does enum List { Node(i32, List), End } not compile, while Node(i32, Box<List>) does?

A Box<List> has the size of one pointer, whatever it points to, so the size of List can be calculated.

2

What does Rc::clone(&a) do?

Cloning an Rc is cheap. The data exists once, and is freed when the last Rc is dropped.

3

What happens when borrow_mut() is called on a RefCell while a borrow() is still active?

RefCell enforces the borrowing rules at run time. A violation is a panic, not a compile error.

4

Two values hold an Rc to each other and nothing else refers to them. What happens?

Reference counting cannot free cycles. Make one of the two directions a Weak pointer.

5

In which order are the local variables of a function dropped?

The variable declared last is dropped first. Later variables may refer to earlier ones, so they must go first.

Guided exerciseA tree of numbers

Define a binary tree: enum Tree { Leaf, Node(Box<Tree>, i32, Box<Tree>) }. Write the methods sum(&self) -> i32 and depth(&self) -> usize (the number of levels, where a Leaf has depth 0). Build a small tree by hand and test both.

Need a hint?

Both methods are a match with two arms. For a node, sum is left.sum() + value + right.sum(), and depth is 1 + left.depth().max(right.depth()).

Show solution and explanation

A recursive data type is handled by recursive functions that have the same shape as the type: one match arm per variant. The helper Tree::node hides the Box::new calls and makes building a tree readable. Each node owns its two subtrees, so dropping the root frees the whole tree.

PracticeCount the clean-ups

Write a struct Tracker with a name and a shared counter of type Rc<Cell<u32>>. Implement Drop so that it adds one to the counter. In main, create three trackers in different scopes, and check after each step that the counter shows how many have been dropped so far.

Need a hint?

All trackers share one Rc<Cell<u32>>, created first. Each tracker gets an Rc::clone of it. In drop, write self.counter.set(self.counter.get() + 1);.

Show solution and explanation

The counter is owned jointly by main and by every tracker (Rc), and each tracker can change it through its shared pointer (Cell). _b is dropped at the end of its block, c by the explicit drop, and _a last, when main ends, after the final println!.

A variable name that starts with an underscore, like _a, tells the compiler “I know this is unused”, but the value still lives to the end of its scope. A lone _ is different: let _ = Tracker { ... }; drops the value immediately.

ChallengeA shared shopping list

Two household members share one shopping list. Model it with Rc<RefCell<Vec<String>>>. Write a struct Member { name: String, list: Rc<RefCell<Vec<String>>> } with the methods add(&self, item: &str) and buy(&self, item: &str) -> bool (removes the item if it is on the list). Show that an item added by one member can be bought by the other.

Need a hint?

self.list.borrow_mut().push(item.to_string()) adds. For buy, get one mutable borrow into a variable, find the position with list.iter().position(|i| i == item), and remove it. Do not call borrow_mut() twice in the same expression chain while the first borrow is still alive.

Show solution and explanation

Both members and main own the same list. In buy, the mutable borrow is taken once and stored in list. It ends when the method returns, so the next call can borrow again. Every borrow here is short and never overlaps with another, which is how RefCell should be used.

A different design avoids Rc<RefCell<…>> altogether: keep the list in one place, and pass &mut Vec<String> to functions that need it. That is often the better choice. Shared ownership is for cases where no single place can own the data.

ChallengeA stack made of boxes

Build a stack (the last value in is the first one out) as a linked list. Every node owns the next node:

Write a type Stack<T> with new, push, pop (returns Option<T>), peek (returns Option<&T>), len, and iter, which gives references to the values from the top down. Then push a million numbers and let the stack go out of scope.

Need a hint?

You cannot move a field out of &mut self and leave a hole. self.top.take() moves the value out of the Option and leaves None in its place. To look without taking, as_ref() turns &Option<Box<Node<T>>> into Option<&Box<Node<T>>>, and as_deref() goes one step further to Option<&Node<T>>. If the program ends with “has overflowed its stack”, think about what dropping one node does to the next node.

Show solution and explanation

Three things in this small program come up again and again in Rust:

  1. take() to move out from behind &mut. push needs the old top as an owned value, to put it inside the new node. take hands it over and leaves None, so self.top is never without a value, not even for a moment. pop does the same, and the ? after take() returns None at once when the stack is empty.
  2. as_ref() and as_deref() to look without taking. peek and the iterator only borrow. The iterator holds Option<&Node<T>>: the node it will give out next.
  3. A drop that does not call itself. Without the impl Drop, Rust would drop the first node, which drops the second node inside it, which drops the third, a million calls deep. Tried without it, this program stopped with thread 'main' has overflowed its stack. The loop unlinks each node before it is dropped, so every node is dropped alone.

For real work, use a Vec: push and pop do the same job, and the values sit side by side in memory, which is much faster to walk through (chapter 52). A linked list is worth writing once, because it trains exactly the moves that the borrow checker asks for.
