Traits in depth

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Use associated types and constants, and know when to prefer them to generic parameters
  • Overload operators such as + and == for your own types
  • Implement a trait for many types at once with a blanket implementation
  • Explain what makes a trait usable as dyn Trait
  • Recognise the marker traits Sized, Send and Sync

Chapter 20 covered the everyday use of traits. This chapter collects the features you meet when you read the standard library, design a library of your own, or wonder how a + b works for your own type. You can read it once now and come back when you need a particular tool.

Real-world analogy
A manager with special rules

A trait is like a job description: it says what a type must be able to do. Associated types are the extra details that each person in that role supplies, like “this team produces numbers, that team produces strings”.

Associated types

Real-world analogy
A country’s power socket vs a universal adapter

Every Iterator implementation has one natural element type (Item), just as each country’s wall socket delivers one fixed voltage: you plug in and ask for Self::Item without listing extra parameters. By contrast, a generic trait parameter (From<T>) is like a travel adapter that can have many implementations (From<&str>, From<char>, From<Box<str>>) for the very same String type.

The Iterator trait has a line type Item;. That is an associated type: a type that each implementation of the trait chooses, once.

Inside the trait, the type is written Self::Item. From outside, it is C::Item, and it can have bounds of its own, as in the where clause above.

Associated type or generic parameter?

A trait could also take a type parameter: trait Container<T>. The difference:

trait Convert<T> (generic parameter)trait Iterator { type Item; } (associated type)
Implementations per typemany: one for each Texactly one
Who chooses the typethe user of the traitthe implementer
ExampleFrom<T>: a String can be made from &str, from char, from Box<str>, …Iterator: a given iterator yields one kind of item

The question to ask: can a type sensibly implement this trait several times, with different types? If yes, use a generic parameter. If there is one natural answer per type, use an associated type. It keeps signatures shorter, because users write impl Iterator<Item = u32> and the compiler never has to guess.

Generic associated types: a type that depends on a lifetime

Everything above has one hidden limitation: an associated type cannot mention a lifetime. type Item = &str is not a type — it is missing the lifetime of the borrow — and type Item<'a> was not allowed until 2022. A generic associated type, or GAT, lets the associated type take parameters of its own, and the usual parameter is a lifetime.

The difference is easiest to see on a type that lends out a view of its insides:

Read the impl line by line:

  • type Item<'a> = (&'a str, &'a [u32]) — the associated type now has a lifetime, and that lifetime is supplied by the method that uses it. Each call to view picks a lifetime; the compiler chooses one no longer than the borrow.
  • where Self: 'a — the promise that the value itself outlives the borrow it lends. Without it, a &'a str taken from self could outlive self, which is the dangling-reference bug Rust exists to prevent. The compiler will not accept a GAT impl that needs this bound and omits it, and the error message says so.
  • fn view(&self) -> Self::Item<'_> — the '_ is the elided lifetime of &self, so the returned tuple cannot outlive the borrow. Try to keep it after the Report is dropped and the borrow checker refuses, exactly as it would for a plain &str.

The pattern GATs were stabilised for is the lending iterator: an iterator whose next returns items that borrow from the iterator itself. The signature says it all —

— and the ordinary Iterator trait cannot express it, because type Item has no lifetime to lend. This is why Iterator only ever yields owned values or references borrowed from somewhere else. The three places GATs earn their keep:

  1. Lending iterators, as above: cursors over a buffer, parsers that yield borrowed tokens, streaming decoders.
  2. Traits over async or fallible work, where the “output” borrows from the input — the reason the async-trait crate existed before async functions in traits.
  3. Borrowing views of a container, like View above: an associated type that is a projection into self.

They are stable since Rust 1.65, so no feature flag is needed; you will meet them mostly when reading library code rather than when writing it. When you do write one, two rules save hours: put the where Self: 'a bound on both the trait and the impl, and keep the borrow as short as the method allows rather than trying to return it from a longer-lived function.

Associated constants

A trait can also demand a constant:

describe has no self parameter. It is an associated function of the trait and is called on the type: Triangle::describe().

Operator overloading

When you write a + b, Rust calls a.add(b), a method of the trait std::ops::Add. Implement the trait for your type, and the operator works for it. This is called operator overloading.

  • type Output is an associated type: the type of the result.
  • Mul<f64> uses the trait’s generic parameter for the right-hand side. That is why Add has both: the right-hand type is chosen by a parameter (a type may be added to several other types), and for each such pair there is one output type.
  • The type is Copy, so a and b can be used again after a + b. Without Copy, the operator would move its operands, since add takes self.
OperatorTraitOperatorTrait
a + bAdda += bAddAssign
a - bSub-aNeg
a * bMul!aNot
a / bDiva[i]Index, IndexMut
a % bRema == bPartialEq
a & b, a | b, a ^ bBitAnd, BitOr, BitXora < bPartialOrd
a << b, a >> bShl, Shr*aDeref, DerefMut
Tip
Overload with restraint

Give an operator only its usual meaning. + for vectors, money or durations is clear. + for “add a user to a group” is a puzzle for every reader. Rust has a fixed set of operators. You cannot invent new ones.

Writing PartialEq and Ord by hand

Usually you derive comparisons. Write them yourself when equality or order should not look at every field:

then_with chains comparisons: if the first one says “equal”, the second decides. Write Ord::cmp once, and let partial_cmp call it, so that the two can never disagree. Keep == consistent with cmp, too: two values that compare as Equal must also be ==.

Blanket implementations

An impl can cover every type that fulfils a bound, all at once:

One impl block gave the method loud to strings, numbers, booleans, and to every type anybody will ever write that implements Display. This is a blanket implementation.

The standard library uses the technique in several well-known places:

  • impl<T: Display> ToString for T is why everything that can be printed has .to_string().
  • impl<T, U: From<T>> Into<U> for T is why implementing From gives you .into() for free.
  • impl<I: Iterator> IntoIterator for I is why every iterator can be used in a for loop.

Two methods with the same name

Two traits may define methods with the same name, and a type may implement both. A plain method call then picks the type’s own method, if it has one. To choose another, name the trait:

The form <Type as Trait>::function(...) is the fully qualified syntax. It is the most explicit way to say which function you mean, and it always works. You need it rarely, mostly for associated functions without self, where there is no argument that tells the compiler the type.

The newtype pattern and the orphan rule

The orphan rule from chapter 20 forbids implementing a foreign trait for a foreign type. The way around it is a newtype: a tuple struct of your own with one field.

Wrapper is your type, so you may implement any trait for it. The wrapper costs nothing at run time: it has exactly the same memory layout as the vector inside. The price is that the methods of Vec are not available on Wrapper directly. You reach them through .0, or pass the calls on, or implement Deref.

The opposite wish: a trait nobody else may implement

Sometimes a library wants everybody to use a trait, but nobody outside to implement it. Then the library can add methods to the trait later without breaking anyone’s code, and it knows the complete list of implementing types. The trick is a supertrait that outsiders cannot name. Such a trait is called a sealed trait:

The compiler even knows the name of the trick: the last note of the message calls Shape a “sealed trait”. Shape requires Sealed, and Sealed lives in a private module. Code outside shapes can call area on a Square, but it cannot write impl shapes::private::Sealed for Triangle, so it cannot implement Shape either. Many traits in the standard library and in popular crates are sealed in this way.

What can be a dyn Trait?

Not every trait can be used as a trait object. A dyn Trait value has forgotten its concrete type, and some methods cannot work without it. A trait is dyn compatible (older texts say “object safe”) if, roughly:

  • none of its methods has a generic type parameter,
  • none of its methods returns Self or takes another Self by value,
  • it does not require Self: Sized.

duplicate returns Self. For a dyn Duplicate, nobody knows what Self is or how large it is. This is the reason Clone cannot be used as dyn Clone.

The message mentions a vtable (“virtual method table”). That is the small table of function addresses that every trait object carries with it. Through it, the program finds the right method at run time. Chapter 37 shows what it looks like in memory.

You can keep such a method in a trait and still use the trait as an object, by telling the compiler that this one method is not available on trait objects:

Asking for the concrete type: Any

A &dyn Shape has forgotten which type it points to. Rust has one small tool for asking: the trait Any, which is implemented for every type that holds no borrowed data. Its method downcast_ref::<T>() returns Some only if the value really is a T:

That is all the “reflection” Rust has. A program cannot list the fields or methods of a type while it runs. (type_name is meant for log messages only.)

The place where you will meet downcasting most often is error handling. A Box<dyn Error> hides the error type, and downcast_ref brings it back when you need to react to one particular kind:

Watch out
Downcasting is a last resort

A chain of downcast_ref calls is a match that the compiler cannot check: add a new type, and nothing tells you that a case is missing. If you know the possible types, use an enum. If the types share behaviour, put a method in the trait. Keep Any for the few places that truly store “anything”, such as the error boxes above, or a container that holds one value per type.

Marker traits: Sized, Send, Sync, Copy

Some traits have no methods. They only state a fact about a type, which the compiler uses. They are called marker traits.

  • Copy you know: values are duplicated instead of moved.
  • Sized means “the size of this type is known at compile time”. Nearly all types are Sized. The exceptions are str, slices [T], and dyn Trait, which is why you only meet them behind a pointer: &str, &[T], Box<dyn Trait>. Every generic parameter has an invisible T: Sized bound. Writing T: ?Sized removes it and allows these types too:
  • Send means “a value of this type can be handed to another thread”. Sync means “a value of this type can be used from several threads at the same time, through shared references”. The compiler works these out for every type automatically, and uses them to reject programs with data races. They are the foundation of Part 7.

Traits with generic methods and supertraits, together

A realistic example brings several features together: a small plug-in system for text filters.

Filter: Debug is a supertrait: every filter must be printable, and the default method describe relies on it. NAME is an associated constant. run is generic over two independent filter types and is compiled separately for each pair that is used.

How other languages do it
How other languages do these things
  • Operator overloading exists in C++, Python (__add__), C# and Kotlin. Java and Go do not have it. Rust’s version is limited to a fixed list of operators, each tied to one trait.
  • Blanket implementations have no real counterpart in Java or C#. The nearest relatives are extension methods (C#, Kotlin), and Haskell’s type class instances with constraints, which inspired the feature.
  • Associated types correspond to Haskell’s associated type families and Swift’s associatedtype. C++ uses nested typedefs in templates for a similar purpose.
Recap
  • An associated type is chosen once per implementation (type Item = u32;). Use a generic parameter when a type should implement the trait several times.
  • Traits can require constants (const NAME: &str;).
  • Operators are traits from std::ops. Implement Add to make + work.
  • A blanket implementation (impl<T: Display> Loud for T) covers all types with a given ability.
  • <Type as Trait>::function() says exactly which implementation to call.
  • A newtype lets you implement foreign traits for foreign data.
  • A trait is usable as dyn Trait only if its methods work without knowing the concrete type.
  • Sized, Send, Sync and Copy are marker traits: facts about a type, with no methods.
Check your understanding
1

Why does Iterator use an associated type Item and not a generic parameter Iterator<T>?

With Iterator<T>, one type could implement Iterator<u32> and Iterator<String> at once, and every call of next would be ambiguous. An associated type fixes the item type per implementation.

2

Why does a generic associated type often need the bound where Self: 'a?

The GAT promises type Item<'a>, and an implementation may hand out &'a str taken from self. Without Self: 'a the borrow could outlive the value it points into, which is exactly the dangling reference the borrow checker exists to reject. The bound states the relationship once, so every caller gets it checked.

3

What must you implement so that a + b works for your type Money?

The + operator is syntax for the add method of the Add trait. Only types that implement the trait can be added.

4

What does impl<T: Display> Summary for T { ... } do?

This is a blanket implementation. Every present and future type with Display gets Summary.

5

Why can the trait Clone not be used as Box<dyn Clone>?

A method that returns Self by value needs the concrete type. That makes the trait not dyn compatible.

6

Which of these types is not Sized?

str is text of unknown length, so its size is not known at compile time. String and Box<str> are pointers with a fixed size.

Guided exerciseMoney that adds up

Define struct Money { cents: i64 } and implement Add (money plus money), Mul<i64> (money times a whole number), and Display (so that 1250 cents print as 12.50). Compute the price of 3 items at 4.99 plus 2.50 for shipping.

Need a hint?

impl Add for Money { type Output = Money; fn add(self, other: Money) -> Money { ... } }. Derive Clone, Copy so that values can be reused. For Display: write!(f, "{}.{:02}", self.cents / 100, self.cents % 100).

Show solution and explanation

With the operators in place, the calculation reads like the arithmetic it describes. The types also protect you: Money * Money does not compile, because no such Mul exists, and multiplying two amounts of money has no meaning. This Display is only correct for amounts that are not negative. A complete version would handle the sign separately.

PracticeA container with an associated type

Define a trait Stack with an associated type Item and the methods push(&mut self, item: Self::Item), pop(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> and is_empty(&self) -> bool. Implement it for Vec<T>. Then write a generic function drain_all<S: Stack>(stack: &mut S) -> usize that pops until the stack is empty and returns how many items it removed.

Need a hint?

The implementation starts with impl<T> Stack for Vec<T> { type Item = T; ... }. Inside it, call the vector’s own methods with the fully qualified form, for example Vec::push(self, item), so that it is clear which push is meant.

Show solution and explanation

impl<T> Stack for Vec<T> is itself a small blanket implementation: it covers vectors of every element type, and each one gets Item = T. drain_all never mentions the item type. It only needs to know that pop returns an Option of something.

The trait’s methods have the same names as the vector’s own. The vector’s inherent methods win in a plain call like numbers.push(4), so the example uses Stack::push(&mut numbers, 4) to call the trait’s version explicitly.

ChallengeA matrix with Index and Mul

Write struct Matrix { rows: usize, cols: usize, data: Vec<f64> }. Implement Index<(usize, usize)> and IndexMut<(usize, usize)>, so that m[(row, col)] reads and writes a cell. Then implement Mul for &Matrix so that &a * &b gives the matrix product. Multiply a 2×3 by a 3×2 matrix.

Need a hint?

The cell (r, c) is at position r * cols + c in data. Index has an associated type Output = f64 and a method fn index(&self, (r, c): (usize, usize)) -> &f64. For the product, the result has a.rows rows and b.cols columns, and each cell is the sum of a[(i, k)] * b[(k, j)] over k. Implement impl Mul for &Matrix, so that the operands are not consumed.

Show solution and explanation

Index returns a reference (&f64). Rust adds the * for you when you write m[(r, c)], and the same expression on the left of = uses IndexMut. The parameter pattern (r, c): (usize, usize) takes the tuple apart right in the signature.

Mul is implemented for &Matrix, a reference, so &a * &b borrows both operands and leaves them usable. An implementation for Matrix by value would consume both matrices on every multiplication. Whether sizes fit is checked at run time here, with assert_eq!. With const generics (chapter 19), a Matrix<const R: usize, const C: usize> could let the compiler check it.

The type system as a design tool

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Convert between types safely with From, TryFrom, FromStr and AsRef
  • Use newtypes and type aliases to make code clearer and safer
  • Explain the never type, zero-sized types and dynamically sized types
  • Encode rules in types so that wrong programs do not compile (the typestate pattern)
  • Apply “parse, don’t validate” and “make invalid states unrepresentable”

So far you have used types to describe data. Experienced Rust programmers use them for something more: to make certain mistakes impossible to write. The compiler checks type rules before the program runs, at no cost while it runs. Types can enforce many important rules, but they complement tests rather than replace them.

This chapter first completes the picture of conversions between types, then presents the less obvious types of the language, and ends with the design techniques that tie them together.

Real-world analogy
Labels on shipping boxes

Every value in Rust carries a type label. A newtype is a label that says, “this is not just a number; it is a percentage, a distance, or an amount in a specific unit.” The compiler checks the label before the code runs, so many dangerous mistakes are impossible to write.

Converting between types

as: quick and quiet

as converts between number types (and a few others). It always succeeds, and that is the problem with it: when the value does not fit, it silently produces a different value.

Use as when losing information is intended or cannot happen: a small integer type to a bigger one, or an integer to a float for a division. For everything else there are conversions that cannot lose data, and conversions that report failure.

From and Into: conversions that cannot fail

From is for conversions that always succeed and are intended to preserve meaning:

There is no i32::from(some_i64) and no f32::from(some_f64). For a narrowing integer conversion, use TryFrom to check the range; for a float conversion, use an explicit cast only when its behavior is acceptable. The standard library avoids providing potentially lossy conversions through From.

TryFrom and TryInto: conversions that may fail

When a conversion works only for some values, it returns a Result:

This is the “safer conversion” promised in chapter 4. Wherever a number crosses from one integer type to another and might not fit, prefer try_from to as.

Implement TryFrom for your own types when construction can fail. It is the conventional home for validation:

FromStr: from text

"42".parse::<i32>() works through the trait FromStr. Implement it, and your type can be parsed in the same way:

strip_prefix returns the rest of the text if it starts with the given character, as an Option. u8::from_str_radix(text, 16) reads a number in base 16. The small closure part avoids writing the same conversion three times.

AsRef: accept many types cheaply

A function that only needs to look at some text can accept “anything that can be seen as a &str”:

AsRef<Path> lets many functions in std::fs accept values such as &str, String, Path and PathBuf through one parameter type.

I have … and want …Use
a number, in a bigger number typei64::from(x) or x.into()
a number, in a type where it might not fitu8::try_from(x)
a number, and I accept cutting it offx as u8
text, and want a valuetext.parse::<T>() (FromStr)
a value, and want textvalue.to_string() (Display)
my type from another type, always possibleimpl From<Other> for Mine
my type from another type, with a checkimpl TryFrom<Other> for Mine
a parameter that accepts several text or path typesimpl AsRef<str>, impl AsRef<Path>

Newtypes: different meanings, different types

A function with the signature fn transfer(from: u64, to: u64, amount: u64) takes three numbers of the same type. Nothing stops a caller from passing them in the wrong order. The mistake compiles, and moves the wrong amount from the wrong account.

Wrap each meaning in its own type:

The mix-up is now a compile error. A newtype costs nothing at run time. In memory, an AccountId is a u64.

Look closely at the fix the compiler proposes: transfer(bob, alice, amount). The types fit now, but the money would flow from Bob to Alice, which is not what was meant. from and to have the same type, so the compiler cannot tell them apart. Types catch exactly the mistakes that you have taught them to catch. (Two different types, Sender and Receiver, would catch this one too.)

Newtypes do three jobs:

  1. Keep apart values with different meanings (ids, units of measurement, kinds of text).
  2. Guarantee a property: with a private field and a checking constructor, as in the Celsius exercise of chapter 17.
  3. Allow trait implementations for foreign types (chapter 28).
Good to know
A famous unit mix-up

In 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter, a spacecraft worth more than 300 million dollars. One piece of software produced a force in pound-seconds, and another expected newton-seconds. Both were plain numbers. With one type per unit, such a program does not compile.

Type aliases: a second name

type gives an existing type an additional name. It does not create a new type:

Aliases shorten long types, and that is all. Since Kilometres and f64 are the same type, the compiler will not notice if you pass miles. For protection, use a newtype. The alias Result<T> with a fixed error type is a common convention: std::io::Result<T> and anyhow::Result<T> are aliases of this kind.

The types at the edges

The unit type ()

() is a type with exactly one value, also written (). It carries no information. It is what a function returns when it has nothing to return, and it is the Ok type in Result<(), Error>: “it worked, and there is nothing more to say”.

The never type !

Some expressions never produce a value at all, because control never comes back from them: panic!(), return, break, continue, an endless loop, and std::process::exit(). Their type is !, the never type. It can stand in for any type, which is why this compiles:

Both arms of a match must have the same type. One arm is a u32, and the other never finishes, so there is no conflict. You have relied on this in every let … else { return; } and every Err(_) => continue.

Zero-sized types

A struct without fields takes up no memory at all. So does (), and so does an array of length zero.

The second line confirms that a newtype is free. The third shows that Option<&T> is no bigger than &T: because references cannot be null, Rust can use the null-pointer representation for None.

Zero-sized types are useful as markers: types that exist only to tell things apart at compile time. They are the basis of the typestate pattern below.

Dynamically sized types

str, [T] and dyn Trait have no size known at compile time, so they cannot be stored directly where a fixed-size value is required. References to them are fat pointers: they carry an address plus metadata, usually a length for str and slices or a pointer to a method table for dyn Trait. On a 64-bit target, these references are typically twice the size of a thin pointer.

(These are the sizes on a 64-bit computer.)

PhantomData: a type parameter with no data

Sometimes a struct should have a type parameter that appears in none of its fields. The compiler rejects unused parameters. The zero-sized type PhantomData<T> says “treat this struct as if it held a T”:

Length<Metres> and Length<Feet> are different types that share all their code. Adding them is a compile error. The unit exists only for the compiler: the struct is 8 bytes, the size of its one f64.

The typestate pattern

Many objects have a life story with rules: a file must be opened before it is read, a letter must be written before it is sent, an order must be paid before it is shipped. Usually such rules are checked at run time, with a state field and error returns. The typestate pattern puts the state into the type, so that calling an operation in the wrong state does not compile.

Each state is its own type, with only the methods that make sense in that state. A Draft has no publish method, so an article cannot be published without a review. A Published has no write method. Every transition takes self by value: the old state is consumed, and ownership makes sure nobody keeps using it.

There is no state field, no run-time check, and no error to handle for “wrong state”. Such mistakes cannot be expressed. Typestates are used in real libraries: builders that refuse to build until all required parts are set, network connections that must complete a handshake before data can be sent, and hardware pins in embedded programming that are configured as either input or output.

Tip
When it is worth it

Typestates shine when the states and transitions are few and fixed, and a mistake would be costly. If the state is only known at run time (loaded from a file, chosen by a user), an enum with a match is the simpler tool.

Two design principles

Make invalid states unrepresentable

Look at this struct for a network connection:

Five fields allow many combinations that mean nothing. Connected and connecting? Connected without a session id? An error together with a session? Every function that receives a Connection must cope with them or hope they do not occur. Now the same information as an enum:

Exactly four situations exist, and each carries precisely the data that belongs to it. A session id can only exist in the Connected state. The meaningless combinations are gone, because there is no way to write them down.

Signs that a type allows invalid states: several bool fields, Option fields that are “only set when …”, and comments such as “must not be empty” or “only valid if kind is 2”.

Parse, don’t validate

A validating function checks its input and returns bool or Result<(), Error>. The knowledge “this was checked” is then lost, and the same string travels on, looking like any other string. Every function further down must trust that someone checked, or check again.

A parsing function checks its input and returns a new type that can only exist if the check passed:

The check happens once, at the edge of the program. From then on, the type Email is the proof. send_welcome needs no check and no error case of its own. You have followed this principle in every project so far: the Command enum of the to-do list, the Config of the search tool, the Sale of the report.

(The check here is deliberately simple. Real address validation has more rules.)

How other languages do it
Type systems compared
  • Python, JavaScript, Ruby are dynamically typed: values have types, variables do not, and a type mistake shows up when the faulty line runs, perhaps in production. Type checkers such as mypy and TypeScript add static checks on top.
  • C has static types but lets you convert almost anything to anything, and has no way to say “this pointer is never null”.
  • Java, C#, Go are statically typed too, but each has different tools for representing nullable values and alternatives. Rust models absence explicitly with Option<T> and can put different data in each enum variant.
  • Rust shares design ideas with Haskell, OCaml, F# and Swift: data-carrying enums, exhaustive matching, and generics checked through traits. In safe Rust, references cannot be null; Rust also adds ownership and lifetimes.
Recap
  • as always succeeds and may change the value. From/Into cannot fail and are intended for value-preserving conversions. TryFrom/TryInto return a Result. FromStr powers .parse(). AsRef makes parameters flexible.
  • A newtype gives a meaning its own type, at no run-time cost. A type alias is only a shorter name.
  • () has one value. ! has none and fits anywhere. Structs without fields take no memory. str, [T] and dyn Trait live behind fat pointers.
  • PhantomData<T> adds a type parameter that exists only at compile time.
  • The typestate pattern makes each state a type, so that operations in the wrong state do not compile.
  • Make invalid states unrepresentable: prefer one enum to several flags and options.
  • Parse, don’t validate: turn checked input into a type that proves the check.
Check your understanding
1

What does 300_i32 as u8 produce?

as never fails. It keeps the lowest 8 bits: 300 − 256 = 44. Use u8::try_from(300) to get an error value in such a case.

2

Why is there i64::from(x) for an i32, but no i32::from(x) for an i64?

For the direction that can fail, the standard library offers TryFrom, which returns a Result.

3

What is the difference between type Metres = f64; and struct Metres(f64);?

An alias gives no protection: Metres and f64 are interchangeable. A newtype is checked by the compiler and has the same size as its content.

4

Why may one arm of a match be panic!("…") while the other arms are u32?

An expression of type ! never produces a value, so it can stand wherever any type is required.

5

In the typestate pattern, why do the transition methods take self by value?

Moving self into the method ends the life of the old state. The only thing the caller has afterwards is the value of the new type.

Guided exerciseA username that is always valid

Write struct Username(String) with impl TryFrom<&str> for Username. The rules: 3 to 16 characters, only ASCII letters, digits and _. The error type is String and says which rule was broken. Add as_str(&self) -> &str. Test with "sara_92", "ab" and "no spaces".

Need a hint?

impl TryFrom<&str> for Username { type Error = String; fn try_from(value: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> { ... } }. Check the length with value.chars().count(), and the characters with value.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || c == '_').

Show solution and explanation

TryFrom is the standard trait for “construct with a check”, so other Rust programmers know at once how to create a Username, and "sara".try_into() works as well. Put the type in its own module, and the private field makes try_from the only door: every Username in the program is then known to be valid.

PracticeParse a duration

Implement FromStr for struct Minutes(u32) so that "90", "45m" and "2h" can be parsed (as 90, 45 and 120 minutes). Anything else is an error.

Need a hint?

Use strip_suffix('h') and strip_suffix('m'), which return an Option<&str> with the rest of the text. Check for h first. Parse the remaining digits with .parse::<u32>() and convert the error with map_err.

Show solution and explanation

Implementing FromStr plugs the type into the standard .parse() method, and into every library that builds on it. The command-line parser clap (chapter 44), for example, can accept a Minutes argument directly. The if let … else if let … else chain produces a pair, which is taken apart in the same let. checked_mul turns an out-of-range hour count into an error instead of allowing an overflow.

PracticeRemove the impossible states

This struct describes a payment. List at least three combinations of field values that make no sense. Then redesign it as an enum in which only meaningful states can be written, and write a function summary(&Payment) -> String.

Need a hint?

Meaningless: paid without a paid_at date. Refunded but not paid. A refund reason without a refund. Not paid, but with a date. The states are really three: pending, paid (with a date), refunded (with a date and a reason). The amount belongs to all of them.

Show solution and explanation

The original struct allowed 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 combinations of flags and options, of which three are meaningful. The enum allows exactly those three. A refund without a payment date cannot be written, and summary has no “should never happen” branch.

If the amount is needed without matching on the state, a common alternative is a struct Payment { amount: u32, status: Status } with the enum inside.

ChallengeA door that cannot be misused

Model a door with the typestate pattern. The states are Open, Closed and Locked. Allowed transitions: an open door can be closed, a closed door can be opened or locked (with a code), and a locked door can be unlocked with the right code. Unlocking with a wrong code must give the locked door back. Use one generic struct Door<State>.

Need a hint?

Use struct Door<State> { state: State }, where the state types are struct Open;, struct Closed; and struct Locked { code: u32 }. Write one impl block per state: impl Door<Open> { fn close(self) -> Door<Closed> } and so on. unlock returns Result<Door<Closed>, Door<Locked>>. The error case hands the still locked door back to the caller.

Show solution and explanation

Door<Open>, Door<Closed> and Door<Locked> are three types that share one struct definition. Each impl block gives one state its methods. Locking an open door, or opening a locked one, is not an error to be handled. It cannot be written.

unlock is the interesting case: whether it works depends on a value known only at run time, so it returns a Result. Because unlock takes self by value, the error variant must give the door back, or it would be lost. Returning the original value in the Err case is a common idiom for operations that consume their input and may fail.

Part 7 · ConcurrencyAdvancedabout 55 min
30

Threads: doing several things at once

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain concurrency, parallelism, threads and data races
  • Start threads, wait for them and get their results
  • Share local data with scoped threads
  • Send data between threads through channels
  • Explain how Send and Sync let the compiler rule out data races

Every program you have written so far did one thing at a time, from the first line of main to the last. Modern computers have several processor cores, typically between 4 and 16, and each can run code at the same moment. A program that uses one of them leaves most of the machine idle. A program may also have to wait for several things at once: a download, a key press, a timer.

Doing several things at once is one of the hardest parts of programming in most languages. It is also where Rust’s ownership rules pay off most. The same rules that prevent dangling references prevent the worst concurrency bug, and they do so at compile time. The Rust community calls this fearless concurrency.

Words first

  • Concurrency means dealing with several tasks in overlapping periods of time. One cook who chops vegetables while the soup simmers works concurrently.
  • Parallelism means really doing several things at the same instant. Two cooks, each at their own stove, work in parallel. Parallelism needs several cores.
  • A process is a running program with its own, separate memory. Your browser and your editor are processes.
  • A thread is one line of execution inside a process. Every program starts with one, the main thread, and can start more. All threads of a process share its memory.
Real-world analogy
Cooks in one kitchen

A restaurant kitchen with one cook can prepare one dish at a time. Hire three more, and four dishes are in progress at once. But the cooks share one kitchen: one fridge, one spice rack, one order board. If two of them grab the same pan, or one changes an order while another is reading it, there is chaos. More cooks means more speed, and it means rules for sharing.

Sharing memory is what makes threads efficient, and what makes them dangerous.

Key idea
What a data race is

A data race happens when two threads access the same piece of memory at the same time, at least one of them writes, and nothing coordinates them. The result depends on tiny timing differences. A program with a data race may work a million times and then corrupt its data once, on a customer’s machine, in a way nobody can reproduce.

Look at the definition again: several accesses, at least one writer. That is exactly what the borrowing rule “many readers or one writer” forbids. Rust extends that rule across threads. A safe Rust program cannot contain a data race. The compiler rejects it.

Starting a thread

thread::spawn takes a closure and runs it in a new thread:

Run it several times. The lines of the two threads mix, and the exact order can change from run to run. The operating system decides when each thread gets to run, and you cannot predict it. That unpredictability is the heart of what makes concurrent programs hard. (thread::sleep pauses the current thread. It is here to give the other thread a chance to run in between.)

spawn returns a JoinHandle. Calling .join() on it waits until the thread has finished.

Watch out
When main ends, everything ends

If the main thread reaches the end of main, the whole program stops, even if other threads are in the middle of their work. Call join on every thread whose work you need.

Getting a result back

The closure’s return value comes out of join:

Four threads calculate at the same time. The results are collected in the order of the handles, so the output is always the same, whichever thread happened to finish first. join returns a Result. It is an Err if the thread panicked:

A panic ends only the thread in which it happens. The other threads go on, and whoever joins the thread learns about the failure.

Threads and ownership: move

A thread may use data from the place where it was started. Borrowing that data does not work:

The new thread might still be running when the function that owns names has returned and names is gone. The compiler cannot know how long the thread will live, so it refuses the borrow. The fix it suggests is move: give the data to the thread.

Ownership has moved into the thread. The main thread can no longer touch names, so the two threads cannot conflict over it. This is the first of three ways to give data to threads: hand it over completely.

Scoped threads: borrowing after all

Often the threads are only needed for a moment, to split up some work, and they should work on data that the caller keeps. Scoped threads allow that. Every thread started inside thread::scope is guaranteed to be finished when the scope ends, so it may safely borrow local variables:

Two threads read two halves of the same vector at the same time, with no move and no copying. Reading is all they do, and many readers are allowed. If one of them tried to change the vector, the borrow checker would object, exactly as it does within a single thread.

Here is the pattern in a reusable form. The data is cut into chunks, one per processor core, and each chunk is summed in its own thread:

thread::available_parallelism() reports how many threads can really run at the same time on this machine. Starting many more threads than that gains nothing for calculations, because the cores are already busy.

Tip
The easy way: Rayon

The crate rayon reduces this whole pattern to one word. Write numbers.par_iter().sum() in place of numbers.iter().sum(), and Rayon splits the work across all cores for you. Chapter 45 shows it.

Channels: passing messages

The second way for threads to cooperate is to share nothing, and to send each other messages. A channel is a one-way pipe: one end sends values in, and the other end takes them out.

Real-world analogy
A conveyor belt

One worker puts parcels on a conveyor belt. Another worker at the far end takes them off, in the order they were put on. The two never touch the same parcel at the same time, and they never need to talk about who has what.

  • mpsc::channel() creates the two ends. The name stands for “multiple producer, single consumer”: many senders, one receiver.
  • sender.send(value) puts a value in. The value is moved into the channel. After sending a String, the sending thread no longer owns it and cannot use it. Ownership travels with the message, so two threads never hold the same data.
  • The for loop over the receiver waits for each message and ends when the channel is closed. A channel closes when all senders have been dropped.
  • receiver.recv() waits for one message, and receiver.try_recv() checks without waiting.

Several threads can send into the same channel. Each needs its own clone of the sender:

The messages arrive in whatever order the threads happen to send them, so the example sorts them before printing. Notice the drop(sender): without it, the original sender would stay alive in main, the channel would never close, and receiver.iter() would wait for ever.

A plain channel can hold any number of waiting messages. If the senders are faster than the receiver, the backlog grows without limit. mpsc::sync_channel(n) creates a bounded channel with room for n messages. When it is full, send waits until there is room, which slows the producers down to the speed of the consumer. This effect is called backpressure.

How other languages do it
“Share memory by communicating”

The Go language made a slogan of this style: do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating. Go’s channels and Rust’s channels work alike. The difference is in what happens when you break the rule. In Go you can still keep and change a value after sending it, and get a data race. In Rust the value has moved, and using it is a compile error.

Send and Sync: how the compiler knows

Why did the compiler accept a Vec<String> being moved into a thread? And how does it know what is dangerous? Through two marker traits (chapter 28):

  • Send: a type is Send if a value of it may be moved to another thread.
  • Sync: a type is Sync if it may be used from several threads at once through shared references.

Almost every type is both, and the compiler works it out automatically: a struct is Send if all its fields are. thread::spawn demands that its closure, and with it everything the closure captures, is Send.

The best known type that is not Send is Rc<T>. Its counter of owners is an ordinary number with no protection. Two threads that clone and drop the same Rc at the same time could corrupt the count, and the value might be freed while still in use.

In C++, the same mistake with a non-atomic counter compiles without complaint and fails rarely and mysteriously. In Rust, it is the message above. The next chapter introduces Arc, the version of Rc that is safe to share.

RefCell and Cell are Send but not Sync: you may give one to another thread, but two threads may not use the same one together, because their borrow tracking is not protected either.

You almost never implement Send or Sync yourself. You only need to understand the error message when a type lacks one of them.

How much faster?

Threads do not make everything faster. Starting a thread takes time (tens of microseconds), so the work per thread must be much larger than that. And the gain is limited by the part of the work that cannot be split.

A test that is easy to split is counting prime numbers. On the two-core machine used to check this guide, counting the primes below three million took 0.51 seconds in one thread and 0.32 seconds in two. The speed-up is less than double, because the work was not split evenly: testing large numbers takes longer than testing small ones, so the thread with the upper half had more to do. Dividing work well is its own craft. One of the exercises lets you measure this on your machine.

Always measure before and after. And use cargo run --release for any timing: a debug build is many times slower and tells you little.

How other languages do it
Threads in other languages
  • C and C++ give you threads and no protection. Data races are undefined behaviour, and finding them needs special tools.
  • Java and C# have threads and locks built in. Forgetting a lock compiles and produces wrong results now and then.
  • Python has threads, but for decades its “global interpreter lock” let only one of them run Python code at a time, so threads did not speed up calculations. (Recent versions offer a build without that lock.)
  • JavaScript runs your code in a single thread. Web Workers are separate, and can only exchange messages.
  • Go has very cheap threads (goroutines) and channels, and a race detector that finds data races at run time, if a test happens to trigger them.
  • Rust checks at compile time. The cost is that you must sometimes convince the compiler. The gain is that a whole class of the hardest bugs is gone.
Recap
  • A thread is a separate line of execution in the same program. Threads share memory.
  • thread::spawn(closure) starts a thread. handle.join() waits for it and returns its result, or an Err if it panicked.
  • Use move to give data to a thread. Use thread::scope to let threads borrow local data for a limited time.
  • A channel moves values from one thread to another. Sending transfers ownership.
  • A data race needs shared access with at least one writer and no coordination. Rust’s borrowing rules, extended by Send and Sync, rule it out at compile time.
  • Threads help when the work is large and can be split. Measure.
Check your understanding
1

What happens to spawned threads when the main thread reaches the end of main?

The process ends with the main thread. Use join (or scoped threads) to wait for work that must complete.

2

Why does thread::spawn(|| println!("{:?}", list)) not compile when list is a local Vec?

The thread’s lifetime is not tied to the current function. Use move to give the vector to the thread, or use a scoped thread.

3

What makes scoped threads (thread::scope) able to borrow local variables?

The scope joins every thread it started before it returns. The compiler can therefore prove that the borrows do not outlive the data.

4

After sender.send(text).unwrap();, can the sending thread still use text (a String)?

Sending transfers ownership. That is what guarantees that two threads never access the same value.

5

Why is Rc<T> not Send?

Two threads updating the plain counter at once could corrupt it. Arc uses an atomic counter and is Send.

Guided exerciseThree workers

Start three threads. Each receives a number (10, 20, 30), computes the sum of all whole numbers from 1 up to it, and returns the result. Collect the three results in order and print them.

Need a hint?

Loop over [10_u64, 20, 30] and call thread::spawn(move || (1..=n).sum::<u64>()) for each. Collect the handles in a Vec, then call join().unwrap() on each.

Show solution and explanation

move copies n into each closure (a u64 is Copy). The handles are joined in the order they were created, so the output is in a fixed order although the threads run at the same time. All three threads are started before the first is joined. If you joined inside the first loop, each thread would finish before the next one started, and nothing would run in parallel.

PracticeCount words in parallel

Write count_words(texts: &[String]) -> usize that counts the words of all texts, using one scoped thread per text. Test it with four texts and compare with a sequential count.

Need a hint?

Inside thread::scope(|scope| { ... }), map over texts.iter() and spawn scope.spawn(move || text.split_whitespace().count()) for each. Collect the handles, then sum the joined results.

Show solution and explanation

Each thread borrows one &String from the slice. That is allowed because the scope guarantees the threads end before count_words returns. collect() is essential: it starts all threads before any is joined. Without it, the lazy iterator would spawn and join one thread at a time.

For texts this short, the threads cost far more than they save. The structure pays off when each piece of work is large, such as a whole file.

PracticeA pipeline

Build a pipeline of three stages connected by two channels. Stage 1 sends the numbers 1 to 5. Stage 2 receives each number, squares it and sends it on. The main thread receives the squares and prints their sum.

Need a hint?

Create two channels: (tx1, rx1) and (tx2, rx2). The first thread owns tx1. The second thread owns rx1 and tx2: for n in rx1 { tx2.send(n * n).unwrap(); }. The main thread computes rx2.iter().sum(). Each stage ends when the previous stage drops its sender.

Show solution and explanation

The shutdown runs through the pipeline by itself. When stage 1 finishes, tx_numbers is dropped, so the loop in stage 2 ends, so tx_squares is dropped, so the iterator in main ends. No thread needs to be told to stop, and no join is needed, because main waits for the last channel to close.

No data is shared at any point. Each number is owned by exactly one stage at a time.

ChallengeMeasure the speed-up

Write is_prime(n: u64) -> bool (test all divisors d with d * d <= n) and count the primes below 3,000,000 twice: in one thread, and split across as many scoped threads as available_parallelism reports. Check that both counts agree, and print both times with std::time::Instant. Run it with cargo run --release.

Need a hint?

Divide the range 0..limit into workers equal parts: part w goes from w * step to (w + 1) * step, limited to limit. Instant::now() before and .elapsed() after gives a Duration, which prints nicely with {:.2?}.

Show solution and explanation

Your times and worker count will differ. This output is from a two-core machine and a release build. The speed-up is about 1.6 and not 2, because the ranges are equal in length but not in work: large numbers need more divisions, so the last thread finishes last while the first one is already idle.

Two ways to balance the load: cut the range into many small pieces and let the threads take the next piece whenever they are free (a work queue), or deal the numbers out in turn (thread 0 takes 0, 4, 8, …). Libraries such as Rayon do the first automatically, with a technique called work stealing.

31

Shared state: Arc, Mutex and atomics

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Share read-only data between threads with Arc
  • Protect changeable data with Mutex and RwLock
  • Use atomic types for simple counters and flags
  • Create global values safely with static, OnceLock and LazyLock
  • Recognise and avoid deadlocks, and choose between messages and shared state

The last chapter showed two ways for threads to work together: give data away with move, or send it through a channel. Both avoid sharing. Sometimes sharing is the natural design: a cache that all threads consult, a counter that all threads increase, a list of connected users. This chapter is about the third way: several threads use the same data, with coordination.

Arc<T>: shared ownership across threads

Rc<T> gives a value several owners, but cannot leave its thread. Arc<T> is the same idea with a counter that is safe to change from several threads at once. The “A” stands for atomic: an atomic operation happens in one indivisible step, so two threads cannot interfere with each other in the middle.

Each thread gets its own Arc, a pointer to the one shared vector. The line let dictionary = Arc::clone(&dictionary); inside the loop creates a new variable with the same name that holds the clone, and the move closure takes that clone. This is the standard idiom. When all threads have finished and dropped their pointers, one owner is left.

Like Rc, an Arc gives read-only access. Many threads reading the same data is always safe. Arc costs a little more than Rc, because atomic operations are slower than plain ones, so use Rc when everything stays in one thread.

Mutex<T>: one at a time

To change shared data, the threads must take turns. A mutex (from “mutual exclusion”) makes sure that only one thread at a time can reach the data.

Real-world analogy
A room with one key

A meeting room has a single key, hanging on a hook. Whoever wants to use the room takes the key. Everyone else who comes by finds the hook empty and waits. When the room is free again, the key goes back on the hook, and the next person takes it.

  • Mutex::new(0) wraps the value. The data lives inside the mutex. There is no way to reach it without going through lock.
  • lock() waits until the mutex is free, and then returns a guard. The guard is a smart pointer: *guard is the protected value.
  • When the guard is dropped, the lock is released. This happens automatically at the end of its scope, by the Drop trait from chapter 27. You cannot forget to unlock.
How other languages do it
A lock that owns its data

In C, C++, Java and Go, a mutex is a separate object that sits next to the data it is meant to protect. The connection exists only in comments and in the programmers’ heads: “always lock m before touching balance”. Forget it once, and you have a data race that compiles without complaint. Rust’s Mutex<T> contains the data. The only path to the data leads through the lock, and the compiler checks every access.

Sharing a mutex: Arc<Mutex<T>>

Several threads need shared ownership of the mutex (Arc) and controlled access to its content (Mutex):

Eight threads each add one, a thousand times. The result is always exactly 8000. Without the lock, the classic race would strike: two threads read the same old value, both add one, and both write back the same new value. One increment is lost. In languages without protection, such a program prints a different number below 8000 on each run.

Arc<Mutex<T>> is the multi-threaded twin of Rc<RefCell<T>>:

One threadSeveral threads
Shared ownershipRc<T>Arc<T>
Change through a shared referenceRefCell<T>Mutex<T>, RwLock<T>
Both togetherRc<RefCell<T>>Arc<Mutex<T>>
If the rules are brokenpanicthe thread waits

What the unwrap is for: poisoning

lock() returns a Result. If a thread panics while it holds the lock, the data may have been left half-changed. The mutex is then marked as poisoned, and every later lock() returns an Err as a warning. Calling .unwrap() passes the panic on, which is usually the right reaction: if one thread crashed in the middle of an update, the others should not carry on with broken data.

Good to know
parking_lot::Mutex and RwLock

Many production Rust codebases replace std::sync::Mutex and RwLock with parking_lot: its locks take less memory (1 byte instead of an OS-allocated lock), are faster under contention, offer fair unlocking, and do not poison—so .lock() returns the guard directly without .unwrap().

Keep the lock short

While one thread holds a lock, all others that want it wait. Hold a lock only for the moment you need the data, and never during slow work such as reading a file or waiting for the network.

In results.lock().unwrap().push(value); the guard is a temporary value. It is dropped at the end of that statement, so the lock is held only for the push.

Deadlock: waiting for ever

Locks bring a new kind of bug. A deadlock occurs when threads wait for each other in a circle, so that none can ever continue.

Real-world analogy
Two keys, two people

Sara holds the key to room A and needs room B as well. Tomas holds the key to room B and needs room A as well. Each waits politely for the other to finish. They wait for ever.

Rust prevents data races. It does not prevent deadlocks. A deadlock is not memory-unsafe: nothing is corrupted, the program just stops making progress. The compiler cannot detect it, so you need habits:

  1. Hold only one lock at a time, whenever you can.
  2. If you need several, always take them in the same order, everywhere in the program. If every thread locks A before B, the circle cannot form.
  3. Keep the locked region small, and do not call unknown code (callbacks, other people’s functions) while holding a lock.
  4. Do not lock the same mutex twice in one thread. The second lock() waits for the first to be released, which never happens.

One thread moves money from A to B, and the other from B to A, two thousand transfers in all. Because both always lock account 1 before account 2, they can never block each other, and the total stays 2000. &mut *first_guard turns the guard into a plain mutable reference to the number inside.

RwLock<T>: many readers or one writer

A mutex lets one thread in, even if all of them only want to read. An RwLock (“read-write lock”) applies the borrowing rule at run time across threads: any number of readers at once, or one writer alone.

read() gives shared access, and write() gives exclusive access. An RwLock is worth it when reads are far more frequent than writes and take some time. For short, simple accesses, a Mutex is just as good and a little cheaper.

Atomics: no lock needed

For a single number or flag, a lock is more than necessary. The atomic types in std::sync::atomic (AtomicUsize, AtomicU64, AtomicI32, AtomicBool, …) offer operations that the processor carries out in one indivisible step:

  • fetch_add(1, …) adds one and returns the previous value, as one step. load reads, store writes, swap exchanges.
  • These methods take &self. An atomic can be changed through a shared reference, with no mut and no lock.
  • A shared AtomicBool is the usual way to tell worker threads to stop: they check it now and then.
What is the Ordering argument?

It tells the compiler and the processor how strictly this operation must be ordered relative to operations on other memory. Ordering::Relaxed promises atomicity on that single number only, which is enough for independent counters. Ordering::Release + Ordering::Acquire work as a pair for publishing data: a writer writes payload data and stores ready.store(true, Ordering::Release), and a reader loads ready.load(Ordering::Acquire)—guaranteeing that once true is observed, all writes made before the Release store are visible. Ordering::SeqCst (“sequentially consistent”) adds one global order across all atomic operations and is the easiest strict default.

A safe rule while learning: use Relaxed for plain counters and statistics, Release/Acquire for flag handoffs, and SeqCst whenever several atomics interact. If you find yourself thinking hard about orderings, use a Mutex.

Atomics are faster than locks and cannot deadlock. They only protect one value. If two values must change together (a balance and a list of transactions), you need a mutex around both.

Read, decide, write: compare_exchange

fetch_add is one step. “Read the value, decide something, write a new value” is three steps, and another thread can get in between. Suppose 100 seats are free, and a thread should take one only if any are left. Written as if free.load(…) > 0 { free.fetch_sub(1, …); }, two threads can both see the last seat and both take it.

The tool for this is compare_exchange: “if the value is still what I read, replace it with my new value; if not, tell me what it is now.”

Eight threads try 400 times, and exactly 100 attempts succeed. The loop “read, compute, compare_exchange, repeat if somebody else was faster” is the basic pattern of all lock-free code. For this common shape there is a ready-made method, fetch_update, which runs the loop for you with a closure.

Global data: static

A static is a value that exists once, for the whole run of the program, at a fixed place in memory. It can be reached from every function and every thread, so it must be safe to share (Sync).

Four tools for four needs:

NeedTool
a global counter or flagstatic X: AtomicU64
global data that changesstatic X: Mutex<T>
a global value that is expensive to build, created on first usestatic X: LazyLock<T>
a global value that is set once at run time (from arguments or a file)static X: OnceLock<T>

LazyLock runs its closure the first time the value is used, exactly once, even if several threads ask at the same moment. The output shows “(building the table)” once, before the first lookup.

A const is different: it is a value that the compiler pastes in wherever the name is used, and it has no fixed place in memory. Use const for plain constants, and static when there must be exactly one instance.

Watch out
Globals are a last resort

Global data makes programs harder to understand and to test, because any function may depend on it invisibly. Prefer passing values as parameters. Good uses for a global are few: a logger, a table that is costly to build, the configuration that is read once at the start. There is also static mut, a global that can be changed without any protection. Using it requires unsafe code, it is almost never needed, and it is easy to get wrong. Use the tools above.

A worker pool

A real program rarely starts a fresh thread for every small job. It keeps a fixed team of threads, a thread pool, and hands them jobs through a queue. This small pool combines everything from the last two chapters: channels, Arc, Mutex, closures and join.

How it fits together:

  • A job is a boxed closure. FnOnce() because each job runs once, Send because it travels to another thread, and 'static because it must not borrow anything that could disappear.
  • The jobs go into a channel. A channel has one receiver, but four workers want to take from it. So the receiver is shared with Arc and guarded by a Mutex.
  • Each worker loops: lock the receiver, take one job, release the lock, run the job. In let job = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv(); the guard is a temporary that is dropped at the end of the statement. The lock is therefore not held while the job runs, and the other workers can fetch jobs in the meantime.
  • finish drops the sender. The channel closes, every worker’s recv() returns Err, the loops end, and join collects the threads.

Twenty jobs are spread over four threads, and the sum of the squares from 1 to 20 is 2870 every time. In real programs you would use a tested pool from a library, such as Rayon’s. Building one once shows that there is no magic inside.

Waiting for something: Condvar

A worker with nothing to do should sleep, and wake up when work arrives. Checking a shared flag in a loop would keep a processor core busy for nothing. A condition variable (Condvar) is the tool for “sleep until somebody tells me that something changed”. It always works together with a mutex:

Three workers share the jobs 1 to 100, and every job is done exactly once. The important line is self.changed.wait(state):

  • wait takes the lock guard, and gives it back. It releases the mutex and goes to sleep as one indivisible step, so no notify can slip through between “I looked, there was nothing” and “I am asleep”. When the thread wakes, it holds the lock again.
  • Always wait inside a loop that checks again. After waking up, another worker may already have taken the job, and a thread is also allowed to wake up with no notification at all. So the code looks again before it trusts anything.
  • notify_one wakes one waiting thread, notify_all wakes all of them. Use notify_all when the change concerns everybody, as closing does.

This is roughly what a channel does inside. When a channel fits, use the channel. A Condvar is the piece you need when you build such a tool yourself. Its smallest relative is thread::park(): the current thread sleeps until another thread calls unpark() on its handle.

Messages or shared state?

Channels (messages)Shared state (Arc<Mutex<T>>)
Ideaeach piece of data has one owner at a timeseveral threads access the same data, in turns
Good forpipelines, handing out work, eventscaches, counters, registries that many threads look up
Risksa forgotten sender keeps a channel open. An unbounded queue can growdeadlocks. Threads waiting on a busy lock
Reasoningsimple: follow the dataharder: think about every possible interleaving

A common and sensible default: start with messages. Give one thread sole ownership of a piece of state, and let the others send it requests. Use shared state when many threads need quick access to the same data, and keep what is shared as small as possible.

One more tool in std::sync for a special need: Barrier makes several threads wait until all of them have reached the same point.

Recap
  • Arc<T> is shared ownership that works across threads. The content is read-only.
  • Mutex<T> holds data that only one thread at a time can reach. lock() returns a guard, and dropping the guard unlocks.
  • Arc<Mutex<T>> is shared, changeable data for threads. RwLock allows many readers or one writer.
  • Atomic types change a single number or flag in one indivisible step, without a lock.
  • static values are global. Use atomics, Mutex, LazyLock or OnceLock for them.
  • Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks. Lock in a fixed order, hold locks briefly, and hold one at a time where possible.
  • Prefer messages. Share state when it is the simpler design, and share little.
Check your understanding
1

Why is Arc<T> used with threads, and not Rc<T>?

Rc’s counter is unprotected, so the compiler refuses to send it to another thread. Arc pays a small price for a thread-safe counter.

2

When is a Mutex unlocked?

The guard releases the lock in its destructor. There is no unlock method to forget.

3

Which bug does Rust’s compiler not prevent?

A deadlock does not break memory safety. Two threads that wait for each other’s lock compile fine. Avoiding it is up to the design.

4

Eight threads each call counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed) a thousand times on a shared AtomicU64 that starts at 0. What is the final value?

fetch_add is atomic: reading, adding and writing happen as one step, so no increment can be lost.

5

Why does the worker pool wrap its Receiver in Arc<Mutex<…>>?

Arc gives each worker access to the same receiver. The Mutex makes sure that only one worker at a time takes a job from it.

Guided exerciseA shared counter

Start 5 threads. Each one adds the numbers 1 to 100 to a shared total, protected by a mutex. Print the total after all threads have finished. What number do you expect?

Need a hint?

The total is an Arc<Mutex<u64>>. Inside the loop that creates the threads, clone the Arc first, then move the clone into the closure. In the thread: for n in 1..=100 { *total.lock().unwrap() += n; }.

Show solution and explanation

The sum of 1 to 100 is 5050, and five threads add it once each. The lock is taken and released for every single addition, which is correct but slow. A better design adds up locally and locks once per thread: let sum: u64 = (1..=100).sum(); *total.lock().unwrap() += sum;. Sharing less is nearly always faster.

PracticeWord frequencies from several threads

Given a list of texts, count how often each word appears in all of them together. Use scoped threads, one per text, and collect the counts in one Mutex<HashMap<String, usize>>. Print the counts for “the” and “fox”.

Need a hint?

With thread::scope, the threads can borrow the mutex directly, and no Arc is needed. To keep the lock short, let each thread build its own local HashMap first, then lock once and merge it into the shared map.

Show solution and explanation

Scoped threads borrow counts and texts directly, so there is no Arc and no clone. Each thread does its counting in a private map without any locking, and holds the shared lock only for the short merge at the end. That keeps the threads from getting in each other’s way.

into_inner() takes the map out of the mutex once the threads are done. It needs no locking, because owning the mutex proves that no one else can be using it.

PracticeStop on request

Start a worker thread that counts upwards in a loop for as long as a shared AtomicBool called running is true. Let the main thread sleep for 50 milliseconds, set the flag to false, and join the worker. The worker returns how far it counted. Print whether the count is greater than zero.

Need a hint?

Share the flag with Arc<AtomicBool>. The worker loop is while running.load(Ordering::Relaxed) { count += 1; }. The main thread calls running.store(false, Ordering::Relaxed).

Show solution and explanation

A thread cannot be stopped from outside in Rust. It must stop itself. A shared flag that the worker checks regularly is the standard way to ask it to. The worker finishes its current step, leaves its loop, and returns normally, so all its values are cleaned up properly. The exact count depends on the speed of the machine.

ChallengeA thread-safe cache

Write struct Cache { entries: RwLock<HashMap<u64, u64>>, computations: AtomicUsize } with a method get(&self, n: u64) -> u64. It returns the square of n. If the result is already in the map, it is read under a read lock. Otherwise it is computed, stored under a write lock, and the computation counter is increased. Call get from 4 threads, each asking for the numbers 1 to 50, and print how many computations happened.

Need a hint?

First try self.entries.read().unwrap().get(&n).copied() in its own statement, so that the read lock is released before you ask for the write lock. Holding the read lock while requesting the write lock on the same RwLock is a deadlock. After taking the write lock, use entry(n).or_insert_with(...), so that the value is computed only if no other thread stored it in the meantime.

Show solution and explanation

Two hundred requests, fifty computations: each value was computed exactly once, although four threads asked for it at nearly the same time.

The method shows a pattern called check, lock, check again. Between the failed read and the write lock, another thread may have stored the value. entry(n).or_insert_with(…) performs the second check under the write lock, so the closure runs at most once per key. The read lock is released at the end of the let known = …; statement, before the write lock is requested. That ordering matters: asking for the write lock while still holding the read lock would block for ever.

get takes &self, yet changes the cache. RwLock and the atomic counter provide interior mutability that is safe across threads, the same idea as RefCell and Cell in a single thread.
