Part 7 · ConcurrencyAdvancedabout 70 min
32

Async Rust: thousands of tasks at once

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain when async is the right tool and when threads are
  • Write async functions and use .await
  • Run tasks concurrently with join!, spawn, select! and timeouts
  • Use async channels and shared state, and avoid blocking the runtime
  • Describe what a future and a runtime are underneath

Threads are perfect when you have a handful of long calculations. Many programs have a different problem. A web server may have ten thousand clients connected at once, and nearly all of them are doing nothing at a given moment: the server is waiting for them to send something. A chat server, a download manager and a web crawler are the same. They are not short of processor time. They spend their lives waiting for the network or the disk.

One thread per waiting client is wasteful. Every thread reserves memory for its own stack, and the operating system needs time to switch between threads. A few hundred are fine. A hundred thousand are not.

Asynchronous programming (“async” for short) is a way to handle huge numbers of waiting tasks with a few threads.

Real-world analogy
One waiter, many tables

A restaurant could hire one waiter per table. Each waiter takes an order, walks to the kitchen, and stands there until the dish is ready. With fifty tables, that is fifty waiters, most of them standing around.

A good waiter works differently. He takes an order at table 1, hands it to the kitchen, and while the kitchen cooks, he goes to table 2, then brings the drinks to table 3. When the kitchen rings the bell, he picks up the dish. One waiter serves many tables, because he never stands still when he could do something else.

An async program is that waiter. Whenever a task has to wait, the thread sets it aside and works on another task that is ready to continue.

ThreadsAsync tasks
Best forlong calculations (CPU-bound work)waiting for network, disk, timers (I/O-bound work)
Cost of onea stack of its own (often megabytes reserved), an operating-system threada small object, often a few hundred bytes
Sensible numbertens to hundredshundreds of thousands
Who switches between themthe operating system, at any momentthe program, only at .await points

A first async program

Async Rust needs a runtime: a library that keeps track of all tasks and runs whichever one is ready. The language provides the syntax, and the runtime comes from a crate. The most widely used runtime is Tokio. Create a project and add it:

That writes the following into Cargo.toml:

The new pieces:

  • async fn declares a function that can pause. Calling it does not run it. It returns a future: a value that stands for a result that will exist later.
  • .await runs a future to its end and gives you the result. If the future has to wait (here: for a timer), .await pauses the current task and lets the thread do other work. Later the task continues exactly where it stopped. Note the position: .await is written after the expression.
  • #[tokio::main] turns async fn main into a normal main that starts the runtime and runs the async code in it.
  • tokio::time::sleep is a timer that waits without occupying a thread.
  • tokio::join! runs several futures concurrently and waits until all are finished.

In the first half, the tea is finished before the toast is started: 200 ms plus 100 ms. In the second half, both wait at the same time, and the total is the longer of the two. The work was not done faster. The waiting overlapped.

When each concurrent branch returns a Result, tokio::try_join! runs them concurrently and stops immediately if any branch fails, dropping (cancelling) the others:

Notice the second call does not wait 500 ms for step("a"): as soon as step("b") returns Err, try_join! drops step("a") and returns Err("step failed").

Futures are lazy

Like iterators, futures do nothing until someone drives them:

Calling greet() only creates the future. The body runs when it is awaited. Forgetting .await is the most common beginner mistake in async code. Usually the compiler catches it, with a type error or with the warning “futures do nothing unless you .await or poll them”:

n is not a number. It is an impl Future<Output = u32>: a future that will produce a u32. Writing fetch_number().await fixes it.

How other languages do it
A difference to JavaScript and C#

In JavaScript, calling an async function starts it running immediately and returns a promise. In Rust, calling an async fn runs nothing. This laziness is deliberate: a future that nobody awaits costs nothing, and you decide exactly when and where it runs.

Tasks: tokio::spawn

join! runs futures concurrently inside the current task. tokio::spawn starts an independent task: the runtime takes the future and runs it in the background, possibly on another thread. It is the async counterpart of thread::spawn, and far cheaper.

spawn returns a JoinHandle, which is itself a future. Awaiting it gives a Result: an Err means the task panicked. Unlike a plain future, a spawned task starts running at once, whether or not you await the handle.

When you want the results in the order in which the tasks finish, use a JoinSet:

async move { ... } is an async block: a future written in place, like a closure. With move it takes ownership of the variables it uses, which a spawned task needs for the same reason a spawned thread does.

Tip
Structured concurrency with JoinSet

Dropping a plain Vec<JoinHandle> detaches those tasks: they keep running in the background with nobody waiting on them, which can leak work after a request finishes or fails. Dropping a JoinSet, by contrast, aborts every unfinished task automatically. Prefer JoinSet (or join! / try_join!) whenever spawned tasks should never outlive the scope that started them.

Tasks must be Send

Tokio may move a task from one thread to another whenever the task is paused. So everything a task holds across an .await must be Send. An Rc is not:

The message is precise: which value, and which .await it lives across. Use Arc in place of Rc, or make sure the value is dropped before the .await.

Timeouts and select!

Anything that waits on the outside world should have a time limit. timeout wraps a future and gives up after a given duration:

select! waits for several futures at once and continues with whichever finishes first. The others are dropped. It is the tool for “wait for a message or a shutdown signal or a timer”.

Key idea
Dropping a future cancels it — and what “cancellation safety” means

When a future is dropped before it finishes, its work stops at whichever .await it was paused on. That is how timeout and select! cancel the losing branches.

When using tokio::select! inside a loop, check whether each branch is cancellation-safe:

  • Cancellation-safe: mpsc::Receiver::recv, TcpListener::accept, and AsyncBufReadExt::read_line lose no partial data when dropped before completing.
  • Not cancellation-safe: creating a fresh tokio::time::sleep(...) inside each loop turn resets the timer every time another branch fires, and multi-step async functions dropped mid-way discard partial work. For a deadline across loop iterations, create the future outside the loop (let timer = tokio::time::sleep(...); tokio::pin!(timer);) and poll &mut timer inside select!, or run stateful work in its own tokio::spawn task.

Channels and shared state

Tokio has async versions of the tools from the last two chapters. Its mpsc channel looks familiar. send and recv are async, so a task that waits for a message does not block a thread:

The channel is bounded: channel(8) holds at most eight waiting messages, and a sender pauses when it is full. Tokio offers more kinds of channel for particular jobs:

ChannelSenders → receiversUse it for
mpscmany → onea queue of work or events
oneshotone → one, a single valuesending back the answer to one request
broadcastmany → many, every receiver gets every messagechat rooms, notifications
watchone → many, only the latest value is keptconfiguration, “current state”

Shared state works with Arc<Mutex<T>>, as with threads:

Tip
Which mutex?

The ordinary std::sync::Mutex is the right choice in async code as long as the lock is taken and released without an .await in between, as above. If you must keep a lock while awaiting something, use tokio::sync::Mutex, whose lock() is async. Holding a standard mutex guard across an .await either fails to compile (the guard is not Send) or risks blocking the runtime.

The golden rule: never block the runtime

Each runtime thread serves many tasks. When a task is polled, it runs until it finishes or returns control to the runtime. An .await may return control if the awaited future is not ready; if it is already ready, execution continues immediately. A slow blocking operation does not return control, so other tasks on that thread must wait.

Things that block:

  • std::thread::sleep (use tokio::time::sleep),
  • the file and network functions of the standard library, such as std::fs::read_to_string (use tokio::fs, tokio::net),
  • long calculations,
  • waiting on a std::sync::mpsc channel or a busy std::sync::Mutex.

For work that is truly blocking or heavy, hand it to a thread that is meant for it with spawn_blocking:

spawn_blocking runs the closure on a separate pool of threads and returns a handle you can await. The async tasks keep running meanwhile. A rule of thumb: if a piece of code can take more than about a tenth of a millisecond without reaching an .await, it does not belong directly in an async task.

A small network server

Here is async Rust doing what it was made for. This program starts a server that accepts TCP connections and answers every line it receives. To keep the example self-contained, the same program then connects to its own server as a client.

TCP is the basic protocol of the internet for sending a stream of bytes reliably from one program to another. A server listens on an address and a numbered port. A client connects to it. Both then read from and write to the connection.

The structure of nearly every async server is in these lines:

  • TcpListener::bind(...) opens a listening address. 127.0.0.1 is the computer itself (“localhost”).
  • The accept loop waits for a client and spawns one task per connection. A task costs so little that ten thousand open connections are no problem.
  • handle_client reads lines and writes answers. Every .await in it is a point where this client’s task steps aside while it waits for the network.
  • into_split() divides the connection into a reading half and a writing half, so that the two can be used independently.
  • ? works in async functions exactly as elsewhere.

In the next chapter this skeleton grows into a chat server.

What happens underneath

You can use async Rust without this section. It is here because knowing what is inside takes away the mystery.

A future is a value with one method, poll. Polling a future asks: “are you finished?” It answers Poll::Ready(value) or Poll::Pending (“not yet, I will let you know”).

An async fn is turned into a state machine by the compiler. It becomes a hidden struct that stores the local variables and remembers at which .await the function is paused. Each poll runs the code up to the next .await that is not ready, and returns Pending. This is why an async task is so small: it stores only its live variables, not a whole stack.

A runtime is a loop that polls futures. It keeps a queue of tasks that are ready, polls them, and puts aside those that return Pending. A pending future has stored a waker (handed in through the Context). When the event it waits for arrives, such as data on a socket or a timer firing, the waker puts the task back into the ready queue.

Here is all of that in a program small enough to read, with no crate at all: a future written by hand, and a runtime of eight lines.

Countdown answers Pending three times and then Ready. block_on is the simplest possible runtime: it polls in a loop until the future is done. A real runtime does not spin like this. It sleeps until a waker tells it that a task can make progress, and it manages many tasks and several threads. The principle is the same.

In plain English
What is Pin?

The state machine behind an async fn may hold references to its own local variables. If such a value were moved to a different place in memory, those references would point to the old place. Pin<&mut T> is a pointer type that promises: “the value behind me will not be moved any more”. poll requires it, so that self-referential futures are safe. In everyday code you never write Pin yourself. When you do need to pin something, the macro pin! (as above) or Box::pin(...) does it.

Most types do not care whether they are moved: numbers, strings, vectors. They carry the marker trait Unpin, and for them Pin changes nothing. The futures that async creates are the important types that are not Unpin. That is why some functions ask you to pin a future before you hand it over, and why the compiler sometimes says that a future “cannot be unpinned”.

Pinning structs and pin-project-lite

Two common situations ask you to think about Pin explicitly:

  1. Reusing one future across a tokio::select! loop. Calling select! on the same future across loop iterations needs &mut future where future is pinned. std::pin::pin!(fut) (or tokio::pin!(fut)) pins it right on the stack with no heap allocation (Box::pin), and gives you a Pin<&mut F> you can poll repeatedly.
  2. Writing a struct that wraps another Future or Stream. Inside fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>), Rust does not automatically turn Pin<&mut Wrapper<F>> into Pin<&mut F>—because you might accidentally swap self.inner while Wrapper is pinned. Pin projection solves this: mark the field with #[pin] using the zero-dependency crate pin-project-lite:

More async features

Async closures capture their surroundings and return a future. They are written async |x| { ... }:

Async functions in traits work directly:

One limit remains: a trait with async methods cannot be used directly as dyn Trait. Where trait objects are needed, the crate async-trait is the usual answer.

An async function that calls itself needs a box. The future of such a function would have to contain a future of the same function, which contains another one, without end. It is the problem of the list that contains a list from chapter 27, and the remedy is the same:

Several futures at once, without spawning. tokio::join! waits for all of a handful of futures and hands back a tuple of their results, and their types may differ. tokio::try_join! does the same for futures that return Result, and returns at the first Err, cancelling the others — the fail-fast shape of “fetch the user, the settings and the avatar, or give up”. select! from above is the third case: it stops as soon as one future is ready and drops the rest. None of them needs spawn, and none needs 'static, because the futures stay in the current task.

WantUseNotes
All of a fixed handful to finishjoin!Different types are fine; returns a tuple
All to finish, or the first errortry_join!Errors must share a type; the rest are cancelled
The first to finish, ignore the restselect!Also the tool for timeout races
Many at once, from a listbuffer_unordered(n)Maps a stream to futures, at most n in flight (chapter 45)
Many independent tasksJoinSetTasks may be cancelled, and tokio-console sees them

A set of futures that grows and shrinks. FuturesUnordered from the futures crate holds futures of one output type, lets you push new ones while it is being polled, and yields results in the order they finish. That is exactly what a worker needs when a finished job may add another job. It is also the honest answer to “how is this different from the other three?”: buffer_unordered needs an iterator of items up front and applies a map function, JoinSet turns each future into an independent spawned task (so it needs 'static, and gains cancellation and visibility), and FuturesUnordered polls them all inside the task that owns it, so the futures may borrow from that task’s data.

Projecting a pin, when the compiler asks. A hand-written Future eventually has to turn Pin<&mut Self> into Pin<&mut Field>, and that operation is only sound if the field is never moved afterwards — which is why it cannot be written in safe Rust. Two escapes: put the self-referential part behind Box::pin, as the recursive async fn above does, or let pin-project-lite generate the projection and its unsafe for you. Libraries that implement Stream, Future or an async trait by hand use the second. Application code almost never needs either, and it is fine to recognise the pattern rather than write it.

Streams are the async relatives of iterators: a sequence of values that arrive over time, such as lines from a connection. They come from the crates futures and tokio-stream, and you will see them in chapter 45.

Other runtimes. Tokio is the default choice for servers and network tools. smol is a small alternative, and embassy brings async to microcontrollers that have no operating system. Libraries are often written for one runtime, so pick one per program. This guide uses Tokio throughout.

Pitfalls to remember

  • A forgotten .await. The future is created and silently does nothing. Heed the compiler’s warning.
  • Blocking in a task. std::thread::sleep, heavy loops, synchronous file access. Use the async versions or spawn_blocking.
  • Async is contagious. An async fn can only be awaited from other async code, so the choice spreads up through the callers to main. This is sometimes called function colouring. Keep the plain logic of your program in ordinary functions and put the async layer around it. That also keeps the logic easy to test.
  • Async does not speed up calculations. For CPU-bound work, use threads or Rayon.
  • Unlimited spawning. A loop that spawns a task for every incoming item, without any limit, can exhaust memory under load. Use bounded channels or a tokio::sync::Semaphore to cap the number of tasks at work.
How other languages do it
Async in other languages
  • JavaScript has one thread and an event loop built into the language. async/await there looks almost the same, and a blocking loop freezes everything, for the same reason as in Rust.
  • Python (asyncio) and C# (Task) follow the same model with a runtime that ships with the language.
  • Go hides the difference: every function may pause, and the runtime moves “goroutines” between threads without async or await. That is simpler to use. The price is a runtime in every program, and less control.
  • Rust compiles each async function to a state machine with no heap allocation of its own, leaves the choice of runtime to you, and runs the same async code on a server with 64 cores and on a microcontroller with 16 kilobytes of memory. It asks for more understanding in return.
Recap
  • Async is for many tasks that mostly wait. Threads are for heavy calculations.
  • async fn returns a future. Nothing runs until it is awaited or spawned. .await pauses the task while it waits, and frees the thread.
  • A runtime such as Tokio runs the tasks. #[tokio::main] starts it.
  • join! waits for all, select! for the first, timeout limits the wait, tokio::spawn starts a background task.
  • Dropping a future cancels it at its current .await.
  • Spawned tasks must be Send. Use Arc, and async channels to communicate.
  • Avoid blocking a runtime thread. Use async I/O, or move blocking work to spawn_blocking.
  • Underneath, a future is a state machine with a poll method, and a runtime is a loop that polls.
Check your understanding
1

What does calling an async fn do, by itself?

Futures are lazy. The call only builds the value that describes the work.

2

Two futures each wait 100 ms on a timer. How long does tokio::join!(a, b) take, roughly?

join! drives both at once. Their waiting times overlap, so the total is the longer of the two, even on a single thread.

3

Why must you not call std::thread::sleep inside an async task?

An .await yields only when its future is not ready. A blocking call keeps the runtime thread busy, so other tasks on it cannot run. Use tokio::time::sleep(...).await instead of std::thread::sleep.

4

What happens to the slower branch of a tokio::select!?

select! continues with the first finished branch and drops the rest. Dropping a future is how cancellation works in async Rust.

5

Which task is async the wrong tool for?

Async helps when tasks wait. A long calculation never waits, and gains nothing. It needs threads on several cores.

Guided exerciseThree things at once

Write three async functions that each wait a different time (100, 200 and 300 ms) and return a number. Run all three with tokio::join!, add up the results, and show that the total time is close to 300 ms and not 600.

Need a hint?

Each function is async fn one() -> u32 { sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await; 1 }. Measure with Instant::now() and .elapsed(). To get an output that is the same on every run, print whether the time was below 450 ms.

Show solution and explanation

One function with parameters replaces three nearly identical ones. join! returns a tuple with the results in the order of its arguments. The three timers run down together, so the total is about 300 ms. Awaiting them one after the other would take 600 ms.

PracticeA deadline for every request

Write fetch(id: u32) -> String, an async function that pretends to be a slow server: it waits id * 60 milliseconds and returns "page <id>". Request the ids 1 to 5 concurrently, each with a timeout of 200 ms, and print for each id whether it arrived or timed out, in order of id.

Need a hint?

Spawn one task per id. Inside the task: timeout(Duration::from_millis(200), fetch(id)).await, which gives Result<String, Elapsed>. Collect the handles in a Vec and await them in order.

Show solution and explanation

Each task returns a pair: its id and the outcome. Pages 1 to 3 need 60, 120 and 180 ms and arrive in time. Pages 4 and 5 would need 240 and 300 ms, and are cut off at 200. Because all five run concurrently, the whole program takes about 200 ms. When a timeout fires, the fetch future is dropped, and its work stops.

PracticeA worker with a mailbox

Give one task sole ownership of a HashMap<String, u32> of word counts. Other tasks send it words through an mpsc channel. When all senders are done, the owning task returns the map. Spawn 3 sender tasks that send the words of three sentences, and print the counts for “the” and “fox”.

Need a hint?

The owner is tokio::spawn(async move { let mut counts = HashMap::new(); while let Some(word) = receiver.recv().await { *counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1; } counts }). Remember to drop the original sender, so that the channel closes when the three tasks have finished.

Show solution and explanation

The map has exactly one owner, the owner task, so it needs no Arc and no Mutex. Everyone else talks to it by sending messages. This design is called the actor pattern: a task that owns some state and a mailbox. Compare it with the mutex version of the same job in the last chapter. Here nothing is shared, and nothing can deadlock.

ChallengeAt most three at a time

You have 10 jobs that each take 50 ms. Run them concurrently, but never more than 3 at the same moment. Use tokio::sync::Semaphore. Track the largest number of jobs that were running together with atomics, and print it.

Need a hint?

let limit = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(3));. In each task, let _permit = limit.acquire().await.unwrap(); waits for a free slot, and the slot is given back when _permit is dropped at the end of the task. Keep two Arc<AtomicUsize>: one for the number currently running (fetch_add at the start, fetch_sub at the end), and one for the maximum seen (fetch_max).

Show solution and explanation

A semaphore is a counter of free slots. acquire().await takes one, and waits if none is free. The permit gives its slot back when it is dropped. All ten tasks are spawned at once, but seven of them wait at acquire until a slot opens.

Limiting concurrency like this is essential in real programs. It keeps a crawler from opening a thousand connections to one server, and keeps a service from being flooded by its own background work.

Project: a chat server

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Design a small network protocol and a concurrent server for it
  • Run one async task per client and connect the tasks with a broadcast channel
  • Wait for two things at once with select!
  • Guarantee clean-up with Drop
  • Test a network server automatically

In this project you write a real network program: a chat server. Any number of people connect to it, choose a name, and whatever one of them types appears on everybody else’s screen. You also write a small client, and a test that starts the server and lets two simulated users talk.

This is what two users see. The lines marked with > are what the person typed. The mark itself is not on the screen.

The project brings together Part 7 (tasks, channels, shared state, select!) with much of what came before: enums and pattern matching for the commands, Drop for clean-up, a library with a thin main, and tests.

Step 0: plan

The protocol

A protocol is the agreement between client and server about what they send each other. Ours is as simple as a protocol can be:

  • Both sides send lines of text, each ended by a line break.
  • The first line a client sends is the name it wants.
  • After that, a line that starts with / is a command (/who, /name sara, /quit, /help). Any other line is a chat message.
  • Lines from the server that start with * are announcements from the server itself.

A text protocol can be tried out by hand and read by eye, which makes mistakes easy to find.

The architecture

  • One task per client. Each task owns its connection and does two things: it reads what its client types, and it forwards what the others say.
  • A broadcast channel is the room. Tokio’s broadcast channel delivers every message to every receiver. A task that wants to say something sends into the channel, and each task holds a receiver.
  • A shared set of names makes sure no two members have the same name, and answers /who.

Notice how little is shared. Messages travel through a channel, as recommended in chapter 31. The only data behind a lock is the set of names, and it is locked for an instant at a time.

The files

Create the project and add Tokio:

Every Rust file placed in src/bin/ becomes an additional program of the package. This package therefore has two programs, chat (from src/main.rs) and client. With more than one, you must say which to run: cargo run --bin chat and cargo run --bin client.

Step 1: the room

All of the following goes into src/lib.rs. Start with the message type and the state that the client tasks have in common:

  • broadcast::channel(100) creates the room. Each receiver gets its own copy of every message, which is why Message must be Clone. The number is the capacity: how many messages the channel keeps for receivers that have not caught up yet.
  • The receiver that channel returns is thrown away (_). Each client task will ask for its own with sender.subscribe().
  • Every client gets a number, its id. A message carries the id of its sender, so that a task can recognise its own messages and need not echo them back. The id 0 stands for the server.
  • send ignores the result with let _ =. Sending fails only when there are no receivers, which is normal for an empty room. This is one of the rare places where ignoring an error is right, and the comment says why.
  • A BTreeSet keeps its elements sorted, so /who lists the names in alphabetical order with no extra work.

Step 2: names

A name must be acceptable and must be free. Taking a name has a counterpart that is easy to forget: the name must be given back when the member leaves, whichever way they leave. They may type /quit, close the window, lose their connection, or the server may hit an error while writing to them.

Rust has a tool that makes forgetting impossible: Drop, from chapter 27. A Member value represents a registered name. When it is dropped, for any reason, the name is released.

  • insert on a set returns false if the value was already there. Checking and inserting therefore happen in one step, under one lock. If the code first asked “is the name free?” and inserted afterwards, two tasks could both get the answer “yes” for the same name.
  • join takes self: &Arc<Self>. That is a method that can only be called on an Arc<Shared>, and it lets the new Member keep its own Arc to the shared state.
  • In rename, the new name is inserted before the old one is removed, so the member never stands without a name. std::mem::replace(&mut a, b) puts b into a and returns the old content of a. Here it stores the new name and hands back the old one for the announcement.
  • drop uses if let Ok(...) and not unwrap(). A destructor should never panic: it may be running because of a panic, and a second panic at that moment ends the whole program.

The only way to get a Member is join, and losing a Member always frees the name. The set of names and the set of living Member values cannot disagree. This is the idea of chapter 29 again: a value whose existence proves a fact.

Step 3: understand the input

Each line from a client is turned into a precise value once, at the edge:

strip_prefix('/') returns the rest of the line if it starts with a slash. If not, the line is an ordinary message. parse is a pure function, so its tests are short. They go at the bottom of src/lib.rs:

The last test checks the Drop behaviour: once the first member is gone, the name is free again.

Step 4: one client’s session

Now the heart of the server: the function that talks to one client from the first line to the last. It has two phases.

Phase 1: the name. The loop asks until shared.join succeeds, and break member hands the new Member out of the loop. lines.next_line().await? yields Some(line), or None when the client has closed the connection. The let … else covers that case.

Phase 2: the conversation. The task must wait for two things at the same time: a line from its own client, and a message from the room. It cannot know which comes first. This is exactly what select! is for. Each time round the loop, select! waits for both, and runs the branch of whichever is ready first.

  • A line from the client is parsed, and the match handles each kind of input. Thanks to the enum, the compiler checks that no case was forgotten.
  • A message from the room is written to the client, unless this client sent it.

Some details that matter:

  • The order of subscribe and the join announcement. The task subscribes first and announces after, so the new member receives its own “joined” line. It serves as the confirmation that the name was accepted.
  • Slow clients. If a client reads more slowly than the room talks, messages pile up in the channel for it. Once more than 100 are waiting, the oldest are discarded, and recv reports Lagged(n). The task tells the client and carries on. One slow client cannot make the server’s memory grow without limit, and cannot hold up the others.
  • Errors. Every write ends in ?. If the client has vanished, the write fails, and the function returns the error.

And the clean-up? There is none to write. When session ends, by /quit, by a closed connection, or by an error passed up with ?, its local variables are dropped. Dropping member frees the name and announces the departure. Dropping writer and lines closes the connection.

Step 5: accept clients

serve is the only public item of the library. It takes a listener that is already bound to an address. That small decision makes the server testable: a test can bind to any free port and hand the listener in.

An error from one client is printed and ends only that client’s task. The accept loop and all other clients are unaffected.

The program itself is short. Put it into src/main.rs:

tokio::signal::ctrl_c() is a future that completes when the user presses Ctrl+C. The select! runs the server until that happens. Then main returns, the runtime shuts down, and all tasks are dropped, which closes every connection.

Step 6: a client

To talk to the server you need a program that connects, sends what you type, and shows what arrives. Tools such as nc (netcat) or telnet can do that, but not every computer has them. A client of our own takes 25 lines. Put it into src/bin/client.rs:

The client has exactly two things to wait for: the keyboard and the server. For that, two plain threads are the simplest tool, and no async runtime is needed. This is the standard library’s own, blocking TcpStream.

  • stream.try_clone() gives a second handle to the same connection, so that one thread can read while the other writes.
  • When the server closes the connection, the reading thread ends the whole program with process::exit. Otherwise the main thread would go on waiting for the keyboard.

Try it

Open three terminals in the project folder.

Type a name in each client, then chat. Try a name that is taken, /who, /name, an unknown command, and /quit. Close one client’s window without /quit and watch the other: * … left appears all the same. Finally press Ctrl+C in the server’s terminal, and both clients report that the connection was closed.

If you just type cargo run, Cargo answers:

Tip
Chat across your network

The server listens on 127.0.0.1, which is reachable only from the same computer. Start it with cargo run --bin chat -- 0.0.0.0:8080 to accept connections from other computers in your network. They connect with cargo run --bin client -- <your address>:8080. Be aware that this server has no passwords and no encryption. Use it among friends on a private network, not on the open internet.

Step 7: test it automatically

Trying things by hand in three terminals does not scale. An integration test can start the server and play several users. Put this into tests/chat.rs:

How the test is built:

  • #[tokio::test] is the async version of #[test]. It starts a runtime for the test function.
  • start_server binds to port 0, which makes the operating system pick a free port. Every test gets its own server on its own port, so the tests can run in parallel without disturbing each other.
  • TestClient hides the plumbing. A test then reads like a script of the conversation: sara.send(...), tomas.expect(...).
  • expect has a timeout. If the server never sends the line, the test fails after two seconds with a clear message. Without the timeout it would hang for ever. Every test that waits for something should have a limit.

The third test, leaving_is_announced, covers both ways of leaving: /quit, and a connection that is simply dropped.

The complete server

Add the test module from step 3 at the end of the file.

What makes this server solid, and what is missing

Worth noticing in the design:

  • No lock is held across an .await. The mutex around the names is taken and released within one statement or one short function.
  • Memory is bounded. The broadcast channel has a fixed capacity, and slow receivers lose old messages.
  • Failures are contained. An error in one session ends one task.
  • Clean-up cannot be skipped, because it lives in Drop.

A server for the real world needs more. It should limit the length of a line (a client that sends gigabytes without a line break would fill the memory), limit how fast a client may send, encrypt the connections with TLS, and identify users with passwords. The crates for those jobs appear in Part 10.

When one server becomes several

This chat server holds every room in one process. That is the right design for thousands of users, and it stops working when you need two servers behind a load balancer: a message sent to server A never reaches the clients connected to server B.

The usual next step is to make the servers stateless and move the shared state out: room membership and message history into a database, and the live fan-out through a message broker — each server subscribes to room.* and delivers to its own clients (chapter 45 covers the brokers). Redis pub/sub is the smallest version of this; NATS is the next.

Beyond that the questions stop being about Rust and start being about distributed systems, and they have names worth recognising before you meet them in an incident report:

  • Service discovery — how does a client find a healthy instance? DNS, a load balancer, or a registry such as etcd or Consul.
  • Consensus — how do several machines agree on one value after a crash? The Raft algorithm is the readable one; openraft is a Rust implementation.
  • Replication and the CAP trade-off — when the network partitions, choose consistency or availability, and know which you chose.
  • Idempotency — every distributed system retries. A retried request must not charge a card twice.

You do not need these to build this project; you need to know the words exist, so that “just run two of them” does not sound like a small change. The book for this territory is Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann, and it is the one every team has a copy of.

Make it better

PracticeActions with /me

Add a command /me <action>. When Sara types /me waves, everybody, including Sara, sees * sara waves.

Need a hint?

Three small changes: a new variant Action(String) in Input, a new arm in parse (model it on the "name" arm), and a new arm in the match inside session. Send the line with the id 0, so that the sender receives it too.

Show solution and explanation

After step 1, the compiler refuses the match in session until step 3 is done: “pattern Input::Action(_) not covered”. The enum made sure the new command could not be half-finished.

The line is sent with from: 0. Messages with the sender’s own id are skipped by the sender’s task, and here Sara should see her own action as everyone else does. A matching test is one line each of sara.send("/me waves") and sara.expect("* sara waves").

PracticeShow what was said before

A newcomer sees an empty screen and has no idea what the conversation is about. Keep the last 10 lines that were sent to the room, and show them to every new member right after the name was accepted, marked with (earlier).

Need a hint?

Add a field history: Mutex<VecDeque<String>> to Shared. In Shared::send, push the text to the back and remove the oldest line when there are more than 10. Add a method recent(&self) -> Vec<String> that returns a copy. In session, write those lines before subscribing. Copy the lines out and let go of the lock before you start writing: a standard mutex must not be held across an .await.

Show solution and explanation

Shared::new also needs history: Mutex::new(VecDeque::new()).

A VecDeque is the right collection: lines are added at the back and removed at the front, both in constant time. recent() clones the lines into a Vec and releases the lock when it returns. Only then does session write them to the client, which involves .await. Holding the guard during those writes would not even compile, because the task would no longer be Send.

When you run the tests after this change, the integration tests fail: a second member now receives (earlier) * sara joined before its own join line. Nothing is broken. The behaviour changed, and the tests noticed. Update TestClient::join so that it skips lines that start with (earlier).

ChallengePrivate messages

Add /msg <name> <text>. Only the named member receives the line, shown as (private) sara: …. If nobody has that name, the sender is told so.

Need a hint?

Give Message a field to: Option<String>: None means “for everyone”, and Some(name) means “only for this member”. Every task still receives every message from the room, and decides whether to show it: a public message is shown unless it is the task’s own, and a private one is shown only if to equals the task’s current name. Add Shared::send_private, which first checks that the name exists.

Show solution and explanation

The private text never leaves the server towards the wrong client: each task filters before it writes. Adding the field to Message made the compiler point at every place that builds one.

This design is simple, and it has a cost: every task wakes up for every private message, only to throw it away. With thousands of members, a different structure is better: a map from each name to that member’s own mpsc sender, so that a private message goes straight to one mailbox. The broadcast channel then carries only what is truly for everyone. Choosing between “simple and good enough” and “more efficient and more complex” is a normal engineering decision. Start simple, and measure before you complicate.

What you have learned

Recap
  • A network server is an accept loop that spawns one task per connection.
  • A broadcast channel delivers each message to every subscriber. It is a natural model for a chat room.
  • select! lets a task wait for its client and for the room at the same time.
  • Shared data is kept small: one set of names behind a mutex that is never held across an .await.
  • A value with a Drop implementation guarantees clean-up on every exit path.
  • Parsing each line into an enum keeps the session loop clear, and the compiler checks that every command is handled.
  • Passing an already bound listener into serve makes the server testable on a free port.
  • Tests that wait for network data need timeouts.

You have finished Part 7. You can now write programs that do many things at once, with threads for heavy work and async tasks for waiting, and you know how Rust keeps both safe. Part 8 covers the advanced corners of the language: macros, unsafe code, calling other languages, and how data is laid out in memory.

Macros: code that writes code

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what a macro is and how it differs from a function
  • Write declarative macros with macro_rules!, including repetition
  • Use the built-in macros and the common attributes
  • Describe the three kinds of procedural macros and write a simple derive macro
  • Decide when a macro is the right tool

Since your first program you have used println!. The exclamation mark means that it is a macro, not a function. vec!, format!, assert_eq!, matches! and #[derive(Debug)] are macros as well. This chapter shows what they are and how to write your own.

Real-world analogy
A rubber stamp

An office that writes the same paragraph into hundreds of letters gets a rubber stamp made. Pressing the stamp produces the full text, and nobody has to write it out again. Some stamps have blanks that are filled in each time, such as a date. A macro is a stamp for code: you write a short form, and the compiler expands it into the full code before the program is built.

A macro runs at compile time. Its input is a piece of source code, and its output is other source code, which the compiler then translates as if you had typed it. This is called metaprogramming: writing programs that produce programs.

FunctionMacro
Works onvalues, when the program runspieces of code, when the program is compiled
Number of argumentsfixedany number (println!("{} {}", a, b))
Can create new items (structs, functions, impl blocks)noyes
Can use syntax that is not ordinary Rustnoyes (vec![0; 10], SQL or HTML inside a macro)
Ease of reading and debuggingeasyharder

That last row is why the rule is: use a function when a function can do the job. Reach for a macro when you hit one of the limits in the table.

Declarative macros: macro_rules!

The simplest way to write a macro works by pattern matching, much like match. It matches pieces of code and fills in a template.

  • macro_rules! square defines a macro called square.
  • ($x:expr) => { ... } is a rule: a pattern on the left, and a template on the right.
  • $x:expr matches any expression and names it $x. The part after the colon is the kind of code to match, a fragment specifier.
  • In the template, $x is replaced by the matched code.

Notice square!(2 + 3), which gives 25. The macro does not paste text. It treats 2 + 3 as one expression, as if it were in parentheses. Macros in C work on raw text, and the same macro there would compute 2 + 3 * 2 + 3, which is 11. This is a classic bug that Rust’s macros cannot have.

The most common fragment specifiers:

SpecifierMatchesExample
expran expression2 + 3, name.len(), "text"
identa name (identifier)count, Point, my_function
tya typei32, Vec<String>, &str
literala literal value42, "hello", true
pata patternSome(x), 1..=5, _
blocka block in braces{ let a = 1; a + 1 }
stmta statementlet x = 5
iteman itema fn, struct, impl …
tta single token, or a group in brackets (“token tree”)almost anything

Several rules

A macro can have several rules. The first one that fits is used:

A function cannot do this. Rust functions have one fixed list of parameters.

Repetition

To accept any number of arguments, a pattern can contain a repetition:

Read $( $number:expr ),* as “zero or more expressions, separated by commas, each called $number”:

  • $( ... ) encloses the part that repeats.
  • , after the parenthesis is the separator.
  • * means zero or more. + means one or more, and ? means zero or one.

In the template, $( + $number )* is written out once for every matched expression. So sum!(1, 2, 3, 4) becomes 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.

Here is a small version of the standard vec! macro, and a macro for map literals, which the standard library does not have:

  • The template has double braces. The outer pair belongs to the macro syntax. The inner pair makes the result one block expression, so that it can stand after let numbers =.
  • $(,)? allows an optional comma after the last item.
  • The map! pattern contains => as plain text that must appear between key and value. A macro can define its own little syntax.
  • A macro can be called with (), [] or {}. All three mean the same. By convention, [] is used for list-like macros and {} for block-like ones.

Macros that call themselves

A rule can use the macro again. This is how to process a list step by step:

maximum!(3, 9, 4) compares 3 with maximum!(9, 4), which compares 9 with maximum!(4), which is 4. The macro works for any type that can be compared, with no generics in sight, because it produces fresh code for each use.

Hygiene

The template of maximum! declares variables called a and b. What if the calling code has its own a?

Nothing goes wrong. Variables created inside a macro live in a separate world from the variables at the place where the macro is used, even when they have the same name. This property is called hygiene, and it removes a whole family of bugs that plague text-based macros in other languages.

Generating items

Macros earn their keep when they remove repetition that functions and generics cannot remove. A typical case is implementing a trait for many types:

Four impl blocks were written by the macro. The standard library does this on a large scale: the arithmetic traits for all the number types are produced by macros.

A macro can also create names. With ident, it can define functions, structs and enums:

One line produced an enum, a list of all its variants, and a method that returns each variant’s name. stringify! turns code into a string literal. If a variant is added later, the list and the method can never be forgotten.

Where a macro is visible

Macros follow slightly different rules from other items:

  • Inside a file, a macro can only be used after its definition. Define macros at the top.
  • To offer a macro to other crates, put #[macro_export] above it. It is then available at the root of your crate: use my_crate::my_macro;.
  • Inside an exported macro, refer to your crate’s own items with $crate::, as in $crate::helpers::run(). That path works wherever the macro is used.

Seeing what a macro produces

When a macro misbehaves, look at its output. Install the tool once with cargo install cargo-expand, and then cargo expand prints your program with all macros expanded. This is what println!("{}", sum!(1, 2)); turns into, slightly simplified:

The macros that come with Rust

You know most of these. A few are worth pointing out.

MacroWhat it does
println!, print!, eprintln!, eprint!print to standard output or standard error
format!, write!, writeln!format into a String, or into a writer
vec!create a Vec
assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!check a condition, panic if it fails
debug_assert! and friendsthe same, but only in debug builds
panic!, todo!, unimplemented!, unreachable!stop the program with a message
matches!does a value fit a pattern? gives a bool
dbg!print an expression with its file and line, and return its value
include_str!("file.txt")put the content of a file into the program as a &'static str, at compile time
include_bytes!("logo.png")the same, as bytes
env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")the value of an environment variable at compile time
concat!, stringify!join literals, or turn code into text
file!, line!, column!, module_path!the current place in the source code
cfg!(...)test a compile-time condition, as a bool
compile_error!("message")stop the compilation with your own error message

dbg! deserves more use than it gets. It is the quickest way to look at a value while hunting a bug:

It prints to standard error, with the file, line and column of each call:

dbg! gives back the value it was handed, so it can be wrapped around any part of an expression without changing the program. Remove it when you are done.

Attributes

An attribute is a note for the compiler, written as #[...] above an item. You have used several. Here are the ones that matter most:

AttributeEffect
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]generate trait implementations
#[cfg(test)], #[cfg(target_os = "windows")]include the item only under a condition
#[test], #[should_panic], #[ignore]mark and configure tests
#[allow(dead_code)], #[warn(...)], #[deny(...)]switch compiler warnings off, on, or into errors
#[must_use]warn when the return value of this function is ignored
#[deprecated(note = "use new_name")]warn everyone who still uses this item
#[inline]suggest that the compiler pastes the function’s body into its callers
#[non_exhaustive]users of this enum or struct must allow for additions in future versions
#[repr(C)]lay out the data as a C compiler would (chapter 37)
#[macro_export]make a macro_rules! macro usable from other crates

An attribute with an exclamation mark, #![...], applies to the whole enclosing file or crate. It goes at the very top.

Conditional compilation with cfg lets one code base serve several platforms:

Only one of the two functions exists in the compiled program. (On Windows, the first line of the output is "\r\n".)

Procedural macros

macro_rules! matches patterns. A procedural macro is more powerful: it is an ordinary Rust function that runs inside the compiler. It receives code as a stream of tokens, can analyse it in any way, and returns new code. There are three kinds:

KindLooks likeExamples
Derive macro#[derive(Name)]Serialize, Deserialize (serde), Parser (clap), Error (thiserror)
Attribute macro#[name] above an item#[tokio::main], #[tokio::test]
Function-like macroname!(...)sqlx::query!("SELECT …"), which checks SQL at compile time

Much of the comfort of Rust’s ecosystem comes from derive macros. You write #[derive(Serialize)] above a struct, and a macro writes the hundred lines that turn it into JSON.

Writing a derive macro

A procedural macro must live in a crate of its own, of a special type. The example has two packages side by side: the macro, and a program that uses it.

Two helper crates do the hard work. syn parses the token stream into a syntax tree that you can inspect. quote turns Rust code that you write, with placeholders, back into tokens.

The macro Describe adds a function describe() that reports the name of a struct and its fields:

The three steps are typical for every derive macro:

  1. Parse. parse_macro_input! produces a DeriveInput, a description of the struct or enum under the #[derive]. input.ident is its name.
  2. Analyse. The match looks into the struct and collects the field names. For an enum, the macro returns a proper compiler error that points at the offending name.
  3. Generate. Inside quote! { ... } you write the code to produce. #name inserts a value from the macro, and #(#field_names),* repeats for every element of a list, like $( ... ),* in macro_rules!.

The program depends on the macro crate through a path:

And deriving it for an enum gives the error the macro defined:

Normal Rust code cannot find out the names of a struct’s fields while it runs. A procedural macro can, because it looks at the source code itself.

Good to know
The cost of procedural macros

Procedural macros must be compiled before the code that uses them, and syn is a large crate. Projects that use many of them compile more slowly. That is a fair price for serde or clap. For your own small conveniences, macro_rules! or a plain function is usually the better choice.

When to write a macro

Ask these questions in order, and stop at the first “yes”:

  1. Can a function do it? Use a function.
  2. Can a generic function or a trait do it? Use that.
  3. Do you need a variable number of arguments, new items, or a special syntax? Then use macro_rules!.
  4. Do you need to analyse the structure of types, as derive does? Then write a procedural macro, or look for a crate that has done it already.

Macros have real costs. Error messages point into expanded code and can be hard to read. Editor features such as “go to definition” work less well inside them. And a reader must learn each macro’s private rules. A good macro is small, well documented, and looks as much like ordinary Rust as possible.

How other languages do it
Macros in other languages
  • C and C++ have a preprocessor that replaces text before the compiler sees it. It knows nothing about the language, is not hygienic, and is behind many subtle bugs. Rust’s macros work on parsed code.
  • Lisp languages are the origin of macros that transform code as data. Rust’s design owes much to Scheme’s hygienic macros.
  • Python decorators and Java annotations look like Rust’s attributes, and serve similar purposes, but work mostly at run time through reflection.
  • C++ templates and Zig’s comptime are other ways to compute at compile time. Rust has const fn for that purpose as well: ordinary functions that the compiler can run while compiling.
Recap
  • A macro transforms code at compile time. The ! marks a macro call.
  • macro_rules! matches patterns such as $x:expr and fills in templates. $( ... ),* repeats.
  • Declarative macros are hygienic: their variables cannot clash with yours.
  • Macros can generate items: functions, impl blocks, enums.
  • Attributes (#[derive], #[cfg], #[must_use], …) give instructions to the compiler.
  • Procedural macros are Rust functions from tokens to tokens: derive, attribute and function-like. syn parses, quote generates.
  • Prefer functions, generics and traits. Use a macro when they cannot express what you need.
Check your understanding
1

When does a macro do its work?

A macro is expanded into ordinary code by the compiler. The running program contains only the result.

2

What does $( $x:expr ),* match?

$( ... ) is a repetition, , is the separator, and * means zero or more.

3

Given macro_rules! twice { ($x:expr) => { $x * 2 }; }, what is twice!(1 + 4)?

A matched expr stays one unit. Rust’s macros do not substitute raw text, unlike the C preprocessor.

4

Which of these can a function not do, so that a macro is needed?

Functions have a fixed parameter list. Generics cover “several types”, and tuples cover “two values”.

5

What kind of macro is #[derive(Serialize)]?

Derive macros are procedural macros that receive the definition of a struct or enum and generate additional code for it.

Guided exerciseA macro with two forms

Write a macro greet! with two rules. greet!() prints Hello, world!. greet!("Sara") prints Hello, Sara!. Then add a third rule that accepts any number of names, separated by commas, and greets each one.

Need a hint?

The first two rules are () => { ... }; and ($name:expr) => { ... };. The third is ( $( $name:expr ),+ ) => { $( greet!($name); )+ };. It calls the macro itself once per name. Put the single-name rule before the list rule.

Show solution and explanation

The rules are tried from top to bottom. A single name fits the second rule. Several names fit only the third, which expands to one greet! call per name, and each of those uses the second rule. Building a list-handling rule out of a single-item rule keeps macros short.

PracticeA set literal

Write a macro set! that builds a HashSet: set![1, 2, 3]. It should accept a trailing comma, and set![] should give an empty set.

Need a hint?

Model it on my_vec!. Create the set with HashSet::new(), and insert each item in a repetition. Remember the double braces, so that the result is one expression.

Show solution and explanation

Duplicates disappear, because the items go into a set. The empty case has a rule of its own. With a single rule and *, the call set![] would expand to a let mut set that is never changed, and the compiler would warn about the needless mut. For the empty set, the element type cannot be worked out from any item, so the variable needs a type annotation. The variable called set inside the macro cannot collide with a variable of that name at the call site, thanks to hygiene.

PracticeGenerate the boring code

You have three newtypes for ids: UserId(u32), OrderId(u32) and ProductId(u32). Each should get #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)], a constructor new, a method value(), and a Display implementation that prints, for example, UserId#7. Write one macro id_type! that creates all of this from the name.

Need a hint?

The pattern is ($name:ident) => { ... }. In the template, write the struct and the two impl blocks, using $name wherever the type’s name appears. stringify!($name) gives the name as text for the Display output.

Show solution and explanation

Three types with identical behaviour, defined in three lines. They are still distinct types: comparing a UserId with an OrderId is a compile error, which is the purpose of the newtypes. Generics could not have produced this, because the task was to create new types with new names.

ChallengeTests from a table

Testing a function with many inputs leads to many near-identical test functions. Write a macro test_cases! that takes a function name and a list of test_name: input => expected entries, and generates one #[test] function per entry. Use it to test fn double(n: i32) -> i32.

Need a hint?

The pattern is ($function:ident, $( $test_name:ident : $input:expr => $expected:expr ),* $(,)? ). The template repeats #[test] fn $test_name() { assert_eq!($function($input), $expected); }.

Show solution and explanation

Each entry becomes a separate test function with its own name. If one case fails, cargo test names exactly that case, and the others still run. A single test with four assertions would stop at the first failure.

The macro generates functions, which only a macro can do. This “table-driven” style is common enough that crates exist for it, such as rstest and test-case. Having written a small version yourself, you know what they do.
