Unsafe Rust: taking over responsibility

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what unsafe allows, what it does not change, and what undefined behaviour is
  • Work with raw pointers
  • Wrap unsafe code in a safe interface and document why it is sound
  • Name the tools that check unsafe code
  • Judge when unsafe code is justified

Everything you have written so far was safe Rust: the compiler guaranteed that no reference dangles, no index reads outside its array, and no two threads race for the same data. It gives these guarantees by being careful. When it cannot prove that some code is correct, it rejects the code, even if the code happens to be fine.

Some things cannot be proved by any compiler: that an address handed over by the operating system really points to usable memory, or that a function written in C keeps its promises. For these cases Rust has a second mode, entered with the keyword unsafe.

Real-world analogy
The maintenance hatch

A machine on a factory floor has guards so that nobody can reach into the moving parts. A trained technician sometimes has to open a guard to repair the machine. The guard is not removed from the factory. It is opened at one marked spot, by someone who knows the procedure, for as short a time as possible. unsafe is that hatch.

unsafe does not mean “this code is dangerous” or “this code is wrong”. It means: ”the compiler cannot check this part. I, the programmer, have checked it, and I take the responsibility.”

What unsafe allows

Inside an unsafe block you may do five things that are forbidden elsewhere:

  1. read or write through a raw pointer,
  2. call an unsafe function (including functions from other languages),
  3. read or change a mutable static variable,
  4. implement an unsafe trait,
  5. read a field of a union.

That is the whole list. Everything else stays as it was. The borrow checker still checks references. Types are still checked. Indexing a vector is still checked at run time. unsafe adds five abilities and takes no checks away.

Undefined behaviour

In exchange for the five abilities, you must keep the rules that the compiler normally enforces. Breaking them causes undefined behaviour, often shortened to UB.

Key idea
What undefined behaviour means

The compiler builds your program on the assumption that certain things never happen. If one of them does happen, there is no rule for what the program does next. It may crash. It may produce wrong results. It may appear to work for years and fail after a compiler update. It may let an attacker take control. “It worked when I tried it” proves nothing.

The most important things that must never happen:

  • reading or writing through a pointer that is null, dangling, or outside its allocation,
  • reading memory that was never given a value,
  • breaking the borrowing rules: a &mut that is not exclusive, or changing data while a & to it exists,
  • a data race,
  • creating a value that is invalid for its type: a bool that is neither 0 nor 1, a char outside the valid range, a reference that is null, an enum with a number that names no variant,
  • calling a function from another language with the wrong signature.

In safe Rust, none of these can happen. That is the meaning of “memory safe”. In C and C++, all of them can happen anywhere. In Rust, they can only originate in an unsafe block, so when something goes wrong, you know where to look.

Raw pointers

A raw pointer is an address in memory with a type attached, and no guarantees. There are two kinds: *const T (for reading) and *mut T (for reading and writing).

Reference &T, &mut TRaw pointer *const T, *mut T
Always points to a valid valueyesnot necessarily
Can be nullnoyes
Borrowing rules enforcedyesno
Has a lifetimeyesno
Freed automatically(does not own)no
Using itsafereading or writing needs unsafe

&raw const number creates a *const i32, and &raw mut number a *mut i32. A reader and a writer to the same value exist side by side here, which references would not allow. The compiler permits creating them, because a pointer that is never used can do no harm. Dereferencing a raw pointer, with *, is the dangerous step, and needs unsafe.

A raw pointer can be made from any number, and then it points wherever that number says:

Raw pointers have methods for the basic operations: is_null(), add(n) to move forward by n elements, read() and write(value).

Unsafe functions

A function can be marked unsafe. That tells callers: “this function has requirements that the compiler cannot check. Read the documentation and make sure you meet them.” It can only be called inside an unsafe block.

Two conventions are visible here, and both are worth adopting from the first day:

  • An unsafe function has a # Safety section in its documentation that lists what the caller must guarantee.
  • Every unsafe block has a // SAFETY: comment that explains why the requirements are met at this spot.

The body of an unsafe function still needs its own unsafe block around each unsafe operation. So the two meanings of the keyword stay apart: unsafe fn states a requirement, and unsafe { } claims that a requirement is fulfilled.

get_unchecked skips the bounds check that list[index] performs. Calling element_unchecked(&numbers, 7) would read memory beyond the array: undefined behaviour.

A safe interface over unsafe code

The main use of unsafe is to build something that is safe to use. The standard library is full of such code: Vec, String, Rc, Mutex and the channels all contain unsafe code inside and offer an interface that cannot be misused.

A classic example is split_at_mut, which divides one mutable slice into two. You cannot write it in safe Rust:

The borrow checker sees two mutable borrows of values. It does not understand that the two ranges do not overlap. They never do, so the function is sound. This is a case where the programmer knows more than the compiler:

as_mut_ptr() gives a raw pointer to the first element. slice::from_raw_parts_mut(pointer, n) builds a slice from a pointer and a length. It is an unsafe function, because it trusts both values blindly.

The function split_at_mut itself is not marked unsafe. Whatever arguments a caller passes, nothing bad can happen: a middle that is too large is caught by the assert!. The assertion is part of the safety argument. Remove it, and safe code could create slices beyond the end of the array.

Key idea
Soundness

A safe function is sound if no possible use of it from safe code can cause undefined behaviour. Making your safe wrappers sound is the whole responsibility you take on when you write unsafe. It is not enough that correct use works. Incorrect use must be either impossible to write or caught with a check.

Managing memory by hand

To see what Vec and Box do inside, here is a small buffer that asks the memory allocator for space directly:

Every hazard of manual memory management appears in these lines, each one answered:

HazardHow Buffer prevents it
The allocation failsthe null check after alloc
Reading memory that was never writtennew fills every element with 0
Reading or writing out of boundsget and set check the index
Forgetting to free (a leak)Drop frees the memory
Freeing twicethe pointer is owned by one Buffer, which is not Clone and is dropped once
Use after freethe pointer is private and never handed out
A data raceset takes &mut self, and a raw pointer field makes the type neither Send nor Sync

The fields are private. That matters: if outside code could change length, all the safety arguments would collapse. The privacy boundary of the module is the safety boundary. All code that can touch the private parts must be reviewed together.

A Layout describes how many bytes are needed and how they must be aligned (chapter 37). In real code you would simply use vec![0; 4]. The point is to see that there is no magic underneath.

A lock built by hand: UnsafeCell

Chapter 27 and chapter 31 showed types that change their content through a shared reference: Cell, RefCell, Mutex, the atomics. All of them are built on one type, UnsafeCell<T>. It is the only legal way in Rust to change data behind a &. Its method get returns a raw pointer to the content, and from there on the responsibility is yours.

To see how the pieces of the last chapters fit together, here is a complete lock. It waits by trying again and again, which is called a spin lock:

Read it from the outside in:

  • The safe interface. A user can only call new and lock, and reaches the value only through a Guard. No call order exists that leads to two threads holding the value at once. That is the claim every unsafe block here depends on, and each // SAFETY: comment says so.
  • locked.swap(true, …) is the whole locking logic, in one atomic step. Acquire and Release are the orderings made for this: everything written before the Release store is visible after the Acquire swap that takes the lock next.
  • The guard is the RAII idea again: Deref and DerefMut give access, and Drop unlocks. Forgetting to unlock is impossible.
  • The two unsafe impl lines are promises to the compiler. The first says that a SpinLock<T> may be shared between threads. The second restricts something: without it, the compiler’s automatic rule would let every guard be shared between threads, even a guard for a type like Cell<i32>, which must never be used from two threads at once. Nothing warns about a mistake like that. Only careful reading finds it.

That last point is the lesson. The lock is about 60 lines long, it follows a well-known design, and it still needed a line that is easy to forget. For real programs, use std::sync::Mutex: it puts a waiting thread to sleep where this one keeps a processor core busy, and many people have checked it.

Memory that has no value yet: MaybeUninit

Safe Rust never lets you read a variable before it has a value. Unsafe code sometimes needs room that is filled in later: an array built element by element, or a buffer that a C function will write to. Reading memory that was never written is undefined behaviour, even for a plain number. The type MaybeUninit<T> is “room for a T that may or may not be there yet”:

assume_init is the unsafe step: you promise that a value has been written. In old code you may see std::mem::uninitialized(). It is deprecated, because almost every use of it was undefined behaviour.

Dropping by hand: ManuallyDrop

The mirror image of building a value by hand is giving it away by hand. A Vec that hands its buffer to the operating system, or a struct that moves one of its fields into a C function, must not free that memory when it is dropped itself. std::mem::ManuallyDrop<T> wraps a value and switches the automatic drop off: the compiler will not run T’s destructor for it, so the destructor runs when you say, or never.

Watch out
Dropping twice is a double free

ManuallyDrop::drop is unsafe for exactly this reason: safe code could call it twice, and the second call would free memory that has already been freed. If you call it, the value must never be dropped again — not at the end of the scope, not by a later mem::take, not by anything else. In ordinary code Option<T> with take() is the better tool, because the None that take leaves behind means “already moved out” and needs no unsafe at all. ManuallyDrop is for the cases where a type must keep its layout — a struct shared with C, or a self-referential type whose fields point into each other — and where the destructor has to be taken over deliberately.

The two tools often appear together: MaybeUninit is “a value may be here”, and ManuallyDrop is “the value is definitely here, but I will decide when it goes”. std::mem::forget(x) is the third form of the same idea — it takes ownership of x and never drops it, which leaks the value but cannot be undone.

The other three abilities

Mutable statics

A static mut is a global variable that can be changed, with no protection at all. Any thread can reach it at any time, so every access is a potential data race.

Even inside unsafe, Rust refuses to create a reference to a static mut (println!("{}", COUNTER) would, and is an error), because such a reference could be made invalid from anywhere. In new code there is almost never a reason to use static mut. An atomic, a Mutex or a OnceLock in a plain static does the same job safely, as shown in chapter 31.

Unsafe traits

A trait is unsafe when implementing it wrongly could cause undefined behaviour in other, safe code. The two you will meet are Send and Sync. The compiler implements them automatically where it can. A type that holds a raw pointer gets neither. If you know that your type is safe to move between threads all the same, you say so, and take the responsibility:

Box::into_raw turns a box into a raw pointer and stops managing the memory. Box::from_raw turns it back, after which the box frees the memory as usual. This pair is the standard way to hand ownership through a raw pointer, and it is how Rust values are passed to and from C code in the next chapter.

Unions

A union is like a struct in which all fields share the same memory. Only one of them holds a meaningful value at a time, and the program itself must remember which. Reading a field is unsafe, because the compiler cannot know that you picked the right one.

Unions exist mainly to exchange data with C code. In pure Rust, an enum does the same job and remembers which variant is active.

Reinterpreting bytes: transmute

std::mem::transmute takes the bytes of a value and declares them to be a value of another type of the same size. It is the most dangerous function in the standard library, because it switches the type system off completely.

The program prints 1, and the compiler itself points out that the transmute is unnecessary. The safe functions say what they mean:

There is nearly always a safe function for the conversion you need: from_bits, to_bits, to_le_bytes, from_le_bytes, as, From. Use transmute only when nothing else exists, and never to change a lifetime or to turn a &T into a &mut T. The latter is undefined behaviour in every case.

Tools that check unsafe code

Unsafe code cannot be verified by the compiler, but you are not without help.

  • Miri is an interpreter that runs your program or tests and watches every memory access. It detects most kinds of undefined behaviour: out-of-bounds access, use after free, uninitialised reads, and violations of the borrowing rules through raw pointers. It needs the nightly toolchain:

Run it on every piece of unsafe code you write. It is slow, and it can only find problems on the paths your tests exercise, so write tests that cover the unusual cases.

  • Sanitizers (AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer) are checks compiled into the program. They are faster than Miri and also cover code from other languages that is linked into your program.
  • Clippy (chapter 40) has lints for unsafe code. clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks demands a SAFETY comment on every block.
  • #![forbid(unsafe_code)] at the top of a crate makes any unsafe a compile error. Use it to state, and enforce, that a crate is entirely safe.
  • cargo geiger counts the unsafe code in your dependencies.

When is unsafe justified?

Good reasons:

  • Talking to other languages and to the operating system. There is no other way (chapter 36).
  • Talking to hardware, in embedded systems and drivers, where memory addresses are device registers.
  • Building basic data structures and synchronisation tools that the borrow checker cannot express: a doubly linked list, a lock-free queue, a memory arena.
  • Performance, in a place that measurements have shown to matter, where a check cannot be removed in any safe way.

Poor reasons:

  • ”The borrow checker is in my way.” It is nearly always pointing at a real problem in the design. Restructure, clone, use indices, or use Rc<RefCell<T>>.
  • ”It is faster”, without a measurement. The optimiser removes most bounds checks on its own, and iterators have none.

Rules for writing it:

  1. Keep it small. A few lines inside a safe function.
  2. Wrap it in a sound, safe interface with private fields.
  3. Write down the invariants: the facts that must always be true (for Buffer: “pointer points to length initialised values”).
  4. Comment every block with // SAFETY:.
  5. Test with Miri.
  6. Look for a crate first. Well-tested crates exist for most needs: bytemuck and zerocopy for reinterpreting bytes, crossbeam for lock-free structures, parking_lot for locks.

Most Rust programmers write unsafe code rarely or never. Application code, web services and command-line tools do not need it. It is still worth understanding, because it explains how the safe parts are built, and how far the guarantees reach.

How other languages do it
Safety in other languages
  • In C and C++, the whole program is “unsafe” in Rust’s sense. Any line can cause undefined behaviour, and reviews must cover everything.
  • Java, C#, Go and Python are memory safe through a garbage collector and run-time checks. They also have escape hatches: sun.misc.Unsafe, C#’s unsafe keyword, Go’s unsafe package, Python’s ctypes.
  • Rust’s contribution is the combination: no garbage collector, safe by default, and unsafe code that is explicitly marked, small, and wrapped. Studies of large Rust code bases find that a few percent of the code is unsafe, and that is where reviewers concentrate.
Recap
  • unsafe permits five things: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions, accessing mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits, and reading unions. All other checks remain.
  • With them comes the duty to avoid undefined behaviour, which the compiler can no longer rule out.
  • Raw pointers (*const T, *mut T) can be null or dangling. Creating them is safe, and using them is not.
  • unsafe fn states requirements for the caller (# Safety). An unsafe { } block claims they are met (// SAFETY:).
  • The goal is a sound safe interface: safe code must not be able to cause undefined behaviour through it. Private fields protect the invariants.
  • Check unsafe code with Miri. Prefer safe alternatives and established crates.
Check your understanding
1

What does an unsafe block switch off?

unsafe adds abilities. References are still borrow-checked, types are still checked, and v[i] still checks its index.

2

Which of these needs unsafe?

Making and handling raw pointers is safe. Dereferencing is not, because the pointer may be invalid.

3

What does “undefined behaviour” mean?

The compiler optimises on the assumption that undefined behaviour never happens. When it does, anything can follow, including wrong results far from the cause.

4

A safe function contains an unsafe block. For which inputs must it be free of undefined behaviour?

A safe function promises soundness. If some input could trigger undefined behaviour, the function must either check for it, or be marked unsafe and document the requirement.

5

Why are the fields of a type that wraps unsafe code usually private?

If anyone could set length to a larger number, the bounds check in front of the unsafe access would be worthless. Privacy keeps the invariant in the hands of the module.

Guided exerciseSwap through raw pointers

Write a safe function swap(a: &mut i32, b: &mut i32) that exchanges the two values using raw pointers. Create the pointers from the references, read both values, and write them back the other way round. Add a SAFETY comment.

Need a hint?

let pa: *mut i32 = a; converts a mutable reference into a raw pointer. Inside unsafe, *pa reads and *pa = value writes.

Show solution and explanation

The function is safe to call, because its parameters are references, and references always fulfil what the raw pointers need. This exercise is for practice only: the same job is done without unsafe by std::mem::swap(a, b), and that is what you should use.

PracticeTwo elements at once

Write a safe function two_mut(list: &mut [i32], i: usize, j: usize) -> Option<(&mut i32, &mut i32)> that returns mutable references to two different elements. It returns None if the indices are equal or out of bounds. Safe Rust rejects (&mut list[i], &mut list[j]). Use raw pointers.

Need a hint?

Do all the checks first: i == j, i >= list.len(), j >= list.len(). Then get let pointer = list.as_mut_ptr(); and build the references with &mut *pointer.add(i) inside unsafe.

Show solution and explanation

The check i == j is the heart of the safety argument. Two &mut to the same element would be undefined behaviour, even if neither is ever written through. The return type ties both references to the borrow of list, so the compiler stops callers from using the slice while they are alive.

The standard library offers this operation: list.get_disjoint_mut([i, j]). As so often, the unsafe code you need has been written and reviewed already.

ChallengeFind the undefined behaviour

Each of these four functions compiles. Three contain undefined behaviour, or allow safe callers to cause it. Find them, explain why, and say how to fix each.

Need a hint?

For each function ask: is there any argument that safe code could pass that breaks a rule from the list at the start of the chapter? Think about dangling pointers, invalid values and bounds.

Show solution and explanation

A is sound. find(' ') returns the byte position of a space, which is always inside the text and on a character boundary, and text.len() is the end. The range ..end is therefore always valid for get_unchecked. A SAFETY comment should say so. The unsafe gains almost nothing here, though: &text[..end] is safe and nearly as fast.

B is undefined behaviour. make_pointer returns the address of a local variable. When the function returns, local no longer exists, and the pointer dangles. Creating and returning the pointer is allowed, which is why it compiles. Dereferencing it in use_it reads memory that has been released. With a reference, the compiler would have refused (E0515). Fix: return the value itself, or a Box<i32>.

C is unsound. A bool must be the byte 0 or 1. as_bool(2) creates a bool with an invalid value, which is immediate undefined behaviour, even if it is never looked at. The function is safe to call and accepts every u8, so safe code can trigger it. Fix: byte != 0, which needs no unsafe.

D is unsound. Nothing checks index. get(&[1, 2, 3], 10) reads beyond the slice. Because get is a safe function, any caller can do that. Fix: check the index first (if index < list.len()), or simply write list[index], or mark the function unsafe fn and document the requirement in a # Safety section.

The pattern in B, C and D is the same: the code works for the inputs its author imagined, and nothing stops other inputs. Reviewing unsafe code means looking for the input nobody imagined. In all three cases the best fix was to remove the unsafe altogether.

36

Working with other languages (FFI)

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what an ABI is and why C is the common language between languages
  • Call C functions from Rust and wrap them safely
  • Compile C code into a Rust project
  • Offer Rust functions to C and to Python
  • Handle strings, structs and ownership across a language boundary

No language lives alone. Decades of proven software are written in C and C++: operating systems, databases, image and audio libraries, cryptography. Other teams work in Python or JavaScript and want one slow part to be fast. Rust was designed to fit into this world. It can call code in other languages and be called by them, with no translation layer in between and no cost at run time. The mechanism is called the foreign function interface, or FFI.

Real-world analogy
A shared language at the border crossing

Different countries speak different languages, but they still need to trade. The point of a shared standard is not that everyone loves it; it is that everyone can agree on the same vocabulary and rules at the border. The C ABI is that common border language for compiled software.

The common language: the C ABI

Real-world analogy
Translating through a diplomatic language

When engineers speaking two unrelated scripts need to sign a treaty that both presses can print accurately, they agree on a single plain format with fixed rules for dates, numbers and margins. In software, each compiler arranges its own types however it likes, but almost every language knows how to read and write C’s binary layout—making the C ABI the shared treaty between Rust, Python, C and everything else.

For one piece of compiled code to call another, both must agree on details far below the level of source code: in which processor registers the arguments are passed, how a struct is laid out in memory, who cleans up afterwards. Such an agreement is an ABI (application binary interface).

Rust’s own ABI is not fixed. The compiler is free to change it between versions, which lets it optimise. The ABI of C, on the other hand, is stable and defined for every platform, and practically every language can speak it. So C is the meeting point: when Rust talks to Python, Swift or Java, both sides pretend to be C.

Three tools make Rust speak the C ABI:

  • extern "C" on a function or block: “use the C calling convention”.
  • #[repr(C)] on a struct or enum: “lay this out in memory as a C compiler would”.
  • The types in std::ffi: c_int, c_char, c_void and so on, which have exactly the size that C’s int, char and void have on the current platform.

Calling C from Rust

The C standard library is linked into every Rust program anyway, so its functions make a ready example. To call a foreign function, you declare its signature in an extern block:

There is a lot to see here.

The extern block is unsafe. The compiler cannot look into C code. It believes the signatures you write. If a declaration is wrong, for example a c_int where C has a long, the result is undefined behaviour. Writing unsafe extern acknowledges that you vouch for the declarations.

Each function is safe or unsafe to call. abs takes a number and returns a number. Nothing can go wrong, so it is declared safe and called like any Rust function. strlen takes a pointer and trusts it blindly, so calling it needs an unsafe block.

C strings are different from Rust strings. A Rust &str is a pointer and a length, and holds valid UTF-8. A C string is only a pointer, and the text ends at the first zero byte. Two types bridge the gap:

TypeIt isUse it to
CStringan owned, zero-terminated stringpass text from Rust to C
&CStra borrowed, zero-terminated stringlook at text that came from C
c"..."a C string literalwrite constant C strings

CString::new fails if the text contains a zero byte in the middle, because C would see the string end there.

C can call back into Rust. qsort is C’s sorting function. It knows nothing about the elements, so it asks the caller for a comparison function. compare_i32 is a Rust function with extern "C", which makes it callable from C. The type *mut c_void is C’s “pointer to anything”.

Watch out
The lifetime of a CString

text.as_ptr() gives a pointer into the CString. The pointer is valid only while text is alive. This line is a classic bug: let pointer = CString::new("hi").unwrap().as_ptr();. The CString is a temporary value that is destroyed at the end of the statement, and pointer dangles. Keep the CString in a variable for as long as C uses the pointer.

Wrap it once, use it safely

Unsafe calls should not be scattered through a program. The usual structure has two layers:

  1. The raw declarations, exactly as C defines them. By convention they live in a module or crate with the suffix -sys (for example openssl-sys).
  2. A safe Rust API on top, which checks arguments, converts types, turns error codes into Results, and frees resources in Drop.

Users of c_length cannot cause undefined behaviour, whatever they pass. That is the job of a wrapper. Most well-known C libraries already have such crates. Look on crates.io before you write your own.

Compiling C code into your project

When the C code is not a system library but a few files of your own, Cargo can compile it together with your Rust code. This needs a build script: a Rust program called build.rs, in the package’s root folder, that Cargo runs before it compiles the package.

The crate cc finds the C compiler of your system and runs it. It is needed only while building, so it is added as a build dependency: cargo add --build cc.

cargo run compiles the C file, links it in, and runs the program. You need a C compiler installed (GCC or Clang on Linux and macOS, the Visual Studio build tools on Windows). A Rust slice turns into the pair that C expects, a pointer and a count, with as_ptr() and len().

Tip
Let a tool write the declarations

Typing extern declarations by hand is tedious for a big library, and a typing error is undefined behaviour. The tool bindgen reads C header files and generates the Rust declarations. It is usually run from build.rs.

Calling Rust from C

The other direction is just as direct. A Rust library can offer functions that look exactly like C functions to the rest of the world.

staticlib produces a library file (libshapes.a) that can be linked into a C program. cdylib produces a dynamic library (.so, .dll or .dylib) that is loaded at run time.

  • #[unsafe(no_mangle)] keeps the function’s name as written. Normally the Rust compiler changes (“mangles”) names so that functions in different modules cannot clash. C looks for the plain name. The attribute is marked unsafe because two functions with the same exported name would collide.
  • pub extern "C" fn uses the C calling convention.
  • #[repr(C)] gives Point the layout a C compiler would choose, so that both sides agree on where x and y are.

The C side needs a header file that declares the functions. You can write it by hand, or let the tool cbindgen generate it from the Rust code.

If the linker reports missing symbols on your system, the Rust library needs some system libraries to be named as well. cargo rustc --release -- --print native-static-libs prints the list to add to the gcc command.

Who frees the memory?

The greeting shows the most important rule of FFI.

Key idea
Memory must be freed by the side that allocated it

Rust and C may use different memory allocators. Memory handed out by one must never be freed by the other. So a library that returns allocated data always provides a matching function to free it.

  • greeting_new creates a CString and gives it away with into_raw(). From then on, Rust no longer manages that memory. The C code owns it.
  • greeting_free takes the pointer back with CString::from_raw and drops the string, which frees the memory with Rust’s allocator.

If the C program called its own free(text), the behaviour would be undefined.

The same technique passes whole Rust objects to C as opaque pointers: Box::into_raw(Box::new(value)) gives C a pointer that it cannot look into but can hand back, and Box::from_raw takes ownership again. C code sees a “handle”, and all work on it goes through your functions.

Panics must not escape

A Rust panic must not travel up into C code, which has no idea what a panic is. In a function with extern "C", a panic that reaches the boundary aborts the whole process. Code that might panic should catch it at the border with std::panic::catch_unwind and return an error code in its place.

Rust and Python

Python is easy to write and slow at heavy computation. The classic remedy was to write the slow part in C. Rust is now a popular choice for that job, and the crate PyO3 hides nearly all the FFI details.

The functions are ordinary, safe Rust. The attribute macros #[pyfunction] and #[pymodule] generate the code that converts between Python objects and Rust types: a Python int becomes a u64, a str becomes a &str, and a Vec<String> becomes a Python list. From Python, the result looks like any other module:

A wrong argument type becomes a normal Python exception. On the machine used to test this guide, counting the primes below 300,000 took 0.57 seconds with the same algorithm written in plain Python, and 0.021 seconds through this Rust function: about 27 times faster.

In practice you build and publish such modules with the tool maturin: maturin develop compiles the crate and installs it into your Python environment. Well-known Python packages built this way include the data-frame library Polars, the validation library Pydantic (its core), and the linter Ruff.

Other languages

LanguageToolNotes
Cbindgen (C → Rust), cbindgen (Rust → C), ccthe foundation for everything else
C++cxxsafe bindings in both directions, with support for C++ strings, vectors and smart pointers
Pythonpyo3 with maturinwrite Python modules in Rust, or run Python inside Rust
JavaScript (Node.js)napi-rs, neonnative Node.js modules
JavaScript (browser)wasm-bindgenthrough WebAssembly (chapter 49)
Java, Kotlinjni, uniffiuniffi generates bindings for Kotlin, Swift and Python from one description
Swiftuniffi, swift-bridgeused for shared code in mobile apps
Rubymagnusnative Ruby extensions

Rules for the border

FFI is where Rust’s guarantees end and yours begin. A short checklist:

  1. Use only FFI-safe types in signatures: the c_* types, fixed-size integers and floats, raw pointers, and #[repr(C)] structs. Not String, Vec, &str, slices, or tuples. Their layout is Rust’s private business.
  2. Check every pointer that comes in for null before using it.
  3. Decide and document who owns each piece of memory, and provide a free function for everything you allocate.
  4. Never let a panic cross the border.
  5. Mind threads. A foreign library may not be thread-safe. Do not implement Send or Sync for a handle unless its documentation says it is safe.
  6. Keep the unsafe layer thin, and put a safe, idiomatic API on top.
  7. Prefer generated bindings to hand-written ones.
How other languages do it
How other languages do FFI
  • Python (ctypes, cffi), Java (JNI, and the newer Foreign Function API), C# (P/Invoke) and Go (cgo) can all call C. In languages with a garbage collector and a runtime, each call across the border has a cost, and data often has to be converted or pinned so that the collector does not move it.
  • Rust has no runtime and no collector, so a call to C costs the same as a C function calling another C function. That makes Rust practical for a job few languages can do: replacing parts of an existing C or C++ program one piece at a time. This is how Rust entered Firefox, Android, the Linux kernel and Windows.
Recap
  • FFI lets Rust call, and be called by, other languages. The shared ground is the C ABI.
  • unsafe extern "C" { ... } declares foreign functions. The declarations are your responsibility.
  • CString and CStr convert between Rust strings and zero-terminated C strings.
  • A build script with the cc crate compiles C files into a Rust project. bindgen and cbindgen generate declarations.
  • #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn and #[repr(C)] offer Rust code to C.
  • Memory is freed by the side that allocated it. Panics stay on the Rust side.
  • High-level tools such as PyO3, cxx, napi-rs and uniffi hide the details for specific languages.
Check your understanding
1

Why do languages usually talk to each other through the C ABI?

Rust’s own ABI may change between compiler versions. C’s is the common denominator that all sides can rely on.

2

Why is an extern "C" block marked unsafe?

The declarations are taken on trust. A mismatch between declaration and reality is undefined behaviour.

3

You want to pass the Rust string "hello" to a C function that expects const char *. What do you use?

C expects a zero byte at the end of the text. A Rust &str has none. CString adds it and owns the memory.

4

A Rust function returns a string to C with CString::into_raw. How must the C code release it?

The memory came from Rust’s allocator and must go back to it. Freeing it with a different allocator is undefined behaviour.

5

What does #[repr(C)] on a struct do?

Without it, Rust may reorder the fields. With it, both languages agree on the position and size of every field.

Guided exerciseCall a C function

The C standard library has int atoi(const char *text), which turns the digits at the start of a text into a number. Declare it, and write a safe wrapper parse_leading(text: &str) -> Option<i32> that returns None if the text contains a zero byte. Try it with "42", "17 apples" and "none".

Need a hint?

Declare fn atoi(text: *const c_char) -> c_int; inside unsafe extern "C" { }. In the wrapper, build a CString with CString::new(text).ok()? and call atoi in an unsafe block.

Show solution and explanation

The call works, and the result shows why Rust’s own parse is better: atoi returns 0 for “none”, which cannot be told apart from a real zero. C had no way to report “this was not a number” except through such conventions. "none".parse::<i32>() returns an Err.

PracticeA counter for C

Design the Rust side of a small library that C programs can use: a counter object. Write four functions with the C ABI: counter_new() -> *mut Counter, counter_add(counter: *mut Counter, amount: u32), counter_value(counter: *const Counter) -> u64, and counter_free(counter: *mut Counter). Then call them from a Rust main, the way C would.

Need a hint?

Box::into_raw(Box::new(Counter { total: 0 })) creates the object and gives up ownership. counter_free takes it back with Box::from_raw and drops it. In counter_add and counter_value, check for null, then turn the pointer into a reference with &mut *counter or &*counter.

Show solution and explanation

This is the opaque pointer pattern. C code receives a Counter * that it cannot look inside. In the C header, the type would be declared as typedef struct Counter Counter; with no fields. Every operation goes through a function, so the Rust side stays in full control of the data.

pointer.as_mut() and pointer.as_ref() turn a raw pointer into an Option of a reference: None for null. They make the null check hard to forget. The life of the object is counter_new → use → counter_free, and each step hands ownership across the border explicitly.

ChallengeA safe handle

The four functions of the last exercise are what a C library typically looks like from the outside. Now be the user: write a safe Rust wrapper SafeCounter around the raw functions. It should create the counter in new(), offer add(&mut self, amount: u32) and value(&self) -> u64, and free the counter automatically. Users of SafeCounter should need no unsafe.

Need a hint?

The struct holds one field, the raw pointer. Implement Drop to call counter_free. std::ptr::NonNull<Counter> is a raw pointer that is guaranteed not to be null, which documents the invariant. Do not derive Clone: two wrappers with the same pointer would free it twice.

Show solution and explanation

All the rules that the C-style interface left to the caller are now enforced by the compiler:

  • Free exactly once: Drop frees, and the type is not Clone.
  • No use after free: after the wrapper is dropped, there is no value left to call methods on.
  • No null: NonNull and the check in new.
  • No data race: add takes &mut self. And because NonNull is neither Send nor Sync, the wrapper cannot be shared with other threads by accident.

This is what binding crates do: a -sys crate with raw declarations, and a safe crate on top that turns the library’s documentation into types.

37

How data sits in memory

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Find the size and alignment of any type
  • Explain padding and why field order matters
  • Control layout with repr attributes
  • Describe how enums, Option, references and trait objects are stored
  • Reason about the cost of allocations, indirection and cache misses

Chapter 8 introduced the stack and the heap. This chapter goes one level deeper and looks at how individual values are stored, byte by byte. You need this knowledge to exchange data with other languages, to read and write binary file formats, and to understand why one data structure is fast and another is slow.

All the numbers in this chapter are for a 64-bit computer, which is what almost everyone uses today.

Size and alignment

Every type has two basic properties:

  • its size: how many bytes a value occupies,
  • its alignment: the value’s address must be a multiple of this number.

Why alignment? Processors read memory most efficiently, and on some machines only, when a 4-byte value starts at an address divisible by 4, and an 8-byte value at an address divisible by 8. So every type demands a suitable starting position.

A char takes 4 bytes, because it can hold any Unicode character. A bool takes a whole byte, although one bit would be enough, because the smallest unit of memory with an address is the byte.

Structs: padding and field order

A struct stores its fields one after another. To give every field its alignment, the compiler may have to leave gaps. These unused bytes are called padding.

Real-world analogy
Packing a suitcase

Imagine a suitcase with fixed compartments, in which large items may only start at certain marks. Put a small item first and a large one after it, and space is left over in between. Put the large items first and the small ones last, and everything fits tightly.

Take a struct with a u8, a u32 and a u16, laid out in the order written:

b needs an address divisible by 4, so three bytes after a are wasted. At the end, two more bytes round the size up to a multiple of the struct’s alignment, so that structs can sit side by side in an array. Total: 12 bytes for 7 bytes of data.

By default, Rust reorders the fields to keep the padding small. That is why Mixed needs 8 bytes and not 12. The order in which you write the fields does not affect the size, and you should not rely on any particular order in memory.

With #[repr(C)], the fields are stored in the order written, as a C compiler does it. Then the order matters, and sorting the fields from the largest alignment to the smallest gives the tightest result.

The repr attributes

AttributeEffectUse it for
(none)Rust chooses the layout and may reorder fieldseverything, unless there is a reason
#[repr(C)]fields in written order, C’s rulesFFI, binary formats
#[repr(transparent)]same layout as the single field insidenewtypes passed through FFI
#[repr(u8)], #[repr(i32)], …on an enum: store the variant number in this integer typeenums shared with C, or written to files
#[repr(packed)]no padding at allexact binary formats. Fields may be misaligned, so use with great care
#[repr(align(64))]raise the alignment to at least 64keeping data on separate cache lines

Level::Mid as u8 gives the number stored for the variant. Enums without data can be given explicit numbers, which is how you match the constants of a C header or of a file format.

Enums and the niche optimisation

An enum must remember which variant it currently is. That information is called the tag or discriminant. An enum with data is as large as its largest variant, plus the tag, plus padding:

Shape needs 16 bytes for the two numbers of a rectangle, and one byte for the tag, which alignment rounds up to 24.

Now look at Option. You might expect Option<T> to always be bigger than T, since it needs a tag. Often it is not:

An Option<u32> needs 8 bytes: every one of the 4 billion bit patterns of a u32 is a valid number, so the tag needs extra space. But a reference can never be the address zero. Rust uses that one impossible value to mean None, and the Option costs nothing. An unused bit pattern like this is called a niche, and the trick is the niche optimisation.

  • References, Box, Rc, Arc, String and Vec all contain a pointer that is never null.
  • A bool uses only the values 0 and 1 of its byte, so 2 can mean None.
  • A char does not use all 32-bit values.
  • NonZeroU32 and its relatives are integers that promise never to be zero, to make room for exactly this.

So “there may be a value or not” costs no memory for the most common cases. A null pointer in C and an Option<&T> in Rust are the same bits in memory. The difference is that Rust’s type forces you to check.

Pointers, thin and fat

A reference or Box to a normal type is one address: 8 bytes. A reference to a type whose size is not known at compile time carries a second piece of information, and is called a fat pointer:

size_of_val measures a concrete value. The String itself, the part on the stack, is always 24 bytes. The text it owns on the heap is 5 bytes here. For the vector, both happen to be 24: the record on the stack, and three u64 on the heap.

Trait objects and the vtable

A Box<dyn Shape> or &dyn Shape is a fat pointer with two addresses:

The vtable (“virtual method table”) is a small table that the compiler creates once for every combination of type and trait. Calling shape.area() means: follow the vtable pointer, read the address of area, call it with the data pointer. That is dynamic dispatch. It costs one extra memory read per call, and it keeps the compiler from pasting the method’s body into the caller, which is usually the bigger loss. Generic code has neither cost.

Where data lives

A running program’s memory has several regions:

RegionHoldsLifetime
Codethe machine instructions of the programthe whole run
Static datastatic variables, string literals, and other constants built into the programthe whole run
Stacklocal variables and function parameters. One stack per threaduntil the function returns
Heapeverything owned by Box, Vec, String, Rc, HashMap …until its owner is dropped

The stack of the main thread is usually 8 MB, and that of other threads 2 MB by default. A very large local array, or recursion that goes too deep, exhausts it. The program then stops with a “stack overflow” message. Large data belongs on the heap: use vec![0; n] and not [0; n] for big buffers.

What costs time

Knowing the layout lets you estimate the cost of a design. Four things matter far more than everything else.

1. Heap allocation. Asking the allocator for memory, and giving it back, costs roughly as much as a hundred simple arithmetic operations. Allocating in a tight loop is a common cause of slow code. Reuse buffers, and reserve capacity in advance with Vec::with_capacity(n) when you know the size.

2. Indirection. Every pointer that must be followed is a memory read at a possibly distant address. A Vec<Box<T>> or a linked list makes the processor jump around. A Vec<T> keeps the values side by side.

3. Cache misses. Reading main memory is slow: about a hundred times slower than a calculation. Processors therefore keep recently used memory in small, fast caches, and fetch memory in blocks of 64 bytes, called cache lines. Data that is close together and visited in order is nearly free after the first access. Data scattered over the heap costs a slow fetch every time.

4. Copying. Moving a value copies its bytes: 24 for a String, whatever its length. Moving a struct of several kilobytes copies all of them. Large values are better kept behind a Box, or passed by reference.

An experiment: array of structs or struct of arrays

A simulation has four million particles, each with eight numbers. A calculation needs only one of them: the mass. Two ways to store the data:

Summing the masses reads the same four million numbers in both cases. On the machine used to test this guide, the first layout took 14 milliseconds and the second 3.5: four times faster. In the array of structs, each particle fills a whole cache line of 64 bytes, of which the loop uses 8. The cache is filled with data nobody wants. In the struct of arrays, eight masses sit in each cache line, and every byte fetched is used.

Neither layout is better in general. If the program usually needs all the fields of one particle together, the first layout wins. The lesson is to put data that is used together close together.

Tip
Rules of thumb for fast data
  • Use Vec<T> as your default collection. It is the friendliest to the cache.
  • Avoid Vec<Vec<T>> for grids. Use one flat Vec<T> and compute the index as row * width + column.
  • Avoid linked lists. They need one allocation and one cache miss per element.
  • Keep often-used structs small. Put large, rarely used parts behind a Box.
  • Check the size of your important types with size_of. An enum with one huge variant makes every value huge: box the big variant.

Moving values out of place

Some standard functions make sense once you think in terms of memory. You cannot move a value out of a &mut reference, because that would leave a hole. But you can swap something else in:

FunctionWhat it does
mem::swap(&mut a, &mut b)exchanges two values
mem::replace(&mut a, new)puts new into a and returns the old value
mem::take(&mut a)puts the default value into a and returns the old value

All three only shuffle a few bytes on the stack. No heap data is copied. Option has a method of the same kind: option.take() leaves None behind and returns what was there.

Byte order

A number of several bytes can be stored with its lowest byte first (little-endian) or its highest byte first (big-endian). Nearly all current processors are little-endian. Many network protocols and file formats use big-endian. When you read or write binary data, always say which order you mean:

Do not copy a struct’s memory straight into a file or onto the network. The padding bytes, the field order and the byte order all depend on the compiler and the machine. Convert each field explicitly, or use a serialisation crate (chapter 43).

Leaks are safe

One last point about memory. Rust guarantees that memory is not used after it is freed. It does not guarantee that all memory is freed. A program can leak memory in safe code:

Box::leak is sometimes useful: it turns a heap value into a 'static reference for data that should live until the program ends. mem::forget discards a value without running its destructor. A cycle of Rc pointers leaks too, as you saw in chapter 27. A leak wastes memory, but it cannot corrupt anything, which is why Rust counts it as safe.

How other languages do it
Layout in other languages
  • C and C++ give you the same control and the same costs. C never reorders fields, so C programmers sort them by hand.
  • Java, C#, Python and JavaScript store almost every object on the heap behind a pointer, with a header of 8 to 16 bytes in front of the data. A Python list of a million integers is a million separate objects. A Rust Vec<i32> of a million integers is 4 MB in one block. This difference in layout, more than raw instruction speed, is why Rust and C are so much faster on large data.
Recap
  • Every type has a size and an alignment. size_of and align_of report them.
  • Structs contain padding to align their fields. Rust reorders fields to reduce it. #[repr(C)] keeps the written order.
  • An enum stores a tag plus its largest variant. Niches make Option<&T>, Option<Box<T>> and Option<String> free.
  • References to str, slices and trait objects are fat pointers: an address plus a length or a vtable.
  • Stack: local values, fast, limited. Heap: owned data of flexible size. Static data: literals and statics.
  • Allocation, indirection, cache misses and large copies dominate the cost. Keep related data together in Vecs.
  • mem::swap, mem::replace and mem::take move values out of &mut places.
  • Always state the byte order when handling binary data.
Check your understanding
1

A #[repr(C)] struct has the fields a: u8, b: u64, c: u8, in that order. What is its size?

a takes 1 byte, then 7 bytes of padding so that b starts at offset 8. b takes 8. c takes 1, and 7 more bytes round the size up to a multiple of 8. Ordered as b, a, c, it would need 16.

2

Why is size_of::<Option<Box<u32>>>() the same as size_of::<Box<u32>>()?

This is the niche optimisation. For a type with no spare bit pattern, such as u32, the Option does need more space.

3

What does a &[u64] consist of?

A slice reference is a fat pointer. Capacity belongs to the owning Vec, not to a borrowed view.

4

Which of these is usually the most expensive single operation?

Allocating involves the memory allocator’s bookkeeping. Moves and arithmetic are a few machine instructions.

5

Why can iterating over a Vec<T> be much faster than over a linked list with the same elements?

Memory arrives in blocks of 64 bytes. Neighbouring elements share a block and come almost for free. Scattered nodes each cost a slow fetch.

Guided exerciseShrink a struct

This #[repr(C)] struct describes a sensor reading. Print its size. Then reorder the fields to make it as small as possible, and print the size again. Finally remove #[repr(C)] from the original and check what Rust does by itself.

Need a hint?

Sort the fields from the largest alignment to the smallest: u64 (8), f32 (4), u16 (2), then u8 and bool (1).

Show solution and explanation

The data is 16 bytes (8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1). The original order wastes 16 more on padding: 7 after valid, 3 after channel, 6 at the end. Sorted from large to small, nothing is wasted. Without repr(C), Rust finds the compact order on its own. With a million readings in a vector, the difference is 16 megabytes, and twice as many readings fit into each cache line.

PracticeRead a binary header

A made-up image format starts with a 12-byte header: 4 bytes with the letters PIX1, then the width as a u32, then the height as a u32, both big-endian. Write parse_header(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<(u32, u32), String> that returns width and height, with clear errors for input that is too short or has the wrong letters.

Need a hint?

Check bytes.len() < 12 first. Compare &bytes[0..4] with b"PIX1", a byte string literal. To get a [u8; 4] from a slice for u32::from_be_bytes, use bytes[4..8].try_into().unwrap(). The length is right, so the conversion cannot fail.

Show solution and explanation

The bytes 0, 0, 3, 32 in big-endian order are 3 × 256 + 32 = 800. The function reads each field explicitly, with a stated byte order, and checks the length before touching the data. It never reinterprets the raw bytes as a struct, so it works the same on every machine. The letters at the start of a file that identify its format are called a magic number.

ChallengeA flat grid

Write struct Grid { width: usize, height: usize, cells: Vec<u8> } that stores a two-dimensional grid in one flat vector. Add new(width, height), get(x, y) -> Option<u8>, set(x, y, value) -> bool, and row(y) -> Option<&[u8]>, which returns a whole row as a slice without copying. Explain why this is better than a Vec<Vec<u8>>.

Need a hint?

The cell (x, y) is at index y * width + x. Check x < width and y < height before computing it. A row is the slice &cells[y * width .. (y + 1) * width].

Show solution and explanation

A Vec<Vec<u8>> for this grid would be four allocations: one for the outer vector, and one per row. Every access follows two pointers, and the rows may lie anywhere on the heap. Each row also carries 24 bytes of bookkeeping, and nothing guarantees that all rows have the same length.

The flat grid is one allocation and one block of memory. An access is one multiplication, one addition and one read. Walking over the whole grid reads memory in order, which the cache handles best. A row is still available as a slice, because a row is simply a continuous part of the vector.

Idiomatic Rust: patterns and habits

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Follow Rust’s naming and API conventions
  • Replace verbose match code with Option and Result combinators
  • Design function signatures that are flexible for callers
  • Apply the builder, newtype, RAII guard and state-machine patterns
  • Recognise and avoid common anti-patterns

Code can be correct and still feel foreign. Every language has its own way of saying things, and code that follows it is called idiomatic. Idiomatic code is easier for others to read, works better with the standard library, and usually has fewer bugs, because the idioms grew out of experience.

This chapter gathers the habits of experienced Rust programmers. Most of the pieces you have seen already. Here they are side by side, as a reference to come back to.

Real-world analogy
Driving on the correct side of the road

Every place has a pattern for how traffic moves. Rust has patterns for names, returns and ownership too. They are not arbitrary—they make the code more predictable, easier to scan and easier to compare across projects.

Names

The compiler warns about the first group. The second group is convention, and it carries real information.

ItemStyleExample
variables, functions, methods, modulessnake_caseword_count, parse_line
types, traits, enum variantsUpperCamelCaseTodoList, Display, Some
constants and staticsSCREAMING_SNAKE_CASEMAX_SIZE
type parametersone capital letter, or a short wordT, K, V, Item
lifetimesshort, lower case'a, 'input

Conversion methods tell you their cost through their prefix:

PrefixCostTakesExample
as_free: a view of the same data&selftext.as_str(), path.as_os_str()
to_may be expensive: creates a new value&selftext.to_string(), slice.to_vec()
into_consumes the value, usually cheapselftext.into_bytes(), vec.into_iter()

More conventions:

  • A getter is named after the field, without get_: user.name(), not user.get_name().
  • Methods that return bool start with is_ or has_: is_empty(), has_children().
  • The main constructor is called new. Others say what they start from: with_capacity(n), from_parts(…).
  • An iterator over a collection comes from iter(), iter_mut() and into_iter().
  • A method that can fail and has a panicking twin uses try_: try_from, try_lock.

Creating values

new and Default

If a type has an obvious empty or starting value, give it both a new() and a Default implementation, and make them agree:

The builder pattern

A struct with many optional settings would need a constructor with a dozen parameters, or a dozen constructors. Rust has no optional or named arguments. The idiom is a builder: a helper type that collects the settings one by one and creates the real value at the end.

Each setter takes self and returns Self, so the calls can be chained. The required value (the address) is a parameter of builder, the optional ones have defaults, and build is the single place where the combination is checked. You will meet builders all over the ecosystem: Command::new("ls").arg("-l"), OpenOptions::new().append(true), thread::Builder.

Working with Option and Result

Beginners write a match for every Option. That is fine, and often clearest. For the simple cases, the combinator methods say the same thing in one line.

I want to …OptionResult
transform the success valuemapmap
transform the errormap_err
chain a step that can failand_thenand_then
use a fallback valueunwrap_or, unwrap_or_default, unwrap_or_elsethe same
try an alternativeor, or_elseor, or_else
keep only if a test passesfilter
convert to the other typeok_or, ok_or_elseok, err
return early from the function??
borrow the insideas_ref, as_mut, as_derefthe same
move the value out, leaving Nonetake

as_deref is worth knowing: it turns an Option<String> into an Option<&str> without copying, so that you can compare or match it against string literals:

A guideline for choosing: use ? to pass problems on, a combinator for a one-step transformation, and match or if let as soon as there are two or more things to do. A chain of five combinators is harder to read than a match.

Function signatures

Accept the most general borrowed type

A function that only reads its argument should ask for the borrowed form that the most callers can provide:

Do not ask forAsk forWhy
&String&stralso accepts literals and parts of strings
&Vec<T>&[T]also accepts arrays and parts of vectors
&Box<T>&Tthe box is an irrelevant detail
&PathBuf&Path
&Option<T>Option<&T>easier to build and to use

Take ownership when you keep the value

If the function is going to store the value, ask for the owned type. The caller then decides whether to move a value in or to clone one, and no hidden copy happens inside your function:

Return owned values, or borrow from the input

A function returns either a new owned value, or a reference into one of its arguments. It cannot return a reference to something it created. When both cases occur, Cow covers them (chapter 27). For sequences, returning impl Iterator<Item = T> lets the caller decide whether to collect:

Iterators over indices

A loop with an index is rarely the best form in Rust. It needs a bounds check on every access, and an off-by-one mistake is easy to make.

Errors

A short summary of the habits from chapter 18:

  • Return Result for anything that can fail for outside reasons. Reserve panic! for bugs.
  • In a library, define an error enum (with thiserror). In an application, use anyhow and add context to errors as they travel up.
  • Use ? to propagate. Handle an error where you can do something useful about it, and that is often near main.
  • Write expect("why this cannot fail") in place of a bare unwrap().
  • Give an error type Debug, Display and std::error::Error, so that it works with ?, Box<dyn Error> and anyhow.

One idiom for validation is the early return, also called a guard clause. Deal with the special cases first and leave, so that the main path is not buried inside nested ifs:

Let types do the work

These patterns were introduced in earlier chapters. They are the centre of idiomatic Rust design.

PatternIn one sentenceChapter
Newtypewrap a value in a struct to give it a meaning and rules of its own12, 29
Parse, don’t validateturn unchecked input into a type that proves it was checked29
Enum for alternativesone variant per case, each with exactly its data. No flags and no “unused” fields13, 29
Typestateone type per state, so that wrong sequences of calls do not compile29
RAII guarda value whose Drop undoes something: unlock, close, deregister27, 33
Extension traitadd methods to a foreign type through your own trait20
Compositionbuild big types out of small ones, and share behaviour through traits20

An RAII guard of your own

A guard is useful whenever something must be undone “no matter what”. This one measures how long a block of code takes:

The message appears on both paths, the normal return and the early error. The variable is called _timer and not _: a plain _ would drop the value at once.

A state machine as an enum

When the states are only known at run time, an enum with a transition function is the idiom. All the rules are in one match, and the compiler checks that every combination is covered:

Matching on the pair (state, event) turns the transition table into code that looks like the table. next is a pure function, so every transition is trivially testable.

Functional core, imperative shell

A design habit that ran through every project in this guide: put the decisions into pure functions that take values and return values, and keep input and output in a thin layer around them. The to-do list’s parse, the search tool’s search, the report’s revenue_by and the chat server’s parse were all written that way. The core is easy to test, and the shell is too simple to need much testing.

Small idioms worth knowing

Five short moves that experienced Rust programmers use without thinking. Each one removes a mut, a match, a Box or a clone.

  1. Mutable while it is built, fixed afterwards. The block needs mut, the rest of the function does not. After the block, nobody can change sorted by accident. For a single line, let numbers = numbers; does the same.
  2. An Option is a sequence of no item or one item. It works wherever an iterator is expected: extend, chain, flatten, even a for loop. That replaces many if let Some(x) = … { list.push(x) }.
  3. transpose swaps the two layers. Here map produces an Option<Result<u16, _>>, and the caller wants “an error, or perhaps a number”: Result<Option<u16>, _>. After transpose, a ? can be applied.
  4. A &dyn Trait chosen at run time. When both values already exist, a plain reference is enough. Box<dyn Trait> is only needed when the value must be owned behind the pointer.
  5. An error that gives the argument back. String::from_utf8 takes ownership of the bytes. If it fails, the bytes are inside the error, and into_bytes returns them. Channels do the same: a failed send returns the message. When you write a function that takes ownership and can fail, consider this, so that callers do not have to clone “just in case”.

Common anti-patterns

Things that work, and that experienced reviewers will ask you to change.

unwrap() on anything that can really fail. It turns a recoverable error into a crash with an unhelpful message. Use ?, a fallback, or expect with a reason.

clone() to silence the borrow checker, as a reflex. One clone to get unstuck is fine. Clones everywhere usually mean that a function should borrow (&T), or that ownership in the program is unclear.

Rc<RefCell<T>> everywhere. This rebuilds the object graphs of garbage-collected languages, with run-time panics in place of compile-time checks. Most programs need it rarely. Ask first whether one owner and some references, or indices into a Vec, would do.

Stringly typed code. Passing states, kinds and commands around as strings (if status == "actve") means that a typing error compiles. Use an enum.

Several bool parameters. resize(true, false, true) cannot be read. Use enums with telling names, or a struct of options.

A catch-all _ => that hides new cases. If a match on your own enum ends with _ => {}, adding a variant later compiles silently, and the new case is ignored. List the variants, so that the compiler reminds you.

Deref to imitate inheritance. Implementing Deref so that a wrapper “inherits” the methods of its field is tempting and confusing. Deref is for smart pointers. Pass the calls on explicitly, or expose the inner value.

Indexing where an iterator would do, and collecting where it is not needed. v.iter().map(f).collect::<Vec<_>>().iter().sum() builds a list only to throw it away. Chain the adapters and consume once.

unsafe or clever tricks for speed, without a measurement. Write the clear version first. Measure. Optimise the part that the measurement points at (chapter 52).

Fighting the language. If a design needs many lifetimes, many RefCells, or parent pointers everywhere, it is probably a translation of a design from another language. Step back and ask who should own the data.

A checklist for public types

When you publish a type for others to use, go through this list. It is condensed from the official Rust API Guidelines.

  • It derives the common traits where they make sense: Debug always, and Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default, PartialOrd, Ord as appropriate.
  • It implements Display if users will want to print it, and Error if it is an error.
  • Conversions use the standard traits: From, TryFrom, FromStr, AsRef.
  • Fields are private, unless the type is plain data with no rules.
  • Constructors that can fail return Result.
  • Functions take the most general borrowed types (&str, &[T], impl AsRef<Path>).
  • Every public item has a documentation comment with an example.
  • Fallible functions document their errors, and panicking ones their panics.
  • It is Send and Sync where possible.
  • Enums and structs that may grow are marked #[non_exhaustive].

Two tools enforce most idioms automatically. rustfmt formats code in the standard style, and Clippy knows several hundred idioms and suggests the better form with an explanation. Both are the subject of chapter 40. Running Clippy on your own code is one of the fastest ways to learn idiomatic Rust.

How other languages do it
Design patterns from other languages

Many classic object-oriented design patterns exist to work around a missing language feature, and shrink in Rust:

  • Strategy is a closure or a trait parameter.
  • Command is an enum with one variant per command.
  • Visitor is a match on an enum.
  • Null object is Option.
  • Iterator and Observer are the Iterator trait and channels.
  • Singleton is a static with LazyLock, and is discouraged for the same reasons as everywhere else.
  • Builder, RAII and newtype matter more in Rust than elsewhere.
Recap
  • Names follow fixed styles. as_, to_ and into_ announce the cost of a conversion. Getters have no get_.
  • Offer new and Default. Use a builder when there are many optional settings.
  • Combinators (map, and_then, unwrap_or, ok_or, filter) replace simple matches. ? propagates.
  • Take &str and &[T] to read, owned values to keep. Return owned values or impl Iterator.
  • Prefer iterators with zip, enumerate and windows to index loops.
  • Let types carry rules: newtypes, enums, typestates, RAII guards.
  • Keep a functional core and an imperative shell.
  • Avoid reflexive unwrap, clone and Rc<RefCell<T>>, strings and bools as stand-ins for types, and catch-all match arms.
Check your understanding
1

By convention, what does a method named as_bytes promise?

as_ conversions are free views that borrow. to_ creates something new, and into_ consumes self.

2

Why is fn count(words: &[String]) a better signature than fn count(words: &Vec<String>)?

The function only reads a sequence. Asking for the slice makes it usable in more situations at no cost.

3

Which expression gives the length of the name, or 0 if there is none, for name: Option<&str>?

map transforms the value inside the Option, and unwrap_or supplies the fallback. unwrap would panic for None, and and_then needs a closure that returns an Option.

4

Why should a match on your own enum usually list all variants, and not end with _ => {}?

Exhaustiveness checking is one of Rust’s best maintenance tools. A wildcard arm switches it off for that match.

5

What problem does the builder pattern solve?

A builder collects options through chained method calls and checks them once in build().

Guided exerciseTidy up with combinators

Rewrite each of these functions as a single expression, using methods of Option and Result. The behaviour must stay the same.

Need a hint?

For port: and_then chains a step that may yield nothing, .ok() turns the Result of parse into an Option, and unwrap_or gives the fallback. For initial: and_then for the first character, then map to change it.

Show solution and explanation

Each nested match had the shape “if there is a value, do the next step, otherwise stay empty”. That shape is and_then. A final “otherwise use this” is unwrap_or, and “change the value if there is one” is map. Both versions compile to the same machine code. The short one shows the flow of the data in one line.

PracticeImprove the signatures

This code works, and its signatures force callers to do needless work. Improve the three functions without changing what they do, and simplify the calls in main.

Need a hint?

longest can take &[String] and return Option<&str>: a borrowed view of the winner, and None for an empty list. max_by_key finds it. greet should take &str. is_admin should take Option<&str>.

Show solution and explanation

What changed:

  • longest no longer clones, no longer indexes, and tells the truth about an empty list by returning None. The old version returned an empty string, which looks like a real result.
  • greet("Sara") works with a literal. No String has to be created only to be borrowed.
  • is_admin(Some("admin")) is a plain comparison. An Option<String> that a caller already has is passed with .as_deref().

In each case the function asks for less, so callers can give it more kinds of things.

PracticeA builder for a pizza

Write a Pizza struct with a size (Small, Medium, Large), a list of toppings, and a flag for extra cheese. Create it through a builder: Pizza::builder(Size::Large).topping("olives").topping("onion").extra_cheese().build(). build returns an error if there are more than 5 toppings.

Need a hint?

The builder holds the same fields as Pizza. Each setter takes mut self and returns Self. build(self) -> Result<Pizza, String> checks self.toppings.len().

Show solution and explanation

The required choice (the size) is a parameter of builder, so it cannot be forgotten. Optional choices have defaults. Because the setters take and return the builder by value, they can be chained, and they can also be used in a loop by assigning the result back. The single check in build guarantees that every Pizza that exists is valid.

ChallengeRefactor a “stringly typed” function

This function computes a shipping price. It works, and it invites mistakes: a typing error in a string compiles, and nothing lists the valid values. Redesign it with enums and a struct, parse the text input at the edge with FromStr, and make the price calculation a match that the compiler checks for completeness.

Need a hint?

Define enum Kind { Letter, Parcel }, enum Zone { Domestic, Abroad }, enum Speed { Normal, Express }, and a struct Shipment { kind, zone, speed, insured }. Implement FromStr for Kind and Zone with an error for unknown text. The price function takes a &Shipment and returns u32: it cannot fail any more, because invalid input can no longer reach it.

Show solution and explanation

What the redesign bought:

  • Typing errors are caught. "parsel" is reported where the text enters the program, with a message that lists the valid words. In the old version it silently produced the price −1.
  • The price function cannot fail. It returns u32. The magic value −1, which every caller had to remember to check, is gone.
  • No more mystery arguments. shipping("parcel", "abroad", true, true) has become a struct with named fields and Speed::Express.
  • The rules are complete by construction. Add Kind::Pallet, and the compiler stops at each match until a price and an insurance rule exist for it.

The code is longer. Nearly all the extra lines are definitions that are written once, and they move mistakes from run time to compile time.
