Cargo in depth

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read and write every important section of Cargo.toml
  • Manage dependencies, versions and features
  • Tune builds with profiles
  • Organise several packages in a workspace
  • Document, install and publish a crate, and manage toolchains with rustup

You have used Cargo since chapter 2: cargo new, cargo run, cargo test, cargo add. Cargo is Rust’s build tool and package manager in one, and one of the main reasons the language is pleasant to use. This chapter covers the rest of what a working Rust programmer needs from it.

Real-world analogy
A project control tower

Cargo is the system that keeps the whole airport moving: which package is in the build, which versions are allowed, which features are active, and which test command the team is running. It turns a pile of files into a repeatable build.

The layout of a package

Cargo works by convention. If you put files in the expected places, no configuration is needed:

The manifest

Real-world analogy
The blueprint vs the parts list

Cargo.toml is your project’s blueprint (“I need a serde crate of version 1.0 or newer”), while Cargo.lock is the exact shipping manifest from the warehouse (“this build used serde 1.0.229 with this exact checksum”). Sharing Cargo.toml lets libraries stay compatible; keeping Cargo.lock for applications guarantees every machine compiles the exact same bytes.

KeyMeaning
namethe package’s name, and by default the name of its library and program
versionthe version, following semantic versioning (below)
editionthe language edition: 2015, 2018, 2021 or 2024
rust-versionthe oldest compiler the package supports. Older compilers refuse to build it, with a clear message
description, license, repository, …information for people and for crates.io. description and license are required for publishing

The three dependency tables differ in when the crates are used:

  • [dependencies]: needed by your code.
  • [dev-dependencies]: needed only for tests, examples and benchmarks. Users of your library never download them.
  • [build-dependencies]: needed only by build.rs.
In plain English
Editions

An edition is a version of the language’s surface: its keywords and a few rules. A new one appears every three years, and may contain changes that would break old code, such as a new keyword. Each crate states its edition, and crates of different editions work together in one program without any trouble. So the language can evolve, and code from 2015 still compiles today. cargo fix --edition updates a package to the next edition automatically.

Reading older code: what the editions changed

Tutorials, answers on the web and old crates are often written for an earlier edition. These are the differences you are most likely to notice:

EditionWhat you see in code written for it
2015extern crate serde; at the top of files. try!(…) where you would write ?. Trait objects without dyn: Box<Error>. Paths in use without crate::.
2018async, await and dyn become keywords. use crate::… paths as in this guide. extern crate is no longer needed.
2021A closure captures only the fields it uses, not the whole struct. array.into_iter() gives the values. TryFrom, TryInto and FromIterator can be used without a use line.
2024unsafe extern blocks and #[unsafe(no_mangle)]. Every unsafe operation inside an unsafe fn needs its own unsafe block. References to a static mut are refused. if let chains with &&. std::env::set_var is unsafe. gen is reserved as a keyword. Temporary values in the final expression of a function and failing if let conditions are dropped before local variables, not after. impl Trait in return position captures every lifetime in scope, unless you narrow it with use<…>. Cargo defaults to resolver = "3" (MSRV-aware).

Code from every edition compiles with today’s compiler, as long as its Cargo.toml names the edition it was written for. If you paste old code into a new project and get puzzling errors, the edition is the first thing to check.

Why did Rust 2024 change temporary drop order? In older editions, if let Some(x) = lock.borrow() { … } else { … } kept the temporary lock guard alive throughout the else branch, causing unexpected borrows or deadlocks if else tried to lock again. In Edition 2024, temporaries created in the if let condition drop before entering else, and temporaries in a block’s final expression drop before local variables in that block.

Three of the 2024 changes are worth recognising, because they arrive as diagnostics rather than as a new keyword, and the message does not always say the word “edition”:

  • Tail-expression drop order. In an older edition, the temporary values created in the final expression of a function body were dropped after the local variables of that body. In 2024 they are dropped before them, at the end of the expression. Consider a function whose last line is cell.borrow().len(). Under the old order the borrow was still alive when the local cell was dropped, so the borrow checker refused the function. Under the new order the borrow ends first and the function compiles. Code that relied on the old order — a guard that read the local variable it outlived — now fails to compile instead of misbehaving, which is the point of the change.
  • unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn. Every unsafe operation inside an unsafe fn must now sit in its own unsafe block. The lint that reports this is named in the error message, and it is a good habit to enable it in older editions too: the body of an unsafe fn was never meant to be an unsafe block.
  • static_mut_refs. Taking a reference to a static mut is an error in 2024, because two threads can do it at once. The fix is one of the tools from chapter 31: an AtomicU32, a Mutex behind a OnceLock, or &raw mut when you really only need the address.
Tip
The Edition Guide is the authority

The Rust Edition Guide lists every change in every edition, with a migration example for each one, and it is short. When an old snippet will not compile and the edition is the suspect, read the page for that edition before changing the code.

Dependencies and versions

Semantic versioning

A version has three numbers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, as in 1.4.2. The rules, known as SemVer:

  • PATCH goes up for bug fixes that change no public API.
  • MINOR goes up when features are added in a compatible way.
  • MAJOR goes up when something changes that can break code using the crate.

For versions below 1.0, the minor number plays the role of the major: 0.3.0 to 0.4.0 may break things.

A version requirement in Cargo.toml describes a range:

You writeCargo acceptsMeaning
"1.4.2"at least 1.4.2, below 2.0.0the default: “compatible with 1.4.2”
"0.3.1"at least 0.3.1, below 0.4.0the same rule for 0.x
"~1.4.2"at least 1.4.2, below 1.5.0only patch updates
"=1.4.2"exactly 1.4.2pinned. Use rarely
">=1.2, <1.8"the given range
"*"anythingnot allowed on crates.io

So serde = "1.0.229" does not mean “exactly this version”. It means “this version or any later one that promises to be compatible”.

Cargo.lock

When Cargo first builds a project, it picks the newest allowed version of every dependency, and of the dependencies of those, and writes the exact result into Cargo.lock. From then on, every build uses exactly those versions, on your machine and on everybody else’s, until you ask for an update.

Commit Cargo.lock to version control. It makes builds reproducible: the program you tested is the program your colleague and your server build.

Everyday commands

CommandEffect
cargo add serde --features deriveadd a dependency
cargo add --dev proptestadd a dev-dependency
cargo remove serderemove one
cargo updatemove all dependencies to the newest allowed versions, and rewrite Cargo.lock
cargo update serdeupdate one crate
cargo treeshow the tree of dependencies
cargo tree -dshow crates that are present in more than one version
cargo tree -i synshow who depends on syn
cargo search http clientsearch crates.io
cargo info tokioshow a crate’s description, versions and features

One line in Cargo.toml can bring in many crates. The tree shows what you really depend on.

Other sources

Features

A feature is a named switch that turns optional parts of a crate on. Features keep compile times and binaries small: you pay only for what you use. tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] } and serde = { features = ["derive"] } are switches of this kind.

You can define features in your own crate:

  • optional = true means that the dependency is only compiled when asked for.
  • serde = ["dep:serde"] defines a feature called serde that switches the optional dependency on.
  • default lists the features that are on unless the user says default-features = false.

In the code, cfg conditions test the feature:

#[cfg_attr(condition, attribute)] applies the attribute only if the condition holds. With the feature off, the crate does not depend on serde at all.

Key idea
Features must only add

If two crates in a program need the same dependency with different features, Cargo builds it once, with all requested features switched on. This is called feature unification. For it to work, a feature must only ever add things. A feature that removes a function, or changes what one does, will break someone who did not ask for it.

Profiles: how the code is built

A profile is a set of compiler settings. Two are used all the time:

dev (cargo build)release (cargo build --release)
Optimisationnone (opt-level = 0)full (opt-level = 3)
Compile timeshortlonger
Run timeslow, often 10 to 100 times slower for calculationsfast
Debug informationyesno
Integer overflowpanicswraps around
Output foldertarget/debug/target/release/
Watch out
Never measure speed in a debug build

A debug build tells you nothing about how fast your program is. Always benchmark with --release. Forgetting this is the most common reason for the question “why is my Rust program slow?”.

Profiles can be changed in Cargo.toml:

The last entry is a useful trick for programs that are too slow to test in debug mode, such as games: your own code compiles quickly, and the libraries run at full speed.

How much the settings matter depends on the program. For the small example program of this chapter, the sizes were:

BuildSize of the program
cargo build (debug)4,542 KB
cargo build --release446 KB
release with strip, lto, codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort"290 KB
the same with opt-level = "z"283 KB

Faster builds

Rust compiles more slowly than most languages. The compiler does much of the work that other languages leave to run time: it makes a separate copy of generic code for every type it is used with, expands macros, and optimises hard. You cannot change that, but you can avoid waiting more than necessary. The measures below are ordered from “free” to “some effort”.

1. Use cargo check while you write. It stops before machine code is generated. These are times for a program of 25 lines that uses regex, serde and serde_json (about 20 crates in all), on a small machine with two cores:

CommandNothing built yetAfter changing one line
cargo check4.3 s0.05 s
cargo build6.6 s0.19 s
cargo build with debug = false5.7 s
cargo build --release13.0 s0.27 s

The first build is the slow one, because every dependency is compiled. After that, Cargo recompiles only your own crate, and that is quick as long as the crate is small.

2. Find out where the time goes. cargo build --timings writes a report to target/cargo-timings/cargo-timing.html. It shows every crate as a bar on a time line: when its build started, how long it took, and what it was waiting for. For the program above, the slowest five were regex-automata (2.3 s), regex-syntax (1.6 s), serde_derive (1.4 s), serde_core (1.3 s) and syn (1.2 s). One line of Cargo.toml can cost more build time than all of your own code.

3. Carry fewer and lighter dependencies. cargo tree shows what each dependency brings along. Many crates switch on more than you need by default:

4. Ask for less debug information. A debug build writes a description of every variable and line for the debugger. If you rarely use a debugger, reduce it:

In the table above this saved about a seventh of the build. The Rust Performance Book reports 20 to 40 % for larger projects.

5. Check the linker. The last step of a build, joining everything into one file, is repeated in full after every change. On Linux, Rust has used the fast linker lld by default since version 1.90. The linker mold is often faster still. On macOS the system linker is fast already.

6. Split a large crate. Cargo compiles crates in parallel, and it rebuilds only the crates that changed and the ones that depend on them. A workspace of several medium crates (next section) builds faster than one huge crate, and a change in one place no longer recompiles everything.

7. Do not compile the same thing twice. The tool sccache keeps compiled dependencies in a cache that all your projects share. On a CI server, keep ~/.cargo and target between runs. For Docker images, cargo-chef builds the dependencies in a layer of their own, so that they are rebuilt only when Cargo.toml changes.

8. Keep generic code thin. A generic function is compiled again for every type it is used with. When only a small part needs to be generic, put the rest in an inner function. The standard library does this in many places:

Measure before and after each step, as with every other kind of performance work (chapter 52).

Workspaces

A larger project is usually split into several packages: a library with the core logic, a command-line program, a web server, some tools. A workspace keeps them in one repository with one Cargo.lock and one target folder, so that they share dependencies and build results.

  • [workspace.package] and [workspace.dependencies] define values once. The members take them over with .workspace = true. All packages then use the same version of every dependency.
  • Commands at the top level apply to all members: cargo build, cargo test. Choose one with -p: cargo run -p shop, cargo test -p shop_core.

Splitting a project into crates also speeds up builds: Cargo compiles crates in parallel and rebuilds only those that changed.

The commands, in one table

CommandWhat it does
cargo new name, cargo new --lib name, cargo initcreate a package (in a new folder, or in the current one)
cargo checkcheck for errors without producing a program. Much faster than build
cargo build, cargo build --releasecompile
cargo run, cargo run --release -- argscompile and run
cargo test, cargo benchrun tests, run benchmarks
cargo doc --openbuild the documentation and open it in the browser
cargo fmt, cargo clippyformat, lint (next chapter)
cargo fixapply the compiler’s suggested fixes automatically
cargo cleandelete the target folder
cargo install name, cargo install --path .build a program and put it on your search path
cargo publishupload the package to crates.io

While writing code, use cargo check most of the time. It stops before the slow step of generating machine code, and reports the same errors.

Frequently used commands can get short names in the file .cargo/config.toml in your project or home folder:

Documentation

Rust has a documentation tool built in. cargo doc turns the comments in your code into a website with the same look as the standard library’s documentation, with search, links between types, and source views.

  • /// documents the item that follows. //! documents the item that contains the comment: the crate or module.
  • The text is Markdown. The first sentence becomes the summary in lists.
  • Conventional sections are # Examples, # Errors (when a Result is returned), # Panics and # Safety (for unsafe functions).
  • A name in square brackets and backticks becomes a link to that item.
  • Code blocks are compiled and run by cargo test, as you saw in chapter 22.

Every crate published on crates.io gets its documentation built and hosted automatically at docs.rs. For any crate you use, https://docs.rs/<crate name> is the place to look.

Tip
Documentation that stays correct as the crate grows

Three habits separate documentation that ages well from documentation that rots:

  • Link by name, not by URL. A name in square brackets inside backticks, like [Product::new] or [Clone], becomes a link that the compiler resolves. If you rename the item, the link breaks and rustdoc tells you. With RUSTDOCFLAGS: -D warnings in CI — the documentation step in the next chapter — a broken link fails the build instead of quietly shipping a dead end.
  • Ask the compiler to notice missing docs. Put #![warn(missing_docs)] at the top of the crate root. Every public item without a doc comment then produces a warning, which is how a public API gets documented by habit rather than by good intentions. Keep it off for programs, where the public surface is your own business.
  • Hide the plumbing. #[doc(hidden)] keeps an item out of the rendered documentation, for generated or internal items that must be public but are not part of the promise. Use it sparingly: a hidden item can still be called, but it is not explained.

cargo doc --open builds and opens the documentation for your crate and its dependencies. cargo doc --no-deps builds only your own, which is what CI should run.

Tip
When rustdoc is not enough

rustdoc answers “what does this function do?”. It is poor at “how do I build something with this crate”: chapters, a tutorial, a table of contents, a search box over prose. For that, the Rust world uses mdBook, the tool that renders the official Rust Book and the Rustonomicon: a folder of Markdown files plus a small book.toml becomes a website with navigation and search. mdbook build writes it, mdbook serve previews it locally, and GitHub Pages can host it for free. API reference and book answer different questions, and a serious library ships both.

Publishing a crate

Sharing a library with the world takes a few minutes:

  1. Create an account at crates.io (it uses a GitHub login) and get an API token. Run cargo login and paste it.
  2. Fill in description and license in Cargo.toml, and write a README.md.
  3. Run cargo publish --dry-run to see what would be uploaded, and check the list of files with cargo package --list.
  4. Run cargo publish.

The metadata is what a stranger sees on crates.io and on docs.rs, so it is worth ten minutes:

rust-version is a promise, not decoration: cargo refuses to build the crate on an older compiler and says so clearly, instead of failing with a confusing error deep inside a macro. cargo msrv measures it for you by trying your crate on a range of toolchains.

Things to know before you do:

  • Publishing is permanent. A version can never be changed or deleted, so that programs depending on it keep building. You can yank a broken version with cargo yank --version 1.0.1, which stops new projects from choosing it.
  • Names are first come, first served.
  • Follow SemVer strictly. People’s builds update to your new minor and patch versions automatically. The tool cargo semver-checks compares your code with the last published version and warns if you are about to break compatibility by accident.
  • The usual licence in the Rust world is the dual licence MIT OR Apache-2.0, the same as Rust itself.

Releasing without the ritual

Publishing by hand becomes a ritual of small mistakes: forget the version bump, forget the changelog, publish in the wrong order. The tools that remove the ritual are all worth knowing by name:

ToolWhat it takes over
release-plzReads the commit history, works out the next version, writes the CHANGELOG.md entry, opens a pull request, and publishes to crates.io when you merge it
cargo-releaseThe manual but scriptable version: one command bumps the version, tags, pushes and publishes a workspace in the right order
cargo-distFor programs rather than libraries: builds binaries for every platform, writes installers, and uploads them to a GitHub release
cargo msrvFinds the oldest Rust version your crate compiles with, so rust-version is measured rather than guessed

Whatever you use, keep a CHANGELOG.md in the format of Keep a Changelog and version strictly by SemVer: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security, newest first. Your users read the changelog far more often than they read the code, and a release that says nothing is a release nobody upgrades to.

rustup: managing the toolchain

rustup installs and updates the compiler and its companions.

CommandEffect
rustup updateupdate to the newest stable release
rustup showshow the installed toolchains and which one is active
rustup toolchain install nightlyinstall another channel
cargo +nightly buildrun one command with a specific toolchain
rustup component add clippy rustfmt rust-analyzeradd tools
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknownadd support for building for another platform
rustup docopen the offline documentation, including the standard library and “the book”

Rust has three release channels:

  • stable: a new release every six weeks. Use this.
  • beta: the next stable release, in testing.
  • nightly: built every night, with experimental features that may change or vanish. Some tools (Miri, certain sanitizers) need it.

A file named rust-toolchain.toml in a project fixes the toolchain for everybody who works on it. rustup installs it on demand:

Building for other platforms

Rust can compile for a different system than the one it runs on. This is called cross-compiling. Each platform has a name, a target triple, such as x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin (Macs with Apple chips), x86_64-pc-windows-msvc or wasm32-unknown-unknown (WebAssembly).

Pure Rust code usually cross-compiles without more ado. When C libraries or a linker for the other system are needed, the tools cross and cargo-zigbuild take care of the setup. For shipping prebuilt binaries, checksums, and installers on GitHub Releases automatically, cargo-dist generates the release workflow directly from Cargo.toml.

Build scripts (build.rs)

When a crate needs generated code at compile time (Protobufs via tonic-build, C libraries via cc, SQLx migration tracking, or embedding the Git commit hash), Cargo runs build.rs before compiling the package. Generated files belong inside OUT_DIR, and instructions back to Cargo use cargo:: directives printed to standard output:

Include generated files inside src/lib.rs with include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/generated.rs"));, and always emit cargo::rerun-if-changed=... so Cargo does not re-run the build script on unrelated edits.

Useful extensions

Cargo can be extended with extra commands, installed with cargo install:

ToolPurpose
cargo-expandshow code after macro expansion
cargo-audit, cargo-denycheck dependencies for known security problems and unwanted licences
cargo-outdatedlist dependencies that have newer versions
cargo-machete, cargo-udepsfind dependencies that are never used
cargo-nextesta faster test runner with clearer output
cargo-watch, baconre-run a command whenever a file changes
cargo-semver-checksdetect accidental breaking changes before publishing
cargo-bloatshow what takes up space in a binary
cargo-binstallinstall tools from ready-made binaries, without compiling
cargo-distautomate multi-platform binary releases and installers

For supply-chain hygiene in CI, pair cargo audit (vulnerability checks against RustSec) with cargo deny check configured by a deny.toml file in the repository root—allowing your team to permit only approved open-source licences (MIT, Apache-2.0), block unmaintained or duplicate crates, and fail pull requests automatically when a security advisory lands.

How other languages do it
Build tools elsewhere
  • C and C++ have no standard build tool or package manager. Projects use Make, CMake, Meson, Bazel, vcpkg, Conan and others, and combining libraries that use different ones is a well-known source of pain.
  • JavaScript has npm, Python has pip together with a shifting set of companions (venv, poetry, uv), and Java has Maven and Gradle.
  • Go and Rust were designed with one official tool from the start. Cargo’s single-tool experience (build, test, document, format, lint, publish) is often cited as a reason people enjoy Rust.
Recap
  • Cargo.toml describes the package and its dependencies. Cargo.lock records the exact versions, and belongs in version control.
  • Versions follow SemVer. "1.4.2" means “1.4.2 or newer, below 2.0”.
  • Features are named switches for optional code and optional dependencies. They must only add.
  • The dev profile compiles fast, and the release profile produces fast programs. Profiles can be tuned.
  • A workspace holds several packages with shared dependencies, one lock file and one target folder.
  • cargo check is the fast everyday command. cargo doc builds documentation from /// comments.
  • Publishing to crates.io is permanent. rustup manages toolchains, components and targets.
Check your understanding
1

Your Cargo.toml says regex = "1.10.2". Which version may Cargo choose?

A plain version number is a “caret” requirement: compatible updates are allowed. The exact version in use is recorded in Cargo.lock.

2

What is Cargo.lock for?

The manifest gives ranges. The lock file pins the concrete choice until you run cargo update.

3

Why should a Cargo feature only add functionality, and never remove or change it?

Because of feature unification, a crate cannot know that a feature is off just because it did not ask for it. Another crate may have switched it on.

4

Your program takes 20 seconds for a calculation when started with cargo run. What is the first thing to try?

The default build is unoptimised. Release builds are often ten to a hundred times faster for calculations.

5

What is the advantage of cargo check over cargo build during development?

check runs all the analysis, including the borrow checker, without generating machine code. It is the fastest way to find out whether the code compiles.

6

What does cargo fix --edition do?

An edition is a set of rules inside one crate, so moving to it is a code-level migration. cargo fix --edition performs the changes that can be done mechanically, and reports the few that need a human decision.

7

You paste a snippet from a 2018-era blog post into a 2024 project and get errors that make no sense. What should you check first?

Old snippets are usually correct for their edition. The differences are listed in the box above and in the Edition Guide, and cargo fix --edition automates most of them.

Guided exerciseRead a manifest

Explain what each numbered line does.

Need a hint?

Go back to the sections on the manifest, version requirements, features and profiles.

Show solution and explanation
  1. The package uses the 2024 edition of the language.
  2. It depends on clap, version 4.6 or newer below 5.0, with the optional derive feature of clap switched on.
  3. It depends on a package in the neighbouring folder core. This is typical inside a workspace.
  4. chrono is an optional dependency: it is compiled only if a feature asks for it. Version 0.4.x is accepted, and 0.5 is not, because for 0.x versions the middle number signals breaking changes.
  5. tempfile is used only by tests, examples and benchmarks. Users of the package never build it.
  6. The feature dates is on by default. A user can switch it off with default-features = false.
  7. The feature dates enables the optional dependency chrono. In the code, parts that need it are marked #[cfg(feature = "dates")].
  8. Release builds use link-time optimisation: the whole program is optimised together, which takes longer and gives a faster and smaller binary.
PracticeBuild a workspace

Create a workspace calc with two members. calc_core is a library with pub fn add(a: i64, b: i64) -> i64 and a unit test. calc_cli is a program that depends on it and prints 2 + 3 = 5. Share the edition through [workspace.package]. Then run the tests of the whole workspace, and run only the program.

Need a hint?

Make the folder, write the top-level Cargo.toml with [workspace], resolver = "3" and members. Inside it, run cargo new --lib calc_core and cargo new calc_cli. In calc_cli/Cargo.toml add calc_core = { path = "../calc_core" }. The commands are cargo test and cargo run -p calc_cli.

Show solution and explanation

There is one Cargo.lock and one target folder at the top. When you change only the program, the library is not rebuilt. The library has no idea that a command-line program uses it, so the same library could later serve a web server or a graphical program as well.

ChallengeAn optional feature

Add a feature colour to a small library. The function warning(text: &str) -> String returns the text unchanged by default. With the feature on, it wraps the text in the terminal codes for yellow: "\x1b[33m" before and "\x1b[0m" after. Write a test for each configuration, and run both.

Need a hint?

Declare the feature under [features] as colour = []. Write the function twice, one version under #[cfg(feature = "colour")] and one under #[cfg(not(feature = "colour"))]. Put the same attributes on the two tests. Run cargo test and cargo test --features colour.

Show solution and explanation

Exactly one of the two functions exists in any build, so they can share a name. A feature with an empty list, colour = [], enables no dependency. It is a pure switch for cfg.

Does this feature keep the rule “features only add”? Not strictly: it changes the result of an existing function. For output decoration that is harmless. For anything other code might rely on, a better design adds a second function, such as warning_coloured, behind the feature. Test both configurations in your automated checks, because code behind a feature that is off is not even compiled.

Tools for quality: formatting, linting, debugging, CI

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Format code automatically with rustfmt
  • Find mistakes and unidiomatic code with Clippy
  • Configure lints for a whole project
  • Debug with dbg!, backtraces and a debugger
  • Set up continuous integration that checks every change

A compiler that catches many mistakes is the first layer of quality. Rust’s standard tools add more layers, and all of them come with the normal installation. Professional Rust projects run them on every change. Learning them early also makes you a better Rust programmer, because they explain what they find.

Real-world analogy
A kitchen check before service

A chef does not wait until the restaurant is full to inspect the pans. Quality tools are the same: they scan the code before the pressure is high, telling you if the style is consistent or if something looks suspicious.

rustfmt: one style for everyone

cargo fmt rewrites your source files in the official Rust style: indentation, spaces, line breaks, the order of imports. Take this cramped code:

After cargo fmt:

The program is the same. Only the layout changed.

CommandEffect
cargo fmtformat all files of the package
cargo fmt --checkchange nothing. Report differences and fail if there are any (for automated checks)

Nearly every Rust project uses the default style, which means that all Rust code looks familiar, and nobody spends time arguing about brace positions. Set up your editor to format on save, and you never think about layout again. A few options can be set in a file rustfmt.toml, for example max_width = 100. To keep a hand-aligned table as it is, put #[rustfmt::skip] above the item.

Clippy: a reviewer that never tires

Clippy is a linter: a tool that reads code and points out constructs that are legal but suspicious, slow, or more complicated than necessary. Such a check is called a lint. Clippy has more than 750 of them.

Here is code that compiles without any complaint from the compiler:

cargo clippy finds six things to improve. Three of its messages, shortened:

The other three are the needless return, total = total + … (use +=), and len() == 0 (use is_empty()). Each message names the lint, shows the better form, and links to a page that explains the reasoning. After following the advice:

CommandEffect
cargo clippylint the package
cargo clippy --all-targetsalso lint tests, examples and benchmarks
cargo clippy --fixapply the suggestions that are safe to apply automatically
cargo clippy -- -D warningstreat every warning as an error (for automated checks)

Lint groups and levels

Clippy’s lints are sorted into groups:

GroupDefaultContents
clippy::correctnesserrorcode that is almost certainly wrong
clippy::suspiciouswarningcode that is probably wrong
clippy::stylewarningunidiomatic code
clippy::complexitywarningcode that can be simpler
clippy::perfwarningcode that can be faster
clippy::pedanticoffstrict lints, with some false alarms
clippy::restrictionofflints for special policies, such as “no unwrap”. Pick single ones, never the whole group

Every lint, from Clippy or from the compiler itself, has a level: allow (off), warn, deny (an error), or forbid (an error that cannot be switched off further down). Levels can be set for one item with an attribute, or for the whole package in Cargo.toml:

When you switch a lint off, add a comment with the reason. #[expect(lint_name)] is a stricter relative of #[allow]: it silences the lint and warns you if the lint no longer fires, so that stale exceptions do not pile up.

Tip
Clippy as a teacher

Run Clippy on everything you write while learning. Its suggestions are the idioms of chapter 38, applied to your own code, at the moment you need them. Read the linked explanations. Do not treat the list as orders, though: if a suggestion makes the code less clear, keep your version and allow the lint with a reason.

The compiler’s own help

  • rustc --explain E0382 prints a long explanation of an error code, with examples. The same texts are online in the error index.
  • cargo fix applies the fixes that the compiler suggests in its messages.
  • cargo check after every few lines keeps problems small.

A method for reading a long error message: read the first line (what), look at the code location and the labels in the excerpt (where), then read the help: and note: lines at the end, which very often contain the fix. Fix the first error and compile again. Later errors are frequently consequences of the first.

rust-analyzer: the tools inside your editor

rust-analyzer is the program that makes an editor understand Rust. It works with VS Code, Zed, Neovim, Emacs, Helix and others, and RustRover has the same features built in. What to learn to use:

  • Inlay hints: the editor shows the inferred type next to each variable. This is a great help while learning.
  • Errors while typing, with quick fixes on a key press: add a missing use, fill in the arms of a match, implement the missing methods of a trait.
  • Go to definition and find all references, which also work for the standard library and your dependencies.
  • Hover for the documentation of anything.
  • Rename a function or type across the whole project.
  • Run and debug buttons above main and above each test.
  • Expand macro, to see what a macro produces.

Debugging

When a program compiles and does the wrong thing, you need to see inside it.

Printing

The simplest tool is often enough. dbg! prints an expression, its value and its location to standard error, and passes the value on:

For structs, derive Debug and print with {:#?}. For a program that runs for a long time, replace ad hoc printing with proper logging, which can be switched on and off by level. The crates for that, log and tracing, are covered in chapter 42.

Backtraces

After a panic, run the program again with RUST_BACKTRACE=1 to see the chain of calls that led there:

Read it from the top down until you reach the first entry that belongs to your own code. The entries above it are the standard library’s panic machinery. Here, the panic happened in lookup, which was called by process, which was called by main, each with its file and line.

A real debugger

A debugger stops the program at a line you choose (a breakpoint) and lets you look at every variable, then continue one line at a time. In VS Code, install the extension CodeLLDB alongside rust-analyzer. A “Debug” link then appears above main and above every test. Click in the margin to set a breakpoint, and start.

ActionWhat it does
Continuerun to the next breakpoint
Step overexecute the current line, without going into the functions it calls
Step intogo into the function that the current line calls
Step outrun until the current function returns
Watchkeep an expression in view while stepping

On the command line, rust-gdb and rust-lldb start the classic debuggers with support for Rust’s types. Debug a debug build: in a release build, the optimiser has rearranged the code and removed variables.

A method for finding bugs

  1. Reproduce it. Find the smallest input that shows the problem.
  2. Write a failing test for it. Now you can tell when it is fixed.
  3. Form one hypothesis and check it with a print or a breakpoint. Halve the search space each time: is the value still right at this point?
  4. Fix the cause, and not only the symptom.
  5. Keep the test.

Checking your dependencies

A program is also everything it depends on.

ToolWhat it checks
cargo auditknown security vulnerabilities in your dependencies, from the RustSec advisory database
cargo denyvulnerabilities, licences, unwanted or duplicated crates, according to rules you set
cargo outdateddependencies that are behind
cargo machetedependencies that are declared and never used
cargo tree -dcrates that are compiled in two different versions

Continuous integration

Continuous integration, or CI, means that a server runs all your checks automatically for every change pushed to the repository. Nobody can forget to run the tests, and a mistake is caught minutes after it is made. On GitHub, a file in the folder .github/workflows/ is enough:

The four steps are the standard quartet: format, lint, test, document. The RUSTDOCFLAGS: -D warnings line turns every documentation warning — a broken intra-doc link, a code example in a doc comment that no longer compiles — into a failed build, which is how documentation stays true.

One more line earns its place in any project that reads a database:

SQLX_OFFLINE=true tells SQLx to check its queries against the saved description in the .sqlx/ folder instead of connecting to a live database (chapter 47). The cache step keeps compiled dependencies between runs, which saves minutes. Larger projects add a matrix that runs the tests on Linux, Windows and macOS, a job on the oldest supported Rust version, and cargo audit on a schedule.

Run the same commands yourself before you push. Many people put them in a script, or use a tool such as just, a simple command runner:

How other languages do it
Tooling in other languages

Formatters and linters exist everywhere: Prettier and ESLint for JavaScript, Black and Ruff for Python, clang-format and clang-tidy for C++, gofmt and go vet for Go. In most ecosystems they are separate projects that must be chosen, installed and configured, and teams differ. Rust follows Go’s example: one official formatter, one official linter, both installed with the compiler. A Rust project you have never seen before is built, tested, formatted and linted with the same four commands as your own.

Recap
  • cargo fmt formats code in the one standard style. cargo fmt --check verifies it.
  • cargo clippy finds likely bugs and unidiomatic, complicated or slow code, and explains each finding.
  • Lint levels (allow, warn, deny, forbid) are set per item with attributes, or per package in [lints].
  • rust-analyzer brings types, errors, quick fixes and navigation into the editor.
  • Debug with dbg!, RUST_BACKTRACE=1, and a debugger with breakpoints. Turn every bug into a test.
  • cargo audit and cargo deny check dependencies.
  • CI runs format, lint, test and documentation checks on every change.
Check your understanding
1

What does cargo fmt --check do?

The --check form is for automation: it fails if formatting is needed, so that unformatted code cannot be merged.

2

Which of these would Clippy typically point out?

The first, second and fourth are compiler errors. Clippy works on code that already compiles, and suggests the clearer or faster form.

3

What does cargo clippy -- -D warnings achieve in CI?

-D warnings means “deny warnings”. The pipeline then fails for any new warning, which keeps the code base clean.

4

A program panics deep inside a call chain. How do you see which functions called which?

The backtrace lists the active function calls at the moment of the panic, with file and line for your own code.

5

Why turn a bug into a test before fixing it?

A failing test is a precise description of the bug. Once it passes, it stays as a regression test.

Guided exerciseClean up with the tools

Create a new project, paste this code into src/main.rs, and run cargo fmt and then cargo clippy. Apply every suggestion until Clippy is silent. The program should still print total: 60.

Need a hint?

Clippy will mention the index loop, the total = total + …, the length comparison, and a vec! where an array is enough. Work through the messages one at a time and run Clippy again after each change.

Show solution and explanation

cargo fmt fixed the spacing. Clippy then led to the rest, one lint after another: an array instead of a Vec that never grows (useless_vec), += instead of total = total + … (assign_op_pattern), an iterator instead of the index loop (needless_range_loop), and is_empty() instead of len() > 0 (len_zero). Once the loop was an iterator, the whole sum became one call. Five lines of careless code turned into four clear ones, guided by the tools.

PracticeFind the bug

This function should return the second-largest number in a list. It gives a wrong answer for some inputs. Find one such input, write a failing test, locate the mistake with dbg! or a debugger, and fix it.

Need a hint?

Try a list in rising order, such as [1, 2, 3]. When a new largest value is found, what should happen to the old largest value?

Show solution and explanation

For [1, 2, 3] the original returned i32::MIN: each number was a new largest, and the previous largest was thrown away. Putting dbg!(n, largest, second); at the end of the loop body shows it at once: second never changes. The falling list [3, 2, 1] happened to work, which is how such a bug survives a quick manual check.

The process matters more than the fix: a concrete failing input, a test that pins it down, a look inside, a one-line correction, and three tests that stay.

ChallengeA CI plan

Write down, as a list of commands, the checks you would run in CI for a library crate that (a) has an optional feature serde, (b) promises to work on Rust 1.85 and later, and (c) must run on Linux and Windows. Explain why each check is there.

Need a hint?

Think about: formatting, lints, tests with and without the feature, the documentation, the minimum Rust version, the two operating systems, and known vulnerabilities.

Show solution and explanation

Why each one:

  1. Formatting and lints are the cheapest checks. They fail fast, before slower jobs start.
  2. Code behind a feature that is switched off is not compiled at all. Only testing with and without serde shows that both configurations build and pass. The operating systems differ in paths, line endings and system calls, so the tests run on both.
  3. Broken links and outdated examples in the documentation are bugs for your users.
  4. Without this job, someone will use a newer language feature by accident, and users on Rust 1.85 will be broken. cargo check is enough to prove that the code compiles there.
  5. A vulnerability can be published for a dependency on a day when your code did not change. A scheduled job notices.

In a GitHub workflow, point 2 is a matrix: one job definition that is run for every combination of operating system and feature set.

Testing strategies for real projects

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Decide what to test at which level
  • Make code testable by passing in its dependencies
  • Write table-driven, property-based and snapshot tests
  • Measure speed with benchmarks and completeness with coverage
  • Know the tools for fuzzing, mocking and faster test runs

Chapter 22 taught the mechanics: #[test], the assertion macros, unit and integration tests. This chapter is about using them well in a growing project, and about the more powerful techniques and tools.

What to test where

Real-world analogy
Checking a car

A car factory tests every bolt and every valve on its own, thousands of times a day, because that is quick and cheap. It tests assembled engines on a test bench, which takes longer. And it drives a finished car around a track now and then. All three are needed, in very different numbers.

LevelTests …SpeedHow many
Unit testsone function or type in isolationmicrosecondsmany
Integration testsseveral parts working together, through the public APImillisecondssome
End-to-end teststhe whole program from outside, as a user would: start it, send input, check outputsecondsfew

This shape is known as the test pyramid: a broad base of fast tests, and a narrow top of slow ones. Fast tests are run constantly, so they find mistakes at once. Slow tests find problems in the connections that unit tests cannot see.

A good test has four properties. It is fast. It is deterministic: the same result on every run. It is independent of other tests. And when it fails, it tells you what is wrong.

Code that can be tested

Some code is hard to test because it reaches out to the world by itself: it reads the clock, a file, the network, a random number. Such a function gives different results at different times, or needs a server to be running.

The cure is to pass in what the code depends on. This is called dependency injection. In Rust, the dependency is described by a trait. The real program passes the real implementation, and a test passes a simple stand-in, called a fake or a test double.

In the real program, a SystemClock implements the trait by asking the operating system. The test controls time completely, and can check 3 o’clock at night without staying up.

The same idea handles storage, the network, and randomness. Write the trait for what your code needs (save_order, send_email), not for everything the outside system can do. A fake that records what was asked of it lets a test check effects:

No e-mail leaves the building during the test. For large traits, the crate mockall generates such stand-ins automatically. A hand-written fake of ten lines is often clearer.

The cheapest way of all to make code testable is the one used throughout this guide: keep the logic in pure functions that take values and return values. They need no stand-ins at all.

Table-driven tests

When many cases differ only in input and expected output, put them in a table:

The message at the end of assert_eq! matters here. Without it, a failure would only say left: false, right: true, and you would not know which row failed. A new case costs one line, which lowers the barrier to adding the next edge case.

Test helpers and test data

Tests are code and deserve the same care. When several tests need similar data, write a helper that builds it with sensible defaults, so that each test states only what is special about it:

For tests that need files, the crate tempfile creates a fresh folder that is deleted when the test ends, so that tests running in parallel cannot disturb each other. Code shared between several integration test files goes into tests/common/mod.rs.

Property-based testing

Example-based tests check the cases you thought of. Bugs live in the cases you did not think of. Property-based testing turns the approach around: you state a rule that must hold for all inputs, and the tool generates hundreds of random inputs to look for one that breaks it.

The standard crate is proptest (cargo add --dev proptest). Here are two functions that pack runs of equal characters, so that "aaabcc" becomes "3a1b2c", and unpack them again:

The property is one line: decoding an encoded text gives back the original. text in "[a-z0-9 ]{0,40}" asks for random strings of up to 40 lower-case letters, digits and spaces. The example test passes. The property test does not:

The tool found a real flaw in the format, one that the hand-picked example missed: if the text itself contains a digit, the encoded form is ambiguous. "0" is encoded as "10", which decodes as “ten of nothing”.

Notice the words minimal failing input. The random input that first failed was probably a long string. proptest then shrinks it: it tries simpler and simpler inputs that still fail, and reports the simplest one. It also saves the failing case in a file, so that the next run tries it first.

Kinds of properties that fit many functions:

PropertyExample
Round trip: doing and undoing gives the originaldecode(encode(x)) == x, parse(format(x)) == x
Invariant: something is always true of the resulta sorted list is in order, and has the same length as the input
Idempotence: doing it twice equals doing it oncesort(sort(x)) == sort(x), trim(trim(s)) == trim(s)
Comparison with a simple versiona fast algorithm agrees with a slow, obviously correct one
No crash: for any input, the function returns without panickinga parser fed with arbitrary bytes

Inputs are described by strategies: any::<i32>() for any number, 0..100_u32 for a range, a regular expression for strings, prop::collection::vec(any::<u8>(), 0..50) for vectors.

Snapshot testing

Some results are large: a formatted report, an error message, a generated file. Typing the expected text into a test is tedious, and updating it after every intended change is worse. A snapshot test stores the output in a file the first time, and compares against that file from then on. The crate is insta.

The first run writes tests/snapshots/snapshot__encoded_report.snap:

Later runs fail if the output differs, and show the difference. The companion tool cargo insta review shows each change and asks you to accept or reject it. The snapshot files are committed with the code, so a reviewer sees exactly how the output changed.

Snapshots are comfortable, and that is their danger: it is easy to accept a change without reading it. Use them for output where the exact text matters, and keep ordinary assertions for logic.

Testing the outside of a program

  • Command-line programs: the crate assert_cmd starts your compiled program with arguments and checks its output and exit code. This is an end-to-end test that Cargo runs like any other.
  • Async code: #[tokio::test] runs an async test function, as in the chat project of chapter 33. Put a timeout around everything that waits.
  • Web services: a server can be tested without opening a network port, by handing requests directly to its router. Chapter 48 shows it.
  • Documentation: every example in a /// comment is a test.

Fuzzing

Fuzzing is property testing taken further. A fuzzer feeds a function millions of inputs, watches which parts of the code each input reaches, and mutates the inputs to reach more. It runs for minutes or days, and it is extremely good at finding inputs that crash parsers and decoders. The tool is cargo fuzz (it needs the nightly toolchain):

Any code that reads data from outside (file formats, network protocols, user input) is a candidate. Fuzzing has found thousands of bugs in widely used software.

Benchmarks

A benchmark measures how long code takes. Measuring time well is harder than it looks: the first runs are slow, other programs disturb the measurement, and the optimiser may remove a calculation whose result is never used. The crate criterion handles all of that. It runs the code many times, analyses the measurements statistically, and compares with the previous run.

The three numbers are the lower bound, the best estimate and the upper bound of the time for one call. On the next run, criterion also reports whether the code got faster or slower, and whether the change is larger than the noise of the measurement.

black_box hides a value from the optimiser, so that the compiler cannot compute the answer in advance or throw the work away. Benchmarks always run in release mode. Chapter 52 is about what to do with the numbers.

How much is tested?

Code coverage reports which lines were executed by the tests. The tool cargo llvm-cov produces the numbers and an HTML page in which untested lines are marked:

Use coverage to find code that no test touches at all. Do not chase a percentage. A line that was executed is not thereby checked: a test without assertions gives full coverage and proves nothing. A sharper tool is mutation testing (cargo mutants): it changes your code in small ways, for example turning < into <=, and reports the changes that no test noticed.

More tools

ToolPurpose
cargo nextesta faster test runner: each test in its own process, clearer output, retries for flaky tests
cargo miri testrun the tests in an interpreter that detects undefined behaviour (chapter 35)
rstest, test-caseparameterised tests and fixtures through attributes
mockallgenerated mock objects for traits
wiremock, httpmocka fake HTTP server for testing code that calls web services
testcontainersstart a real database in a container for the duration of a test
loomtest concurrent code by trying the possible interleavings of threads
trybuildcompile-fail tests: assert that a bad program fails to compile with the message you expect
pretty_assertionscoloured, line-by-line diffs when an assert_eq! fails
quickcheck, proptestgenerate random inputs and check properties instead of examples (above)
instasnapshot tests: compare against a reviewed, committed output (above)

Habits that keep a test suite healthy

  • Test behaviour, not implementation. A test that checks private details breaks with every refactoring and protects nothing.
  • Every bug gets a test before it is fixed.
  • Fix or delete flaky tests. A test that fails now and then teaches everyone to ignore failures. The usual causes are shared state, real time, real network, and dependence on the order of a HashMap.
  • Keep tests fast. A suite that takes ten minutes is not run.
  • Name tests as statements about behaviour: large_orders_ship_free.
  • Run everything in CI, on every change (chapter 40).
How other languages do it
Testing tools in other languages

Property-based testing comes from Haskell’s QuickCheck and exists in most languages now: Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for JavaScript, jqwik for Java. Snapshot testing became popular through Jest in JavaScript. Fuzzing grew up around C and C++ with AFL and libFuzzer, which cargo fuzz uses underneath. Rust adds two things of its own: the type system removes whole categories of tests that dynamic languages need (“what if this is null?”, “what if this is the wrong type?”), and a fuzzer that finds a panic in safe Rust has found a bug, and not a security hole.

Recap
  • Many fast unit tests, some integration tests, a few end-to-end tests.
  • Pass dependencies in through traits. Tests use simple fakes for the clock, storage and network.
  • Table-driven tests make adding a case cheap. Helper functions build test data with defaults.
  • Property tests check a rule for hundreds of generated inputs and shrink failures to a minimal case.
  • Snapshot tests store large outputs in files and show differences for review.
  • criterion measures speed reliably. cargo llvm-cov shows untested code. cargo fuzz hunts for crashes.
  • A healthy suite is fast, deterministic, and run on every change.
Check your understanding
1

Why does the test pyramid have many unit tests and few end-to-end tests?

Speed and precision decide the proportions. Each level catches problems the others cannot.

2

A function calls SystemTime::now() inside and behaves differently in the evening. How do you make it testable?

Injecting the dependency puts the test in control. The production code passes the real clock.

3

What does “shrinking” mean in property-based testing?

A random failing input is usually long and confusing. The shrunk one, such as "0", shows the heart of the bug.

4

Which is a property suitable for a function sort?

The first is an example. A property is a statement about all inputs, which the tool can check with generated data.

5

A project has 100 % line coverage. What does that prove?

Coverage finds untested code. It cannot tell whether the tests assert anything meaningful.

Guided exerciseA table of cases

Write fn grade(points: u32) -> Result<char, String>: 90 to 100 points give 'A', 75 to 89 'B', 60 to 74 'C', below 60 'F', and more than 100 is an error. Test it with one table-driven test that covers every boundary on both sides.

Need a hint?

The table is an array of pairs (points, expected), where expected is a Result<char, ()> or simply an Option<char> with None for “error”. Boundaries: 100 and 101, 90 and 89, 75 and 74, 60 and 59, and 0.

Show solution and explanation

Each boundary appears twice: the last value on one side and the first on the other. That is where “off by one” mistakes hide, such as > where >= was meant. .ok() turns the Result into an Option, so that the table stays simple and the error text is not part of the comparison. The message "for {points} points" identifies the failing row.

PracticeA fake for storage

A function register(store: &mut impl UserStore, name: &str) -> Result<u32, String> should refuse empty names and names that already exist, and otherwise save the user and return the new id. Define the trait UserStore with the methods exists(&self, name: &str) -> bool and save(&mut self, name: &str) -> u32. Write an in-memory fake, and three tests.

Need a hint?

The fake is a struct with a Vec<String>. save pushes the name and returns the new length as the id. The tests: a successful registration, a duplicate, and an empty name. In the last two, also check that nothing was saved.

Show solution and explanation

The rules of registration are tested without any database. In the real program, a type that talks to a database implements UserStore, and register does not change. The tests check the returned value and also the state of the store afterwards: a refused registration must leave no trace. The second assertion in the first test shows that names are trimmed before saving, a detail that would be easy to lose in a later rewrite.

ChallengeProperties of a function

Write distinct_sorted(values: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<i32>, which returns the distinct values of a list in rising order. Then write three property tests with proptest: (1) the output is strictly rising, (2) every input value appears in the output and nothing else does, and (3) applying the function twice gives the same as applying it once.

Need a hint?

The function is sort followed by dedup. A strategy for a vector is prop::collection::vec(any::<i32>(), 0..100). “Strictly rising” is result.windows(2).all(|pair| pair[0] < pair[1]). For property 2, use a small range such as -50..50_i32, so that duplicates really occur.

Show solution and explanation

Together, the first two properties describe the function completely: the result contains exactly the input’s values, each once, in order. No concrete example was needed, and each test run checks 256 random lists per property, including the empty list and lists of one element.

The choice of strategy matters. With any::<i32>(), two equal numbers almost never occur by chance, so the removal of duplicates would hardly be exercised. The narrow range in the second property makes duplicates frequent. When you write a property, ask whether the generated inputs really reach the interesting cases.

Try breaking the function, for example by removing values.dedup(), and watch which property fails and what minimal input proptest reports.

The crate ecosystem: finding and using libraries

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Find crates for a task and judge their quality
  • Read a crate’s documentation efficiently
  • Use the everyday crates: rand, regex, chrono, itertools, tracing
  • Name the standard choice for each common task
  • Keep dependencies safe and under control

Rust’s standard library is small on purpose. It has no random numbers, no regular expressions, no dates, no JSON and no HTTP. All of these live in crates: libraries published on crates.io, the community’s registry, which holds well over 150,000 of them. Knowing the language is half of being productive in Rust. The other half is knowing which crate to reach for.

This chapter shows how to find and judge crates, and introduces the ones you will use in almost every project. The chapters after it go deeper into the main areas: data formats, command-line tools, async and web, databases, and applications.

Real-world analogy
A toolbox with a label on every drawer

The standard library is the set of tools that comes with the workbench. Crates are the tools you choose for a particular job. A label helps you reach for the right tool, but before using one you still check that it fits, is maintained, and has no hidden damage. In the same way, learn a crate’s job and check its source, docs, dependencies and release history before trusting it in a project.

Where to look

SiteWhat it gives you
crates.iothe official registry: search, download numbers, versions, links
lib.rsa different view of the same crates, with better categories and ranking
docs.rsthe documentation of every version of every crate, built automatically
blessed.rsa short, hand-picked list of recommended crates for each task
The Rust Cookbookexample code for common tasks, using well-known crates
This Week in Rusta weekly newsletter with new releases and articles

On the command line, cargo search json searches the registry, and cargo info serde_json shows a crate’s description, licence, versions and features.

Judging a crate

Real-world analogy
Choosing parts for a bridge

Before bolting a third-party girder into a bridge, an engineer checks who manufactured it, whether it has been stress-tested on other bridges, and whether the supplier still answers the phone. Picking a crate from crates.io works the same way: download counts, maintenance activity, documentation, dependency tree weight and licence tell you within two minutes whether you can trust a dependency in production.

Anyone can publish a crate, so you need to look before you depend on one. A checklist that takes two minutes:

  1. Is it widely used? The download numbers and the list of “dependents” on crates.io tell you. A crate used by thousands of others has had its bugs found.
  2. Is it maintained? Look at the date of the last release and at the repository: are issues answered, are pull requests merged? A finished, stable crate may be quiet, and that is fine. Unanswered bug reports are not.
  3. Is it documented? Open docs.rs. Is there an introduction and an example? Do the main types have descriptions?
  4. What does it pull in? cargo tree shows its dependencies. Fewer is better, for build time and for risk.
  5. Which licence? MIT and Apache-2.0 are the usual ones and allow nearly everything. Check that the licence fits your project, especially for commercial work.
  6. Is it at version 1.0 or above? Many excellent crates are at 0.x. Below 1.0, expect breaking changes between minor versions.
  7. Does it use unsafe, and with care? For low-level crates that is normal. Look for a test suite, and for the use of Miri and fuzzing.
Watch out
Check the name letter by letter

Attackers sometimes publish crates whose names look almost like popular ones, hoping for a typing mistake. This is called typosquatting. Copy the name from the crate’s documentation, or use cargo add, and look at what was added.

Reading documentation on docs.rs

Every crate’s documentation has the same structure, which makes any crate quick to learn:

  • The front page has an introduction, usually with a complete example. Start here.
  • Modules, structs, enums, traits, functions are listed with one line each. Click through to the main type.
  • On a type’s page, look at the methods first, then at trait implementations: these tell you whether it is Clone, Debug, Send, or can be used with ?, for, or serde.
  • The search box at the top searches names, and also signatures: &str -> u32 finds functions that turn text into a number.
  • ”Source” links show the implementation. Reading good crates is a fine way to learn.
  • The feature flags page lists the optional features.

The examples in documentation are compiled as tests, so they work with the version you are looking at.

Everyday crates

The examples below can be tried in any project after cargo add with the crate’s name. The versions are those current when this guide was written.

rand: random numbers

The program prints facts about the random values, and not the values themselves, so that its output is the same on every run. Three points to remember:

  • rand::random_range(1..=6) is all you need for simple cases.
  • The methods on a generator (random, random_range) come from the trait RngExt, which must be imported.
  • A generator created with a seed produces the same numbers every time. Use it for tests and for simulations that must be repeatable. The default generator is safe for security purposes such as tokens. A seeded one is predictable by design.

regex: searching text with patterns

A regular expression is a small pattern language for text: \d is a digit, {4} means “four times”, parentheses capture a part.

  • Patterns are written as raw strings, r"...", in which a backslash is an ordinary character.
  • Building a Regex is costly. Do it once, and not inside a loop. For a pattern used in many places, keep it in a static with LazyLock.
  • This crate guarantees that matching time grows only in proportion to the length of the text. Some regex engines in other languages can be brought to a standstill by a crafted input. This one cannot.

For simple checks, the standard string methods (contains, split, strip_prefix, find) are simpler and faster than a regex.

chrono: dates and times

  • A ”naive” date or time has no time zone: NaiveDate, NaiveDateTime. DateTime<Utc> and DateTime<Local> are moments in a specific zone.
  • Constructors such as from_ymd_opt return an Option, because 30 February does not exist.
  • Utc::now() reads the clock. Dates can be subtracted, and a Duration can be added.
  • Format codes like %Y-%m-%d follow the convention of C’s strftime.
Tip
Store UTC, show local time

Keep and compare moments in UTC (or as timestamps), and convert to the user’s time zone only for display. Mixing local times causes bugs around daylight saving changes. The standard library’s std::time::Instant is the right tool for measuring how long something takes. Besides chrono, the crates time and jiff are good modern choices. jiff is especially careful about time zones.

Time zones, durations, and the format on the wire

Almost every date bug comes from mixing up three questions that look like one. Ask them separately and the bugs disappear:

  1. Which instant in time is it? Store this. A moment is universal; it is the same moment in every city.
  2. Which zone should the reader see it in? A display decision, made at the edge, from the user’s setting — not stored.
  3. How is it written down? One format on the wire, chosen once for the whole system.

The consequence: store UTC, display local, and always store an instant rather than a wall-clock time. 2026-11-14T09:12:03Z and 2026-11-14T12:12:03+03:00 are the same moment written two ways. That format is RFC 3339 (a profile of ISO 8601), and it is what JSON APIs and HTTP headers use, because it is sortable as text, unambiguous, and readable by a human. In PostgreSQL the column type is TIMESTAMPTZ; in SQLite, store the RFC 3339 string or a Unix timestamp as an integer. Always parse incoming offset strings with DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339 and normalise immediately to DateTime<Utc>:

A time zone is more than an offset: it is a set of rules that a government can change. That is why the rules ship as a database (tzdata, the IANA list) and why a program that calculates “9 a.m. tomorrow in Berlin” needs one. chrono-tz provides the zone list for chrono.

Two traps worth naming:

  • Daylight saving. One hour of the year is skipped and one is lived twice. A local time such as 02:30 on a changeover day may not exist (LocalResult::None), or may exist twice (LocalResult::Ambiguous). Never call .unwrap() when converting a NaiveDateTime into a zoned local time. Arithmetic on local wall-clock times is therefore ambiguous — do it in UTC or on an Instant, and convert only for display. A zone with no daylight saving, such as East Africa Time (UTC+03:00 all year), does not have this problem, which is why code written there can look fine and fail in Berlin.
  • A birthday is not an instant. A birth date, an invoice date or a business day is a calendar date: NaiveDate in chrono, Date in jiff. Storing it as a timestamp at midnight UTC makes it the wrong day for half the planet.

The three crates, honestly compared:

CrateStrengthChoose it when
chronoThe most widely used, with the widest ecosystem support (sqlx, serde, uuid) and the examples in this bookYou want the default, and the docs you will find everywhere
timeStricter API, no implicit local-time reading, good formattingYou want compile-time checks on formats and a smaller surface
jiffModern design, built-in IANA TZDB (Zoned), RFC 3339 as the native formatTime zones and human-facing dates are central to the program. For new code in 2025 onwards, a good first choice

For the wire: with the serde feature, chrono’s DateTime<Utc> serialises to an RFC 3339 string and parses back from one, which is exactly what you want in JSON. Durations in configuration are best written for humans — "30s", "5m", "2h" — and parsed with humantime (or humantime_serde as a serde attribute) rather than a raw number of milliseconds that nobody can read six months later.

itertools: more iterator tools

Importing the trait Itertools adds dozens of methods to every iterator. counts() is the word-count map of chapter 15 in one call, and into_group_map_by is the grouping loop of chapter 25.

tracing: logging

A program that runs for hours cannot be debugged with println!. Logging writes messages with a time, a severity level, and structured data, and lets you choose at run time how much you want to see. The modern standard is tracing, with tracing-subscriber to print the messages.

  • The five levels, from most to least detailed: trace!, debug!, info!, warn!, error!. A program in production usually shows info and above.
  • Messages can carry fields (result = …, code = 7) in addition to text. Tools can filter and search by them.
  • #[instrument] wraps a function in a span: a named stretch of time. Every message inside shows which call it belongs to, with the arguments (divide{a=1 b=0}). In async programs, where many tasks are interleaved, this is what makes logs readable.
  • The example switches off the time stamp and colours to keep the output stable. Normally you would just call tracing_subscriber::fmt::init().

tracing is powerful, but a small program does not need spans and fields. The crate log is a facade: it provides the macros (error!, warn!, info!, debug!, trace!) and nothing more. A library should depend on log and call its macros — and never decide where messages go. The crate env_logger is a small logger implementation, and the environment variable RUST_LOG chooses how much to see.

A tiny program with a logger:

  • The format closure decides what each line looks like; here it is just the level and the message. env_logger writes to standard error by default; this example explicitly uses standard output so the captured lines are visible here.
  • default_filter_or("trace") shows everything during development. Without any RUST_LOG setting, info and above would be enough for production.
  • error! shows even though nothing catches it: logging does not stop the program.

hides info and debug. The filter is a pattern: mycrate=debug shows debug messages from one crate only, and info shows the rest.

log + env_loggertracing
What you writeone message per callmessages with fields, inside named spans
Async taskshard to tell which task said whatspans follow the task (#[instrument])
Best fitsmall tools, command-line programsservices, servers, async code

This chapter introduces the basics for scripts and small programs. For structured JSON logging in production, request IDs across async tasks, OpenTelemetry distributed traces, Prometheus metrics, and health probes, see chapter 51.

How other languages do it
Logging, not printing

A library logs; an application decides where the logs go. log and tracing both leave the decision to main. A library that calls println! forces its output on everybody.

Watch out
Never write your own cryptography

Use the established crates for passwords, encryption and secure connections. A home-made cipher or hash is broken in ways its author cannot see. Passwords are stored with a slow, salted hash made for the purpose, such as argon2, and never in readable form.

Keeping dependencies healthy

Each dependency is code you did not write, running with all the rights of your program.

  • Add what you need, and no more. For a ten-line helper, writing it yourself may be better than a new dependency.
  • Disable features you do not use: default-features = false, and then enable what is needed.
  • Update regularly: cargo update for compatible versions, cargo outdated to see newer major versions. Read the changelog for major updates.
  • Audit: cargo audit checks against the database of known vulnerabilities. Run it in CI.
  • Watch for duplicates: cargo tree -d lists crates that are compiled twice in different versions.
  • Remove what is no longer used. Cargo warns about a dependency that no code uses (warning: unused dependency). cargo remove <name> deletes it from Cargo.toml.
  • Commit Cargo.lock.
How other languages do it
Package ecosystems
  • JavaScript’s npm is the largest registry of all, with a culture of very small packages. Python’s PyPI is similarly broad, and the standard library there is large (“batteries included”).
  • C and C++ have no central registry, and adding a library is real work, so programmers often rewrite things.
  • Rust sits in between: a small standard library, a central registry, and a culture of focused, well-documented crates. Because adding a crate is one command and the compiler checks how you use it, Rust programs tend to use many of them. The other side of that ease is the need to choose with care.
Recap
  • The standard library is small. Most functionality comes from crates on crates.io, documented on docs.rs.
  • Judge a crate by use, maintenance, documentation, dependencies, licence and version.
  • rand for randomness, regex for text patterns, chrono for dates, itertools for extra iterator methods, tracing for logging.
  • log is a logging facade for libraries; an application can install env_logger and let RUST_LOG control its output.
  • For every common task there is a well-known standard crate. The table in this chapter is your map.
  • Keep dependencies few, current and audited.
Check your understanding
1

Where do you find the documentation of any published crate?

docs.rs builds and hosts the documentation for every release of every crate, in the same format as the standard library’s.

2

Which sign suggests that a crate may be a risky choice?

A quiet crate can simply be finished. Unanswered reports mean that nobody is looking after it. Many solid crates are below 1.0.

3

Why build a Regex once and reuse it, and not inside a loop?

Regex::new parses and compiles the pattern. Doing that for every item wastes most of the running time.

4

When is a random number generator with a fixed seed the right choice?

A seeded generator is repeatable, which is valuable for testing and useless for security. Secrets need the default, unpredictable generator.

5

What does #[instrument] from tracing add to a function?

Spans give log messages context. In concurrent programs they show which request or task a message belongs to.

Guided exerciseDice statistics

Roll a six-sided die 60,000 times with a generator seeded with the number 2026, count how often each face appears, and print whether every face came up between 9,500 and 10,500 times.

Need a hint?

let mut rng = StdRng::seed_from_u64(2026);, then rng.random_range(1..=6) in a loop. Count in an array [0_u32; 6], using face - 1 as the index.

Show solution and explanation

Each face is expected 10,000 times. With a fair generator, a count is almost never more than a few hundred away from that. Because the generator is seeded, the program gives the same counts on every run, which makes the result checkable. Replace the seeded generator by rand::rng(), and the exact counts change from run to run while the conclusion stays.

PracticeAge and days

Write age_on(birthday: NaiveDate, today: NaiveDate) -> u32 that returns a person’s age in whole years. Test it for someone born on 14 March 1995, on the day before and on the day of their birthday in 2027. Then print how many days lie between 13 March 2027 and New Year’s Day 2028.

Need a hint?

Start with today.year() - birthday.year(), and subtract one if the birthday has not yet come this year. Comparing the tuples (month, day) does that in one step. Two dates can be subtracted, which gives a duration with a method num_days().

Show solution and explanation

Tuples are compared element by element, so (month, day) < (month, day) asks exactly “is today earlier in the year than the birthday?”. The function takes today as a parameter and does not call Utc::now() itself. That is the dependency injection of chapter 41: the function can be tested for any date. Date arithmetic by hand, with month lengths and leap years, is a classic source of bugs. The crate has them right.

ChallengeAnalyse a log

Combine three crates. Given the log text below, use regex to take each line apart, chrono to parse the time, and itertools to summarise. Print the number of valid entries, the count per level in alphabetical order, the number of minutes between the first and the last entry, and every error message that occurs more than once.

Need a hint?

A pattern with three groups: ^(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) (\w+)\s+(.*)$. Use filter_map twice: once to drop lines that do not match, once to drop times that do not parse. counts() gives the per-level map, minmax() the first and last time, and duplicates() the repeated messages.

Show solution and explanation

Each crate does the part it is good at. The regex separates the fields and rejects the broken line. chrono turns the text into a real time that can be subtracted. itertools supplies the summaries as single method calls. The glue between them is ordinary iterator code, and the borrowed &str pieces point into the original log text with no copies.

This is what working in Rust looks like much of the time: a few well-chosen crates, joined by a small amount of your own code.
