Data formats with Serde: JSON, TOML and more

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what serialisation is
  • Convert your structs and enums to and from JSON with derive
  • Control the result with Serde attributes
  • Read configuration from TOML and handle data of unknown shape
  • Validate data while it is being read

Programs exchange data all the time: they save it to files, send it over the network, and read configuration. For that, a value in memory must be turned into a sequence of bytes in an agreed format, and back again. The first direction is called serialisation, and the second deserialisation.

In Rust, nearly all of this is done with one library: Serde (from “serialise” and “deserialise”). You describe your data as ordinary structs and enums, add one line, and Serde converts them to and from JSON, TOML, YAML, CSV and a dozen other formats.

Real-world analogy
A universal adaptor

A travel adaptor has two sides: one for your plug, and one for the foreign socket. With one adaptor, any of your devices works in any country. Serde is the adaptor between Rust types on one side and data formats on the other. A type that works with Serde works with every format, and a new format works with every type.

Setting up

Serde itself defines the two traits Serialize and Deserialize. Each format is a separate crate.

The feature derive provides the derive macros, which generate the conversion code for your types.

To JSON and back

JSON is the most common format for exchanging data, especially on the web. It knows objects ({ "key": value }), lists ([1, 2]), strings, numbers, true, false and null.

  • #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] is all the type needs.
  • serde_json::to_string produces JSON, and to_string_pretty adds line breaks and indentation for people.
  • serde_json::from_str reads JSON. The target type comes from the annotation: let dune: Book = ….
  • The mapping is what you would expect: a struct becomes an object, a Vec a list, Option is the value or null, and numbers and strings are themselves.
  • r#"…"# is a raw string that may contain double quotes, which makes JSON in source code readable.

For files and network connections there are serde_json::to_writer(file, &value) and serde_json::from_reader(file), which avoid building the whole text in memory.

Wrong data is an error, with a position

Deserialising checks the data against your types. Whatever does not fit is reported, with the line and column:

A wrong type, a missing field, a number too big for a u8, and a missing brace are all caught. This is “parse, don’t validate” from chapter 29, for free: once you hold a User, the data has the right shape, and the rest of the program needs no checks. In languages where JSON becomes a loose dictionary, such mistakes surface later, somewhere deep in the program.

Shaping the output with attributes

The names and rules of an existing format rarely match Rust’s conventions exactly. Attributes adjust the mapping without changing your types:

AttributeEffect
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]convert all field names: user_name ↔ userName. Others: "snake_case", "kebab-case", "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE", "lowercase"
#[serde(rename = "mail")]a different name for one field
#[serde(alias = "e-mail")]accept a second name when reading
#[serde(default)]if the field is missing, use Default::default()
#[serde(default = "function")]if the field is missing, call this function
#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]leave the field out when writing, if the test is true
#[serde(skip)]never read or write this field
#[serde(flatten)]put the fields of a nested struct directly into the parent
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]reject input with fields the struct does not have
#[serde(with = "module")]use custom functions for this field

By default, unknown fields in the input are ignored. Together with default, that makes formats able to grow: an old program reads new files and skips what it does not know, and a new program reads old files and fills in defaults.

Enums

Enums map to JSON in several ways. The default wraps the data in an object named after the variant. Often you want a field that names the kind, and one attribute does that:

RepresentationAttributeJSON for Login { user: "sara" }
externally tagged (default)none{"Login": {"user": "sara"}}
internally tagged#[serde(tag = "type")]{"type": "Login", "user": "sara"}
adjacently tagged#[serde(tag = "t", content = "c")]{"t": "Login", "c": {"user": "sara"}}
untagged#[serde(untagged)]{"user": "sara"}: the first variant that fits is chosen

The internally tagged form is what most web APIs use. A list of events of different kinds becomes one Vec<Event> that you handle with a match.

Data of unknown shape

Sometimes you do not know the structure in advance, or need only one value from a large document. serde_json::Value is an enum that can hold any JSON:

  • Indexing with ["key"] or [0] never panics. A missing entry gives Value::Null.
  • as_str(), as_u64(), as_array() and their relatives return an Option, because the value may be of another kind.
  • The json! macro builds a Value from JSON-like syntax, with Rust expressions inside.

Use Value for exploring and for truly free-form data. For anything with a known structure, define structs. You then get checking, documentation and auto-completion.

Configuration files with TOML

TOML is the format of Cargo.toml, and the usual choice for configuration files in Rust programs. It is easy for people to read and edit. The crate toml works exactly like serde_json:

The TOML syntax in brief: key = value lines, [section] for a nested struct, and [[name]] for one element of a list of structs. The port and the debug flag are missing from the file and get their defaults.

In a real program, read the text with std::fs::read_to_string("config.toml"). A typical start-up sequence is: read the file, deserialise it into a Config struct, report any error with its position, and pass the Config on. From then on the configuration is a checked, typed value.

Other formats

Since the conversion is described once by the derive, switching the format is a matter of calling a different crate:

FormatCrateTypical use
JSONserde_jsonweb APIs, data exchange
TOMLtomlconfiguration files
YAMLserde_yaml and its successorsconfiguration, Kubernetes files
CSVcsvtables, spreadsheets
MessagePackrmp-serdecompact binary exchange between languages
bincode, postcardbincode, postcardvery compact binary data between Rust programs. postcard suits embedded devices
CBORciboriumbinary, standardised
RONrona Rust-like text format, used for game data
URL query strings and formsserde_urlencodedweb forms

Web frameworks, database libraries and command-line parsers build on Serde as well. A struct with Deserialize can be filled from an HTTP request body, a row of a database, or environment variables.

Binary formats: bincode and MessagePack

JSON and TOML are text: easy to read and debug, but verbose and slow to parse. When the data never needs to be read by a person — saved to a file, sent between two services, kept in a message queue — a binary format is smaller and faster. Both sides must agree on the type, usually by sharing the same crate; the bytes themselves contain no schema and no field names unless the format adds them.

bincode turns a Serde type into the smallest possible bytes: field names disappear, and numbers are written in their binary form. It is the natural choice when both sides are Rust.

rmp-serde implements MessagePack: a binary form of JSON-like data (maps, lists, strings, numbers). Other languages can read it, so it fits services written in more than one language.

  • Four bytes for three values, and none of them are the words sensor, temperature or ok. The reader must know the struct shape in advance — that is the contract of a binary format.
  • The size difference matters at scale: ten thousand readings take about 40 kilobytes with bincode, roughly ten times less than the same data as JSON.
bincodermp-serde (MessagePack)JSON
Field names in the datanoyesyes
Readable by other languagesrarelyyesyes
Sizesmallestsmalllarger
Best forRust ↔ Rustmixed-language servicesfiles people edit

Because the bytes carry no names, adding or removing a field can break files written by an older version of the program. Use Option, #[serde(default)] and #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "…")] to tolerate change (described earlier in this chapter), or keep a text format for data that must last years.

Tables: CSV

Chapter 26 read a table of sales by splitting lines at commas, and noted that real CSV files are harder: a field may contain a comma or a quote. The crate csv knows these rules, and with Serde each row becomes a struct:

  • The columns are matched to the fields by the names in the first line, so their order in the file does not matter.
  • "Smith, John" is one field with a comma inside, and "" inside quotes stands for one quote character. The hand-written parser of chapter 26 would have split the first row into five fields.
  • deserialize returns an iterator of Results. A bad row (here many is not a number) gives an error with its line number, and the program decides whether to skip it or to stop.
  • To work with a file, use csv::Reader::from_path("sales.csv") and csv::Writer::from_path(…).

Validating while reading

Serde can call your own conversion code, which lets a type protect its rules even when the data comes from outside. The attribute try_from says: “to deserialise me, first read this simpler type, then run my TryFrom”:

A Sale with a discount of 150 percent cannot come into existence, whether it is built in code or read from a file. The error from TryFrom is reported with the position in the input. This closes a common gap: without it, #[derive(Deserialize)] would fill the private field directly and bypass the constructor’s check.

For full control, you can implement Serialize and Deserialize by hand. That is rarely necessary.

Tip
How Serde stays fast

Serde does not build an intermediate tree of generic values. The derive macro generates code for exactly your type, which the compiler optimises like hand-written parsing code. Deserialising into structs is therefore fast and uses little memory. A field of type &str can even borrow directly from the input text, with no copy at all.

How other languages do it
Serialisation in other languages
  • JavaScript (JSON.parse) and Python (json.loads) return loose objects and dictionaries. Nothing checks the shape, unless you add a validation library such as Zod or Pydantic.
  • Java (Jackson, Gson) and C# (System.Text.Json) fill classes using reflection: they inspect types while the program runs, which costs time and finds some mistakes late.
  • Go uses struct tags and reflection. A missing field silently becomes a zero value.
  • Serde does the work at compile time. Missing fields and wrong types are errors unless you say otherwise, and no reflection is involved.
Tip
When the error does not say which field

Serde’s error message names the problem but not always its address: on a deep configuration file it can say “invalid type: string, expected a boolean” without telling you which of two hundred fields. The crate serde_path_to_error wraps the deserialiser and reports the path — server.tls.require_client_cert, not just “field”. It is ten lines of integration and it pays for itself the first time a user sends you a broken configuration file.

Recap
  • Serialisation turns values into bytes in some format, and deserialisation turns them back.
  • #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] makes a type work with every format Serde supports.
  • serde_json::to_string, to_string_pretty and from_str convert to and from JSON. Errors name the problem and its position.
  • Attributes adjust names (rename, rename_all), fill gaps (default), omit fields (skip…) and choose the enum representation (tag).
  • serde_json::Value and json! handle free-form JSON.
  • toml reads configuration files into typed structs, with defaults for missing settings.
  • #[serde(try_from = "…")] runs your validation during deserialisation.
Check your understanding
1

What do you have to add to a struct so that it can be written as JSON and read back?

The two derives generate implementations of Serde’s traits. Any format crate can then convert the type.

2

The JSON {"name": "Sara"} is deserialised into struct User { name: String, age: u8 }. What happens?

Missing fields are errors by default. Use Option<u8> or #[serde(default)] if the field may be absent.

3

Which attribute makes the Rust field user_name appear as userName in JSON, for all fields of the struct?

rename_all converts every field name to the given style. rename does it for a single field.

4

What does #[serde(tag = "type")] on an enum do?

This is the internally tagged representation: {"type": "login", "user": "sara"}.

5

When is serde_json::Value the right tool, and not a struct?

Value can hold anything, at the price of checking kinds by hand. Known structures are better served by structs.

Guided exerciseA round trip

Define a struct Recipe with a name, a number of servings, a list of ingredients (strings), and an optional note. Create one, convert it to pretty JSON, print it, read it back, and check that the result equals the original.

Need a hint?

Derive Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize. Use serde_json::to_string_pretty and serde_json::from_str. The return type of main can be Result<(), serde_json::Error>.

Show solution and explanation

A round-trip test like this (from_str(to_string(x)) == x) is the basic check for any type you serialise. It is also a natural property test: generate random recipes and assert the same equality. The None appears as null. With #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")] on the field, it would be left out, and reading would still work, because a missing Option field is read as None.

PracticeSettings with defaults

Define a Settings struct for a game: player_name: String (required), volume: u8 (default 80), fullscreen: bool (default false), and keys: Keys with jump and fire (both strings, with the defaults "space" and "ctrl", and the whole [keys] section may be missing). Read it from TOML, and show that a file with only player_name = "Sara" works.

Need a hint?

#[serde(default = "function_name")] for volume. For the whole keys field, #[serde(default)] needs Keys to implement Default: write that impl by hand so that it returns the two key names. Put #[serde(default)] on the struct Keys as well, so that a section with only one of the two keys is accepted.

Show solution and explanation

Three levels of defaults work together. A field with default = "…" calls a function. A field with plain default uses the type’s Default. And #[serde(default)] on a whole struct fills every missing field from the struct’s Default, which is why fire is "ctrl" when only jump is given. The required field stays required: a file without player_name is an error.

PracticeMessages of several kinds

A chat protocol sends JSON messages of three kinds: {"kind": "text", "from": "sara", "body": "hi"}, {"kind": "join", "user": "tomas"}, and {"kind": "ping"}. Model them as one enum, deserialise a list containing one of each, and print a line for each with a match.

Need a hint?

Use #[serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "lowercase")]. The variants are Text { from: String, body: String }, Join { user: String } and Ping.

Show solution and explanation

The enum is the protocol’s specification in code. An unknown kind is rejected at the border, and the match must handle every kind that exists. When a fourth message kind is added to the enum, the compiler leads you to every place that needs to deal with it. This is how the chat server of chapter 33 would look with a JSON protocol.

ChallengeSave the to-do list as JSON

In chapter 18 you saved the to-do list in a home-made text format that broke on special characters. Replace it with JSON. A TodoFile has a version number and a list of tasks. A Task has an id, a title, a done flag, a priority (low, normal or high) and a list of tags. Files written by an older version, without done, priority and tags, must still load. Write save and load with helpful error messages, using anyhow.

Need a hint?

Use #[serde(default)] on the three newer fields. Priority needs Default: derive it and mark the Normal variant with #[default]. Use #[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")] on the enum. In save and load, add context to errors with .with_context(|| format!(…)). Print an error with {error:#} to see the whole chain in one line.

Show solution and explanation

Compared with the hand-written format, there is no parsing code at all, and titles may contain any character, including quotes and line breaks. Three design points:

  • Growing the format. The fields added later have #[serde(default)], so the old file with only id and title loads, and the missing values are filled in. The version field is there for the day when a change cannot be handled by defaults.
  • Tidy output. skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty" keeps empty tag lists out of the file.
  • Errors with context. Serde says what is wrong and where in the text. with_context adds which file it was. {error:#} prints the chain: the file, then the cause.

#[default] on an enum variant, together with #[derive(Default)], chooses the default variant.

Command-line tools with clap

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Describe what makes a command-line tool pleasant to use
  • Define arguments, options, flags and subcommands with clap
  • Get help texts, validation and error messages generated for you
  • Build a complete to-do tool that stores its data as JSON
  • Test a command-line program

Command-line tools are where many people first use Rust in earnest. The language suits them well: a Rust tool starts instantly, is a single file that needs nothing else installed, and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows. Many of the popular modern terminal tools are written in Rust: ripgrep (search), fd (find files), bat (show files), eza (list files), and uv and ruff for Python.

In chapter 23 you parsed arguments by hand. That works for two switches. Real tools have dozens of options, need help texts and error messages, and should behave the way users expect. The crate clap (“command line argument parser”) does all of that from a description of your options.

The parts of a command line

  • An argument (or positional argument) is identified by its position: "call Sara".
  • An option has a name and a value: --priority high. Most have a long form (--priority) and a short one (-p).
  • A flag is an option without a value. It is either there or not: --all.
  • A subcommand selects one of several operations, each with its own arguments: git commit, cargo build, todo add.

Conventions that users rely on, and that clap gives you by default:

  • --help and -h print help. --version and -V print the version.
  • Short flags can be combined: -av means -a -v.
  • -- ends the options. Everything after it is an argument, even if it starts with a dash.
  • Results go to standard output, messages and errors to standard error.
  • The exit code is 0 for success, and something else for failure.

A first program with clap

You describe the command line as a struct. Each field is one argument:

How the struct turns into a command line:

FieldBecomes
name: String (no attribute)a required positional argument
#[arg(short, long)] loud: boola flag -l / --loud. False unless given
#[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)] count: u8an option -c / --count with a value. The text is converted to u8, and anything else is an error
#[arg(long)] title: Option<String>an optional option. None if absent
files: Vec<String>any number of values
the /// commentsthe help texts

Args::parse() reads the real command line. If something is wrong, it prints an error with a usage hint and ends the program with exit code 2. If --help is given, it prints the help and exits. Your code only ever sees a valid, typed Args value. This is “parse, don’t validate” once more, done by a library.

Args::try_parse_from(list) does the same for a list of strings and returns a Result. It is the key to testing a command-line definition, and this chapter uses it to make the examples repeatable.

More control

  • An enum with #[derive(ValueEnum)] becomes an option with a fixed set of values. The help lists them, and a wrong value is rejected with the list.
  • value_parser!(u32).range(1..=10_000) restricts a number to a range.
  • ArgAction::Count counts how often a flag is given: -v, -vv, -vvv.
  • A type that implements FromStr can be used directly as a field type, such as the Minutes of chapter 29.
  • The whole help text at the end was generated from the struct and its comments.

The project: a to-do tool

You will now rebuild the to-do list of chapter 16 as a proper command-line tool. Each call does one thing and ends, and the tasks are kept in a JSON file between calls:

Step 0: plan

The design follows the pattern of all the projects so far:

  1. The command line is described by types. clap turns the arguments into a Cli value.
  2. The data is a TodoList that Serde reads from and writes to a JSON file.
  3. The logic is one function, run(command, &mut list), that changes the list and returns the text to print. It reads no files and prints nothing, so it is easy to test.
  4. main connects the three: parse, load, run, save, print, and choose the exit code.

Step 1: describe the command line

Subcommands are an enum. Each variant is one subcommand, and its fields are that subcommand’s arguments. It is the same Command enum as in chapter 16. There you wrote the function that turns text into the enum. Here clap generates it.

  • #[command(version, about)] takes the version number from Cargo.toml and the description from the /// comment.
  • global = true lets --file be written before or after the subcommand.
  • PathBuf is the owned type for file paths.

With no further work, the tool has help for itself and for every subcommand:

Step 2: the data and its file

Priority shows how well the ecosystem fits together: one enum derives ValueEnum for clap and Serialize/Deserialize for Serde. It is a command-line option and a JSON value at once. It also derives Ord. Enum variants are ordered as they are written, so Low < Normal < High.

  • load treats a missing file as an empty list. The first todo add then just works.
  • Result here is anyhow::Result. with_context on an Option (as in find) turns None into an error with that message.
  • The next id is one more than the largest id in use, so an id is never given out twice while its task exists.

Step 3: the logic

run returns two things: the text for the user, and whether the list was changed, so that main knows whether to save. The sorting key is a tuple, which is compared part by part: open tasks before finished ones, then the highest priority first (Reverse turns that part around), then by id.

Step 4: main, errors and exit codes

main returns an ExitCode. That is tidier than process::exit, because the program ends in the normal way and all values are dropped properly. The real work is in try_main, where ? can be used freely. Every error ends up in one place, is printed to standard error with its chain of causes ({error:#}), and gives exit code 1.

The first error comes from your code. The other two come from clap, which exits with code 2 for a wrong command line. (echo $? shows the exit code of the last command in most shells.)

Step 5: tests

Since run takes a Command and a list, and returns text, the tests need no files and no processes. Cli::try_parse_from lets them start from the words a user would type:

The first test is a gift from clap: debug_assert checks the whole definition for mistakes such as two options with the same short letter. Without it, such a mistake would only show when a user runs the program.

To test the finished program from outside, with a real file and real exit codes, the crate assert_cmd runs the compiled binary inside a test:

The complete program

Install it with cargo install --path ., and todo is available in every folder.

Good manners for command-line tools

  • Be quiet when things go well, and clear when they do not. Say what failed, with which file, and if possible what to do about it.
  • Work in pipelines. Read from standard input when no file is given, and write plain results to standard output, so that the tool can be combined with others: cat notes.txt | mytool | sort.
  • Do not decorate output that is not going to a person. std::io::IsTerminal tells you whether standard output is a terminal or a pipe. Colours and progress bars belong only on a terminal.
  • Offer machine-readable output, such as --json, when other programs may want to read the result.
  • Never lose data. Ask before destructive actions, or offer --dry-run, which shows what would happen.
  • Follow the conventions for --help, --version, --verbose, --quiet and exit codes.

(The example was run here without a terminal and with empty input.)

When the reader leaves early

Try any program that prints many lines with println!, and cut its output short: mytool | head -2. head reads two lines and ends. The next println! has nobody to write to, and it panics:

A user who only asked for the first two lines should not see a crash. A tool that prints a lot writes with writeln!, which returns the error as a value, and treats a closed pipe as a normal end:

Locking standard output once, as this program does, also makes the writing faster (chapter 52).

The other early exit is the one the user asks for: Ctrl+C. By default it kills the program where it stands, which is fine for a tool that only prints, and wrong for one that is holding a lock file, a temporary file or a half-written download. Handle the interrupt and tidy up:

  • In an async program, tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await is one line in a select! next to the real work; the server chapters use it for a graceful shutdown.
  • In a synchronous program, the crate ctrlc installs a handler that runs your closure.
  • Exit with code 130 (128 + SIGINT), so scripts and shells know the program was interrupted rather than failed. A Drop guard that removes the temporary file is often all the tidy-up you need.

A program that ignores Ctrl+C entirely, or that swallows it and keeps working, is worse than one that dies: the user’s only remaining option is kill -9, which leaves the mess behind.

Running other programs

Command-line tools often start other tools: a compiler, git, an editor. std::process::Command does that:

  • Three ways to start. output() waits and collects everything the program printed. status() waits and lets the program use your terminal directly. spawn() returns at once with a Child that you can talk to and wait for later.
  • A failing program is not an Err. An Err means that the program could not be started at all. If it started and failed, you get Ok with an exit code other than 0. Check status.success() every time.
  • Arguments are passed one by one, with arg or args. No shell is involved, so a file name with spaces or with a ; in it is passed on exactly as it is. Do not build one long command string and hand it to sh -c. With text from a user, that is the same mistake as building SQL from input (chapter 47).
  • Close the input when you are done. sort waits for the end of its input. Dropping the handle closes the pipe.

Configuration files and precedence

Well-behaved command-line tools combine three sources in a predictable order, where each layer overrides the one below it:

  1. Built-in defaults (for example, color = "auto").
  2. User configuration file in the operating system’s standard folder—found portably with directories::ProjectDirs::from("", "", "myapp") (~/.config/myapp/config.toml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/… on macOS, %APPDATA% on Windows).
  3. Environment variables (with clap’s #[arg(env = "MYAPP_FORMAT")]).
  4. Command-line flags (--format json), which always win for a single invocation.

See chapter 46 for layered configuration with figment and protecting secret settings with secrecy.

More crates for the terminal

CratePurpose
clap_completegenerate tab-completion scripts for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell
indicatifprogress bars and spinners
owo-colors, colored, anstylecoloured text
dialoguer, inquirequestions, menus and password prompts
ratatui with crosstermfull-screen terminal interfaces
comfy-table, tabledtables
directoriesthe right folders for configuration and data on each system
assert_cmd, predicates, trycmdtesting command-line programs
cargo-distbuild and publish installers for all platforms

Tab completion and man pages

A tool that people use daily should complete its own arguments. clap knows the whole grammar already, so clap_complete turns that structure into a completion script for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell — no second definition to keep in sync. The usual pattern is a hidden subcommand that writes the script to standard output:

clap_complete::generate takes the shell, the command definition (Cli::command()), the program name and any Write — usually std::io::stdout() — and writes the script there. Wire it to a hidden completions <shell> subcommand, so the script is produced by the binary itself and can never drift out of step with the parser.

The user then installs it once:

Keep the subcommand #[command(hide = true)]: it is plumbing, not a feature to advertise in --help. The same idea for documentation: clap_mangen renders the same definition as a man page, so todo completions and man todo describe exactly what the program accepts. Distributions that package your tool will ask for both.

Full-screen interfaces

Some programs are not a command that prints and exits but a place you stay in: a log viewer, a file browser, a dashboard, a mail client. They need the whole terminal — a fixed layout, panels that update independently, keys that act on a selection.

ratatui is the standard crate for this, with crossterm underneath it for the terminal itself. Its model is immediate mode, and that phrase is the whole idea: you do not build a widget tree once and mutate it. On every tick — say thirty times a second — you describe the entire screen from your current state, and the library redraws it. There is no hidden state to fall out of sync with your data, and no callbacks:

In outline the loop is four steps: terminal.draw(|frame| render(frame, &app))? to describe the whole screen, one blocking read of a key, app.on_key(key) to change the state, and a break when the state says the user asked to quit. Everything the program knows lives in app; the screen is a function of it.

Three things are different from a program that prints:

  • The terminal becomes state you borrowed. You enter raw mode and the alternate screen, and you must leave them again — including when the program panics. A terminal left in raw mode with no cursor is a support call. ratatui’s examples show the restore-on-panic hook; copy it.
  • Layout is code. You split the screen into rectangles with constraints (Length(3), Percentage(40), Min(10)), and each widget draws into its rectangle.
  • Test the logic, not the pixels. Keep the application state and the key handling in plain structs with plain methods, tested as in chapter 22. The drawing function is then the only part you cannot unit-test, and it should contain no decisions.

Which crate for which job, in one table:

JobCrateExample
Show progress on a long taskindicatifa download bar, a spinner during a build
Ask a question and read an answerdialoguer, inquirea menu, a confirmation, a password prompt
Print an aligned table and exitcomfy-table, tabledtodo list
Own the screen and stay runningratatui + crossterma dashboard, a file browser, a TUI client

Start with the first three. Reach for ratatui when you notice that you are clearing the screen and reprinting it yourself.

Questions and progress: dialoguer and indicatif

clap parses what the user types. Two crates handle the rest of a pleasant terminal program: asking questions, and showing that work is under way.

dialoguer shows prompts: confirm (yes or no), input (free text), password (hidden keystrokes), select (a menu), multi-select. It reads the keyboard directly, so it needs a real terminal — run these programs yourself; they do not work in the playground or when standard input is piped.

A small interview:

A typical run looks like this (your terminal may show colours):

The returned values are ordinary Rust values: a String, the index of the chosen item, a bool. Validate them afterward (if name.is_empty() { ... }) just as you would with clap.

indicatif draws progress bars and spinners for work that takes seconds or minutes. It writes to standard output, so a well-behaved tool checks std::io::stdout().is_terminal() and stays quiet when its output is piped (“When the reader leaves early”, above):

A run prints something like:

  • ProgressBar::new(100) declares the total; inc(1) advances it by one.
  • The template controls what is shown: a spinner, elapsed time, the bar, position, total and the estimated time left.
  • finish_with_message replaces the bar with a final line, so the screen never ends on a half-drawn bar.
CrateUse it for
dialoguerquestions, menus, passwords — anything the user must answer while the program runs
indicatifprogress bars and spinners for long work
clap_completetab completion for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell
owo-colors, anstylecoloured text on a terminal

A progress bar piped into a file fills it with escape sequences. Check is_terminal, or offer a --quiet flag.

Make it better

PracticeEdit a task

Add a subcommand todo edit <id> <new title> that changes the title of a task.

Need a hint?

Add a variant Edit { id: u32, title: String } to Command, with /// comments for the help. The compiler then demands a new arm in run. Reuse list.find(id)? and the empty-title check.

Show solution and explanation

Adding the variant was enough to get the argument parsing, the help entry and the error messages. The only code to write was the behaviour. The empty-title check now exists twice, which is a hint to move it into a small function, or into a Title newtype that cannot be empty.

PracticeOutput for machines

Add a flag --json to the list subcommand. With it, the shown tasks are printed as JSON, so that other programs can read them.

Need a hint?

Add #[arg(long)] json: bool to the List variant. In run, after filtering and sorting, return serde_json::to_string_pretty(&shown)? when the flag is set. A Vec<&Task> can be serialised, because Serde implements Serialize for references and vectors.

Show solution and explanation

With JSON output, the tool can be combined with others: a script can read the list, and a tool such as jq can filter it. The empty case now prints [], which is valid JSON, and not the sentence “Nothing to do.”, which would break a program reading the output. Human-readable and machine-readable output have different rules, and good tools offer both.

ChallengeDue dates

Add an optional due date to tasks: todo add "pay rent" --due 2027-01-31. Show the date in the list, and add a flag todo list --overdue that shows only open tasks whose date has passed. Old files without the field must still load.

Need a hint?

Add chrono with its serde feature: cargo add chrono --features serde. NaiveDate implements FromStr and Serde’s traits, so it can be the type of the clap option and of the struct field: due: Option<NaiveDate>. Put #[serde(default)] on the field. For “today”, do not call the clock inside run. Pass today: NaiveDate in as a parameter, so that the tests can choose the date.

Show solution and explanation

A wrong date such as --due 2027-02-30 is rejected by clap with a message from chrono, before your code runs: the field’s type does the validation. The date travels through three layers without any conversion code of your own: clap parses it with FromStr, Serde stores it as "2027-01-31", and chrono compares it.

Passing today into run keeps the logic free of the system clock. The test decides that it is the first of February 2027, and gives the same result on every day it runs. #[serde(default)] keeps old files readable, and skip_serializing_if keeps the file free of "due": null lines.

Configuration: where values come from

A program that hard-codes its path, port or API key has to be rebuilt for every machine it runs on. A program that reads everything from the environment is untestable and unpleasant to use. The good answer is a layered one: every setting can come from several places, and the closest-to-the-user source wins.

The precedence chain, which is the same in almost every well-built tool:

The order is not arbitrary. A flag is chosen by the person running the command now, so it must win. An environment variable is set by whoever deployed this instance. A file is a shared, versioned configuration. A default is the author’s guess. Each layer overrides the one after it, and every setting has a default, so a program with no configuration at all still starts.

A file, with defaults

Environment variables that override it

Two conventions make this pleasant. Prefix everything (TDL_), so the program’s variables cannot collide with the hundreds of others in the environment. And parse once, at start-up, into one typed struct, using serde and its #[serde(default)] attribute: the file and the environment are merged into a Config, and the rest of the program never looks at an environment variable again. A mistyped port then fails immediately with a clear message instead of at the first request.

The crates for the layering are:

CrateWhat it addsWhen to choose it
figmentMerge several sources (TOML file, environment with a prefix, defaults) into one serde struct, with a report of where each value came fromThe layering above, without writing it yourself. The usual choice in Axum applications
configThe same idea with more file formats (JSON, YAML, RON) and a different APIYou need YAML or a watching file
dotenvy (successor to dotenv)Loads a .env file into the environment for developmentLocal work only. Never ship a .env; add it to .gitignore and commit a .env.example with the keys and no values
secrecyA SecretString wrapper that prints as [REDACTED], is zeroed on drop, and must be unwrapped explicitlySettings that are secret, so a Debug print or a log line cannot leak them
humantimeParses "30s", "5m", "2h" into a DurationTimeouts, intervals, retention periods
Tip
Print the resolved configuration at start-up, with the secrets redacted

One INFO line at start-up that shows every setting and where it came from turns “it works on my machine” into a five-second diagnosis. With secrecy, the parts that must not be seen print themselves as [REDACTED], so the log line is safe to keep.

Watch out
An environment variable is not a secret store

Environment variables are visible to anything that can read the process — a crash dump, a debugging endpoint, /proc, a child process. They are the conventional way to pass configuration, not a way to protect it. For real secrets use the host’s secret store: Docker secrets, Kubernetes Secret objects, or the secret manager of your cloud. In particular, never bake a secret into a Docker image: image layers are readable for ever by anyone who can pull it, even if a later layer deletes the file. Pass secrets at run time, and rotate them.

This is what the twelve-factor app means by “config in the environment”. The name comes from 12factor.net, and the rule is about one idea: the same artefact, built once, runs in every environment, and only its configuration differs. Chapter 48 shows the same chain implemented for a web service in a few dozen lines, without a crate.

What you have learned

Recap
  • A command line consists of arguments, options, flags and subcommands. Users expect --help, --version, sensible errors and exit codes.
  • With clap’s derive, a struct describes the command line, and an enum describes the subcommands. Help, validation and error messages are generated.
  • Cli::parse() gives a typed value, or explains the problem and exits. try_parse_from does the same for tests.
  • The same enum can serve clap (ValueEnum) and Serde.
  • Keep the logic in a function that takes the parsed command and returns the output. main loads, calls, saves, prints and sets the exit code.
  • Send results to standard output and errors to standard error, and work well in pipelines.

Concurrency in practice: Rayon, Tokio, streams, HTTP clients and tower

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Use all processor cores for a computation with Rayon
  • Set up a Tokio runtime, run heavy work beside it, and shut it down cleanly
  • Process values that arrive over time with streams
  • Call web APIs with async reqwest or blocking ureq
  • Add timeouts and limits with tower layers

Part 7 explained the machinery of concurrency: threads, locks, channels and async tasks. In daily work you rarely build on that machinery directly. A handful of crates package the common patterns, and this chapter is a tour of them.

The workThe toolWhy
A calculation over a large collectionRayonsplits the work over all cores, with one changed word
Many things that mostly wait: connections, requests, timersTokiothousands of tasks on a few threads
A sequence of values that arrive over timestreamsiterators for async code
Calling a web APIreqwestan HTTP client
Timeouts, limits, retries, logging around a servicetowerreusable layers
A few long-running background jobsplain threads and channelssimple, and no crate is needed

Rayon: all cores for one calculation

Real-world analogy
A team of movers

Four movers empty a lorry. Each one gets a quarter of the boxes. One of them has only light boxes and is finished early. A good mover does not sit down then: he walks over to a colleague who is behind, and takes boxes from the far end of that pile. Nobody plans this in advance, and still everyone is busy until the lorry is empty. Rayon’s worker threads behave this way. The technique is called work stealing.

Rayon gives data parallelism: the same operation is applied to many pieces of data, on all cores at once. Its main idea is the parallel iterator. You write an iterator chain as in chapter 25, and replace iter() by par_iter():

  • use rayon::prelude::*; brings the parallel methods into scope.
  • par_iter() borrows the items, par_iter_mut() borrows them mutably, and into_par_iter() takes them. These are the three familiar forms, with par_ in front. Ranges, vectors, slices, hash maps and strings all have them.
  • Rayon starts one worker thread per core, once, and reuses them for every parallel operation in the program. You never create or join a thread.
  • collect on a parallel iterator keeps the order of the input, although the pieces are computed in any order.

How much faster?

In chapter 30 you counted the primes below three million with two hand-made threads. It took 0.51 seconds on one thread and 0.32 seconds on two, because the upper half of the numbers is more work than the lower half. With Rayon, the whole program is this line:

On the same two-core machine it takes 0.25 seconds: twice as fast as one thread, and faster than the hand-made version. The reason is work stealing. Rayon does not cut the range into two fixed halves. It keeps splitting it into smaller pieces, and a thread that runs out of work takes pieces from the other one. Uneven work is balanced without any planning.

More parallel tools

MethodPurpose
map, filter, flat_map, sum, count, min, max, collectas on ordinary iterators
for_eachrun a closure for every item. The order is not defined
any, all, find_any, find_firstsearching. find_any returns whichever match is found first in time, find_first the first in order
par_sort, par_sort_unstable, par_sort_by_keysorting a slice
par_chunks(n), par_chunks_mut(n)work on pieces of n items, such as the rows of an image
fold + reducebuild a partial result per thread, then merge the partial results
par_bridge()turn any ordinary iterator into a parallel one
rayon::join(a, b)run two closures, possibly at the same time

In a parallel fold, every thread builds its own map without any locking. reduce then merges the maps in pairs. This “split, work alone, merge” pattern is much faster than one shared map behind a Mutex.

The compiler still watches

Parallel code in most languages is risky, because nothing stops two threads from changing the same variable. In Rust the same rules as always apply. This attempt to add numbers into a shared variable is rejected:

Rayon’s for_each asks for a closure that is Fn + Sync + Send: one that several threads may call at the same moment. A closure that changes a captured variable is FnMut, so it does not qualify. The data race is caught before the program exists. The fixes are the ones you know: let Rayon combine the values (.sum()), or use an atomic or a Mutex.

This is what “fearless concurrency” means in practice. You can change iter to par_iter in a large program, and if it compiles, it has no data race.

Divide and conquer with join

rayon::join runs two closures and returns both results. If another core is free, they run at the same time. Used inside a recursive function, it spreads a problem over all cores:

The two closures borrow left and right from the caller. That is allowed because join returns only when both are finished, as with scoped threads. Below 1,000 items the function stops splitting, because handing out very small pieces costs more than computing them.

Dynamic scoped tasks with rayon::scope

rayon::join runs two tasks. When the number of parallel pieces is known only at run time (for example, traversing a tree or updating chunks of a slice) and those tasks need to borrow local data, use rayon::scope:

Like std::thread::scope, rayon::scope guarantees every task spawned inside finishes before scope returns—so closures can hold short-lived & and disjoint &mut borrows safely without 'static bounds or Arc.

When Rayon does not help

  • Small jobs. Handing work to other threads costs time. Measured on the test machine: adding up 1,000 numbers, repeated 1,000 times, took 0.05 milliseconds with iter() and 20 milliseconds with par_iter(). That is 400 times slower. Parallelism pays when each call has real work to do: roughly, when the sequential version takes at least a tenth of a millisecond.
  • Waiting. Rayon’s threads are meant for computing. Tasks that wait for the network or the disk belong to Tokio. A waiting task would block one of Rayon’s few threads.
  • Work that depends on order. for_each runs in any order. If you print inside it, the lines come out mixed.
  • Already parallel code. If the outer loop is parallel, a parallel inner loop adds little.

So measure before and after, with --release.

Tokio in practice

Chapter 32 introduced async programming with Tokio: tasks, join!, select!, channels and timeouts. Here are three things that every real service needs in addition.

Choosing and building the runtime

#[tokio::main] creates a runtime with one worker thread per core. The attribute takes options, and a runtime can also be built by hand:

FormMeaning
#[tokio::main]multi-threaded runtime, one worker per core
#[tokio::main(worker_threads = 4)]a fixed number of workers
#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]everything on the calling thread. Good for small tools and for tests
Builder::new_multi_thread()…build()by hand, for full control
runtime.block_on(future)run a future to completion from ordinary, non-async code

block_on is the bridge from synchronous code into async code. A program that is mostly synchronous can keep a runtime in a variable and call block_on where it needs an async library.

Three async runtimes

Tokio is the runtime you will meet most often, but it is not the only one:

Tokioasync-stdsmol
APIits own types (tokio::spawn, tokio::time::sleep)deliberately similar to std (async_std::task::spawn, async_std::stream)small and explicit (smol::scale, your own Executor)
How it starts#[tokio::main] or a Runtime you build#[async_std::main]smol::run(async { … })
Ecosystemthe largest: Axum, reqwest, SQLx, tower all assume Tokiosmallersmallest
Best fitweb services and most async programscode that should read like stdtiny binaries and constrained devices

All three run many tasks on a few threads, and all three follow the same golden rule: never block a worker thread. Tokio is the default choice because nearly every async crate is tested with it first.

Heavy work beside async tasks

The golden rule of chapter 32 was: never block the runtime. A calculation that takes 50 milliseconds holds up every other task on that worker thread. There are two ways to move it out of the way:

  • spawn_blocking is for code that blocks: a slow calculation, a synchronous library, a file operation. Tokio runs it on a separate pool of threads.
  • For work that should use all cores, start it with rayon::spawn and send the result back through a oneshot channel, which carries exactly one value. Awaiting the receiver does not block anything.

The two runtimes then work side by side: Tokio’s threads handle the waiting, and Rayon’s threads handle the computing.

Shutting down cleanly

A server should not simply vanish when it is stopped. It should stop accepting new work, let running requests finish, save what must be saved, and then end. This is called a graceful shutdown. The crate tokio-util has two helpers for it:

  • A CancellationToken is a signal that can be cloned and handed to every task. cancel() sets it, and cancelled().await completes when it is set. Each task checks it in a select!, next to its normal work.
  • A TaskTracker remembers the tasks it spawned. close() followed by wait().await waits until all of them have returned.

The pattern is always the same: wait for the stop signal, cancel the token, wait for the tasks, and add a time limit in case one of them hangs.

More of Tokio

PartContents
tokio::fsasync versions of the file functions
tokio::processstart other programs and talk to them
tokio::signalCtrl+C and other signals from the operating system
tokio::timesleep, timeout, interval (a tick every so often), Instant
tokio::syncmpsc, oneshot, broadcast, watch (the latest value of something), Mutex, RwLock, Semaphore, Notify, OnceCell
tokio::taskspawn, spawn_blocking, JoinSet, yield_now, LocalSet (for futures that are not Send)
tokio::ioBufReader, copy, split, and duplex (a connection in memory, for tests)
tokio-utilcancellation tokens, task trackers, and codecs that cut a byte stream into messages
tokio-consolea live view of all the tasks in a running program

Streams: values that arrive over time

An iterator hands out values that are already there. A stream hands out values that arrive over time: messages from a connection, rows from a database, ticks of a timer. Getting the next value is something you await.

IteratorStream
The next valueiterator.next()stream.next().await
The loopfor x in iteratorwhile let Some(x) = stream.next().await
Traitstd::iter::Iteratorfutures::Stream
Adaptorsmap, filter, take, …the same, from StreamExt

The standard library has no stable stream trait yet (as of Rust 1.100), so streams come from the crate futures, with helpers in tokio-stream:

  • use futures::stream::StreamExt; provides next and the adaptors, as Iterator does for iterators.
  • There is no for loop for streams yet. while let Some(item) = stream.next().await takes its place.
  • Some adaptors of futures expect a closure that returns a future. For a plain test, std::future::ready(value) wraps a value into a future that is finished at once. That explains the filter line.

Many at a time, but not too many

The most useful stream tool controls how many async operations run at the same time. map turns each item into a future, and buffer_unordered(n) runs up to n of those futures at once:

AdaptorBehaviour
.then(f)one at a time, in order
.map(f).buffered(n)up to n at a time. Results in the order of the input
.map(f).buffer_unordered(n)up to n at a time. Results as soon as each is ready
.for_each_concurrent(n, f)run f for each item, up to n at a time, with no results

Why limit at all? Ten thousand downloads at once would overload your network, the other server, or the limit on open files. A limit of some tens keeps the speed and stays polite.

FuturesUnordered and custom Streams

When you want to poll a dynamic set of futures inside the current task—without spawning them onto Tokio (so they can borrow local variables and do not even need to be Send)—reach for FuturesUnordered from futures::stream:

Choose between the three dynamic concurrency tools like this:

ToolRuns whereBounds requiredCancellation on drop
tokio::task::JoinSetSpawned across Tokio worker threadsFutures must be Send + 'staticAborts all spawned tasks when dropped
FuturesUnorderedPolled cooperatively inside the current taskCan borrow local data; no Send neededDrops all inner futures when dropped
.map(f).buffer_unordered(n)Polled inside the current task with concurrency cap nDriven lazily as you pull from the streamStops polling remaining items when dropped

You can also implement futures::Stream on your own wrapper type by projecting Pin<&mut Self> with pin-project-lite (chapter 32):

Channels and timers as streams

tokio-stream wraps Tokio’s types as streams, so that the adaptors work on them:

tokio_stream::StreamExt is a second trait with the same name as the one in futures. Its filter takes a plain closure. Import one of the two in a file, not both, or the compiler will complain that method names are ambiguous.

reqwest: calling web APIs

Programs talk to web services through HTTP, the protocol of the web. The idea is simple:

  • The client sends a request: a method (GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to change, DELETE to remove), a URL, some headers (extra information as name–value pairs), and sometimes a body (the data).
  • The server returns a response: a status code (200 means OK, 404 means not found, 500 means the server failed), headers, and a body.

Most web APIs send and expect JSON bodies. An HTTP client is a library that sends requests. In Rust the standard choice is reqwest. It builds on Tokio and works with Serde.

A practice server

The examples need a server to talk to. So that they work without an internet connection and always give the same answers, each example starts a tiny server inside the same program, with the function below. It uses Axum, which is the subject of the next chapter, so there is no need to understand it yet. In the examples that follow, this function is part of the program but is not printed again.

It answers at /hello with a text, at /users/1 and /users/2 with a user as JSON, at /numbers/<n> with a number, and at /slow only after two seconds. With a real service, base would be an address such as https://api.example.com.

A first request

There are two awaits. The first waits for the status and the headers. The second, in text(), waits for the body, which may be large and arrive later.

JSON in both directions

  • A Client keeps connections open and reuses them. Create one for the whole program and share it. It is cheap to clone, because it holds an Arc inside.
  • A request is built step by step: client.get(url) or .post(url), then optional parts, then .send().await.
  • .json(&value) serialises a value as the request body. response.json::<T>().await deserialises the response body. Both use Serde.
Builder methodAdds
.header("X-Api-Key", "…")a header
.bearer_auth(token)a login token in the Authorization header
.query(&[("page", "2")])parameters at the end of the URL: ?page=2
.json(&value)a JSON body
.form(&value)a body in the format of web forms
.body(text_or_bytes)a raw body
.timeout(duration)a time limit for this request

What can go wrong

Watch out
A 404 is not an Err

send() returns Ok whenever the server answered at all, even with “404 Not Found” or “500 Internal Server Error”. Check response.status(), or call .error_for_status()?, which turns error statuses into an Err. Forgetting this is the most common mistake with HTTP clients.

Watch out
Always set a timeout

reqwest has no time limit by default. A request to a server that never answers waits for ever, and so does your task. Set .timeout(…) on the client.

A smaller client: ureq

reqwest is powerful, and it needs Tokio. A script or a command-line tool often does not want an async runtime at all. ureq is a minimal, blocking HTTP client: one call does the whole request and waits for the answer.

A tiny server and a client that talks to it, all in one program:

  • .call() performs the request and waits. No async, no await, no runtime.
  • response.status() is the status code, and into_body().read_to_string() reads the whole body as text.
  • timeout_global sets an upper bound: a server that never answers does not wait forever. In ureq 3, set it with .config().timeout_global(Some(duration)).build().
  • Other builders: .header("header", "value") for headers, .send_json(&value) for a JSON body, and ureq::Agent to reuse connections across many requests (the equivalent of reqwest’s Client).
reqwestureq
Asyncyes, on Tokiono
Best fitservices, many requests at oncescripts and command-line tools

Choose reqwest for a server or for many requests at once; choose ureq when a small dependency and no runtime matter more.

Many requests at once

Streams and reqwest together give the standard recipe for calling an API many times: a limited number of requests in flight, and a time limit for each.

The practice server answers number 5 only after two seconds, and number 7 with an error. Each result is kept together with its id, so one failure does not hide the other answers. This is the same idea as in chapter 25: decide per item what an error means.

Good to know
Encrypted connections

An address that starts with https:// is encrypted with TLS. reqwest handles this for you. In version 0.13 it uses rustls by default, a TLS library written in Rust, so that no system library has to be installed. For a small script that needs no async code, reqwest::blocking offers the same API without await (enable the feature blocking). The crate ureq is a smaller, blocking alternative.

ureq: a synchronous HTTP client

Choose ureq when a command-line program makes a few HTTP calls and a blocking request is simpler than introducing an async runtime. It is not a faster way to make many concurrent requests: while a call waits, its current thread is blocked. Its Agent owns reusable client configuration and a connection pool; borrow one agent across calls instead of rebuilding a client each time.

call() and body reading both return errors, so ? reports connection, protocol and I/O failures. Check the returned status before treating a body as successful application data; an HTTP response such as 404 is not the same kind of failure as a DNS or TLS error. Configure request timeouts and response-size limits for the service you call. In an async Tokio handler, do not call this blocking client directly on an executor thread; use async reqwest or deliberately isolate blocking work with spawn_blocking.

tower: layers around a service

A request should have a time limit. There should not be too many at once. Each one should be logged. Failed ones might be retried. These wishes are the same for every server and every client, whatever the request means. tower is the crate that lets such behaviour be written once and reused everywhere.

Real-world analogy
An onion

A tower service is built like an onion. In the middle is your own code. Around it are layers: one checks the time, one counts, one writes the log. A request passes through the layers from the outside to the middle, and the response travels back out through the same layers. Each layer can change the request, refuse it, or act on the response.

Two ideas are enough:

  • A Service is an async function with a name: it takes a request and returns a future of Result<Response, Error>.
  • A Layer wraps a service and gives back a new service. Code that sits in the path of every request like this is called middleware.
  • ServiceBuilder stacks layers. The first one listed is the outermost.
  • service_fn turns an async function into a service.
  • service.ready().await? waits until the service can take a request (the concurrency limit may make it wait), and .call(request) sends it.
  • The function lookup knows nothing about timeouts or limits. The layers add them from outside.
LayerEffect
timeoutfail a request that takes too long
concurrency_limitat most n requests at the same time. The others wait
rate_limitat most n requests per period
load_shedrefuse at once when the service is busy, without waiting
retryrepeat failed requests, by a policy you define
bufferput a queue in front of the service, so that it can be shared

The crate tower-http adds layers that understand HTTP: request logging (TraceLayer), compression, CORS headers, limits on body size, time limits, and serving files. In the next chapter you will add them to a web server with one line each.

The real value of tower is that the ecosystem agrees on it. The web framework Axum, the gRPC library tonic and the HTTP library hyper all speak in tower services. A layer written once works with all of them, for servers and for clients.

How a layer is built

You will rarely write a layer yourself. Seeing one removes the mystery. This layer counts the requests that pass through:

The Service trait has two methods. poll_ready says whether the service can accept a request now. call takes the request and returns a future. Count<S> is generic over the inner service S, so it wraps any service at all. That is all there is to middleware: a struct that holds the next service, does something, and passes the request on. For simple cases, Axum offers a shorter way with an async function, as the next chapter shows.

gRPC services with tonic

Between internal backend services, HTTP + JSON is sometimes slower or looser than you want: every field name is repeated as text on the wire, and clients and servers only discover schema mismatches when parsing fails. gRPC solves both with Protocol Buffers (.proto schemas) over HTTP/2: compact binary frames, generated client and server structs in Rust, and bidirectional streaming built in.

In Rust, tonic (built on Tokio, Hyper, and Tower) is the standard gRPC crate, paired with prost and tonic-build:

Because tonic runs on tower, timeouts, concurrency limits, and request-ID / OpenTelemetry layers attach to a gRPC server the exact same way as to Axum. Choose REST/JSON for public browser APIs and simple integrations; choose gRPC (tonic) for high-throughput internal service-to-service contracts and streaming RPCs.

Watching a service in production: logs, metrics and traces

A program that works on your laptop is half of the job. In production nobody can attach a debugger to the machine that is failing, and the failure happens at three in the morning. What you have instead are three kinds of signal that the program emits while it runs. Between them they answer almost every question you will ever ask about a service.

SignalThe question it answersSizeAn example
LogsWhat exactly happened in this one event?Grows with traffic: one line per interesting thingorder 8123 rejected: card declined
MetricsHow much, how fast, how often — as numbers over timeTiny and constant per serieshttp_requests_total{route="/notes",status="500"} 12
TracesWhere did this request spend its time, and in which service?Sampled, so a fraction of requestsa tree of spans: GET /notes → db.query → redis.get

They are not alternatives. Metrics tell you that something is wrong; traces tell you where; logs tell you why. A service with only logs is expensive to search and blind to trends. A service with only metrics tells you the error rate is up but not which request failed.

Logs that a machine can search

println! is fine for a program you run yourself and useless for a service. The difference is structure: instead of one sentence, emit one line of JSON per event, with the parts you will want to filter on as fields.

Any log system — Loki, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch, Datadog, jq on a file — can then answer “every request slower than 500 ms on /notes yesterday” without a regular expression written by hand. The message field stays human, the fields stay machine-readable.

In Rust the crate for this is tracing, which chapter 42 introduced: an event is a log line, a span is a named region of work with fields attached, and every event inside that region inherits them. It is the same crate for logs and traces, which is why the ecosystem settled on it. The subscriber decides the format:

  • tracing_subscriber::fmt() prints human-readable lines, as in chapter 48;
  • tracing_subscriber::fmt().json() prints one JSON object per line — the production format;
  • EnvFilter reads RUST_LOG, so you can raise the level of one dependency at run time without rebuilding: RUST_LOG=info,my_crate=debug,sqlx=warn.
Watch out
What never goes into a log

Never log a password, session cookie, Authorization header, API key, card number or full personal record. Logs are copied to other machines, indexed, kept for months, and read by people who are not you. Log an identifier and look the record up in the database instead. When you must log a value to debug it, log a hash or a prefix, and delete the line before merging.

Metrics: a few numbers that never grow

A metric is a number with a name and a set of labels, sampled over time. Three shapes cover almost everything:

KindWhat it doesRust typeExamples
CounterOnly goes up. Rate = per secondCounterhttp_requests_total, errors_total, jobs_processed_total
GaugeGoes up and downGaugequeue_depth, connections_open, cache_bytes
HistogramCounts observations in buckets, so you can compute quantilesHistogramhttp_request_duration_seconds

The labels are the powerful part, and also the trap: http_requests_total{route="/notes",status="500"} lets you ask for the error rate of one route. A label with unbounded values — a user id, a raw URL, an order number — creates a new time series for every value, and the monitoring system falls over. Keep labels to a handful of low-cardinality values (route not path, status not request id).

For a web service the four numbers worth having on day one are the RED set: Rate (requests per second), Errors (the proportion that failed), and Duration (the distribution, not the average).

Watch out
Never average a latency

The average request time hides the problem: with one 30-second request in a thousand fast ones, the average barely moves while one user waited half a minute. Store a histogram and look at the 99th percentile (p99) — the time within which 99% of requests finished. That is the number your users feel.

The facade is metrics: your code calls counter!, gauge! and histogram! once, and a recorder installed at start-up decides where the numbers go. The usual recorder for a service is metrics-exporter-prometheus, which keeps them in memory and serves the standard Prometheus text format from one route:

That text is what GET /metrics returns. Prometheus (or Grafana Agent, or VictoriaMetrics) scrapes it every fifteen seconds, and Grafana draws it. The prometheus crate is the alternative to the metrics facade when you want its client library directly; the metrics facade is the choice when a library needs to record something without forcing an exporter on its users.

Traces: one request, many services

A trace follows a single request through the system. Each step is a span: a name, a start, an end, and the parent span it belongs to. Collect them and you can see, for one slow checkout, that 900 ms of 1,000 were spent in one database query — which no amount of grep on log lines will tell you.

The vendor-neutral standard is OpenTelemetry (often shortened to OTel). The Rust crates are opentelemetry for the API and SDK, opentelemetry-otlp for the exporter, and tracing-opentelemetry to connect the two worlds: your tracing spans become OTel spans, so you instrument once and export anywhere. The exporter speaks OTLP to a collector — a sidecar or a service — which forwards to Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, or whatever the team already runs. That indirection is the point of the facade: you can change backend without touching a line of application code.

Practical rules that save hours:

  • Instrument spans, not log lines. A span for GET /notes, one for the database call inside it, one for the cache lookup. Field names come free, and the trace is assembled from the nesting.
  • Sample. Traces are bulky. Keep every request when the rate is low, a small percentage when it is high (head sampling in the SDK), and make sure errors are always kept.
  • Propagate the context. The trace id travels in a request header (traceparent) between services. That is what makes one trace span several processes instead of one.

Health and readiness

Two tiny endpoints, with different meanings, and both needed by every orchestrator:

RouteQuestionAnswerWhen it fails
GET /healthIs the process alive and serving HTTP?200 with {"status":"ok"}Restart me
GET /readyCan it do useful work right now?200 when dependencies answer, 503 otherwiseSend me no traffic yet

/health must not touch the database. A liveness probe that fails because the database is down will restart a healthy process in a loop and make the outage worse. /ready is where the dependency checks belong: it returns 503 while the connection pool is still connecting after start-up, so the load balancer holds traffic back. Chapter 48 already has the first of the two; in Kubernetes they are livenessProbe and readinessProbe, and the handler patterns are those of chapter 46.

Request ids: one string that makes support possible

Give every incoming request an id, put it in the log lines of that request, and return it in a response header such as x-request-id. Then a user can say “my request 8f3c1d0e failed” and you can find the three log lines and the trace in seconds. In Axum, tower-http provides SetRequestIdLayer and PropagateRequestIdLayer with MakeRequestUuid; if you prefer to write it, it is the same layer pattern as the timeout in the tower section above.

Looking at a running process

tokio-console attaches to a running Tokio program and shows every task: how long it has waited, what woke it, and which task is holding a thread and blocking everything else. It is the tool that finds “one task does blocking work” in minutes instead of days. It needs the console-subscriber crate and a rebuild with --cfg tokio_unstable.

Tip
Start with three lines of output

A brand-new service does not need a full observability stack. It needs: one structured log line per request, one counter of failures, and a /health route. Those three take an hour and cover most incidents. Add traces when there is more than one service, and dashboards when someone asks a question twice. For complete Rust code wiring tracing-subscriber JSON logs, OpenTelemetry OTLP export, metrics-exporter-prometheus, and /health/live vs /health/ready, see chapter 51.

More crates for networking

NeedCrates

gRPC (typed calls between services)tonic, with prost for Protocol Buffers
WebSockets (a lasting two-way connection)tokio-tungstenite. Axum has them built in

QUIC and HTTP/3quinn, h3

E-maillettre
DNShickory-resolver
