Databases: SQL with SQLx, Diesel and SeaORM

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain tables, rows, keys and the basic SQL statements
  • Query a database from Rust with SQLx and map rows to structs
  • Prevent SQL injection with bound parameters
  • Keep data consistent with transactions and row locking
  • Size connection pools, paginate with cursors and avoid N+1 queries
  • Manage the schema with migrations and check queries at compile time
  • Pair SQL with Redis caching, NoSQL or embedded key-value stores

So far, your programs kept their data in memory or in a file that they read and wrote as a whole. That stops working when the data grows, when several users change it at the same moment, or when you need questions answered such as “all orders of last month above 100 birr, by customer”. A database is a program made for exactly this: it stores data safely, finds it fast, and lets many clients work at once.

Real-world analogy
A library with a librarian

In a large library you do not walk along the shelves yourself. You hand the librarian a precise request: “all books by this author, newest first”. The librarian knows the catalogue, finds the books quickly, and makes sure that two readers never take the same copy home. A database is the library together with its librarian, and the language of the requests is called SQL.

Words first

  • A relational database stores data in tables. A table looks like a spreadsheet: every row is one thing (a book, a user), and every column is one property (title, year).
  • Each column has a type, such as integer or text, and may forbid empty values.
  • A primary key is a column whose value identifies a row, usually a number named id.
  • A foreign key is a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table. It links the two: an order belongs to a customer.
  • The set of tables and columns is the schema.
  • SQL (“structured query language”) is the language for defining tables and for reading and changing rows. One request in it is a query or statement.

Three database systems cover most uses:

SystemWhat it isTypical use
SQLitea library inside your program. The database is one fileapps, tools, embedded devices, small web sites, tests
PostgreSQLa server that many programs connect tothe default for web services
MySQL, MariaDBservers as wellwidespread in web hosting

This chapter uses SQLite, because there is nothing to install: the examples create a database in memory and run on the spot. Nearly everything carries over to PostgreSQL, and a table at the end lists the differences.

SQL in ten minutes

SQL reads almost like English. These statements are the core of it:

  • SELECT … FROM … WHERE … is the workhorse. * means all columns.
  • WHERE chooses the rows. Without it, UPDATE and DELETE affect every row.
  • NULL means “no value”. It is the database’s None. Test for it with IS NULL, not with =.
  • Text is written in single quotes. Keywords are written in capitals by convention.

You will meet JOIN, GROUP BY and transactions further down.

SQLx: SQL with Rust types

SQLx is a widely used SQL toolkit for async Rust. You write plain SQL, and SQLx sends it, fills in the parameters, and converts the rows into Rust values. It supports SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL.

The pieces:

  • A connection pool keeps a set of open connections to the database and lends one out for each query. Opening a connection is slow, so they are reused. Create one pool when the program starts, and share it. It is cheap to clone.
  • sqlx::query(sql) prepares a statement. .bind(value) supplies a value for the next ? in the SQL text.
  • .execute(&pool) runs a statement that returns no rows. Its result tells how many rows were changed.
  • sqlx::query_as(sql) converts each row into a struct that derives FromRow. The column names must match the field names. A column that may be NULL needs an Option field.
  • sqlx::query_scalar(sql) is for a single column.
MethodReturnsUse when
.execute(&pool)the number of changed rowsINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE
.fetch_all(&pool)Vec<T>a list of rows
.fetch_one(&pool)T. An error if there is no rowexactly one row must exist
.fetch_optional(&pool)Option<T>zero or one row: “find by id”
.fetch(&pool)a stream of rowsvery many rows, handled one at a time
SQLite typeRust type
INTEGERi64 (also i32, bool)
REALf64
TEXTString
BLOBVec<u8>
NULL allowedOption<T>
dates and timeschrono or time types, with the feature of the same name
JSONsqlx::types::Json<T>, with the feature json
Good to know
In memory and on disk

sqlite::memory: creates an empty database in memory. Each connection gets its own, which is why these examples limit the pool to one connection. For a database in a file, connect to sqlite://app.db, and use SqliteConnectOptions with create_if_missing(true) so that the file is created at the first start.

Never build SQL from input

The values in the examples went through bind, never into the SQL text. This is the most important rule of database programming. Here is what happens otherwise:

The attacker’s quote character ended the text value early, and the rest of the input became SQL: OR '1'='1' is true for every row, so every secret was returned. This attack is called SQL injection. For decades it has been among the most common causes of stolen data.

With bind, the SQL text and the values travel to the database separately. The input is only ever a value. It is compared with the names, matches none, and the query returns nothing.

SQLx goes one step further. It accepts only string literals as query text. Did you notice AssertSqlSafe in the wrong version? Without it, the example does not compile:

A query must be a &'static str, which in practice means a literal in your source code. A String built at run time is refused, unless you wrap it in AssertSqlSafe and so state that you have checked it. A security rule has become a type rule.

Queries that depend on the input

Sometimes the shape of a query varies: a search form with optional filters, or an insert of many rows. QueryBuilder assembles such a query from fixed pieces of SQL and bound values:

push adds SQL text that you wrote, and push_bind adds a ? together with its value. The printed SQL shows that no value ever enters the text. (WHERE 1 = 1 is a small trick: every further condition can then start with AND.)

Transactions: all or nothing

Some changes belong together. Moving money takes two updates: less on one account, more on the other. If the program stops between them, money has vanished. A transaction groups statements so that either all of them take effect, or none.

  • pool.begin() starts a transaction. Statements run on it with &mut *transaction in place of &pool.
  • commit() makes the changes permanent.
  • If the transaction value is dropped without a commit, everything is undone. This is called a rollback. An early return or a ? therefore cleans up by itself. It is RAII from chapter 12, applied to a database.
  • CHECK (cents >= 0) is a constraint: a rule that the database enforces for every row, whoever writes. Rules that must always hold belong into the schema, as the last line of defence.

Databases promise four properties for transactions, known as ACID: atomic (all or nothing), consistent (the rules hold afterwards), isolated (transactions running at the same time do not see each other’s half-done work), and durable (what is committed survives a crash).

Several tables: JOIN and GROUP BY

Real data lives in several tables that refer to each other. Each fact is stored once: the name of a product stands in the products table, and an order refers to it by id. A JOIN puts the rows that belong together side by side again, and GROUP BY summarises.

  • REFERENCES customers(id) declares a foreign key. The database can then refuse an order for a customer that does not exist.
  • JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id attaches to each order the customer row with the matching id. The short names o, c and p are aliases for the tables.
  • A plain JOIN drops rows without a partner. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table: Lena appears with zero orders.
  • GROUP BY c.id makes one output row per customer. COUNT and SUM then compute over each group. COALESCE(x, 0) replaces NULL (the sum of nothing) by 0.
  • AS names an output column. query_as matches those names with the struct fields.
  • sqlx::raw_sql runs several statements at once, without parameters. It is meant for set-up scripts.
Watch out
The N+1 problem

A tempting way to print orders with customer names is: load all orders with one query, and then, in a loop, load the customer of each order with another query. For 1,000 orders that makes 1,001 queries, each with a trip to the database. One query with a JOIN gets the same data in one trip, often a hundred times faster. Whenever you run a query inside a loop, ask whether a JOIN or a WHERE id IN (…) could replace it.

Indexes

To find the rows with a certain author, a database must by default read the whole table. An index is a sorted look-up structure for a column, like the index at the back of a book. With it, the database jumps to the matching rows. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows which way a query will be executed:

SCAN means reading every row. SEARCH … USING INDEX means a direct look-up. On a table with a million rows, that is the difference between seconds and a fraction of a millisecond. The primary key always has an index.

Indexes are not free: each one takes space and must be updated with every insert. Create them for the columns that your frequent queries filter, join or sort by, and for nothing else. A column that must not contain the same value twice gets a UNIQUE index, which enforces that rule as well.

Migrations: the schema changes too

A program grows, and its tables change with it: a new column here, a new table there. The database on your machine, the test database and the production database must all receive the same changes, in the same order. A migration is a small SQL file that makes one such change. The files are numbered, kept in the repository with the code, and applied in order. The database remembers which ones it has run.

SQLx has a command-line tool for this. Install it once with cargo install sqlx-cli. It reads the database address from the environment variable DATABASE_URL:

Fill the new file with SQL:

A later change is a new file, here sqlx migrate add add_rating with the content ALTER TABLE books ADD COLUMN rating REAL;. Then apply everything that is pending:

Running sqlx migrate run again does nothing, because both are recorded as installed. A program can also apply its migrations itself when it starts. The macro sqlx::migrate!() builds the files of the migrations folder into the executable:

The macro reads the folder while the program is compiled. Cargo compiles again only when a Rust file changes, so a new migration file alone would go unnoticed. A build script (chapter 36) next to Cargo.toml tells Cargo to watch the folder. The command sqlx migrate build-script writes it for you:

Watch out
Never edit a migration that has been applied

Once a migration has run anywhere but on your own machine, treat it as history. To change something, add a new migration. Editing an old file leaves the databases that already ran it in a different state from the new ones, and SQLx will refuse to continue when it notices that a recorded file has changed.

Queries checked at compile time

A query in a string has a weakness: a typing mistake in a column name is found only when that line runs. SQLx can do better. The macros query! and query_as! connect to your development database while compiling, ask it to check the SQL, and learn the types of the parameters and the result columns.

Output of the first run:

The parameters follow the SQL text as macro arguments. query! returns a value with one field per column, which is why row.count and row.newest exist, with the right types. Now a column name with a typing mistake, titel, stops the build:

A field of the wrong type is caught as well. With year: String in the struct, the compiler reports that String cannot be made from the i64 that the column delivers. A whole class of mistakes moves from “found by a user” to “found by the compiler”. When a migration renames a column, the build shows every query that must change.

The price is that compiling needs a database. With DATABASE_URL set, the macros use it. For builds without one, such as in CI, run cargo sqlx prepare once. It saves the answers of the database into a folder .sqlx, which you commit:

sqlx::query("…")sqlx::query!("…")
SQL checkedwhen the line runswhen the program is compiled
Parameters.bind(value)macro arguments
ResultFromRow struct, tuple or Rowa generated type, or your struct with query_as!
Needs a database to compilenoyes, or the saved .sqlx data

Then set SQLX_OFFLINE=true wherever no database is available — CI, a Docker build, a colleague’s laptop before the first docker compose up. The macros read the committed .sqlx data instead of connecting, and the build works. Commit the folder and re-run cargo sqlx prepare whenever a query changes; a stale .sqlx gives a confusing error that mentions neither the folder nor the migration. This one variable removes the most common “works locally, fails in CI” complaint about SQLx.

The examples of this guide use the function form, so that they run anywhere. For a real project with a fixed schema, the macros are worth their set-up.

A database behind a web server

Putting SQLx under an Axum server takes little: the pool is the state.

(The helper send is the one from the previous chapter.)

  • The same Book struct derives FromRow for the database and Serialize for JSON. A row becomes a struct, and the struct becomes the response.
  • INSERT … RETURNING id, title, year inserts a row and returns it in one statement, with the id that the database chose.
  • impl From<sqlx::Error> for ApiError lets ? convert database errors. They become a 500 response with a neutral message, and the details are logged.
  • Compared with the notes API of the last chapter, the Mutex is gone. The database handles concurrent access, and the data survives a restart.

Testing with a database

Because an in-memory SQLite database is created in microseconds, every test can have its own, fresh and empty, and the tests can run in parallel without disturbing each other. SQLx has an attribute that does the set-up, including the migrations:

Other ways: Diesel and SeaORM

SQLx has you write SQL yourself. An ORM (“object-relational mapper”) takes another route: you describe the tables in Rust, and build queries by calling methods. The library generates the SQL.

Diesel is the oldest and strictest. A table! description tells the compiler about the columns and their types. A query that compares a number column with a text, or selects a column that does not exist, does not compile. No database is needed for that check. Diesel is synchronous. (The crate diesel-async adds async support.)

SeaORM is async and built on top of SQLx. It follows the style of ORMs in other languages: a struct called Model is a row, and an “active model” holds changes to be saved. Its tools can generate these structs from an existing database.

For small synchronous programs that only need SQLite, rusqlite is the direct and light choice:

SQLxDieselSeaORMrusqlite
You writeSQLRust query methodsRust query methodsSQL
Checked at compile timewith the query! macros, against a databasealways, against the table! descriptiontypes of the modelno
Asyncyesno (add-on crate)yesno
DatabasesSQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQLSQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQLSQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQLSQLite
Good forservices where you want to see and control the SQLlarge schemas with many query variationsfast development of typical create-read-update-delete applicationstools and apps with a local database

Which one? If you know SQL or want to learn it, start with SQLx: there is nothing between you and the database, and the knowledge carries over to every other language. If the application is mostly forms over tables and you prefer methods to SQL text, take SeaORM. If you want the strongest compile-time guarantees and can work synchronously, take Diesel. All three are mature and widely used.

PostgreSQL in place of SQLite

SQLitePostgreSQL
Cargo featuresqlitepostgres
Pool typeSqlitePool, PgPoolOptionsPgPool, PgPoolOptions
Addresssqlite://app.dbpostgres://user:password@host/database
Placeholders?$1, $2, …
Auto-numbered keyINTEGER PRIMARY KEYBIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, or GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
Typesfew and flexiblemany and strict: BOOLEAN, TIMESTAMPTZ, UUID, JSONB, arrays (TEXT[])
Concurrent writersone at a timemany (row-level locks & MVCC)

Many projects use SQLite for tests and small single-node tools, and PostgreSQL when several app instances share one database. Switching SQLx to PostgreSQL replaces SqlitePoolOptions with PgPoolOptions and uses $1, $2 placeholders:

Notice how PostgreSQL’s richer type system maps cleanly in SQLx:

  • JSONB maps to sqlx::types::Json<Metadata> without manual serde_json string conversions.
  • Custom Postgres ENUMs map directly via #[derive(sqlx::Type)].
  • Arrays (TEXT[]) map straight to Vec<String>, letting you batch lookups cleanly with WHERE id = ANY($1) instead of loops!

Pool sizing and timeouts

Resist setting max_connections(500). A PostgreSQL server handles only a modest number of active queries concurrently before context-switching and lock contention slow everything down. Size each service pool around (2 × CPU cores) + disk spindles (typically 10–25 connections per app instance), always set a bounded acquire_timeout (so overload returns 503 promptly instead of hanging forever), and place PgBouncer in front when running dozens of application containers.

Preventing race conditions: FOR UPDATE vs optimistic locking

When two concurrent checkouts read stock = 1 at the same instant and update afterward, both succeed unless the database coordinates them:

  • Pessimistic locking (SELECT … FOR UPDATE): Inside pool.begin(), lock the row (SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE). The second transaction waits until the first commits or rolls back.
  • Optimistic concurrency control (version column): Read version = 4, then run UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2. Check result.rows_affected() == 1—if 0, someone updated the row concurrently, so return a conflict (409 Conflict) or retry cleanly without holding row locks!

Pagination: keyset/cursor vs OFFSET

LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000 forces the database to scan and discard 10,000 rows on every page—and if a new row arrives between page 1 and page 2, items shift and appear twice! For feeds, logs, and large tables, prefer keyset (cursor) pagination backed by an index:

Caching and Redis

Relational databases should not answer the same hot read or session lookup ten thousand times a second. Redis (or Valkey) is an in-memory key-value server used for short-lived caches, distributed sessions, and rate-limit counters. In Rust, redis (with tokio-comp) or fred gives an async multiplexed connection you can share cheaply across handlers without a separate pool:

Always set an explicit TTL (set_ex) on cached items, and decide how writes invalidate stale entries (delete the key on update or tolerate brief staleness). Never treat an eviction-prone cache as your only source of truth.

Three PostgreSQL features are worth knowing by name, because they solve problems that otherwise turn into polling loops or guesswork:

  • LISTEN / NOTIFY — a table’s changes can wake other processes. NOTIFY events_changed inside the same transaction as the write, and every connection that ran LISTEN events_changed receives it after the commit. It is the cheapest way to push a change to a second service without adding a broker; the Rust side holds a connection and awaits the notifications. Ordering is not guaranteed and nothing is persisted, so use it for “something changed, go and look”, not as a queue.
  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE — the answer to “why is this query slow”. EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT … runs the query and prints the plan with real times per step. A sequential scan on a table with a million rows, where you expected an index, is the single most common finding.
  • COPY — bulk loading. Inserting a million rows one statement at a time takes minutes; COPY … FROM STDIN takes seconds, and sqlx can copy from a stream.

Other kinds of storage

A relational database is the right default: it gives you transactions, constraints and a query language that answers questions you did not plan for. These are the tools you reach for when one of those is in the way.

NeedCratesChoose it when
A cache, or data shared between serversredis, fredReads outnumber writes, the data is rebuildable, and you need it shared between processes
DocumentsmongodbThe shape varies between records, and a record is read as a whole
A key-value store inside the program, without SQLredb, fjall, sledA desktop or CLI program needs durable keyed data without a server
Full-text searchtantivyReal ranked search over many documents; SQLite’s FTS5 is the built-in alternative below a few hundred thousand rows
Files in cloud storage (S3 and similar)object_store, aws-sdk-s3Blobs belong in an object store, never in the database
A low-level PostgreSQL clienttokio-postgresYou need protocol features SQLx does not expose
Pooling any driverdeadpool, bb8You use Diesel, tokio-postgres or a client with no pool of its own

Redis: the shared memory between your servers

Redis is a server that holds key–value data in memory. It is fast because it never touches the disk on the read path, and it is honest about the trade: assume the data can disappear, and never let Redis be the only copy of anything you cannot rebuild.

The five operations that cover most uses, run from redis-cli:

Three habits make Redis pleasant to live with:

  • Namespace every key — session:, cache:, rate: — because a shared Redis is shared, and a key called user42 will collide with someone else’s.
  • Always set an expiry on anything that is a cache. A cache without a TTL is a database with none of the guarantees.
  • Use the patterns the types give you. A sorted set is a leaderboard, INCR is a rate-limit counter, and SET … EX is a session with a timeout already in it.

In Rust, redis is the crate. Use redis::aio::ConnectionManager rather than a bare client in a web service: it reconnects by itself after the server restarts, and it is cheap to clone into every handler. fred is the alternative with more of Redis 6 and 7 built in. The operations are commands, not SQL: cmd("SET").arg(key).arg(value).arg("EX").arg(3600).query_async(&mut conn).await?.

MongoDB: documents instead of rows

A document is one self-contained record, nested as deeply as the data is. Reading it is one lookup with no JOIN; bson::doc! writes queries that look like the documents themselves; mongodb plus serde maps a document to a struct. Choose documents when each record has its own shape and you always read it whole. Choose rows when several records must agree with each other — an order and its stock level — because that is what transactions and foreign keys are for, and MongoDB’s transactions are newer and more constrained than PostgreSQL’s.

Embedded key-value stores

redb, fjall and sled are storage engines that live inside your program: no server, no port, one file. Choose them for a desktop application, a CLI tool that keeps state, or a cache that must survive a restart. redb is the simplest and most stable of the three for new work; sled is the best known but has been at beta for years; fjall is LSM-based and shines on write-heavy local workloads. All three store bytes, so pair them with serde and you have a durable typed store in about twenty lines. None of them give you SQL, indexes on arbitrary fields, or concurrent access from other processes. For example, redb stores typed key-value tables in a single crash-safe file:

Object storage and full-text search

Files — images, PDFs, exports, backups — belong in object storage, not in a database column: object_store gives one API over S3, GCS, Azure and the local filesystem, and aws-sdk-s3 is the S3-specific official SDK. Both stream, so a 2 GB upload never has to fit in memory.

For search, tantivy is a search engine library: you define a schema, index documents, and query with ranked results, highlights and facets, all inside your process. Below a few hundred thousand rows, SQLite’s FTS5 extension gives you keyword search with ranking in the database you already have, through a virtual table and MATCH — often the right first answer.

How other languages do it
Databases in other languages
  • Python has SQLAlchemy and Django’s ORM, and JavaScript has Prisma and Drizzle. Mistakes in queries and in the mapping of rows show up when the program runs.
  • Java uses JDBC and the ORM Hibernate. C# has Entity Framework, where queries are written in the language itself (LINQ) and checked by the compiler, which is close to Diesel’s approach.
  • Go has database/sql in its standard library, with rows scanned into variables by hand. The tool sqlc generates checked code from SQL files, an idea related to SQLx’s macros.
  • In most languages, building SQL from strings is possible and the injection risk is left to discipline. SQLx makes the unsafe way a compile error.
Recap
  • A relational database stores rows in tables with typed columns. SQL defines, reads and changes them.
  • SQLx runs SQL from async Rust. A pool hands out connections. query, query_as and query_scalar run statements, and FromRow maps rows to structs.
  • Values always go through bind. Building SQL from input opens the door to SQL injection, and SQLx refuses non-literal query strings.
  • A transaction makes several statements all-or-nothing. Dropping it without commit rolls back.
  • JOIN combines tables, GROUP BY summarises, and indexes make look-ups fast.
  • Migrations are numbered SQL files that change the schema step by step.
  • query! and query_as! check SQL against a real database at compile time.
  • Size pools modestly (~2 × cores, with bounded acquire_timeout), prefer keyset/cursor pagination over large OFFSETs, and use FOR UPDATE or optimistic version checks for concurrent writes.
  • Use redis (with explicit TTLs) for shared ephemeral caches and rate-limit counters, or redb for zero-server embedded key-value storage.
  • Diesel and SeaORM are ORMs that build the SQL from Rust code. rusqlite is a light, synchronous SQLite library.
  • Redis is shared memory between servers: cache, sessions, counters, rankings. Namespace the keys, and give every cache entry an expiry.
  • MongoDB stores documents instead of rows, and redb/fjall/sled store key–value data inside your own program with no server at all.
  • object_store and s3-style services hold blobs; tantivy (or SQLite’s FTS5) holds a search index.
  • SQLX_OFFLINE=true plus a committed .sqlx folder is what makes compile-time-checked queries work in CI.
Check your understanding
1

Why is format!("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'") dangerous when name comes from a user?

This is SQL injection. With .bind(name), the value is sent apart from the SQL text and can never be read as SQL.

2

A function starts a transaction, runs one UPDATE, and then returns early with ? because the next statement failed. What happens to the UPDATE?

Dropping a transaction rolls it back. Only an explicit commit() makes the changes permanent.

3

Which method fits “find the user with this id, who may not exist”?

fetch_optional returns Option<T>. fetch_one would return an error for a missing row, which makes an expected case look like a failure.

4

What does an index on a column do?

An index is a sorted look-up structure. It speeds up reads that filter or sort by the column, and must be kept up to date on writes.

5

What is special about sqlx::query! compared with sqlx::query?

The macro asks the development database (or the saved .sqlx data) to describe the query. Wrong column names and types become compile errors.

6

Why is keyset (cursor) pagination (WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)) usually better than LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000 for large tables?

With an index on (created_at, id), keyset pagination jumps straight to the next page in constant work per page, regardless of how deep the user scrolls.

7

Why should you avoid setting max_connections(500) on each instance of a web service’s database pool?

Keeping each pool modest (around 10–25 connections with a short acquire_timeout, and PgBouncer in front at scale) gives far higher throughput under load than opening hundreds of idle or contending connections.

Guided exerciseA table of tasks

Create an in-memory database with a table tasks (id, title, and a flag done that is false by default). Insert three tasks, mark one as done, and print the open ones. Then print how many of all tasks are finished, with one query.

Need a hint?

SQLite accepts done BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE, and SQLx maps it to a Rust bool. Derive FromRow for a Task struct. For the last part, SELECT COUNT(*), COALESCE(SUM(done), 0) FROM tasks returns two numbers, which query_as can put into a tuple (i64, i64).

Show solution and explanation

The INSERT names only the title. The database fills in the id and the default for done. Tuples implement FromRow too, which is handy for small results that do not deserve a struct. Summing a boolean column counts the true values, because SQLite stores true as 1.

The counting happens in the database, in one query. Loading all rows and counting them in Rust would give the same number, and would move the whole table over the connection to do it.

PracticeCount words with an upsert

Write async fn count_word(pool, word) -> Result<i64, sqlx::Error> that records one more occurrence of a word and returns its new count. The table words has the word as its primary key and a count. If the word is new, a row is inserted with count 1. If it exists, the count is increased. Do it in a single statement, ignoring upper and lower case.

Need a hint?

SQL has a form for “insert, or update if the key exists”, often called an upsert: INSERT INTO words (word, count) VALUES (?, 1) ON CONFLICT (word) DO UPDATE SET count = count + 1. Add RETURNING count to get the new value back, and read it with query_scalar and fetch_one.

Show solution and explanation

The obvious alternative is two steps: SELECT the row, then INSERT or UPDATE depending on the answer. That has a gap. Two clients can both find no row and both insert, and one of them fails. The upsert is a single statement, and the database carries it out as one indivisible step. Whenever you catch yourself writing “check, then act” against a database, look for a single statement that does both, or use a transaction.

ORDER BY count DESC, word sorts by a second column when counts are equal, so the result is the same on every run.

PracticeOrders that cannot oversell

A shop has a table products (name, stock) and a table orders. Write place_order(pool, customer, product, quantity) that records the order and reduces the stock, as one unit. It must fail without changing anything if the product is unknown or the stock is too small. Return the new order’s id, or an error that says which of the things went wrong.

Need a hint?

Start a transaction with pool.begin(). Read the stock with fetch_optional on the transaction (&mut *transaction). Return early with your own error for the two refusals: dropping the transaction undoes everything. Define the error enum with thiserror, with a variant Database(#[from] sqlx::Error) so that ? works on SQLx results.

Show solution and explanation

The read of the stock, the update and the insert run inside one transaction. The two refusals return before any change. And if the insert failed after the update, the ? would leave the function, the transaction would be dropped, and the stock would be restored.

The error type separates what the caller did wrong (unknown product, too many) from what went wrong inside (the database). A web handler would turn the first two into 4xx responses and the last into a 500.

The CHECK (stock >= 0) in the table is a second line of defence. Even if a bug in some other function forgot the check, the database would refuse a negative stock.

ChallengeA store type for tasks

Hide the SQL of a to-do application behind a type. Write struct TaskStore that owns a pool, with the methods in_memory() (creates the table), add(title, priority), list(&Filter), complete(id) -> bool and stats(). Filter has three optional conditions: done, min_priority and search (a text that the title must contain). stats returns the number of open and finished tasks, computed by the database. Titles are trimmed, and an empty title must be refused.

Need a hint?

Build the list query with QueryBuilder, adding AND … with push and push_bind for each condition that is Some. For the text search use title LIKE ? with the value format!("%{search}%"): in LIKE, % stands for any text. stats can use SELECT done, COUNT(*) FROM tasks GROUP BY done, read as Vec<(bool, i64)>. A CHECK (length(title) > 0) constraint refuses empty titles at the database.

Show solution and explanation

A type like TaskStore is often called a repository. The rest of the program calls store.add(…) and store.list(…) and never sees SQL, a pool or a row. Three gains follow:

  • One place to change. If a column is renamed or the database is swapped, only this type changes.
  • Easy tests. TaskStore::in_memory() gives each test its own database in an instant.
  • A typed border. Rows become Task values here, and nothing untyped leaves.

complete reports through rows_affected whether a row was changed, which saves a separate “does it exist?” query. The search text goes through push_bind like every other value, so a ' in it is harmless. And the empty title is refused by the CHECK constraint after trimming: the rule lives in the schema, where no code path can bypass it.

In the next chapter, a store like this sits behind a web API.

Project: a link shortener with a web API and a database

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Plan a web service as three layers: HTTP, rules and storage
  • Keep all SQL inside one repository type
  • Turn every failure into a clear JSON response
  • Protect routes with an API key
  • Test the whole API without opening a network port
  • Prepare a service for a real server

In this project you build a complete web service: a link shortener. It turns a long web address into a short one. When somebody opens the short address, the service sends the browser on to the long one and counts the visit. Services such as bit.ly work this way.

This is the finished program at work. curl is the command-line HTTP client from chapter 46. -X POST chooses the method, -H adds a header, -d supplies the body, and -i also shows the status line and the headers of the response.

The first request stores a link under the code book. The second one follows it: the answer 307 Temporary Redirect with a location header tells a browser where to go next. The third one shows the facts about the link, with one visit counted.

The project brings Part 10 together: Axum for HTTP (chapter 46), SQLx with SQLite for storage (chapter 47), Serde for JSON (chapter 43), and thiserror, anyhow, tracing and rand from chapter 42. It also keeps a promise of chapter 41: the tests exercise the whole API without a network.

Real-world analogy
A cloakroom for web addresses

A link shortener works like the cloakroom of a theatre. You hand over a bulky coat (a long address) and get a small ticket (a short code). Whoever shows the ticket is led to the coat.

The cloakroom also shows how the program is organised. The attendant at the counter talks to the visitors. A sheet of rules says which coats are accepted. And only the clerk in the back walks among the racks. Each of the three has one job, and none does the job of another.

Step 0: plan

The API

RequestWho may call itWhat it doesSuccess
POST /linkseverybodystores a link. The body is JSON: {"url": "…"}, or {"url": "…", "code": "…"} to choose the code201 Created
GET /{code}everybodysends the browser to the long address and counts the visit307 Temporary Redirect
GET /links/{code}everybodyshows the facts about one link200 OK
GET /linksthe ownerlists links, the most visited first. ?limit=20&offset=0 selects a page200 OK
DELETE /links/{code}the ownerremoves a link204 No Content
GET /healtheverybodyanswers ok if the service and its database work200 OK

The owner proves who they are with a secret API key, sent in the header x-api-key.

Every failure is answered with a fitting status code and a small JSON document:

StatusWhen
400 Bad Requestthe body is not valid JSON
401 Unauthorizedthe API key is missing or wrong
404 Not Foundthere is no such link, or no such path
409 Conflictthe chosen code is taken
415 Unsupported Media Typethe body is not declared as JSON
422 Unprocessable Entitythe JSON is readable, but a value breaks a rule
500 Internal Server Errorthe database failed
Good to know
A GET that counts

By the rules of HTTP, a GET request should only read. Following a short link also adds one to a counter. That is accepted practice: the client did not ask for a change, and a visit counter is comparable to a line in a log file.

The data

One table is enough:

ColumnTypeMeaning
codetext, primary keythe short code, such as book
urltextthe long address
hitsintegerhow often the link was followed
created_attextwhen the link was stored

The layers

The program has three layers, and each knows only the one below it:

Why bother with layers in a small program? Because each layer can then be understood, tested and replaced alone:

  • The rules are plain functions. They are tested in microseconds, with no database and no HTTP.
  • The store is the only place that contains SQL. This is the repository idea from the end of chapter 47.
  • The routes translate between HTTP and the two layers below. They contain no SQL and few decisions.

The files

The package contains a library (lib.rs) and a program (main.rs), as in chapter 23. Nearly all code lives in the library. That is what makes the tests in tests/ possible, because an integration test can only use a library.

Every file is printed in full in this chapter. A file that is printed in several blocks continues where the block before stopped.

Step 1: the project and the table

Create the project and add the crates:

The last line adds tower as a dev-dependency: a crate that only the tests use. Cargo.toml now looks like this (your version numbers may be newer):

CrateIts job here
axum, tokiothe web framework and the async runtime
sqlxtalks to the SQLite database. SQLite itself is compiled into the program
serde, serde_jsonJSON in and out
thiserrorthe error type of the service
anyhowerrors while starting up
randrandom codes
tracing, tracing-subscriber, tower-httpthe log, with one line per request, and a time limit
tower (tests only)hands a request to the router without a network

The table

The table is created by a migration (chapter 47): a numbered SQL file that is applied once to every database. Create the folder migrations and in it this file:

  • PRIMARY KEY makes code unique. The database refuses a second row with the same code, whatever our Rust code does. It also builds an index, so finding a link by its code stays fast with millions of rows.
  • DEFAULT values are filled in by the database: a new link starts with 0 hits and the current time.
  • SQLite has no type for dates. CURRENT_TIMESTAMP stores a text such as 2026-11-14 16:00:38, in UTC.

The number in front of the file name is a timestamp. It decides the order in which migrations run. If you installed sqlx-cli, the command sqlx migrate add create_links creates such a file for you.

The program will apply its migrations itself when it starts, with the macro sqlx::migrate!(). The macro reads the folder while the program is compiled and stores the files inside the executable. That has a catch: when you add a migration later and change no Rust file, Cargo sees no reason to compile again, and the new migration is silently missing. A two-line build script (chapter 36) closes the gap. Create it next to Cargo.toml:

The library

Replace nothing in src/main.rs yet. Create src/lib.rs with one line of documentation. The modules are added to it step by step:

Step 2: one error type

Before any feature, decide how failures travel. Every function of the service that can fail returns the same error type. And that type knows how to become an HTTP response, as in chapter 46.

Create src/error.rs:

And register the module in src/lib.rs:

What to notice:

  • One variant per kind of failure. The #[error("…")] texts are what the client reads. {0} and {1} insert the first and second field of the variant.
  • status is a match without a catch-all arm. When you add a variant later, the compiler stops until you have decided on its status code.
  • #[from] sqlx::Error generates impl From<sqlx::Error> for ApiError. So in a function that returns Result<_, ApiError>, a database call can simply end in ?.
  • From<JsonRejection> is written by hand, because it stores two values. A JsonRejection is what Axum produces when it cannot read a JSON body. Axum has already chosen a status code (400, 415 or 422) and written an explanation. We keep both and only change the wrapping, so that these errors are JSON as well.
  • The database error is logged, not shown. Its text may contain table names, SQL or file paths, which are of no use to a client and of some use to an attacker. The client reads “something went wrong on the server”, and the details go to the log.

cargo check should pass now. Cargo warns that some dependencies are not used yet. The warnings go away as the project grows.

Step 3: the rules

The second layer answers three questions. Is this an address that we are willing to shorten? Is this a code that we accept? And what does a new random code look like?

Create src/validate.rs:

Add pub mod validate; to src/lib.rs.

check_url reads from top to bottom like the rules it enforces:

  • The address must start with http:// or https://. strip_prefix returns the rest of the text after the prefix, or None. or_else tries the second prefix if the first one did not fit, and ok_or_else turns a final None into our error (chapter 18).
  • Something must follow the prefix, and it must contain no spaces or control characters.
  • The function returns the trimmed address as a &str that borrows from the parameter. Nothing is copied.

The list of allowed beginnings is a security rule, and it is written as an allow list: everything that is not expressly permitted is refused. A short link to an address that starts with javascript: would run a script in the browser of whoever follows it. Listing the two good cases is safer than trying to list all the bad ones.

check_code allows 3 to 20 ASCII letters, digits, - and _. Two words are reserved. A link with the code links could never be followed, because the path /links already belongs to the API.

random_code picks six characters from an alphabet of 32. The look-alikes 0/o and 1/l are left out, because people read codes aloud and type them from paper. Six characters give 32⁶ = 1,073,741,824 different codes.

These functions are pure: the result depends only on the parameters. Nothing is easier to test. Append the tests to the same file:

Run cargo test. The four tests pass.

The test lists are worth a second look. A table of bad inputs in a for loop makes it cheap to add a case, and the message "{url:?} should be refused" names the culprit when one fails.

Step 4: the store

The third layer owns the database. Create src/store.rs:

  • Link mirrors one row. FromRow lets SQLx fill it from a query result.
  • LinkStore wraps the connection pool. The field is private: no code outside this file can reach the pool, so no code outside this file can run SQL.
  • open is for the real program. create_if_missing creates the database file on the first start. sqlx::migrate!().run(…) then applies every migration that this database has not seen.
  • journal_mode(Wal) switches SQLite to its write-ahead log. In this mode, readers and one writer can work at the same time, which is what a server needs. While the program runs, you will see two helper files next to the database: links.db-wal and links.db-shm.
  • in_memory is for tests. It gives a complete, empty database in a few milliseconds. The pool is limited to one connection, because every connection to sqlite::memory: would get its own separate database.

Now the queries. The file continues:

Add pub mod store; to src/lib.rs.

Three of these methods deserve a closer look.

insert lets the database decide. A tempting way to refuse a duplicate code is to ask first (“is there a row with this code?”) and insert afterwards. That has a gap. Two requests for the same code can both ask at the same moment, both hear “no”, and both insert. The pattern is called check-then-act, and it is a classic source of rare, unrepeatable bugs.

The store does not ask. It inserts, and the PRIMARY KEY of the table refuses the second row. error.is_unique_violation() recognises this refusal, and the match arm with the guard translates it into ApiError::CodeTaken. Every other database error passes through unchanged.

visit does two things in one statement. UPDATE … SET hits = hits + 1 … RETURNING url adds one to the counter and hands back the address. The database computes hits + 1 itself, inside one statement. So two visits at the same instant cannot both read 5 and both write 6. With fetch_optional, an unknown code simply gives None.

list never returns everything. LIMIT and OFFSET are bound like all other values. The second sort key, code, makes the order definite when two links have the same number of hits. Without it, pages could overlap.

Notice the return types. insert returns an ApiError, because it knows a failure with a meaning: the code is taken. The other methods return a plain sqlx::Error. The routes will turn that into an ApiError with ?.

Test the store

Append to src/store.rs:

Run cargo test: seven tests pass. The new ones are async, so they are marked with #[tokio::test] (chapter 32). Each creates its own database, so they cannot disturb each other, and they run in parallel.

matches!(second, Err(ApiError::CodeTaken(code)) if code == "docs") checks the variant and its content in one expression (chapter 14). ApiError cannot be compared with ==, because sqlx::Error does not implement PartialEq.

Step 5: the routes

Now the layer that speaks HTTP. Create src/routes.rs. It begins with the imports and the data types:

  • AppState is what every handler can reach: the store, the secret key, and the address under which the service is reachable from outside (needed to print complete short links). Axum clones the state for every request. The store clones cheaply, because a pool is a handle to shared data. The two texts are Arc<str>: shared, read-only strings. Cloning one copies a pointer and adds one to a counter, where cloning a String would copy the text (chapter 31).
  • NewLink is what a client sends. code is an Option, so the field may be missing.
  • LinkView is what a client receives. It is not the same as Link: it has an extra field, short_url, which is computed and not stored.

Keeping the three types apart (input, stored, shown) looks like repetition in a small program. It pays off with the first field that must not be accepted from a client, or must not be shown to one.

The router

The file continues with the function that builds the application:

  • Two groups of routes. The admin router holds what only the owner may do. route_layer wraps exactly these routes in the middleware require_key. A route that is added to this group later is protected without anybody having to remember it.
  • from_fn_with_state is the sibling of from_fn from chapter 46, for middleware that needs the state. Here it needs the key to compare with.
  • /links and /{code} do not collide. For the path /links, both patterns fit. Axum prefers the fixed text over the placeholder. That is the reason for the reserved words in step 3.
  • fallback answers every request that no route matches, so that even an unknown path gets our JSON error.
  • The limits. A body may have at most 16 KB, and a request may take at most 10 seconds. Both are far more than an honest client needs.
  • TraceLayer writes one log line per request. It is added last, which makes it the outermost layer: it sees every request, including those that the other layers refuse.

The handlers

The file continues:

Each handler is short, because the layers below do the work:

  • health asks the store for a sign of life. A hosting platform can call this route every few seconds and restart the program if the answer is not 200.
  • create_link takes the body as Result<Json<NewLink>, JsonRejection>. With a plain Json<NewLink>, Axum would answer a broken body itself, in plain text. With the Result, the handler receives the failure, and input? turns it into our ApiError. Then come the rules, then the store. A chosen code that is taken ends the request with 409.
  • insert_with_random_code covers the rare case that a random code exists already. It tries again with a new one. All other outcomes, good or bad, are returned as they are: other => return other.
  • follow is the heart of the service, in four lines. Redirect::temporary answers 307. A permanent redirect (308) would be wrong here: browsers remember permanent redirects and would skip our server from the second visit on. Visits would no longer be counted, and a deleted link would keep working in those browsers.
  • list_links reads limit and offset from the query string. clamp(1, 100) forces the limit into a sane range, whatever the client asks for.
  • delete_link uses the bool from the store to choose between 204 and 404.

The file ends with the middleware:

require_key runs before the handlers of the admin group. With the right key in the header, it passes the request on with next.run(request). Otherwise it returns an error, and the handler never runs.

Watch out
Production upgrade: constant-time key comparison

Notice given == Some(&*state.api_key) uses ordinary string equality (==), which stops at the first mismatching byte. In a production service, hash both keys with SHA-256 and compare the fixed-length digests with subtle::ConstantTimeEq as shown in chapter 46, so response timing never leaks how many leading bytes matched.

Finally, complete src/lib.rs. It lists all modules, and re-exports the two names that main and the tests need most:

(config is created in the next step. cargo check will complain about it until then.)

Step 6: settings and main

A service should not contain its settings. The same executable must run on your laptop, on a test server and in production, and a secret in the source code ends up in the version history for ever. The custom of web services is to read settings from environment variables, which are the layer between a configuration file and a command-line flag (the full precedence chain is in the CLI chapter). Here it is in a few dozen lines, with no crate:

VariableMeaningIf it is not set
API_KEYthe secret of the owner, at least 16 charactersthe program refuses to start
PORTthe port to listen on3000
DATABASE_URLwhere the database file issqlite://links.db
BASE_URLthe public address of the servicehttp://localhost: plus the port

Create src/config.rs:

This file uses anyhow, not ApiError. The division follows chapter 18: an error that some code must tell apart and react to gets its own type. An error that is only reported to a human is a job for anyhow. A wrong setting is reported once, to the person who starts the program, and the program ends.

There is no default for API_KEY, on purpose. A service that starts with a well-known default secret is open to everybody who has read its source code. For larger services that combine TOML files, .env files, environment overrides, and redacted SecretString fields, see the layered figment + secrecy pattern in chapter 46.

Now replace the content of src/main.rs:

main only connects parts: read the settings, open the store, build the state, listen, serve. The two with_context calls add what the bare errors lack. Compare the message for an occupied or forbidden port with and without it:

When you press Ctrl+C, shutdown_signal completes. The server then stops accepting connections, finishes the requests that are under way, and serve returns. Only then is the store closed.

Start the service. The key is given for this one run:

If a request with -d '{…}' is refused as broken JSON, save the body in a file body.json and send it with -d "@body.json", which works in every shell.

In a second terminal, talk to it. This is a real session:

  • The fourth request chose no code, so the service made one up. Yours will differ.
  • The error messages for a broken body come from Axum. Our ApiError only wrapped them in JSON.
  • Without the key, the list is refused with 401.
  • Open http://localhost:3000/ plus one of your codes in a browser. You land on the long address.

Meanwhile, the first terminal shows the log, with one line per request:

Stop the server with Ctrl+C and start it again. The links are still there, because they live in the file links.db. Add the line links.db* to the file .gitignore, so that the database does not end up in version control.

Try a wrong setting too:

Step 7: test the whole API

Trying things by hand with curl is fine once. It is no way to make sure that everything still works after every change. The service needs automatic tests that cover the same ground.

The obvious method would be to start the server on a port and send real HTTP requests, as the tests of the chat server did in chapter 33. Axum offers something better. A Router is a tower Service (chapter 45): a value that turns a request into a response. So a test can build a Request value, hand it to the router, and inspect the Response value. No port is opened and nothing is sent over a network, yet the request passes through all of our code: routing, middleware, extractors, handlers, rules, store and database.

Create the folder tests and in it api.rs. The file starts with a few helpers:

  • test_app builds the complete application the way main does, with two differences: the database lives in memory, and the settings are fixed values. Every test calls it and gets a service of its own.
  • send is the central piece. oneshot comes from the trait tower::ServiceExt and means: call this service with one request. It consumes the service, so the router is cloned first. Cloning a router is cheap. The function then reads the whole body and tries to parse it as JSON.
  • call builds a request from a method, a path, an optional key and an optional JSON body. get and create are shortcuts for the two most frequent cases.

Helpers like these are worth their lines. They make each test read like a description of behaviour:

Run them:

Seventeen tests on three levels:

LevelTestsThey check
rules (validate.rs)4which addresses and codes are accepted
store (store.rs)3that the SQL does what the method names say
API (tests/api.rs)10that everything works together, through HTTP

This is the test pyramid of chapter 41 in small. The ten API tests together take about two hundredths of a second, each with a database of its own. Tests this fast get run after every change.

What the API tests pin down is the behaviour that clients rely on: status codes, the shape of the JSON, who may do what. They do not mention SQL or the names of handlers. You could replace SQLite with PostgreSQL, or rewrite every handler, and these tests would tell you whether clients would notice.

Step 8: make it ready for a server

Build the optimised version:

The result is one file, target/release/shortener. On the machine used for this guide it has about 7 MB, with SQLite and all migrations inside, and the running service occupies about 6 MB of memory. To run it on a server, copy the file there and set the four variables. Nothing else needs to be installed.

Before real users arrive, go through the list of chapter 46:

  1. HTTPS. Put a reverse proxy in front that handles the certificates, and set BASE_URL to the public address, such as https://sho.rt.
  2. The key. Generate a long random API_KEY, and keep it in the settings of your host, not in a file of the project.
  3. The data. Put the database file on a disk that survives restarts, for example with DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///data/links.db (three slashes: an absolute path). Copy it regularly to another place.
  4. The health check. Tell your host to call GET /health.

In a container, the Dockerfile of chapter 46 fits after you change the name of the executable. The migrations folder does not need to be copied into the final image, because its content is inside the program.

What makes this service solid, and what is missing

Worth noticing in the design:

  • Every value from a client is checked before it is used, in one place, by an allow list.
  • Every value reaches SQL as a bound parameter. No SQL text is ever built from input, so SQL injection is impossible (chapter 47).
  • Uniqueness and counting are left to the database, in single statements. There is no moment between a check and an action in which another request could interfere.
  • Errors are data. Each failure is a variant of one enum, each variant has one status code, and internal details never reach a client.
  • Resources are bounded: the size of a body, the duration of a request, the length of a list, the number of database connections.
  • The program contains no secrets and no settings.

A public shortener needs more than this:

  • Rate limiting. Anybody can create links as fast as they can send requests. A layer that limits requests per client address belongs in front (the crate tower_governor provides one).
  • Protection against abuse. Shorteners hide where a link leads, which makes them attractive for fraud. Real services check addresses against block lists and offer a preview page.
  • Observability. The service logs, but it counts nothing. A request counter and a duration histogram, exposed on GET /metrics, are what turn “it feels slow” into “p99 rose at 14:20” (chapter 45). The GET /health route is a start; a separate readiness check that also asks the database is the other half.
  • A real login. One key for one owner works for a machine client, not for people. Sessions for a browser, signed tokens for an app, and the difference between authentication and authorisation are in chapter 46.
  • Accounts. One key for one owner is the simplest possible scheme. With several users, each gets a key of their own, stored as a hash like a password. Keys should also be compared in constant time (the crate subtle does that), so that the duration of a comparison reveals nothing about the key.
  • A real URL parser. check_url covers the basics. The crate url implements the complete standard.
  • More than one machine. SQLite is a file on one disk. To run several copies of the service, switch to PostgreSQL. Thanks to the store, only store.rs and the migration change.
  • Honest numbers. Chat programs fetch links to show a preview, and each fetch counts as a visit. Real services filter such automatic visitors.
How other languages do it
The same service in other languages
  • In Python (Flask or FastAPI) or JavaScript (Express) this service takes fewer lines. Whether a field can be missing, whether every error case has a status code, and whether a value is text or a number are found out when a request hits the wrong spot, unless tests or additional type checkers catch it earlier. Both need an installed interpreter with the right packages on the server.
  • In Java (Spring) or C# (ASP.NET), types are checked at compile time, and null remains possible nearly everywhere. A running service typically needs a hundred megabytes of memory or more.
  • Go produces a single executable as well. Its errors are values that are easy to ignore, and a missing JSON field silently becomes an empty value.
  • In Rust, the optional field is an Option, the forgotten error case is a compiler error, the forgotten check of a Result is a warning, and the result is one file of a few megabytes.

Make it better

Three extensions, from simple to demanding. Do them in this order, because each builds on the one before. For every one, write the test first, see it fail, and then make it pass.

PracticeChange where a link points

The owner wants to correct the address of an existing link without changing its code. Add the route PATCH /links/{code}. It requires the API key and takes a body such as {"url": "https://new.example"}. It answers with the changed link, with 404 for an unknown code, and with 422 for an address that breaks the rules.

PATCH is the HTTP method for changing part of a resource.

Need a hint?

The store needs a method update_url(&self, code: &str, url: &str) -> Result<Option<Link>, sqlx::Error>. A single statement, UPDATE links SET url = ? WHERE code = ? RETURNING … with fetch_optional, changes the row and tells you whether it existed.

A second method on a path that already has one is added by chaining: delete(delete_link).patch(change_link).

Show solution and explanation

In src/store.rs, inside the second impl LinkStore block:

In src/routes.rs, a type for the body and a handler:

And in the function app, the route of the admin group gets a second method:

The test, appended to tests/api.rs:

The new route sits in the admin group, so it is protected by the key without one more line. The first assertion of the test makes sure of that. The handler reuses check_url, so a changed address must pass the same rules as a new one. And UPDATE … RETURNING with fetch_optional again does two jobs in one statement: it changes the row, and its None says that there was no such row.

Nothing had to change in error.rs, validate.rs, config.rs or main.rs. That is the layering at work.

PracticeRemember the last visit

Show in the facts about a link when it was followed most recently: a field last_visited, which is null until the first visit.

This changes the table, so it needs a new migration. Do not edit the first migration file: databases that exist already would never see the change.

Need a hint?

The migration is one statement: ALTER TABLE links ADD COLUMN last_visited TEXT;. Give the file a later timestamp than the first one. A column without NOT NULL may be empty, and an empty column maps to Option<String> in Rust.

Set the column in the same UPDATE that counts the visit. Then add the field to Link, to every list of columns in the store, and to LinkView.

Show solution and explanation

The new migration:

In src/store.rs, the struct gets a field, and the method visit sets the time:

The four other queries name their columns. Each list becomes code, url, hits, created_at, last_visited.

In src/routes.rs, LinkView gets the field last_visited: Option<String>, and LinkView::new copies it with last_visited: link.last_visited.

The test:

Now start the program on the database file from before. It applies the new migration by itself, and the old links are still there, with an empty last_visited:

Three observations:

  • The struct and the queries must agree with the table. If you forget the column in one of the lists, FromRow fails when that query runs, with an error that names the missing column. The tests catch it, which is one more reason to have a test for every route. The checked macros of chapter 47 (query_as!) would catch it at compile time.
  • An Option<String> field is written as null in JSON when it is None.
  • Migrations only go forward. If you start the old program on the migrated database, SQLx refuses to continue, because the database has seen a migration that this program does not know. That protects the data from a program that does not understand its shape.
ChallengeLinks that expire

Let clients create links with a limited lifetime. The body of POST /links gets an optional field ttl_seconds (“time to live”). After that many seconds, following the link answers 410 Gone with the error the link '…' has expired, and the visit is not counted. A link without the field never expires. The lifetime must be at least 1 second and at most 10 years.

The interesting part is the test. A test must not wait 60 seconds to see a link expire. So the service must not ask the computer for the time directly. Give it a clock that tests can replace.

Need a hint?

Store the moment of expiry in a new column expires_at INTEGER, as seconds since 1970 (Unix time). NULL means “never”.

For the clock, add a field to AppState: pub clock: Clock, with pub type Clock = Arc<dyn Fn() -> i64 + Send + Sync>;. That is a shared closure which returns the current time in seconds (chapter 24, chapter 31). The real program passes a closure that reads SystemTime::now(). A test passes a closure that reads an AtomicI64, which the test can set to any moment.

Let the database decide about the expiry in the same statement that counts: … WHERE code = ? AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ?). If no row was changed, a second query finds out whether the link is unknown or expired. An enum with three variants is a good return type for visit.

Show solution and explanation

The migration:

A new rule in src/validate.rs:

A new variant in src/error.rs, and its arm in status:

In src/store.rs, Link gets the field pub expires_at: Option<i64>, and every list of columns gets expires_at. insert takes the moment of expiry as a third value, and visit gets a new return type:

In src/routes.rs, the clock and the state:

NewLink gets the field ttl_seconds: Option<i64>, and LinkView gets expires_at: Option<i64>. Two handlers and the helper change:

src/lib.rs re-exports the new names with pub use routes::{AppState, Clock, app, system_clock};, and main adds one line to the state: clock: system_clock(),.

In tests/api.rs, the application is built around a time that the test owns (this needs use std::sync::Arc; and use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicI64, Ordering};):

And the test travels through time without waiting:

The existing tests of the store must pass the new arguments, for example store.insert("docs", "https://docs.rs", None) and store.visit("docs", 0), and compare with Visit::Go(…) and Visit::Unknown.

What this exercise shows:

  • Time is an input. A function that reads the clock of the computer gives a different result on every call, which makes it hard to test. Passing the time in, as the parameter now of visit and as the closure in the state, makes the code deterministic: the same inputs give the same result. The same idea works for random numbers, for the file system and for other services. It is known as dependency injection.
  • (state.clock)() calls a closure that is stored in a field. The parentheses around state.clock are needed. Without them, Rust would look for a method named clock.
  • The expiry check is part of the UPDATE. Checking first and counting afterwards would again leave a gap between check and action.
  • Visit has three variants where an Option had two cases, and the match in follow must handle all three. A bool or a second Option would have hidden the third case.
  • 410 Gone says more than 404: the link existed, and it will not come back.
  • expires_at > ? means that the link is dead at the exact second of expiry. The test pins this down with the two moments 1,059 and 1,060. Boundaries are where mistakes of one hide, so test both sides.

What you have learned

Recap
  • A web service is easier to build and to change in layers: one speaks HTTP, one holds the rules, one owns the storage.
  • A repository type with a private pool keeps all SQL in one file, and gives tests a database of their own in an instant.
  • One error enum with IntoResponse gives every failure a status code and a uniform body. Internal details go to the log, not to the client.
  • Input is checked with allow lists, and reaches SQL only as bound parameters.
  • Let the database enforce uniqueness and do the counting, in single statements. A check followed by a separate action leaves a gap.
  • Routes that need protection live in a router of their own, wrapped by route_layer.
  • Settings and secrets come from environment variables, and a missing secret stops the program at the start.
  • oneshot hands a request straight to the router. Tests then cover everything from routing to SQL, without a network and in milliseconds.
  • A build script makes Cargo notice new migration files. The program applies them when it starts.
  • What is hard to test, such as the current time, becomes easy when it is passed in.
