Apps with a user interface: WebAssembly, Tauri and native windows

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain what WebAssembly is and what a module may and may not do
  • Compile a Rust function for the browser and call it from JavaScript
  • Change a web page from Rust, by hand and with the framework Leptos
  • Recognise the same ideas in Yew and Dioxus
  • Describe how a Tauri app divides the work between a web page and Rust
  • Tell apart the three designs of native GUI libraries, with egui, iced and Slint
  • Choose a toolkit for a given kind of app

Until now your programs talked through a terminal or answered HTTP requests. This chapter is about programs that people click on: pages in a browser, and windows on a desktop. Rust offers three roads to them:

  1. Rust inside a web page. The Rust code is compiled to WebAssembly and runs in the browser, next to JavaScript or in place of it.
  2. A web page inside a desktop window, with Rust behind it. This is the design of Tauri.
  3. Windows drawn by Rust itself. The libraries egui, iced and Slint stand for three different ways to do that.

To make the tools easy to compare, most examples build the same tiny program: a counter, which is a number, a button that raises it, and a button that sets it back to zero.

Good to know
How the programs of this chapter were tested

A program with a window cannot run in the playground, so the code blocks here have no Run button. Every program was built and started for this guide, with the crate versions shown: the WebAssembly examples in a real browser (Chromium), the desktop examples on Linux, with real mouse clicks on their buttons. Numbers and outputs are from those runs. This corner of the Rust world changes faster than the language itself. If a newer version rejects a line, the documentation of the crate shows the new spelling. The ideas stay.

WebAssembly: Rust in the browser

Real-world analogy
A calculator in a locked room

Imagine you hire a brilliant calculator, a person who computes anything you ask at great speed. For safety, this person sits in a locked room without windows. Slips of paper with numbers go in through a slot, and slips with numbers come out. The calculator cannot see your house and cannot touch anything in it. Whatever needs doing outside the room, you must do yourself, on request. A WebAssembly module is this calculator, the browser is the house, and JavaScript stands at the slot.

WebAssembly, short Wasm, is a compact format for program code. It is the machine language of an imagined, very simple computer. Every current browser contains a part that runs this code at high speed, next to its JavaScript engine. A compiler can produce Wasm in place of the machine code for your real processor, and the Rust compiler is one of the best at it.

Three properties shape everything that follows:

  • A module can only compute. By itself it cannot read a file, open a network connection or change the page. It may call the functions that the surrounding program hands to it, the imports, and it offers functions of its own, the exports. The surrounding program is called the host. In a browser, the host is the page with its JavaScript. A closed box like this is called a sandbox.
  • Only numbers cross the border. A Wasm function takes numbers and returns numbers. A text or a struct must be copied into the memory of the module, and then its address and length are passed. You met this problem in chapter 36, and the solution is the same: generated glue code.
  • Rust needs no helper inside the module. There is no garbage collector to ship, so the files are small. The first module of this chapter has 16 kilobytes.

The tools:

ToolWhat it does
target wasm32-unknown-unknownlets rustc produce Wasm. In this target triple (chapter 39), wasm32 is the processor, and the two unknowns say: no vendor, no operating system
crate wasm-bindgengenerates the glue: Rust code on one side of the border, a JavaScript file on the other
program wasm-packone command that runs Cargo, the glue generator and a size optimiser, and puts the result into a folder pkg

The wasm-bindgen documentation moved to wasm-bindgen.github.io. The older rustwasm.github.io documentation site is no longer maintained; this is a documentation move, not a statement that the crate itself has been discontinued.

A Rust function for a web page

Create a library with cargo new --lib wasm_hello. The manifest asks for a cdylib, the kind of library that a foreign host loads (chapter 36):

  • #[wasm_bindgen] exports a function and generates its glue. Without the attribute, a function stays private to the module, like is_prime here.
  • &str and String are allowed in the signature. The glue copies the text across the border in both directions.
  • Use u32, i32 and f64 for numbers. They match the JavaScript type number. (A u64 would arrive as a JavaScript BigInt, which is clumsier to use.)
  • The logic is plain Rust. cargo test runs the test on your own machine, without any browser.

Build the package:

On its first run, wasm-pack downloads the helper programs that it needs. The note about optional fields matters only if you publish the package. The folder pkg now holds four files that matter:

FileSizeContent
wasm_hello_bg.wasm15,724 bytesthe compiled Rust code
wasm_hello.js7,142 bytesthe glue: one JavaScript function for each export, and a loader
wasm_hello.d.tstype declarations for TypeScript, with your doc comments
package.jsonmakes the folder an npm package that can be published

The type declarations show how the two functions look from the other side:

What the glue does with a string

Here is the generated JavaScript function for greet, unchanged. It copies the name into the memory of the module and gets an address and a length (ptr0, len0). The Wasm function receives these two numbers and returns two numbers, the address and length of the answer. The glue reads the answer out as a JavaScript string, and finally asks the module to free the memory:

This is the hand-written FFI of chapter 36, written for you by a tool.

Now the page. Put this file next to Cargo.toml:

  • <script type="module"> lets the page use import.
  • init() downloads the .wasm file and prepares it. It is the default export of the glue file. After the await, the exported functions can be called like any JavaScript function.

A browser does not load modules from a page that was opened straight from the disk. The files must come from a web server, and a tiny one on your own machine is enough. Two that work:

Open http://localhost:8000. The page greets Sara, and a click on the button gives:

How fast is it?

The same loop was measured three ways on the same machine:

VersionTime
Rust, compiled for the processor (cargo run --release)0.51 s
Rust, compiled to Wasm, in Chromium0.52 s
the same loop written in JavaScript, in Chromium0.51 s

The three times are the same. (The last digit moves by one from run to run.) This loop spends nearly all of its time dividing, and a division takes the processor equally long, whoever asks for it. So the Wasm version reaches the full speed of a native program here. But so does JavaScript.

Key idea
What WebAssembly is good for

Wasm is not a magic “faster” button. A modern JavaScript engine compiles a simple number loop to very good machine code. Wasm pays off when you want to use Rust code in the browser: the validation rules that your server also uses, a parser, image or sound processing, a physics simulation, a crate from crates.io. It also gives steady speed, without pauses for garbage collection. And remember that every call across the border costs something, above all when texts are copied. Let one call do a lot of work.

wasm-pack can also build for other hosts. With --target nodejs, the result is a module for Node.js, the program that runs JavaScript outside the browser:

The default, --target bundler, produces a package for the build tools of large JavaScript projects, such as Vite or webpack.

Tip
Wasm outside the browser

The same module runs on a server, and that is how many teams sell “plug-ins with a safety rail”. wasmtime embeds a Wasm runtime in a Rust program: you load a module, give it a narrow set of allowed functions, and it can compute but cannot read your files or open a socket unless you hand it the capability. extism wraps that idea as a plug-in framework with host functions and a memory model for passing data both ways. The pattern is the one this chapter opened with — the calculator in the locked room — applied to user-supplied code: untrusted code runs at near-native speed, inside limits you set.

When a panic happens

A panic inside the module arrives in JavaScript as an error that says very little:

The crate console_error_panic_hook improves this. Call console_error_panic_hook::set_once(); once at the start, and the browser console shows the usual message:

Open the console with F12 in most browsers. It is the first place to look when a page with Wasm stays empty.

Changing the page from Rust

A web page is kept in the browser as a tree of objects: one for each heading, paragraph and button. This tree is the DOM (“document object model”). JavaScript changes the page by changing this tree. Rust can do the same through two crates of generated bindings:

  • web-sys covers what the browser offers: the DOM, network requests, drawing surfaces, storage, and much more.
  • js-sys covers what JavaScript itself offers: arrays, dates, promises.

web-sys is huge, so every browser type sits behind its own Cargo feature. If the compiler cannot find a method that the documentation shows, the feature for its type is missing.

The page only loads the module:

After wasm-pack build --target web, the page shows “Clicks: 0” and a button, and three clicks make it “Clicks: 3”. The new pieces:

  • #[wasm_bindgen(start)] marks a function that runs by itself as soon as the module is ready.
  • Browser functions that can fail return Result<_, JsValue>. A JsValue is “any JavaScript value”, here the error that was thrown.
  • Closure::new wraps a Rust closure so that JavaScript can call it. The closure owns clicks and label, which is why it is a move closure.
  • on_click.as_ref().unchecked_ref() hands the closure over as the JavaScript function that add_event_listener_with_callback expects.
  • on_click.forget() is the surprising line. The page will call the closure for as long as it lives, but JavaScript knows nothing about Rust ownership. If on_click were dropped at the end of start, the next click would call a closure that no longer exists, and the glue would report an error. forget gives the value up without dropping it. This small, deliberate leak is the normal pattern for a listener that stays for the whole life of the page.

It works, and the module is still small (21,891 bytes). But it took thirty lines for two elements and one event. Nobody builds a whole application this way. That is the job of a framework.

Wasm outside the browser

The locked room is useful in other houses too. Programs called Wasm runtimes run modules on a server or inside another application, as a safe way to run plug-ins and code from strangers. For these hosts there is a standard set of imports named WASI, which gives a module files, clocks and arguments, but only the ones that the host allows. Rust has targets for it. An ordinary main program compiles without changes:

The file notes.txt exists in the folder, and still the program cannot see it. The runtime wasmtime shows a module nothing unless told to. With permission for the current folder, the file appears:

How other languages do it
Other languages in the browser

JavaScript and TypeScript are at home in the browser. C and C++ reach it through Wasm as well, with a toolchain named Emscripten. Go and C# can be compiled to Wasm too, but they bring their runtime and garbage collector along, which makes the downloads much larger. Rust and C++ need neither, and Rust adds its safety and Cargo. This is why Rust became one of the most used languages for WebAssembly.

Web frameworks: Leptos, Yew, Dioxus

A framework for user interfaces turns the work around. You do not create elements and listeners by hand. You describe how the page looks for a given state, and the framework changes the page whenever the state changes. The description is split into components: functions that return a piece of the interface and can be used like new HTML tags.

Real-world analogy
A spreadsheet

In a spreadsheet, you type =A1*2 into cell B1 once. From then on, whenever A1 changes, B1 shows the new result by itself. Nobody writes code that says “when A1 changes, update B1”. Modern interface frameworks work like this. A piece of state is a cell, and the parts of the page that show it are the formulas.

A counter with Leptos

In Leptos, such a cell is called a signal: a value that remembers who reads it. The whole counter:

This is a normal binary project (cargo new), and the page is almost empty. The build tool for it is Trunk: it compiles the program to Wasm, generates the glue, adds the <script> to the page, and serves the result.

The first build takes a minute or two. Then Trunk serves the page at http://127.0.0.1:8080, opens it in the browser, and builds again whenever a file changes. trunk build --release writes the finished files into a folder dist, ready to be put on any web server.

Line by line:

  • #[component] turns a function into a component. Its parameters are the properties that the caller sets: <Counter start=0 />.
  • signal(start) creates a signal and returns two handles: count for reading and set_count for writing.
  • The view! macro contains the description. It looks like HTML and is checked by the compiler: a tag that is never closed is a compile error. Fixed text stands in quotes, and Rust expressions stand in braces.
  • {count} puts the signal into the page. Leptos notes that this spot depends on count.
  • on:click=… attaches a Rust closure to the click event. set_count.update(…) changes the value in place, and set_count.set(…) replaces it.
  • {move || if count.get() % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }} is a formula like =A1*2. Leptos runs the closure again each time a signal that it reads changes.

The function Counter itself runs only once. A click does not rebuild the page. It changes the signal, and the signal updates exactly the two spots that read it. The feature name csr stands for client-side rendering: the whole interface is built in the browser.

The same counter with Yew and Dioxus

Yew is the oldest of the three, and its design follows the JavaScript library React:

use_state keeps a value between runs of the function. Here the model is different from Leptos. count.set(…) asks Yew to run the whole function again. Yew compares the new description with the previous one and changes only what differs in the real page. This comparison is the technique known as the virtual DOM. The handle must be cloned into the closure, because both the closure and the html! block use it.

Dioxus uses signals as well, and writes the description in a syntax that looks like Rust instead of HTML:

The special strength of Dioxus is its range: the same components can run in a browser, in a desktop window and on a phone. It has its own build tool, dx. (For this guide, all three counters were built with Trunk. Dioxus looks for a page element with the id main to draw into.)

LeptosYewDioxus
Descriptionview!, like HTMLhtml!, like HTMLrsx!, like Rust
Statesignalshooks such as use_statesignals
On a changeonly the spots that read the signalthe component runs again, then a comparisonthe component runs again, then a comparison
Also offersrendering on the serverrendering on the serverdesktop and mobile apps, rendering on the server

What does a framework cost in download size? Measured for the counters above, as release builds:

CounterWasm filecompressed for transfer (gzip)
by hand with web-sys22 KB10 KB
Leptos210 KB54 KB
Yew338 KB93 KB

These are the sizes with default settings. The size settings of chapter 39 (opt-level = "z", lto = true) make them smaller. Most of the size is the framework itself, which is paid for only once.

One language on both sides

The examples above build the page in the browser, and the server only delivers files. Leptos and Dioxus can also run the same components on the server:

  • With server-side rendering, the server runs the components and sends finished HTML. The page is visible at once, even before the Wasm file has arrived, and search engines can read it.
  • In the browser, the Wasm program then takes over the existing HTML and attaches its event handlers. This step is called hydration.
  • A server function is a function that is written among the components, but runs on the server. The browser version of the program contains only a small stand-in with the same name, which sends an HTTP request.

The attribute #[server] generates both versions, and a type SaveNote that stands for a call of the function. The body is compiled only into the server program, so it may use the database and secrets. The component sends its form to save_note and shows the answer. The argument and the result travel as serialised data. Both sides are compiled from the same source, so their types cannot drift apart. (This listing was compiled in both modes for this guide, but not run. A complete project also needs a server program, usually built on Axum, and the build tool cargo-leptos sets one up.)

How other languages do it
JavaScript frameworks

If you know React, Yew will feel familiar: function components, hooks, a virtual DOM. Leptos is closer to SolidJS, where signals update the page directly and components run once. Dioxus sits between the two. Compared with JavaScript frameworks, the Rust ones give you the compiler’s checks across the whole application, and they let server and browser share types. The price is a longer build and a larger first download.

Tauri: a web page in a desktop window

Real-world analogy
A restaurant

A restaurant has a dining room and a kitchen. The dining room is what the guests see, and it can be redecorated freely. The kitchen holds the knives and the fire. Guests never enter the kitchen. They order from the menu, a waiter carries the order through the door, and brings back a dish. In a Tauri app, the dining room is a web page, the kitchen is a Rust program, and the menu is a list of Rust functions that the page may call.

A Tauri app is one program with two parts:

  • A window that shows a web page. Tauri does not bring a browser. It uses the webview that the operating system already has: a component that displays web pages inside another program.
  • A Rust program behind it, which may do everything a Rust program may do: read files, talk to devices, start threads.

The page can be made with anything that produces HTML: plain HTML and JavaScript, a JavaScript framework, or one of the Rust frameworks from the previous section.

The project

Tauri needs a few system libraries. On Linux these are the development packages of WebKitGTK and GTK. On Windows it is the WebView2 component, which current Windows versions include, and on macOS the developer tools of Xcode. The “Prerequisites” page of the Tauri documentation lists the exact packages for each system.

Two small tools create and run projects:

The options answer the questions that the tool would otherwise ask one by one. -t vanilla chooses the template with a page in plain HTML and JavaScript, and -m cargo says that no JavaScript tooling is used. The identifier is a unique name for the app, written like a web address in reverse. -y accepts the defaults for the rest. The project has two halves:

The example app does something that a page in a browser cannot do: it reads a file from the disk by its path, and counts its lines and words. Replace the generated lib.rs, index.html and main.js with these:

Start it from the project folder:

The first build compiles a few hundred crates and takes several minutes. Then a window opens. Type the path of a small text file and press Count. For a test file of four lines, the window shows:

A path that does not exist gives the message from the Err branch:

Cargo also prints a warning: the dependency tauri-plugin-opener is unused. The template needed it for the two links on its page. To get rid of the warning, delete that line from src-tauri/Cargo.toml, and the entry "opener:default" from src-tauri/capabilities/default.json.

How the two halves talk:

  • #[tauri::command] puts a function on the menu. The page calls it by name with invoke("file_stats", { path: … }).
  • The arguments travel as JSON, and Serde fills the Rust parameters from it. The return value travels back the same way: FileStats derives Serialize and arrives as a JavaScript object with the fields lines, words and bytes.
  • invoke returns a promise. Ok(value) fulfils it, and Err(message) rejects it, which lands in the catch block. The error type must be serialisable, and a String is the simplest choice.
  • State<'_, History> is data that lives as long as the app. It is registered once with .manage(…), and any command can ask for it as a parameter. Several commands may run at the same moment, so the data sits in a Mutex (chapter 31).
  • generate_handler![…] is the menu itself. A function that is not listed there cannot be called from the page.
Watch out
Names change their style at the border

JavaScript names are written in camelCase, and Tauri converts the names of arguments. A Rust parameter file_path must be passed from JavaScript as filePath. With the wrong spelling, the call is rejected with this message: “invalid args filePath for command file_stats: command file_stats missing required key filePath”.

Treat the page like a client on the network. Check every argument inside the command, as you do in a web handler (chapter 46). Tauri adds a second line of defence, the capabilities: the files in src-tauri/capabilities list which built-in features of Tauri a window may use, such as file dialogs, notifications or the clipboard. What is not listed is refused. Most of these features come as plug-in crates with names like tauri-plugin-dialog.

cargo tauri build produces the installers for the system it runs on. For the example, the package for Debian and Ubuntu came to 1.8 MB, with a program of 5 MB inside. The package names the WebKitGTK library of the system as a requirement, which is exactly why it can be this small.

How other languages do it
Electron

Electron is the best-known way to build desktop apps from web pages. Editors and chat programs that you may use every day are built with it. An Electron app ships a complete browser and the Node.js runtime, so even a small one is a download of roughly a hundred megabytes, and each running app holds its own browser in memory. Tauri uses the webview of the system and a compiled Rust program, which makes apps much smaller. In exchange, the page is shown by a different engine on each system, and must be tested on each.

Native windows: egui, iced, Slint

The third road uses no web technology. The library opens a window and draws everything in it. Two words first:

  • A widget is a building block of an interface: a label, a button, a text field, a slider.
  • The event loop is the endless loop at the heart of every graphical program: wait for the next event (a click, a key, a timer), react, draw, repeat. The library runs this loop. Your code is called from inside it, which is why main ends with a call like run that returns only when the window closes.

The libraries differ in how your code is called, and there are three main designs. All three programs below were built and clicked for this guide. Each library brings 240 to 350 crates, so the first build takes a few minutes.

egui: describe the window again for every frame

egui is an immediate mode library. (eframe is the companion crate that opens the window for it.) The closure runs each time the window must be drawn, which happens after every event. Each run describes the complete content of the window from top to bottom. There are no widget objects that live on. ui.button("Click me") draws the button and reports in the same call whether it was clicked just now, so the reaction is an ordinary if.

The state is a normal variable, and the label shows its current value simply because the label is described anew every time. No signals, no messages, no callbacks. For tools, editors for game data, and control panels, this is the fastest way to a working window. The costs: the whole description runs again for every frame, complex layouts are harder to express, and egui draws its own style of widgets, which looks the same on every system and native on none. egui programs can also be compiled to Wasm and run inside a web page.

iced: state, messages, update, view

iced follows a design that is named the Elm architecture, after the language that made it popular. It has four parts:

  • the state: one struct, here Counter;
  • the messages: an enum with one variant for everything that can happen;
  • update: the only place where the state changes, by handling one message;
  • view: a function that describes the window for the current state. Widgets do not change anything. They only say which message to send: .on_press(Message::Clicked).

iced runs the cycle: draw the view, wait for a message, call update, draw the view again. This is more to write than the egui version. In return, every change in the program passes through one match, which is easy to read, to log and to test: update is a plain method that needs no window. The exercise at the end of the chapter tests one. iced is the base of COSMIC, a complete desktop environment for Linux.

Slint: the interface in its own language

Slint describes the interface in a small markup language of its own, a language made for describing what is on the screen. The slint! macro compiles this description into a Rust struct, here CounterWindow. Larger projects keep the markup in .slint files, and an editor extension shows a live preview of them.

  • in-out property <int> count declares a piece of state that Rust can read and write. The macro generates get_count and set_count.
  • text: "Clicks: " + root.count; is a binding: a formula as in the spreadsheet. When count changes, the text follows.
  • Simple reactions stay in the markup: clicked => { root.count += 1; }.
  • callback reset(); declares an event that the Rust side handles. The macro generates on_reset, which takes a closure.
  • The closure must not own the window, because the window owns the closure, and the two would keep each other alive for ever. as_weak() gives a weak handle, the same idea as Weak in chapter 27.

Slint was designed for devices with small screens and little memory as well as for desktops, and the same markup can be used from C++, JavaScript and Python. Read its licence before you use it in a product: Slint is offered under the GPL, under a free licence with conditions, and under a paid one. egui and iced use the permissive MIT licence (egui also Apache-2.0), like most Rust crates.

eguiicedSlint
Designimmediate modeElm architecturemarkup with bindings
State lives inyour variablesone state structproperties of the components
A click becomestrue from .clicked()a message for updatea callback or a line of markup
Good first choice fortools, debug panels, quick resultsapplications with a clear structuredesigned interfaces, small devices
Good to know
Check toolkit maturity before choosing

These projects do not all promise the same stability. The egui documentation warns that it is under heavy development and that releases may include breaking changes. The iced project describes itself as experimental and its own documentation may assume advanced Rust knowledge. Before adopting either for a long-lived product, check the exact release’s changelog, minimum supported Rust version, supported platforms, and migration policy. The examples here teach their core models; they are not a guarantee of API stability.

More names you will meet: gtk4 with relm4 on top binds the GTK toolkit of the GNOME desktop. cxx-qt connects Rust to the Qt toolkit. And ratatui builds full-screen interfaces inside a terminal (chapter 44).

How other languages do it
GUI libraries elsewhere

egui is modelled on Dear ImGui, a C++ library that is popular for tools in game studios. The Elm architecture of iced is the idea behind Redux in the JavaScript world. The markup of Slint will remind you of QML from Qt, and its bindings of SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose. In C++, C# or Swift, one toolkit usually dominates a platform. Rust has no such standard yet, and several good candidates.

Phones

Rust runs well on Android and iOS, and there are two ways to use it there. Both need the development tools of the platform (Android Studio, Xcode), and neither was tried for this guide.

  • A whole app from one of the toolkits. Tauri 2 and Dioxus can build Android and iOS apps from the same project as the desktop version.
  • A Rust core under a native interface. The data model, the rules and the network code are written once in Rust. The interface is written in Swift and Kotlin, the languages of the two platforms. The tool uniffi generates the bindings between them. Large apps use this to share one tested core between their iPhone, Android and desktop versions.

Choosing

You want to…A good first choice
speed up one part of a web site, or use Rust code in itwasm-bindgen with wasm-pack
write a whole web application in RustLeptos, Dioxus or Yew
build a desktop app, and you know HTML and CSSTauri
make a tool or a control panel quicklyegui
build a desktop app in pure Rust with a clear structureiced
realise a designed interface, also on small devicesSlint
stay in the terminalratatui
build a phone app with the native looka Rust core with uniffi
Key idea
Keep the logic out of the interface

Whichever toolkit you choose, put the rules of your program into plain functions and types, in a library crate without any interface code. count_primes and the update method of the iced counter are tested with cargo test, without a browser or a window. The same crate can then serve a command-line tool, a web server, a Wasm module and a desktop app. Toolkits change quickly. Well-tested logic stays.

Recap
  • WebAssembly is a compact code format that browsers run in a sandbox. A module can only compute, and reaches the outside through imports and exports.
  • wasm-bindgen generates the glue between Rust and JavaScript, and wasm-pack build produces a ready package. web-sys gives Rust the browser’s own functions.
  • Wasm is worth it for using Rust code in the browser and for steady speed. A simple loop is not faster than in JavaScript.
  • WASI and runtimes such as wasmtime run Wasm modules outside the browser, with only the permissions that the host grants.
  • Leptos, Yew and Dioxus describe the page as components. Signals update the spots that read them. Yew runs the component again and compares.
  • A Tauri app is a web page in the system’s webview with a Rust program behind it. The page calls #[tauri::command] functions with invoke.
  • egui describes the window anew for every frame. iced sends messages to one update function. Slint uses a markup language with bindings.
  • Keep the logic in a library crate, where it is tested without any interface.
Check your understanding
1

What can a WebAssembly module do without any help from its host?

A module is a sandbox. Files, the network and the page are reachable only through functions that the host passes in as imports. This is what web-sys and WASI do.

2

Why does the hand-written counter call on_click.forget()?

JavaScript holds only a reference to the closure and knows nothing about Rust ownership. Without forget, the closure would be dropped at the end of start, and the next click would fail.

3

In the Leptos counter, what happens when set_count.update(…) runs?

A signal knows its readers. The component function ran once, and afterwards the signal updates exactly the text node and the closure that use it.

4

Why is a Tauri app much smaller than an Electron app?

The window of a Tauri app is drawn by the system’s own web component. The app contains only your page and the compiled Rust program.

5

Which sentence describes an immediate mode library such as egui?

The second answer is the Elm architecture of iced, and the last one is Slint. In egui, if ui.button("…").clicked() both draws and asks.

Guided exerciseText statistics in the browser

Build a page with a text area. While the user types, the page shows the number of lines, words and letters of the text. The counting is done by one Rust function text_stats that returns all three numbers at once.

Need a hint?

wasm-bindgen can export a struct: put #[wasm_bindgen] on a pub struct whose public fields are numbers. In JavaScript the returned value is then an object with these fields. Listen for the input event of the text area.

Show solution and explanation

The manifest is the one of wasm_hello with another name. For the text “Selam, world!” followed by a second line “2 lines”, the page shows 2 lines, 4 words, 15 letters.

An exported struct stays inside the memory of the module, and JavaScript receives a small object that points to it. Reading stats.lines calls a generated function that fetches the number. Since the data lives in the module, somebody must free it: stats.free() does it at once. Without the call, the glue frees the struct when the JavaScript object is collected as garbage, at some later time. The test runs with plain cargo test.

PracticeA temperature converter with Leptos

Write a Leptos page with one text field for a temperature in degrees Celsius. Below it, the page shows the temperature in Fahrenheit (multiply by 9/5, then add 32), and follows every keystroke. If the field does not contain a number, the page says so.

Need a hint?

Keep the text of the field in a signal, and compute the output in a move || closure that parses it. An input reports changes through on:input, and the helper event_target_value(&event) returns its current text. prop:value=… sets the content of the field.

Show solution and explanation

Cargo.toml and index.html are the ones of the Leptos counter. The field starts with 20 and the page shows 68.0 °F. Typing 100 gives 212.0 °F, and abc gives the request for a number.

Only one signal is needed. The Fahrenheit text is not state of its own: it is derived from the Celsius text, like a formula cell. The closure fahrenheit reads the signal with .get(), so Leptos runs it again after every set. Storing the result in a second signal would be an invitation for the two to disagree.

ChallengeA counter with a step, in iced

Extend the iced counter. A text field holds the step, and a button “Add” adds the step to the count. The step may be negative. While the field does not contain a whole number, the Add button is disabled. Write a test for update that needs no window.

Need a hint?

The view must not change the state, so the text of the field is part of the state, and every keystroke is a message: text_input("Step", &self.step_text).on_input(Message::StepChanged). Parse the text in view. A button made with .on_press_maybe(option) is disabled when the option is None.

Show solution and explanation
  • The message Add carries the step that was valid when the button was drawn, so update has nothing left to check. step.map(Message::Add) turns the Option<i64> into an Option<Message>, because a tuple variant can be used as a function.
  • Message can no longer be Copy, since one variant holds a String.
  • saturating_add stops at the largest i64 where + would overflow and panic in a debug build. A user can type a very large step.
  • The test drives the program through its messages, exactly as the window would, and runs in a fraction of a second with cargo test.

Games, small devices and data

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain the game loop and why movement is multiplied by the frame time
  • Write a small game with macroquad
  • Describe entities, components and systems, and run a Bevy app
  • Say what no_std means and what core still offers
  • Run a program for a microcontroller in an emulator and read its layers: PAC, HAL, embedded-hal, drivers
  • Test device logic on your own machine with a fake pin
  • Calculate with tables of numbers in ndarray and summarise data with Polars
  • Explain how a program learns a line from data

Three more fields where Rust is used, and each of them could fill a book of its own. This chapter gives you a first working program in each field, the two or three ideas that everything else builds on, and a map of the crates.

Good to know
How the programs of this chapter were tested

The games were built and played on Linux with real key presses. The program for a microcontroller ran in an emulator. The program for the Raspberry Pi Pico was compiled for that chip, but not loaded onto a real board. The other examples that show an output were run by the checker of this guide, like the examples of the earlier chapters.

Games

Real-world analogy
A flip book

A flip book is a stack of drawings, each a little different from the one before. Flip through it quickly and the figure moves. A game does the same thing, but it makes each drawing at the moment it is needed: it looks at what the player is doing, moves everything a tiny step, draws the picture, and starts again. Sixty times a second.

One round of this is a frame, and the endless repetition is the game loop:

  1. Input: which keys are down, where is the mouse?
  2. Update: move things, detect collisions, count points.
  3. Draw: paint the new picture.

A complete small game with macroquad

The library macroquad gives you exactly this loop and a handful of drawing functions, and nothing to configure. The game below has a ball that bounces off the walls, and a paddle that the player moves with the arrow keys. Every hit with the paddle is a point. When the ball falls past the paddle, the game starts over.

cargo run opens a blue window with a yellow ball, a white paddle, and the score.

  • #[macroquad::main("Keep it up")] opens the window with this title and then runs your function. The function is async for a simple reason: next_frame().await is the place where it pauses, the finished picture goes to the screen, and the library collects new input. You need no async runtime for this.
  • The body of loop is one frame, and the three steps are easy to see.
  • The variables before the loop are the whole state of the game.

The most important detail is * seconds. Frames do not take equally long. A fast machine draws more of them per second than a slow one. If the ball moved a fixed distance per frame, the game would run faster on a faster machine. So speeds are given in pixels per second, and each frame moves things by speed × the time that has passed since the last frame. This time is called the delta time.

Tip
Start small

macroquad compiles in well under a minute and needs about 30 crates. It is a good place to learn how games work. The usual next steps are pictures with load_texture, sounds, and a struct for each kind of thing in the game.

Bevy: entities, components, systems

A larger game has hundreds of kinds of things: players, enemies, bullets, doors, sounds, particles. Keeping each in its own variable and its own block of the loop stops working. Bevy, the best-known game engine written in Rust, organises a game in a way called ECS:

  • An entity is a thing in the game. By itself it is only an identity number.
  • A component is a piece of data attached to an entity: a position, a velocity, a health value. An entity is defined by the components it carries.
  • A system is a function that runs every frame and works on all entities that have certain components.
Real-world analogy
A table with optional columns

Think of a big table. Every row is an entity, and every column is a kind of component. A cell may be empty: a tree has a position but no velocity. A system is a rule such as “for every row that has both a position and a velocity, add the velocity to the position”. The rule does not care what else the row contains, or what the thing “is”.

Here is that rule as a program. It runs three frames without opening a window:

  • A component is an ordinary struct with #[derive(Component)].
  • commands.spawn(…) creates an entity from a tuple of components.
  • A system is an ordinary function. Its parameters say what it needs, and Bevy passes it in. You saw the same trick with the extractors of Axum in chapter 46.
  • Query<(&mut Position, &Velocity)> means: every entity that has both components, with the position writable. The tree has no Velocity, so movement never sees it. report asks only for a label and a position, and gets all three.
  • add_systems(Startup, …) registers systems that run once. Those under Update run every frame. .chain() fixes their order: first move, then report.
  • The tree is printed first although it was created last. Bevy stores entities with the same set of components together, and a query walks through these groups. Never rely on the order.

Two things make this design more than a matter of taste. It composes: to make the tree fall over, you add a Velocity to it, and the existing system moves it. No class has to be rewritten. And it is fast: the components of one kind lie side by side in memory, as in the “struct of arrays” layout of chapter 37. Bevy also reads from the parameters which systems touch the same data. Systems that do not get in each other’s way run on several cores at the same time. These are the borrowing rules, applied to whole functions: many readers or one writer.

A window and the keyboard

A real Bevy game adds DefaultPlugins, which brings the window, the renderer, input and sound. This program shows a square that follows the arrow keys:

  • Camera2d is the eye that looks at the 2D world. Without a camera, nothing is drawn.
  • Sprite is a coloured rectangle or a picture, and Transform is its position, rotation and size. Both are components that Bevy provides, and its own systems draw every entity that has them.
  • Player is a component without data, a marker. With<Player> picks the entity without reading anything from it.
  • Res<…> asks for a resource: a value that exists once for the whole game, such as the clock (Time) or the state of the keyboard.
  • Single<…> is a query that expects exactly one match.
  • time.delta_secs() is the delta time. The speed is 200 pixels per second, however many frames the computer manages to draw.

The first build of a Bevy program compiles about 400 crates and takes many minutes. Later builds are much faster. On Linux, Bevy needs the development packages for sound and input devices (ALSA and udev). The setup page of the Bevy documentation lists them for each distribution.

CrateWhat it is
macroquada small library for 2D games: a loop and drawing functions
ggezanother small 2D library, in the style of the LÖVE framework
bevya complete engine built on ECS, for 2D and 3D
fyroxa 3D engine that comes with a scene editor
godotlets you write the scripts of the Godot engine in Rust
wgputalks to the graphics card. Most of the others build on it
rapier2d, rapier3dphysics: gravity, collisions, joints
How other languages do it
Game engines elsewhere

Unity (C#), Unreal (C++) and Godot (its own language, C# or C++) are complete studios with a visual editor, where levels are built with the mouse and scripts are attached to objects. In Bevy, the game is described in code. ECS is not a Rust invention. Large studios use it in C++ for its speed. But it suits Rust well, because data that lives in tables and is borrowed by systems never needs the webs of pointers between objects that the borrow checker dislikes.

Small devices

A microcontroller is a complete computer on one small chip: a processor, some memory, and pins that can switch things on and measure things. It sits in washing machines, keyboards, cars and toys, costs about as much as a cup of coffee, and has perhaps 64 kilobytes of memory where your laptop has billions of bytes. Programming such chips is called embedded programming.

There is no operating system on such a chip. Your program is the only program. It starts when the power comes on, and it must never end. Nothing protects it: no system stops a program that writes outside its memory. This is called running on bare metal, and it is where Rust’s guarantees are worth the most. Rust also fits for a second reason. It has no garbage collector and no runtime, so a whole program can fit in a few kilobytes.

no_std: Rust without an operating system

The standard library assumes an operating system: files, threads, a heap, a clock. On a chip none of this exists, so embedded programs start with the attribute #![no_std] and use a smaller library instead:

LibraryNeedsContains
corenothingnumbers, Option, Result, slices, str, iterators, closures, traits, formatting, atomics
alloca heap that you set upBox, Vec, String, Rc, Arc, BTreeMap
stdan operating systemall of the above, and files, network, threads, HashMap, println!

Nearly everything you learned about the language is in core. std re-exports it, which is why std::option::Option and core::option::Option are the same type.

A program for a chip, run in an emulator

You do not need hardware for a first try. The program QEMU imitates whole computers, among them a board with an ARM Cortex-M3 chip. Install it from your package manager or from its web site. The part needed here is called qemu-system-arm. The compiler needs the target for this processor family, which has no operating system in its name:

The project has four small files besides Cargo.toml:

What is new:

  • #![no_main] and #[entry]: there is no operating system that could call main. The crate cortex-m-rt contains the start-up code of the chip, and #[entry] tells it which function to jump to.
  • -> !: the function never returns. There is nothing to return to.
  • memory.x tells the linker where the chip keeps its program (FLASH, which survives without power) and its working memory (RAM). Every chip has its own numbers.
  • hprintln! prints through a channel to the developer’s computer, called semihosting. A chip has no screen. On real hardware the text travels through the debug cable.
  • use panic_semihosting as _; selects a panic handler. Without an operating system, somebody has to say what a panic does, and a no_std program does not compile without one. This crate prints the message and stops. A product would rather restart the device.
  • .cargo/config.toml sets the target for the project and makes cargo run start the emulator.

Now look at the last two lines of the output. The index 7 is outside the array, and the program stopped with a clear message, on a chip, without an operating system. The same mistake in C would read whatever happens to lie behind the array and carry on with a wrong number. All checks of Rust work on bare metal, because they are part of the compiled program and need no help from outside.

The release build of this program occupies 5,996 bytes of the chip’s 256 kilobytes.

The layers of embedded Rust

Nobody writes to the registers of a chip by hand for long. The crates form layers:

LayerWhat it gives youExamples
PAC, “peripheral access crate”every register of one chip by name, generated from the maker’s descriptionrp-pac, stm32-metapac
HAL, “hardware abstraction layer”safe types for the pins, timers and serial ports of one chip familyembassy-rp, stm32f4xx-hal, esp-hal
embedded-haltraits that all HALs implement: OutputPin, InputPin, I2c, SpiBus, DelayNs
driverscode for a sensor, a display or a radio, written against the traitshundreds on crates.io

The third layer is the clever one. A driver that asks for “anything that implements OutputPin” works on every chip that has a HAL. The same idea also lets you test device logic at your desk. This controller for a fan knows nothing about any chip:

On a device, FanControl::new would receive a real pin from the HAL. In the test it receives FakePin, and the logic can be checked in milliseconds, without a soldering iron. This is the dependency injection of chapter 48, with a pin in the role of the clock.

In a HAL, every pin is a value, and you can only get it once. Two parts of a program cannot drive the same pin by accident, because one of them does not own it. The type of a pin also records whether it is set up as an input or an output, so reading an output pin is a compile error. Ownership and the typestate pattern of chapter 29 turn wiring mistakes into compiler messages.

Async on a chip: Embassy

A device often does several things at once: blink a light, watch a button, read a sensor every second. Without an operating system there are no threads. The classic answer is a hand-written state machine driven by interrupts. Rust has a better one. async functions are state machines that the compiler writes (chapter 32), and they need no heap. Embassy is an async runtime for microcontrollers, with HALs for many chip families. This program for the Raspberry Pi Pico blinks two lights at different speeds:

  • embassy_rp::init returns all peripherals of the chip as one struct of values, each of which can be moved out once.
  • Each spawner.spawn(…) starts a task. pool_size = 2 reserves room for two tasks of this kind at compile time, because there is no heap to take it from.
  • Timer::after_millis(…).await does not spin in a loop. The task sleeps, and when all tasks sleep, the processor itself sleeps and saves power until a timer wakes it.

Compiled for the Pico (target thumbv6m-none-eabi), the whole program, with the runtime, two tasks and the timer driver, occupies 13,224 bytes of flash memory and 516 bytes of RAM. It was not loaded onto a board for this guide. The usual tool for that step is probe-rs, which flashes the binary through a debug probe and streams logs back over RTT. On tight microcontrollers, pair probe-rs with defmt (“deferred formatting”): instead of formatting numbers into text on the chip, the firmware emits compact numeric token IDs (defmt::info!("temp={=i16}", t)) and probe-rs formats them on your laptop, saving kilobytes of flash and cycles.

Collections and messages without a heap

Two crates replace things that are missing without std. heapless offers collections with a fixed capacity, which is part of their type. They live wherever the variable lives, and a full collection gives the value back instead of growing:

postcard is a Serde format (chapter 43) for small devices. It works without a heap and produces very few bytes, which matters when a message travels over a slow radio link:

The five bytes contain no field names and no punctuation, only the values in the order of the struct. Both sides must therefore use the same struct definition, which is easy when both are written in Rust and share a crate.

How other languages do it
Embedded programming elsewhere

C and C++ run on almost every chip ever made, and the makers’ own tools are written for them. They give the same control as Rust and none of its checks. MicroPython and the Arduino environment are friendlier for a first blinking light, at the price of speed, memory, or safety. Rust is younger here, and not every chip has a good HAL yet. Where it has, you get the speed and size of C with ownership, Result, async and Cargo.

Data and machine learning

Tables of numbers: ndarray

Science and statistics work with whole tables of numbers at once. The crate ndarray provides arrays with any number of dimensions and arithmetic on all their elements, in the style of NumPy from the Python world:

  • An operator between an array and a number, or between two arrays of the same shape, works element by element.
  • An axis is a direction through the array. “The mean along axis 1” walks across the columns and leaves one number per row.
  • s![0..2, 2..] describes a slice with one range per dimension. Like a slice of a Vec, it is a view, and nothing is copied.
  • dot is the matrix product. Here it multiplies every row with the weights and adds up.

For small vectors and matrices of fixed size, as games, robots and graphics need them, the crate nalgebra is the usual choice.

Tables of records: Polars

Business data looks different: rows of records with named columns of mixed types. A table of this kind is called a data frame. Polars is a data frame library written in Rust. It is best known through its Python version, and it is used from Rust in the same way. The next program computes the first table of the sales report from chapter 26, from a file sales.csv with the valid rows of that chapter:

  • The program first describes the work: read, add a column, group, summarise, sort. Nothing happens until collect(). Polars then plans the whole job, reads only the columns that are needed, and uses all processor cores. This is the laziness of iterators (chapter 25) on a larger scale.
  • col("quantity") * col("unit_price") is not a multiplication of two numbers. It builds a description of a calculation for whole columns.
  • The types of the columns are found by looking at the file.

In chapter 26 this table took a struct, a parser and a HashMap. That was the right exercise. For real data work, a data frame library is the right tool: it handles millions of rows, missing values, joins between tables and many file formats. Be prepared for the cost: Polars is one of the largest crates there is, and its first build takes a long time.

How a program learns

Machine learning means that a program finds the numbers of a formula by itself, from examples. The smallest example fits on one screen. Given a few pairs of “hours studied” and “mark”, find the line mark = slope × hours + offset that fits them best:

The loop is the heart of nearly all machine learning:

  • The model is a formula with adjustable numbers, the parameters. Here there are two. A large language model has billions.
  • The loss is one number that says how wrong the model is on the examples: here the average squared error.
  • The gradient says, for each parameter, how the loss changes when that parameter grows a little. The formulas for it come from calculus.
  • Each step moves every parameter a little in the direction that lowers the loss. The size of the step is the learning rate. This procedure is called gradient descent.

Run it and watch the loss fall. After a thousand steps the program has found a slope near 5 and an offset near 50, although nobody told it these numbers.

A machine learning library does the same with more comfort. It stores the numbers in arrays with many dimensions, called tensors, computes the gradients automatically for any formula, and runs the arithmetic on a graphics card.

CrateWhat it is for
ndarray, nalgebraarrays and linear algebra
polarsdata frames
arrow, parquetthe standard formats for tables in memory and on disk
datafusionan engine that runs SQL queries over such tables
linfaclassic methods: regression, clustering, decision trees
burna deep learning framework written in Rust, with training, for processors, graphics cards and the browser
candlea small framework for running neural networks, from the company Hugging Face
ort, tchbindings to the ONNX Runtime and to the engine of PyTorch
tokenizerssplits text into the pieces that language models read
rig-core, async-openaibuilding LLM-powered applications, structured prompts, embeddings, and tool-calling agents

Choosing between them, in three lines each:

  • candle — a small, readable framework from Hugging Face for running models, with Metal and CUDA backends. Choose it to serve an inference endpoint or run a model on a device; the weights of most published models load directly.
  • burn — a full framework with training, a backend abstraction (CPU, GPU, browser through WebAssembly) and its own tensor library. Choose it when you are training as well as running, and want one codebase for several targets.
  • tch and ort — bindings to LibTorch (PyTorch’s engine) and the ONNX Runtime. Choose them when you must run an existing model exactly as its authors trained it, and accept shipping a large native library alongside your binary.
  • linfa — the classic algorithms: regression, clustering, decision trees, with an API modelled on scikit-learn. Choose it for tabular prediction where a small, explainable model beats a neural network — which is most of the time.
  • polars, datafusion, duckdb — three ways to the same goal: query tables without loading them into a database. Polars is the data-frame library, DataFusion is an engine you embed in a program, DuckDB is a SQL database that reads Parquet and CSV files directly.
  • arrow and parquet — Arrow is the in-memory column format that Polars, DataFusion, pandas and Spark all speak; Parquet is its compressed form on disk. Together they are why a Rust data pipeline can hand its output to a Python notebook without a conversion step.
How other languages do it
Rust and Python in data science

Python is the language in which data scientists think and try things out, and that will not change soon. But much of what makes Python fast today is Rust underneath: Polars, the tokenizers library, the validation core of Pydantic, the tools ruff and uv. They are Python modules built with PyO3, like the one in chapter 36 that was 27 times faster than its Python version. Reach for Rust when a data job must run fast and reliably day after day, when a trained model has to answer requests with little memory, when it has to run in a browser or on a device, or when a Python library needs a fast core.

Recap
  • A game repeats input, update and draw for every frame. Speeds are multiplied by the delta time, so that the game runs equally fast on every machine.
  • macroquad offers a loop and drawing functions. Bevy organises a game as entities, components and systems, and runs systems in parallel when their data allows it.
  • A microcontroller has no operating system. #![no_std] programs use core, choose a panic handler, and describe the memory of the chip to the linker.
  • Rust’s checks work on bare metal: an index out of bounds stops the program instead of reading foreign memory.
  • PAC, HAL, the embedded-hal traits and drivers are the layers of embedded Rust. Logic written against the traits is tested on a normal computer with fake pins.
  • Embassy runs async tasks on a chip, without threads and without a heap. heapless and postcard provide collections and messages of fixed, small size.
  • ndarray calculates with whole arrays, and Polars with tables of records, lazily and on all cores.
  • Machine learning adjusts the parameters of a model step by step to lower a loss. Gradient descent is the basic procedure.
Check your understanding
1

A game moves a ball with ball.x += 5.0; once per frame. What is wrong with that?

The distance should depend on the time that has passed, not on the number of frames: ball.x += speed * delta_time.

2

In the Bevy example, why does the system movement never touch the tree?

A query matches the entities that have all the requested components. What an entity “is” follows from the components it carries.

3

Which of these is available in a #![no_std] program without any further setup?

They are part of core, which needs nothing from the outside. Vec needs a heap (alloc), and files and println! need an operating system (std).

4

What is the point of the traits in embedded-hal?

FanControl<P: OutputPin> runs on any chip, and on your desk with FakePin. This is ordinary generic programming with traits.

5

In the line-fitting program, what does one step of gradient descent do?

The gradient tells for each parameter which way the loss falls. Many small steps in that direction lead to parameters that fit the data.

Guided exerciseGravity for some

Take the Bevy example with labels, positions and velocities. Add a marker component Falling. A new system gravity reduces the vertical velocity of every falling entity by 10 per frame. Another system removes entities that have dropped below the height 0, and says so. Create a falling stone and a rising balloon, both at height 100, and run five frames.

Need a hint?

Query<&mut Velocity, With<Falling>> selects by the marker without reading it. To remove an entity, a query can ask for its identity with the special type Entity, and commands.entity(entity).despawn() deletes it. Chain the four systems in an order that makes sense: gravity, movement, removal, report.

Show solution and explanation

gravity changes only velocities, and movement is the unchanged system of the chapter: it moves the stone faster each frame without knowing why. The balloon has no Falling marker and keeps rising. Commands such as despawn are collected and carried out between systems, so the stone is already gone when report runs in the same frame.

PracticeA long press

Write a type LongPress<P> for a push button on any chip. Its method check is meant to be called at a regular pace. It returns true once when the button has been held down for a given number of checks in a row. A pressed button connects its pin to ground, so “pressed” means that the pin is low. Test the type on your machine with a fake pin that plays back a list of states.

Need a hint?

The trait for reading is embedded_hal::digital::InputPin, with the methods is_high and is_low. Both take &mut self and return a Result. Count consecutive low readings, and reset the count on a high one. Returning true only when the count equals the limit reports each long press once.

Show solution and explanation

The button is released at check 2, so the first two readings do not count. Checks 3, 4 and 5 are low, and the third of them reports the long press. Checks 6 and 7 are still low, but the count has passed 3 and nothing more is reported. The same LongPress compiles for a real chip, where a timer would call check every few milliseconds.

ChallengeStandard scores

Take the table of test scores from the ndarray example. Write a function that scales every column so that its mean is 0 and its standard deviation is 1. This makes tests of different difficulty comparable. Write a second function that returns, for every test, the row number of the best student.

Need a hint?

table.mean_axis(Axis(0)) and table.std_axis(Axis(0), 0.0) give one number per column. When you subtract a one-dimensional array from a two-dimensional one, ndarray applies it to every row, which is called broadcasting. table.columns() iterates over the columns.

Show solution and explanation

(table - &mean) / &deviation contains no loop. The row of four means is subtracted from each of the three rows, and the result is divided in the same way. In the output, a positive number is a result above the average of that test. The first student’s 85 in the second test is one standard deviation above its mean, a stronger result than the 90 in the third test, where everybody did well.

Observability: logging, traces, metrics, and health

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Emit structured JSON logs and spans with tracing and tracing-subscriber
  • Avoid async span bugs by using .instrument() instead of .entered() across .await
  • Propagate request IDs and W3C trace contexts across tasks and HTTP calls
  • Export distributed traces with OpenTelemetry and OTLP
  • Record counters, gauges, and histograms with metrics and serve /metrics
  • Separate /health/live and /health/ready probes cleanly

When a program runs on your laptop, println! or dbg! is enough to see what it did. When a service runs on a server and serves thousands of requests at once, println! falls apart. Lines from different requests mix together, you cannot filter by user or latency, and when a request jumps between three services, plain text cannot tie them back together.

Observability is designing a program so that operators can understand what is happening inside it purely from its external signals. In production Rust services, those signals rest on three pillars: structured logs, distributed traces, and numeric metrics — paired with health endpoints so load balancers know when an instance can take traffic.

Real-world analogy
The cockpit instruments and the black box

Flying an aircraft at night without instruments and reading a crash note afterwards is like debugging a production outage with scattered println! lines. Modern aircraft carry two complementary systems: live cockpit gauges (speed, altitude, fuel flow — your metrics and health checks) and flight-data recorders that record timestamped events linked to exact flight legs (logs and traces). Together they let you notice a rising engine temperature before anything catches fire, and reconstruct the exact chain of events if something fails.

The three pillars: logs, traces, and metrics

PillarWhat it answersExampleTypical Rust crate
LogsWhat discrete event happened at this moment, and with what fields?order failed order_id=42 err="card declined"tracing + tracing-subscriber
TracesWhere did one request spend its time across async tasks and services?GET /checkout (84 ms) -> charge_card (71 ms)tracing + tracing-opentelemetry
MetricsHow many, how full, or how fast overall?http_requests_total=18420, p99 latency 45 msmetrics + metrics-exporter-prometheus

Every signal serves a different question:

  • Metrics are cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts (“alert if 5xx error rate exceeds 1% for 5 minutes”), because millions of requests collapse into a handful of numbers.
  • Traces capture the tree of nested steps (spans) for individual requests so you can see why a single request took 1.2 seconds or failed downstream.
  • Logs record detailed events attached to those spans, searchable by exact identifiers such as order_id or request_id.

Structured logging and spans with tracing

Chapter 42 introduced the basics of tracing and log. In a service, two upgrades turn development logging into production telemetry: machine-readable JSON and runtime filtering with EnvFilter.

Instead of calling the one-line tracing_subscriber::fmt::init(), real applications build a registry() and compose layers on top of it. That lets you swap formatting between local development and production, and later plug OpenTelemetry right into the same subscriber:

  • EnvFilter::try_from_default_env() reads RUST_LOG from the environment. If it is unset, the fallback keeps noisy libraries at info while keeping your own crate at debug.
  • Setting .json().flatten_event(true) writes one JSON object per line so log collectors (Loki, Datadog, CloudWatch, Elasticsearch) index every field without fragile regular expressions:

Annotating functions cleanly with #[instrument]

#[tracing::instrument] wraps a function in a span whose lifetime matches the call. In real handlers you almost always want to skip arguments that are huge (state, pool) or sensitive (password, token, api_key), and explicitly record only safe identifiers:

Notice the sigils in fields(...):

  • %value formats using Display (clean text, no surrounding quotes).
  • ?value formats using Debug (useful for enums and structs).
  • skip(...) is mandatory for secrets and non-Debug types. Never let auth_token or a password struct end up in span attributes.
Watch out
Never hold span.enter() across an .await

Entering a span synchronously (let _guard = span.enter();) records “this OS thread is now inside span” until _guard drops. In async Rust, a task can pause at .await, another task can resume on the same OS thread while _guard is still inside the suspended future, and the logs of both tasks become scrambled.

Always attach spans to async work with .instrument(span) (from tracing::Instrument), or use #[tracing::instrument] on async fn, which expands to .instrument(...) automatically:

Even tokio::spawn drops span context unless you attach it to the spawned future: tokio::spawn(run_job(id).instrument(tracing::Span::current())).

Request IDs and correlation across hops

When two hundred clients call /checkout at the same second, seeing WARN card gateway timed out in the log tells you nothing unless you know which request timed out, which route triggered it, and what happened right before and after.

In Axum + tower-http, three layers solve this cleanly:

  1. SetRequestIdLayer::x_request_id(MakeRequestUuid) checks whether the incoming request already has an x-request-id header; if not, it generates a fresh UUID v4.
  2. TraceLayer::new_for_http() creates one request span per request and copies x-request-id onto that span via make_span_with.
  3. PropagateRequestIdLayer::x_request_id() copies x-request-id onto the HTTP response so clients and support engineers can quote it back when reporting a bug.
Tip
Layer order matters in ServiceBuilder

ServiceBuilder applies layers from top to bottom on the incoming request (and in reverse on the response). Always place SetRequestIdLayer above TraceLayer so the request ID exists before make_span_with reads it. If you flip them, request_id shows up as "-" on every span!

When your service calls another HTTP API with reqwest, pass the correlation header along so the downstream service logs the same ID:

Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry and OTLP

Request IDs link log lines by text search. OpenTelemetry takes the next step: it turns tracing spans into structured timing trees and exports them over OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol) to collectors such as Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, or an OpenTelemetry Collector sidecar.

Why does tracing-opentelemetry fit Rust so naturally? Because your application code still uses ordinary tracing::info_span!, #[tracing::instrument], and tracing::info!. Adding OpenTelemetry only adds one more layer inside tracing_subscriber::registry():

Two practical rules for OpenTelemetry in production:

  1. Always flush on shutdown. The batch exporter buffers spans in memory and sends them every few seconds. Keep the SdkTracerProvider handle in main and call let _ = provider.shutdown(); after axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(...) finishes, or the final spans of a shutting-down container are lost.
  2. Propagate traceparent across service boundaries. TraceContextPropagator reads and writes the standard W3C traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-01 HTTP header so an upstream trace ID continues seamlessly inside downstream services. Crates such as reqwest-tracing or a small middleware injecting global::get_text_map_propagator(...) automate this header injection.

Metrics with metrics and Prometheus

Logs and traces tell stories about individual requests. When traffic spikes to 20,000 requests per second, you cannot inspect every request — you need metrics that answer “what is the p99 latency and 5xx rate right now?”.

The metrics crate works like tracing or log: libraries and handlers call macros (counter!, gauge!, histogram!), while main installs one exporter such as metrics-exporter-prometheus.

Metric typeBehaviourWhen to use it
counter!Only goes up (resets on restart); Prometheus turns it into a rateRequest counts, error counts, jobs processed
gauge!Goes up and down freelyActive DB connections, queue length, items in cache
histogram!Collects observations into latency/size bucketsRequest latency (seconds), payload sizes (bytes)

When Prometheus scrapes GET /metrics, it receives standard text lines ready for Grafana charts:

Watch out
Beware of cardinality explosion in metric labels

Every unique combination of (label_name, label_value) allocates a separate time series in memory — permanently until restart. Putting user_id, email, request_id, or raw paths (/users/1, /users/2, …, /users/999999) in a metric label creates millions of series and crashes either your service or Prometheus.

Keep metric labels to small, bounded sets (method, route template via MatchedPath, coarse status class). High-cardinality IDs belong in logs and traces, never in metric labels.

Health and readiness probes

Orchestrators such as Kubernetes, Amazon ECS, and Nomad continuously ask your container two distinct questions:

  1. Liveness (GET /health/live) — ”Is this process stuck or deadlocked? Should I kill and restart it?”
    • Must do zero external I/O. Do not query the database or Redis here! If your database goes down for 5 seconds and /health/live returns 500, the orchestrator restarts all healthy app servers at once — turning a brief database hiccup into a full outage.
  2. Readiness (GET /health/ready) — ”Should the load balancer send user traffic to this instance right now?”
    • Checks critical dependencies (for example, SELECT 1 on the SQLx pool under a tight timeout) and returns 200 OK when ready or 503 Service Unavailable when warming up, overloaded, or temporarily unable to reach the database.

Also keep /health/* and /metrics quiet: either attach TraceLayer only to your business router or exclude probe paths in your logging filter/middleware, and make sure /metrics is not exposed directly to the public internet (serve it on an internal admin port or restrict it at your reverse proxy).

How other languages do it
Observability in Rust vs Python, Go, and Java
  • Python (logging / structlog) and Node (pino): Easy to start, but async correlation relies on thread-local or AsyncLocalStorage context variables, and logging adds measurable CPU and reflection overhead per call.
  • Go (log/slog + OpenTelemetry): Clean standard structured logger, though you pass context.Context explicitly into every function to carry trace spans.
  • Rust (tracing): Span filtering compiles down to fast integer bitmasks checked before formatting arguments, so disabled debug! / trace! logs cost a few nanoseconds. And instead of wiring a Context parameter through every function signature, .instrument(span) rides directly inside the state machine of each async future.
Recap
  • Logs record discrete events, traces track timing trees across async tasks and services, and metrics aggregate numbers for alerts and dashboards.
  • Compose tracing_subscriber::registry() with EnvFilter, fmt::layer().json() in production, and tracing_opentelemetry::layer() for OTLP spans.
  • Never hold span.enter() across an .await. Attach spans to futures with .instrument(span) or #[tracing::instrument].
  • Always skip(...) passwords, tokens, and huge values in #[instrument].
  • Place SetRequestIdLayer above TraceLayer in ServiceBuilder so request spans record the ID, and propagate x-request-id / traceparent to downstream services.
  • Keep Prometheus labels low-cardinality (use MatchedPath, never user IDs or raw URLs).
  • Separate /health/live (fast in-process check, never touches the DB) from /health/ready (bounded dependency check returning 200 or 503).
Check your understanding
1

Why should you avoid calling let _guard = span.enter(); before an .await inside an async fn?

An entered guard marks the current thread until dropped. When an async task yields at .await, another task can run on that thread and inherit the wrong parent span. Use .instrument(span) instead.

2

A handler has #[tracing::instrument(skip(password))] on async fn login(email: String, password: String). Why is skip(password) essential?

Never log secrets, API keys, or tokens. Use skip(...) on sensitive or large parameters, and prefer logging only safe IDs.

3

In Axum with ServiceBuilder, you notice request_id is empty inside TraceLayer’s make_span_with, even though SetRequestIdLayer is present. What is the likeliest cause?

ServiceBuilder runs layers top-to-bottom on incoming requests. SetRequestIdLayer must appear above TraceLayer so the ID exists when make_span_with inspects the headers.

4

Why should metric labels use MatchedPath (/users/{id}) instead of req.uri().path() (/users/42)?

Each unique combination of metric label values creates a permanent time series. Keep metric labels bounded; put IDs in logs and traces.

5

Your Postgres server restarts for 4 seconds. Which health endpoint should return 503 Service Unavailable, and which should keep returning 200 OK?

Liveness checks whether the process itself is alive; readiness checks whether dependencies allow serving traffic. Restarting healthy pods during a brief DB blip causes cascading outages.

Guided exerciseConfigure JSON logging and safe instrumentation

Write a small library function charge_user(user_id: u64, card_token: &str, amount_cents: u64) annotated with #[tracing::instrument] so that card_token is never logged, user_id and amount_cents are recorded, and an init_tracing(json: bool) helper configures tracing_subscriber with EnvFilter (defaulting to info).

Need a hint?

Use #[tracing::instrument(skip(card_token))] and check both fmt::layer().json() and fmt::layer().compact() under tracing_subscriber::registry().with(filter).

Show solution and explanation

With LOG_FORMAT=json, the line prints user_id and amount_cents as structured JSON fields and omits card_token completely.

PracticeLiveness, readiness, and bounded metrics

Extend an Axum service so that:

  1. GET /health/live always returns 200 OK without checking the database.
  2. GET /health/ready checks a ping_db() async flag under a 200 ms timeout and returns 503 Service Unavailable if it times out or returns false.
  3. A track_metrics middleware records http_requests_total using MatchedPath so /items/1 and /items/2 share the single label path="/items/{id}", and /health/* routes are placed outside that middleware.
Need a hint?

Build one Router for business routes (api) with .route_layer(middleware::from_fn(track_metrics)), and merge it with an ops router containing /health/live, /health/ready, and /metrics.

Show solution and explanation

Separating api and ops keeps probe scrapes out of business latency histograms and ensures /items/1 and /items/999 map to the single bounded label /items/{id}.

ChallengeCorrelating requests end-to-end

Write an Axum router using ServiceBuilder with SetRequestIdLayer, TraceLayer (extracting x-request-id into a span field), and PropagateRequestIdLayer. Add a handler GET /proxy that reads x-request-id from the request headers and attaches it to an outbound reqwest::RequestBuilder, and test with tower::ServiceExt::oneshot that sending a custom x-request-id: req-777 echoes the exact same header back on the HTTP response while a request without the header receives a generated UUID.

Need a hint?

Put SetRequestIdLayer::x_request_id(MakeRequestUuid) first inside ServiceBuilder, then TraceLayer, then PropagateRequestIdLayer::x_request_id(). Pass HeaderMap into the handler to read "x-request-id".

Show solution and explanation

SetRequestIdLayer preserves caller-provided IDs when valid and mints a fresh 36-character UUID otherwise, TraceLayer attaches it to the span, and PropagateRequestIdLayer echoes it on the response.
