Performance: measure first, then improve

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Follow the three rules: measure a release build, find where the time goes, change one thing at a time
  • Compare whole programs with hyperfine and single functions with criterion
  • Read a flame graph
  • Count allocations and remove the needless ones
  • Recognise the common causes of slow programs: the algorithm, allocations, unbuffered files, hashing
  • Tell a real difference between two measurements from noise
  • Decide when a program is fast enough

Rust programs are fast without special effort. For fifty chapters you have written plain, clear code, and it ran at a speed close to that of C and C++. So the first advice about performance is: do nothing, until something is too slow for its purpose.

When that day comes, this chapter gives you a method. It has three rules, and they matter more than any single trick:

  1. Measure a release build.
  2. Find out where the time goes before you change anything.
  3. Change one thing, and measure again.

Chapter 38 asked you to write the clear version first and to optimise only what a measurement points at. Here is how to get that measurement.

Real-world analogy
The slow restaurant

A restaurant gets complaints: the food takes too long. The owner is sure that the cooks are slow, and buys a faster stove. Nothing improves. Then somebody stands in the kitchen for an evening with a watch. Cooking a dish takes six minutes. But every plate waits ten minutes on the counter, because one waiter serves the whole room. The stove was never the problem. Programs are like this. The slow part is very often not where you would bet, and only a watch can tell you.

Good to know
The numbers in this chapter

All times were measured on the machine that tests this guide: Linux, two processor cores, Rust 1.100. Your numbers will differ, but their proportions should be similar. The Run buttons of this chapter open the playground in release mode.

A program to make faster

The patient for this chapter makes a long text of two million words and then counts how often each word occurs. It carries two measuring tools with it, which are explained below:

The function measure is the watch. It runs a piece of work, and prints how long that took and how often it asked for memory on the heap.

The count of allocations comes from the first lines of the program. #[global_allocator] replaces the part of the program that hands out heap memory. Our Counting passes every request on to System, the normal allocator, and adds one to a counter on the way. The counter is an atomic number from chapter 31, because any thread may ask for memory. Implementing GlobalAlloc needs the word unsafe (chapter 35): the compiler cannot check that an allocator returns valid memory. Here that duty is passed straight on to System. When a String or a Vec grows into a larger buffer, that counts as an allocation too.

Rule 1: measure a release build

cargo run builds for debugging: quick to compile, with all checks, without optimisation. The speed of such a build says nothing about the program that your users will run. cargo build --release makes the optimised program in target/release.

The tool hyperfine measures the running time of whole commands. It runs each of them many times and does the statistics:

The release build is 4.3 times faster, and not one line of the code has changed. In the line of the release build, 188.2 ms is the mean of 15 runs, and ± 7.6 ms says how much the single runs differed from each other. Keep an eye on that second number. It returns later in this chapter.

Watch out
The most common mistake

“Rust is slow” in a forum post nearly always means “I measured a debug build”. Before you compare Rust with anything, and before you optimise anything, add --release.

Rule 2: find out where the time goes

Look again at the output of the program:

The program is called a word counter, so the natural suspect is the counting loop with its hash map. The watch says something else. Making the text takes longer than counting it, and asks for memory four million times: twice for every word. Whoever starts by tuning the hash map works on the smaller half of the problem.

Timing the large steps by hand, as measure does, is the simplest way to find the slow part. Often it is enough.

A profiler

For larger programs there are profilers. A profiler interrupts the running program several thousand times a second, and notes which function is running at that moment and which functions called it. Each note is a sample. A function that appears in many samples is one where the time goes.

The result is drawn as a flame graph. The tool cargo flamegraph does all of it in one step:

The second command builds the release version, runs it under the profiler, and writes the picture flamegraph.svg, which any browser can show. -F 5000 asks for 5,000 samples per second, because this program runs for only a fifth of a second. A profiler needs the names of the functions, which a release build normally leaves out. Keep them with two lines in Cargo.toml:

Here is the result for the word counter, reduced to its widest bars:

How to read a flame graph:

  • Every bar is a function. Its width is the share of the samples in which that function was running, or was waiting for a function that it had called.
  • A bar sits on top of its caller. main called make_text, which called format!, which called fmt::write.
  • The order from left to right is alphabetical, and the colours mean nothing. Only the widths count.
  • Look for wide bars near the top. That is where the processor really spends its time.
  • A narrow bar has no room for its name. Point at it to read the name, or click it to zoom in. A click on the bar at the bottom zooms out again. The real picture works the same way, and so does the drawing above.

The graph agrees with the watch: each of the two steps takes about half of the time. And it shows what happens inside them:

  • In make_text, nearly everything is format!. Inside it, three bars deal with memory: alloc creates the small String, realloc moves it to a larger buffer when the number arrives, and drop gives the memory back. Together they take 24 per cent of the whole running time. That is nearly half of make_text, spent on asking for memory and returning it.
  • In count_words, the hash map takes most of the time: 20 per cent for finding the key and 12 for computing its hash. to_string adds 9 per cent, and nearly all of that is its allocation.

A surprise

The real picture has many more bars than this drawing, and a Search button in its corner. Search for atomic_add, and several narrow bars light up, with the note Matched: 11.0%. That function is the fetch_add of our own allocation counter. The watch itself uses a tenth of the time.

A test confirms it. Without the two lines of #[global_allocator], hyperfine measures 167.8 ms for the program instead of 188.0 ms: 10.8 per cent less. Nobody would have guessed that an addition costs so much. (An atomic addition has to be safe against all other threads, and it happens six million times.) Finding what nobody guessed is what a profiler is for.

There are two lessons in this. Every measuring tool disturbs what it measures, so take your instruments out before the final measurement. And a counter that is only a tool should not be mistaken for a part of the problem: the allocation counts stay in the examples below, because they explain why a version is slow.

ToolWhat it does
cargo flamegraphbuilds, profiles and draws the flame graph. On Linux it uses perf
perfthe profiler of Linux. perf record and perf report work with any program
samplyrecords a profile and shows it in the Firefox Profiler, a viewer that runs in the browser
dhat (dhat-rs)profiles heap allocations and reports peak live memory by call site
heaptrack, valgrind --tool=massiftracks total heap usage and memory leaks over time on Linux without modifying code
cargo-bloatlists the largest functions and crates inside a compiled binary to shrink executable size

Everything in this chapter was run on Linux. cargo flamegraph and samply describe macOS and Windows in their documentation too. For explicit vector processing when the compiler cannot auto-vectorise a hot inner loop, the crate wide provides portable SIMD types (f32x4, u32x8) on stable Rust (and std::simd on nightly).

Rule 3: change one thing, and measure again

Both steps of the program allocate once or twice per word. That is the trail to follow.

The counting. word.to_string() creates a new String for every one of the two million words, only to look it up. For all but 5,000 of them the key exists already, and the fresh String is thrown away at once. But the words are all in text. A map with keys of the type &str can simply point at them.

The text. format!("w{word}") builds a small String, push_str copies it into the text, and then it is dropped. The macro write! puts the characters straight into the String that exists already. And since the final size is roughly known, the buffer can be reserved once.

Here are the two new functions, and a main that measures the old and the new versions side by side. The rest of the program is the same as before and is not shown again. The Run button has all of it.

Both steps are at least twice as fast, and together they went from 185 to 80 milliseconds. The allocations fell from six million to thirteen. Four details of the method:

  • Each change was measured by itself, next to the old version. A change that does not help is taken out again, because it only makes the code harder to read.
  • The results are compared, with assert_eq!. A fast function with a wrong answer is worthless, and it is easy to break something while tuning.
  • The instrument was checked. Without the allocation counter, the four lines read 83, 37, 75 and 39 milliseconds. The conclusion is the same.
  • The price is visible in the types. HashMap<&str, u32> borrows from the text, so the text must live as long as the map. If the caller needs keys that it owns, convert the 5,000 keys at the end. That is still 400 times fewer allocations than before.

One more measurement: with String::new() instead of String::with_capacity(12_000_000), the new make_text_fast takes 46 ms and allocates 22 times. So nearly all of the gain comes from write!, and the reserved capacity adds a little. Without a measurement, you would not know which of the two ideas did the work.

Where the time usually goes

A handful of causes explains most slow programs. They are listed here from the most important to the least.

The algorithm

No tuning can save a program whose work grows with the square of its input, the O(n²) of chapter 15. Here are two functions that answer the same question: is any number in this list twice?

Read down the columns. Each time the input doubles, the first function takes four times as long, and the second one about twice as long. At 80,000 numbers the difference is a factor of 170, and it keeps growing. contains on a slice looks harmless, but it is a loop, and here it sits inside another loop. A HashSet answers “have I seen this?” in a time that does not depend on its size.

Always test with input of a realistic size. With 100 numbers, both functions are too fast to tell apart.

Allocations

Asking for heap memory is not expensive once. It is expensive two million times. You have seen the effect above. The usual places:

  • to_string(), to_owned() and clone() on values that are only read. Borrow them.
  • format! when the result is only appended to another string. Use write!.
  • A String or Vec that is created anew in every round of a loop. Create it once before the loop and empty it with clear(), which keeps its memory. Reading two million lines from a file took 70 ms with lines(), which makes a new String per line, and 52 ms with read_line into one String that was emptied each time.
  • collect() into a Vec that is then walked through only once. Keep working with the iterator.

with_capacity is on every list of performance tips, so here is its measurement as well. Filling a Vec with ten million numbers took about 34 ms from Vec::new() and about 31 ms with the right capacity. The gain is small, because a growing Vec doubles its buffer each time and so has to move only rarely. Reserve the capacity when you know the size, and do not expect wonders.

Tip
A finished tool for counting

The crate dhat replaces the hand-made counter of this chapter. It needs three lines:

For the first program of this chapter it reported:

That is the six million allocations that our counter found, 64 megabytes in total, and at most 17 megabytes at the same moment. The saved file also says which lines of the code asked for the memory. While dhat watches, the program runs about twenty times slower, so use it for counting and not for timing.

Files without a buffer

Every write to a File is a request to the operating system, and such a request costs far more than the few bytes that it carries:

A factor of 80, for one more word in the code. BufWriter collects the output in memory and passes it on in pieces of several kilobytes. BufReader does the same for reading, as you know from chapter 18.

The terminal is a file as well. println! passes every line on at once. Printing 500,000 lines into a file took 384 ms with println!, and 14 ms with writeln! into a BufWriter::new(std::io::stdout().lock()). For a program that prints a few lines this does not matter. For one that prints a whole report it does.

Hashing, and idle cores

The standard HashMap uses a hash function that is built to withstand attackers: people who choose keys on purpose so that a server gets slow. That safety costs time. When strangers have no control over the keys, a simpler hash function is a fair exchange. The crate rustc-hash offers FxHashMap, which the Rust compiler itself uses. And with Rayon (chapter 45), the counting can use all cores:

The simpler hash function saves 40 per cent. The second core saves only another fifth, far from the half that one might hope for. The text has to be cut into pieces, and the partial maps have to be merged at the end, and that work is extra. Parallel code pays best when each piece of work is large and its result is small.

Not the iterators

Beginners often fear that the comfortable style of chapter 25, with its chains and closures, must be slower than a plain loop with an index. Measure it:

Both take the same time: 0.18 nanoseconds for each pair of numbers. No processor multiplies and adds that fast one pair at a time, so the compiler must have turned both loops into machine code that handles several pairs in one step. The chain of zip, map and sum costs nothing. This is what people mean by a “zero-cost abstraction”. The indexed version contains checks (a[i] panics when i is too large), and here they did not slow it down. Where such checks do cost time, an iterator is the cure, because it has no index to check.

The debug build tells a different story. There, the indexed loop needs 22,000 nanoseconds per call and the iterator version 45,000: thirty and sixty times slower than the release build. All the small functions of an iterator chain are really called, one after the other, until the optimiser melts them together. This is rule 1 again. Never judge a style of code by its debug build.

The layout of the data

Processors are much faster with data that lies close together in memory. Chapter 37 measured it: summing one field took 14 ms in an array of large structs, and 3.5 ms when that field had an array of its own. The same effect decides between collections. Here are the times for adding up two million numbers:

The numbers are stored inTime
Vec<u64>0.6 ms
Vec<Box<u64>>, the boxes created one after the other3.0 ms
LinkedList<u64>3.1 ms
Vec<Box<u64>>, the boxes scattered over the heap11.1 ms

In the first row the numbers lie side by side. In the others, the processor has to follow a pointer for every single number, and in the last row each pointer leads to a different corner of the memory. When in doubt, use a Vec of plain values.

Smaller tools from the same box

A few more techniques come up in every discussion of fast Rust. Each of them matters in some programs and does nothing in most, so measure before and after.

  • Bounds checks. v[i] checks on every access that i is inside the list. People often blame these checks, and they are rarely the cause. A test for this chapter added two slices into a third in three ways: with indices (three checks in every round), with indices after cutting all three slices to the same length first (let a = &a[..n];), and with zip. All three took about 260 nanoseconds for 4,096 numbers: the compiler had moved the checks out of the loop on its own. If a profile does show time in a check, an iterator or a slice taken before the loop removes it safely. get_unchecked needs unsafe, and it is the last thing to try.
  • Inlining. Calling a very small function can cost more than the work inside it. The compiler copies small functions into their callers by itself (the debug numbers for iterators above show what happens when it does not). #[inline] on a function is a suggestion to do so, and #[inline(never)] and #[cold] mark code that should stay out of the fast path, such as error handling. Add them only when a profile points at one function, and measure: the result is sometimes slower.
  • Short lists without the heap. A Vec always puts its elements on the heap. The crates smallvec and arrayvec keep a few elements inside the value itself and use the heap only when there are more. That helps where millions of very short lists are created, and costs elsewhere, because the type gets bigger.
  • Reading the machine code. For a small, hot function, you can look at what the compiler made of it: paste it into the Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org), or run cargo asm from the crate cargo-show-asm in your project. You do not need to understand every instruction. A loop that became a handful of instructions with registers named xmm, ymm or zmm works on several numbers per step, and a call inside a hot loop means that something was not inlined.
  • Letting the compiler learn from a run. With profile-guided optimisation, you build the program, run it on typical input while it records what happens, and build again with that record. The tool cargo-pgo does the steps. Large programs such as the Rust compiler itself are built this way.

Settings of the compiler

Chapter 39 presented the settings of the release profile. Two of them, and one flag for the compiler, are meant to make code faster:

They cost a line each, so they are worth a try. Here is the word counter with them, measured by hyperfine with 30 runs each:

BuildTimeCompared with the first
cargo build --release188.8 ms ± 10.7 ms
with lto and codegen-units = 1192.6 ms ± 13.6 ms+2.1 %
with target-cpu=native182.4 ms ± 8.8 ms−3.4 %
with all three181.8 ms ± 8.8 ms−3.7 %

The differences are a few milliseconds, and single runs of one and the same program differ by ten. For this program, the settings change nothing that can be measured. (lto did make the program file smaller: 411 KB instead of 495 KB.) Other programs gain more, above all those that call many small functions across the borders of crates. The only way to know is to measure. One warning: a program built with target-cpu=native may not start at all on an older processor, so never build that way for other people.

A different allocator is a similar one-line experiment. With the crate mimalloc instead of System, the times of the word counter stayed the same.

Compare all of this with the changes to the code: twice as fast by removing allocations, and 170 times as fast with a better algorithm.

Numbers you can trust

Noise

Run the same program twice and you get two different times. Other programs, the temperature of the processor and the state of its caches all play a part. This variation is called noise. A difference between two versions means something only when it is clearly larger than the difference between two runs of the same version. That is what the ± of hyperfine tells you, and why “3.4 % faster” in the table above is no result at all.

You have seen noise in this chapter already. The function make_text took 106.8 ms in the first listing and 104.3 ms in the second one, and nothing had changed.

The benchmark library criterion (chapter 41) does this reasoning for you. It remembers the last measurement of every benchmark. Here is its report for the counting function, after the change from String keys to &str keys:

The three numbers after change are the lower bound, the best estimate and the upper bound of the difference. The whole range lies far below zero, so the improvement is real. Then the benchmark was run once more, without touching the code:

The best estimate says “3 % slower”, for identical code. But the range reaches from below zero to above zero, and criterion draws the right conclusion: this is the noise of the machine. A tool that knows about noise keeps you from celebrating a gain, or hunting a loss, that does not exist.

So this is what to do with the numbers of a benchmark: run cargo bench, change the code, run cargo bench again, and read the line change.

The benchmark file

The setup in Cargo.toml is the one from chapter 41. The benchmark uses 100,000 words instead of two million, because criterion calls the function many hundred times.

Work that disappears

The optimiser removes calculations whose result is known in advance or never used. Usually that is what you want. In a measurement it can fool you:

A million multiplications and additions in 86 nanoseconds would be more than ten thousand operations per nanosecond. No processor can do that. The compiler has recognised the pattern and replaced the whole loop with a formula for the sum of squares, so no loop runs at all. black_box (chapter 41) hides the limit from the optimiser, and it does not help here, because the formula works for any limit. (The debug build of the same program needs 6 milliseconds.)

There is a second trap in these numbers. Reading the clock takes time too: a measurement with nothing at all between its start and its end shows 50 to 90 nanoseconds on the same machine. So the program above measured mostly its own clock. Never time anything that short with Instant. Let criterion repeat it a million times.

The program is honestly this fast, and nothing is wrong with it. But if the question was “how long does a loop of this kind take?”, the measurement answered a different question. Be suspicious of a result that looks too good, and let the measured work depend on data that the compiler cannot know, such as the two million words above.

When to stop

Optimised code is usually longer and harder to change than the first, simple version. Every step in this chapter added a constraint: a map that borrows from the text, a capacity that must be estimated, a second hash function to know about. So decide what “fast enough” means before you start: “the report appears within one second”, “the server answers a thousand requests per second”. Stop when the goal is reached. Time that you spend beyond it buys nothing that anybody will notice.

And if a measurement shows that only unsafe code can reach the goal, chapter 35 applies: a small block, behind a safe function, with a comment that says why it is correct, and with the benchmark that justifies it.

How other languages do it
Performance work in other languages

In Python or JavaScript, making code faster often means leaving the language: the hot loop moves into NumPy, into C, or into Rust. In Java, Go and C#, much of the effort goes into producing less garbage for the collector. That is the same hunt for allocations as in this chapter, with less control over the result. C and C++ offer the same toolbox as Rust: release builds, profilers, flame graphs. The difference is the risk. Restructuring C++ code for speed can introduce memory errors that show up months later. In Rust, the borrow checker reviews every such change. The map with &str keys in this chapter is an example: in C, such a map full of pointers into another buffer would be a classic source of bugs, and here the compiler guarantees that the text outlives the map.

Recap
  • Do nothing until something is too slow. Then measure a release build, find where the time goes, and change one thing at a time.
  • hyperfine compares whole programs. criterion compares functions and reports whether a change is real. A profiler draws a flame graph, in which the wide bars are the functions that take the time.
  • The biggest gains come from a better algorithm. Then come needless allocations, files without a buffer, and the hash function.
  • Borrow instead of cloning, write with write! into a String that exists, and wrap files in BufReader and BufWriter.
  • Iterators are as fast as hand-written loops with an index, in a release build.
  • Settings of the compiler are cheap to try and often bring little.
  • Measuring tools cost time themselves. A difference smaller than the noise is not a result. A result that looks too good probably measured something else.
  • Decide beforehand what is fast enough, and stop there.
Check your understanding
1

A friend says: “My Rust program is slower than the same program in Python.” What do you ask first?

A debug build is not optimised. In this chapter, the release build of the word counter was 4.3 times faster than the debug build, and the small loop over two slices was thirty times faster.

2

A program reads a file, parses it, and writes a report. It is too slow. What is the best first step?

Without a measurement you may spend a day on a step that takes five per cent of the time. In the example of this chapter, the slowest step was not the one that the name of the program suggested.

3

Why was counting with HashMap<&str, u32> twice as fast as with HashMap<String, u32>?

Both maps hold the same 5,000 keys, and they hash and compare the same bytes. The difference is two million allocations against twelve.

4

In a flame graph, the bar of the function parse is very wide, and on top of it sits a bar to_string that is nearly as wide. What does that tell you?

The width of a bar includes the time of everything that the function calls, and a bar sits on top of its caller. So parse itself does little. To make it faster, look at why it calls to_string.

5

Two builds of a program are measured with hyperfine: 188.8 ms ± 10.7 ms and 182.4 ms ± 8.8 ms. What can you conclude?

Six milliseconds of difference mean little when single runs vary by ten. More runs on a quieter machine could settle it. Until then there is no result.

6

A benchmark reports that a loop over one million elements takes 90 nanoseconds. What is the most likely explanation?

Ninety nanoseconds are a few hundred steps of the processor, far too few for a million rounds. A result that looks too good usually means that the work was optimised away.

Guided exerciseTwo numbers with a given sum

The function below answers this question: are there two numbers in the list, at different places, whose sum is target? It tries every pair. Write a second function that needs only one pass over the list. Check that both agree, and measure both with 30,000 numbers.

Need a hint?

For a number n, the partner that completes the sum is target - n. Walk through the list once, and keep the numbers that you have seen in a HashSet. For each number, ask the set whether its partner came earlier. For the measurement, use a list in which no pair exists, so that neither function can stop early.

Show solution and explanation

With 30,000 numbers there are about 450 million pairs, and the first function looks at every one of them. The second function does 30,000 look-ups. The order inside its loop matters: the look-up comes before the insert. So a number is never paired with itself, but two equal numbers at different places are found, as the test with [5, 5] shows. The small cases at the start protect you from a fast function that is wrong.

PracticeA line without waste

This function joins numbers into one line such as 37,74,111. For 1,000 numbers it allocates more than a thousand times. Write a version that allocates once, and prove it with the counting allocator from this chapter.

Need a hint?

Two things allocate here. to_string() makes a temporary String for every number, and line has to move to a larger buffer again and again. write!(line, "{number}") writes the digits straight into line. It needs use std::fmt::Write;. A u32 has at most ten digits, so String::with_capacity(numbers.len() * 11) is always enough.

Show solution and explanation

The slow version allocates once per number for to_string(), and eleven more times because the line outgrows its buffer: 8 bytes, then 16, then 32, up to 8,192. (line + "," itself does not allocate. The + of a String appends to its left side.) The fast version reserves more than it needs: 11,000 bytes for a line of 5,700. That is a good trade. And if the estimate were too small, the program would still be correct, because the String would simply grow.

ChallengeThe third column

A text has 500,000 lines of the form id,customer,amount,status. The function below adds up the amounts. Find out what it does that is not needed, write a faster version, and measure both.

Need a hint?

For every line, the function creates four Strings and a Vec, uses one of them, and throws all five away. split is an iterator, and nth(2) takes its third item without storing the others. That item is a &str that points into the line, and parse is content with it.

Show solution and explanation

Nearly three times as fast, with shorter code. The slow version allocated five times per line, 2.5 million times in total, and the fast one never. nth(2) also stops splitting after the third field, so the rest of each line is not even looked at. What remains is the real work: finding the commas and parsing the numbers. In a real program, both unwraps would become proper errors (chapter 18), and that would not make it slower.

Project: a personal library with a web API and a CLI

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Plan a program in layers: HTTP, rules, storage
  • Share one data model between a web API and a command-line tool
  • Store books in SQLite with SQLx
  • Import and export JSON with Serde
  • Handle errors uniformly with thiserror and anyhow
  • Test the API and the CLI without a network
  • Prepare the program for a server

The earlier chapters each taught one ecosystem: Axum for HTTP, SQLx for databases, clap for command lines, Serde for JSON, thiserror and anyhow for errors. This capstone brings them together into one real program: a personal library manager. You can add books, mark them as reading or read, list and search them, and export them to JSON — either through a web API in a browser or through a command-line tool in a terminal.

The finished program works like this:

Both the command and the web API talk to the same database. The command-line tool is useful for bulk work; the web API is useful for a small web page or a phone app.

The project brings Part 10 together:

  • Axum for HTTP (chapter 46)
  • SQLx with SQLite for storage (chapter 47)
  • Serde for JSON (chapter 43)
  • clap for the command line (chapter 44)
  • thiserror and anyhow for errors (chapter 18)
  • tracing for logs (chapter 42)
  • tokio for the async runtime (chapter 45)

It also keeps the promises of the tooling chapters: format, lint, test, document, and a CI-style checklist at the end.

Real-world analogy
A library card catalogue

A library has a card catalogue: one card per book, filed so that any librarian can find a book by title, author or subject. The catalogue is the database. The librarian behind the desk is the rules layer — they check that a new book has a title before filing it. The public catalogue terminal and the telephone are the web API and the CLI: two different ways to ask the same librarian about the same cards.

Step 0: plan

The API

RequestWhat it doesSuccess
GET /healthanswers ok if the service and database work200 OK
GET /bookslists books, newest first. ?status=read and ?q=… filter200 OK
POST /booksadds a book. Body is JSON: {"title": "…", "author": "…", "isbn": "…"}201 Created
GET /books/{id}shows one book200 OK
PATCH /books/{id}changes fields. Body is JSON with only the fields to change200 OK
DELETE /books/{id}removes a book204 No Content

Every failure is answered with JSON:

StatusWhen
400 Bad Requestthe body is not valid JSON
404 Not Foundthere is no book with that id
422 Unprocessable Entitythe JSON is readable but breaks a rule (empty title, bad rating)
500 Internal Server Errorthe database failed

The data

One table is enough for a first version:

ColumnTypeMeaning
idinteger, primary keythe book’s number
titletext, not nullthe book’s title
authortext, not nullthe author’s name
isbntextthe ISBN, optional
statustext, not null, default to-readto-read, reading or read
ratinginteger1 to 5, only when read
created_attext, not nullwhen the book was added

The layers

LayerJobCrates
HTTPparse requests, return JSON responsesAxum, Serde
Rulescheck titles, ratings, statuses; decide what may changeyour own code
Storagerun SQL against SQLiteSQLx
CLIparse arguments, call the rules, print resultsclap, anyhow

The rules layer is plain Rust with no web and no database. That makes it easy to test, and easy to reuse from both the web API and the CLI.

The files

Step 1: the project and the table

Create the project and add the dependencies:

Then create the migration and the build script so that Cargo notices new migration files:

The rerun-if-changed line tells Cargo to rerun the build script when a migration file changes. SQLx’s migrate!() macro embeds the migration files in the program at compile time.

Step 2: the data model and errors

The model types are shared by the store, the routes and the CLI. Keeping them in one file means a change to a book’s shape is made in one place.

NewBook is what a client may send. Book is what the store returns — it adds the id and the creation date that the client never chooses. This separation, first seen with notes in chapter 46, keeps the client from inventing ids.

Now the one error type for the whole program. thiserror writes the Display and Error implementations; #[from] lets ? convert SQLx errors.

Step 3: the store

The store owns the SQLx pool. Every query lives here, so the rest of the program never sees SQL. A Library handle is cheap to clone because it holds an Arc inside the pool.

BookRow is a private helper: SQLx maps a row into it, and find_book converts it into the public Book. The conversion point is where the database’s rating: Option<i64> becomes the model’s Option<u32>, and where the status text is parsed. All SQL stays in this file.

The sqlx::migrate!() call runs automatically when the program starts. Migrations that were already applied are skipped.

Test the store

Because SQLite in memory is fast, each test gets a fresh database:

Each test uses its own in-memory database, so tests never interfere and run in parallel.

Step 4: the rules

The rules layer sits between the store and the outside world. It knows nothing about HTTP or the command line — it takes values and returns values.

The rules reject bad input before it reaches the database. set_rating converts a plain u32 into a Rating, which is only valid between 1 and 5 — so a book can never have a rating of 0 or 99, whatever calls the rules.

Step 5: the routes

The routes turn HTTP requests into calls on the Library. Errors become uniform JSON responses.

LibraryError::into_response is the one place that decides status codes and bodies. Database errors are logged with their details but the client sees only a neutral message — the security rule from chapter 46.

Step 6: settings and main

Settings come from environment variables, never from the source code. For multi-environment config files, .env loading, and secrecy::SecretString redaction, see chapter 46 and the configuration section of the CLI chapter; for separating /health/live and /health/ready, see chapter 51. main wires everything together: logging, the store, the router, and the server.

main parses the command line inside Tokio’s async runtime. The same Library value also serves the web API when serve is called.

Note how Library is shared: the CLI uses it directly, and AppState puts it behind State<AppState> for Axum. One set of rules, two interfaces.

Try it

Build and run the server in one terminal:

Then in another:

And the CLI in a third terminal (or the same one, after stopping the server):

The web API and the CLI see the same books because they share one Library and one Store.

Step 7: test the whole API

The tests hand requests straight to the router, exactly as in chapter 46. No network port is opened, so the tests run in milliseconds.

The AppState clone is cheap: Library holds an Arc-backed pool. Each test gets a fresh in-memory database.

What makes this service solid, and what is missing

Solid:

  • One error enum gives every failure a status code and a uniform JSON body.
  • All SQL lives in store.rs; the rules and routes never touch it.
  • Bad input is rejected by the rules before it reaches the database.
  • Database errors are logged, not shown to the client.
  • Settings come from environment variables.
  • The program shuts down gracefully on Ctrl+C.
  • Tests cover the API without a network.

Missing (deliberately, for the exercises):

  • list_books ignores the status and search filters in the CLI-only path (they work in the web API).
  • There is no pagination: GET /books returns every book.
  • No authentication: anybody may add or delete books.
  • No protection against a very large request body.
  • The serve subcommand starts the web API, while the other subcommands operate on the same database.

Make it better

PracticeAdd the missing filters

Make GET /books?status=read and GET /books?q=dune work. The route already parses them and passes them to list_books; the store already builds a dynamic query with QueryBuilder.

Need a hint?

Check that the status query parameter maps to Status::ToRead, Status::Reading or Status::Read, and that q is passed as a search string. Add tests that request ?status=read and check that only read books come back.

Show solution and explanation

Add tests that request ?status=read and check that only read books come back.

PracticePagination

Add ?limit=20&offset=0 to GET /books. limit defaults to 50, offset to 0. Add SQL LIMIT ? OFFSET ? to the store query, and test that a page returns at most limit books.

Need a hint?

Add limit: Option<u32> and offset: Option<u32> to list_books, push LIMIT and OFFSET with push_bind at the end of the QueryBuilder, and convert to i64 for SQLx.

Show solution and explanation

Test that asking for 1 book from a database with 3 returns exactly 1, and that asking for offset 1 skips the first.

ChallengeProtect the writes

Add an API key. POST /books, PATCH /books/{id} and DELETE /books/{id} require the header x-api-key to match the API_KEY environment variable. Reading stays open. Use Axum middleware from chapter 46, and keep the key out of the source code.

Need a hint?

Write a require_key middleware function like the one in chapter 46. Put the write routes in their own router with .route_layer(middleware::from_fn(require_key)). Read API_KEY in Config and pass it into AppState.

Show solution and explanation

Test that a write without the key gets 401, and with the right key succeeds.

ChallengeA second migration

Add a last_visited column that records when a book was opened through GET /books/{id}. Write the migration SQL, apply it at start-up, update the handler to set the column, and add a test that checks the column exists.

Need a hint?

Create migrations/20261115090000_add_last_visited.sql with ALTER TABLE books ADD COLUMN last_visited TEXT;. sqlx::migrate!() applies it automatically. Add the column to BookRow and Book, and datetime('now') in the GET /books/{id} handler path.

Show solution and explanation

sqlx::migrate!() applies both migrations in order, and skips any already applied.

What you have learned

Recap
  • A program in layers — HTTP, rules, storage — is easy to test and easy to reuse.
  • One data model shared by the web API and the CLI means both interfaces see the same data.
  • SQLx keeps all SQL in one file, with bound parameters and compile-friendly queries.
  • thiserror gives libraries a precise error enum; anyhow gives applications quick context.
  • LibraryError::IntoResponse turns every failure into a fitting JSON answer.
  • Settings come from environment variables; secrets never appear in source code.
  • tokio::runtime::Runtime::block_on connects a synchronous CLI to an async library.
  • Tests hand requests straight to the router; each test gets its own in-memory database.
  • Migrations evolve the schema safely, and build.rs makes Cargo notice them.

What comes next

You have reached the end of Part 11 and of this guide, and the last of its eight projects. You now know how to build command-line tools, web services, database-backed programs, graphical applications, observability pipelines, and embedded software in Rust. Head to chapter 54 for the books, crates, and communities where Rust developers keep learning.

Where to go from here

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Choose what to study next, by goal and by level
  • Find the best book or course for each topic
  • Practise with small tasks and with real projects
  • Stay up to date and take part in the Rust community

You have worked through the whole language, the tools around it, and eight projects. This chapter is a map of what lies beyond: the books and courses that go deeper than this guide, places to practise, and ways to stay in touch with a language that gets a new version every six weeks.

You do not need to cover every topic to move forward. Keep the core path from chapter 1 through chapter 26, then choose the route closest to what you want to build:

GoalA focused next route
Command-line toolsCargo, error handling, Serde, Clap
Web services and APIsasync Rust, Tokio and the async ecosystem, Axum, databases, then the API project
Browser or desktop appsSerde, then WebAssembly and app interfaces
Embedded devices or gamesmemory and ownership, smart pointers, unsafe Rust, then games and embedded Rust
Deeper language understandingadvanced traits, type design, memory layout, and idioms

Treat these as starting points, not prerequisites. Follow a link when a project needs that skill, and return to the route later.

Real-world analogy
After the driving test

A driving licence does not make an experienced driver. It means that you can now learn safely on your own, on real roads. You are at that point with Rust: you can read the documentation of any crate, understand what the compiler tells you, and build things. The experience comes from kilometres driven.

How other languages do it
Learning Rust vs learning another skill

Some people expect a language to be mastered by reading alone. In practice, every programming language is learned in a loop: you read a bit, you try a small thing, you fix the errors, and you build something real. Rust is unusual in that the compiler gives excellent feedback, which makes that loop efficient once you know the basic rules.

How to keep learning

Three activities, in a loop. Each one feeds the others.

  1. Build something you want to exist. A tool for your own work, a small game, a bot, a web service for your club. A project that you care about keeps you going when it gets difficult, and it forces you to solve problems that no tutorial planned for you.
  2. Read code that is better than yours. The documentation of every crate has a “source” link next to each item. Follow it. Start with small, well-kept crates that you already use.
  3. Explain what you learned. Write a short note, answer a beginner’s question, or show your project to someone. Gaps in your understanding become visible the moment you try to explain.

Other guides, and what each one is best at

This guide owes ideas to all of the following. None of them is a replacement for the others: each teaches something better than the rest. Everything in the first table can be read free of charge on the web.

One at a time

What this guide leaves out

Every ecosystem has corners that a guide starting from zero cannot teach honestly. Rather than mention them once and move on, here they are with a reason and a direction. This is the written coverage policy of the guide: a topic is either taught with a compiled example, named with advice so that you know what to look up, or declared out of scope here.

AreaWhy it is out of scopeWhere to go
Blockchain and Web3 (solana, anchor)Domain-specific, fast-moving, and needs a blockchain mental model before Rust helpsthe Solana developer docs
Operating systems and kernels (blog_os, Rust for Linux)Needs low-level hardware knowledge that comes before this guide, not after itWriting an OS in Rust
Robotics (ROS 2 bindings)The hard part is robotics, not Rustr2r and the ROS 2 tutorials
High-frequency trading and market dataLatency engineering at that level is its own discipline, and much of it is closed-sourcemeasure first: chapter 52
Cloud-provider SDKs (aws-sdk-*, azure_*, google-cloud-*)Each vendor ships its own generated SDK and its own documentation; the pattern is the same for all of themthe vendor’s Rust SDK docs, and object_store for a vendor-neutral API
GraphQL and full-screen terminal UIs (async-graphql, ratatui)Real subjects with their own books. This guide names them, says when they are the right choice, and stops there rather than half-teaching themthe crate books linked in the table above and in chapter 44

Everything else you meet in chapter 42 is either taught in a chapter or described with advice about when to choose it. If you find a crate that is only a name in a table, that is a gap worth reporting.

Practice

Small tasks train the hands:

  • Rustlings, if you have not done it yet. After this guide it takes a few evenings.
  • Exercism has about a hundred Rust tasks with automatic tests. You can ask for comments from a volunteer mentor.
  • Advent of Code publishes a series of puzzles every December, each in two parts, and all earlier years stay open. Each puzzle is practice in parsing text, in iterators and in collections.

Projects train the judgement. Ideas, ordered roughly by size:

IdeaWhat it trains
Your own version of a Unix tool: wc, head, tree, grep with coloursfiles, arguments, iterators, tests
A tool that renames or sorts your photos by datepaths, folders, errors, dry runs
A program that watches a web page and tells you when it changesHTTP, async, timers, storing state
A text adventure or a small roguelike game in the terminalenums, state machines, a game loop
A static site generator: Markdown in, HTML outparsing, templates, a whole pipeline
A chat bot for a platform you usean API from someone else, JSON, long-running tasks
An interpreter for a tiny language of your ownrecursion, Box, enums, error messages
A key-value store with a network protocolTCP, concurrency, files that survive a crash
A ray tracer that writes an image filenumbers, traits, Rayon, performance
A contribution to a crate you usereading foreign code, tests, review

Finish small things. Three finished tools teach more than one huge project that never runs.

Reading good code

Code to learn from, once your own projects raise questions:

  • The standard library. Option, Vec and String are written in Rust that you can now read. Click “source” in their documentation.
  • ripgrep, a fast search tool: how a larger command-line program is split into crates.
  • mini-redis, written by the Tokio team as a teaching project: an async server and client, with comments that explain the choices.
  • The examples folder of Axum, Bevy, egui or any other crate you use. Examples are the fastest way into a library.

Staying up to date

  • A new stable version of Rust appears every six weeks. Run rustup update now and then. The Rust blog explains what each version brings.
  • This Week in Rust is a weekly newsletter: articles, new crates, events, jobs.
  • A new edition arrives about every three years. cargo fix --edition does most of the moving (chapter 39).
  • Talks from conferences such as RustConf, EuroRust and RustNation are published as videos.

This guide was tested with Rust 1.100. Rust keeps old code working, so the examples will compile with later versions. Crates outside the standard library move faster. When an example with a crate no longer compiles, look at the changelog of that crate first.

Guided exercisePick one next step

Write a short plan for the next two weeks: one project you will build, one book or article you will read, and one community place you will visit or follow. Keep the plan visible.

Need a hint?

Do not pick everything at once. Choose one real need and one learning resource that supports it.

Show solution and explanation

A good plan is concrete and small enough to finish. Example: “I will build a CLI that renames photos by date, read one chapter of Rustlings or the Rust book, and ask a question in the users forum when I get stuck.” The important part is that the plan connects learning to a real task.

PracticeChoose a reading habit

Pick one resource from this chapter and explain in one sentence why it matches the project you want to build next. Then write down one action you will take when you finish the chapter: a code sample, a note, or a small experiment.

Need a hint?

Match the resource to your audience: learn ownership from a book, learn compiler messages from Rustlings, or read async docs if you need a server.

Show solution and explanation

A strong answer names both the task and the reason. Example: “I need to build a small web service, so I will read Zero To Production in Rust because it starts with a single service and keeps growing systematically.” The action is the step that turns reading into understanding.

ChallengeDecide what to revisit

Choose one topic from this guide that you still find unclear. Write a one-paragraph note saying what you understand, what you do not yet understand, and what you will do next to close the gap.

Need a hint?

Use a concrete question: “I understand ownership in simple cases but not in a struct that contains a Vec and a reference; I will revisit that chapter and write one tiny example.”

Show solution and explanation

This exercise trains the habit of making your confusion precise. The goal is not to feel bad about the gap; it is to convert uncertainty into a next action. That is how Rust learning becomes durable.

Check your understanding
1

Why is a loop of build, read code, and explain useful?

Learning in a loop keeps your knowledge connected to real work and helps you notice where you are still guessing.

2

Which resource is best for a beginner who wants to improve compiler-message reading?

Rustlings is built for small fixes, so it helps you practice reading compiler messages as you make mistakes on purpose.

3

Why is it valuable to choose just one topic at a time?

One topic at a time keeps your attention on the skill that matters right now.

4

What is a good first contribution to open source?

Small, well-described contributions are the easiest way to start helping in a project and to learn from experienced maintainers.

People

  • The users forum is the place for questions of every level, and answers there are patient.
  • The official Discord and Zulip chats, and the r/rust forum on Reddit, are active every day.
  • Many cities have a Rust meetup. Showing a small project there is a good first talk.
  • When you are stuck, write a good question: a small program that shows the problem, the full compiler message, and what you expected to happen. Making the small program often answers the question before you send it.

Giving back

Open-source projects need more than code. Good first contributions are a fix in the documentation of a crate after it confused you, a missing example, a test for a reported bug, or a clear bug report with a small program that shows the problem. Many projects mark suitable tasks with a label such as “good first issue”. And when you have written a tool that others could use, publish it (chapter 39).

Guided exercisePlan the next thirty days

Pick the project you wrote down in chapter 1, or a new one. Write three steps, each small enough to finish in one evening, and put a date next to each. The first step should be something you already know how to do — creating the project and printing one line is allowed.

Need a hint?

If a step takes longer than an evening, it is not a step yet. “Add a database” is a month. “Make the program read one line from a file” is an evening.

Show solution and explanation

There is no single right plan, but a workable shape looks like this:

  1. By Tuesday: cargo new mytool, print one hard-coded line, commit it.
  2. By Thursday: read a file given on the command line, print its first ten lines.
  3. By Sunday: count the words in that file and print the count.

Notice the direction: each step is runnable and each one changes one thing. A plan whose steps you cannot run is a wish list. When a step turns out to be harder than expected, split it — that is not failure, it is the normal way plans are made.

PracticeWrite a question worth answering

Think of the last problem you could not solve. Write the forum post you would send: what you wanted, the smallest program that shows the problem, the full compiler message, and what you expected instead. Do not send it anywhere.

Need a hint?

Four ingredients: what you tried, what happened, what you expected, and the smallest complete program that shows it. The smallest program is the part people skip, and it is the part that gets answers.

Show solution and explanation

A post that gets answered looks like this:

Title: Iterator::sum gives 0 on a Vec<f64> I filled in a loop

I am reading numbers from a file and summing them. The count is right but the total is 0.

I expected 45. I get 0. The real code adds inside a loop first and sums afterwards, which is where it differs from this sketch.

There is a good chance that writing it down solves it before you post: the act of shrinking the program is the debugging technique. Judging by the sketch, the loop that fills the vector probably produces integers and the sum is taken over an empty or shadowed binding — and you would have found that while trimming. If not, the post is now easy to answer.

ChallengeReturn something to a crate that confused you

Find a sentence, an example or a missing type signature in the documentation of a crate you use that cost you time. Open an issue or a pull request on that crate’s repository with a better wording.

Need a hint?

Small documentation pull requests are merged quickly, and maintainers are grateful for them. Mention which version you used and paste the confusing sentence verbatim, so the maintainer does not have to search for it.

Show solution and explanation

The recipe:

  1. Find the documentation source. Most crates keep it in the repository as doc comments above the code, or as a docs/ folder, not on docs.rs.
  2. Edit the comment, keeping the meaning, and add the example you wish you had found.
  3. Run the crate’s tests locally if you can: cargo test also runs the examples in doc comments, so a wrong example fails there.
  4. Open a pull request that says what confused you and what you changed. One sentence is enough.
  5. If the repository has a CONTRIBUTING.md, read it first; it usually says how to sign commits and what to run.

Do this once and you are a contributor to the Rust ecosystem, which is a different relationship with the language from being a reader of it.

Check your understanding
1

How often does Rust publish a new stable release?

Rust ships a stable release every six weeks. Editions — batches of opt-in language changes — arrive roughly every three years, so “a new version” and “a new edition” are different events.

2

Your program compiles today. A new stable release arrives. What happens to it?

Backwards compatibility is the promise: code that compiles on one stable release keeps compiling on later ones. Moving to a new edition is a separate, opt-in step in Cargo.toml, helped by cargo fix --edition.

3

Two crates do the same job. Which signal tells you the most?

Popularity is a proxy, not evidence. A recent release, a maintainer who answers issues, and documentation with real examples tell you what the next year of your project will feel like.

4

Which is the best first contribution to the ecosystem?

Start where your own confusion was. A documentation fix is small, obviously useful, and almost always welcome; the larger contributions come later, once you know the code.

5

This guide says a topic is “out of scope”. What does that mean in practice?

The coverage policy is written down in chapter 0 and applied here: taught, named with advice, or declared out of scope. A declared gap is honest; a silent one is a trap for the reader.

Recap
  • Keep a loop going: build, read good code, explain.
  • Pick resources by need: the Brown edition of the book for ownership, Rustlings for compiler messages, Effective Rust and the API Guidelines for style, the specialised books for async, unsafe, concurrency and performance.
  • Practise with small tasks, and learn judgement with projects that you finish.
  • Update Rust regularly, read the release notes, and ask and answer questions in the community.
  • A declared gap is honest, a silent one is not: this chapter lists what the guide deliberately leaves out, and where to read instead.

A

Glossary

The technical words of this guide, in plain language. Type in the box to filter the list. Where a chapter explains the word in full, the entry links to it.

ABI
The exact rules by which compiled code calls other compiled code: where arguments go, how values are laid out. The C ABI is the common language between programming languages. See chapter 36.
aliasing
Reaching the same value through more than one name. Rust allows it only while nobody changes the value. See chapter 10.
alignment
The rule that a value must start at an address divisible by a certain number, usually its size. It is the reason for padding inside structs. See chapter 37.
allocation
Asking for a block of memory on the heap. It takes time, so fast code avoids doing it in a loop. See chapter 52.
API
The set of functions and types that a library or a web service offers to its users.
argument
A value that is passed to a function in a call. The function receives it in a parameter.
array
A list with a fixed length, known at compile time, whose elements all have the same type: [i32; 3]. See chapter 4.
associated function
A function that belongs to a type but has no self parameter, called as Type::name(). String::new() is one.
associated type
A type that a trait leaves open and each implementation fills in, such as Item in Iterator. See chapter 28.
async
A way to write code that waits (for the network, for a timer) without blocking a thread. An async fn returns a future. See chapter 32.
atomic
A type whose operations happen in one indivisible step, so that several threads can use it without a lock. See chapter 31.
attribute
An instruction for the compiler written above an item, such as #[derive(Debug)] or #[test].
backtrace
The list of function calls that were active when a program panicked. Switch it on with RUST_BACKTRACE=1.
benchmark
A measurement of how long a piece of code takes, repeated often enough to be trusted. See chapter 52.
binary
A file that the computer can run directly. Also called an executable or a program file.
binding
A name attached to a value. let x = 5; binds the name x to 5.
bit
The smallest unit of data: 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte.
block
Code between { and }. A block is an expression: its value is the value of its last expression.
borrow checker
The part of the compiler that checks the rules for references: many readers or one writer, and no reference outlives its value. See chapter 10.
borrowing
Using a value through a reference, without becoming its owner.
bound
A requirement on a type parameter: T: Display means “any type T that can be printed”. See chapter 19.
Box
A pointer that owns a value on the heap. See chapter 27.
buffer
A block of memory that collects data so that it can be read or written in large pieces, not byte by byte.
bug
A mistake in a program that makes it behave wrongly.
build script
A file build.rs that Cargo runs before it compiles a package, for example to generate code in OUT_DIR or compile C code. See chapter 36 and chapter 39.
byte
Eight bits. The unit in which memory and files are measured.
cancellation safety
Whether an async operation can be dropped mid-.await (for example in tokio::select!) without losing data or leaving corrupt state. See chapter 32.
Cargo
Rust’s tool for building, testing, documenting and publishing packages, and for fetching dependencies. See chapter 39.
channel
A queue for sending values from one thread or task to another. See chapter 30.
CI
Continuous integration: a server that builds and tests the project automatically after every change. See chapter 40.
Clippy
A tool with several hundred extra checks that suggests better ways to write code: cargo clippy.
clone
An explicit, complete copy of a value, made with .clone(). It may be expensive.
closure
A function without a name that can use variables from the place where it was written: |x| x + offset. See chapter 24.
collection
A type that holds many values: Vec, HashMap, HashSet and others. See chapter 15.
compile time
The moment when the compiler translates the program. A mistake found “at compile time” never reaches a user.
compiler
The tool that translates your source code into a program the computer can run, and checks it for mistakes first. Rust’s compiler is called rustc.
concurrency
Dealing with several tasks during the same period of time. They may take turns on one processor core.
const
A value that is fixed when the program is compiled, with a name in capital letters.
constant
See const.
Copy
A trait for small values that are duplicated bit by bit instead of moved, such as numbers and bool. See chapter 9.
crate
The unit that the compiler translates in one go: one library or one program. Also the word for a library published on crates.io. See chapter 17.
crates.io
The public registry where Rust libraries are published.
dangling pointer
A pointer to memory that has already been freed. Using it is a serious bug, and safe Rust makes it impossible.
data race
Two threads touching the same memory at the same time, at least one of them writing, with nothing to coordinate them. Safe Rust rules it out at compile time.
deadlock
Two threads that each wait for a lock the other one holds, for ever. See chapter 31.
debug build
The quick, unoptimised build that cargo build makes. Good for development, far too slow for measuring speed.
dependency
A crate that your package uses. It is listed in Cargo.toml.
dereference
To follow a reference or pointer to the value behind it, written *r.
derive
To let the compiler write a trait implementation for you: #[derive(Debug, Clone)].
deserialisation
Turning data in a format such as JSON into Rust values. See chapter 43.
destructuring
Taking a value apart with a pattern: let (x, y) = point;. See chapter 14.
discriminant
The hidden number in an enum value that says which variant it is.
documentation comment
A comment that starts with ///. cargo doc turns such comments into web pages, and their examples are run as tests.
drop
The moment a value is cleaned up, when its owner goes out of scope. Types can run their own code then, through the trait Drop.
dyn
Marks a trait object: dyn Shape is “some type that implements Shape, decided while the program runs”.
dynamic dispatch
Choosing which function to call while the program runs, by looking it up in a table. It is what dyn Trait does.
edition
A version of the language’s surface, such as 2021 or 2024. A crate chooses one, and crates of different editions work together. See chapter 39.
enum
A type whose value is exactly one of several named variants, each of which can carry its own data. See chapter 13.
error
Either a message from the compiler that stops the build, or a value of type Err(…) that a function returns when something went wrong.
executable
See binary.
expression
A piece of code that produces a value: 2 + 3, a function call, an if with its branches. See chapter 5.
feature
A named, optional part of a crate that can be switched on in Cargo.toml. See chapter 39.
FFI
Foreign function interface: calling code written in another language, or being called by it. See chapter 36.
field
A named piece of data inside a struct.
flame graph
A picture of where a program spends its time: one bar for each function, as wide as its share of the time. See chapter 52.
float
A number with a fractional part, stored with limited precision: f32 or f64.
function
A named piece of code with parameters and a result. See chapter 5.
future
A value that stands for a result that will be ready later. Awaiting it gives the result. See chapter 32.
fuzzing
Testing a function with huge numbers of random inputs to find the ones that make it crash. See chapter 41.
garbage collector
A part of many languages that searches for unused memory and frees it while the program runs. Rust has none.
GAT
Generic associated type: an associated type inside a trait that takes lifetime or type parameters of its own, such as type Item<'a>. See chapter 28.
generic
Written once for many types, with a type parameter such as T. See chapter 19.
guard
A value whose only job is to undo something when it is dropped, such as the guard that unlocks a mutex. Also: an extra if condition on a match arm.
handle
A value that stands for something you cannot hold directly, such as an open file or a running thread.
hash
A number computed from a value, used to find it quickly in a HashMap.
HashMap
A collection that finds a value by its key. See chapter 15.
heap
The part of memory for data whose size is not known in advance or that must live longer than one function call. See chapter 8.
idempotency
Performing the same operation or delivering the same message more than once without changing the outcome beyond the first execution. See chapter 45.
idiomatic
Written the way experienced users of the language would write it. See chapter 38.
immutable
Not changeable. Variables and references are immutable unless marked mut.
impl
The block in which the methods of a type, or the implementation of a trait for a type, are written.
inlining
An optimisation that copies the body of a small function into the place where it is called.
integer
A whole number. Rust has signed ones (i8 to i128, isize) and unsigned ones (u8 to u128, usize).
integration test
A test in the folder tests/ that uses a crate from the outside, as a user would. See chapter 22.
interior mutability
Changing a value through a shared reference, with the safety check moved to run time or to the processor. Cell, RefCell, Mutex and atomics do this. See chapter 27.
invariant
Something that must always be true for a value, such as “the percentage is between 0 and 100”. Private fields and constructors protect invariants.
item
Something defined at the top level of a module: a function, struct, enum, trait, constant, impl block or module.
iterator
A value that hands out a sequence of items one by one. See chapter 25.
JSON
A widespread text format for data, used by nearly every web API. See chapter 43.
keyword
A word that belongs to the language and cannot be used as a name, such as fn or let. The list is in the reference appendix.
lazy
Doing work only when the result is asked for. Iterators and futures are lazy.
library
Code meant to be used by other programs. It has no main function.
lifetime
The stretch of the program during which a reference is valid. Written 'a where the compiler needs to be told. See chapter 21.
linker
The tool that joins all compiled pieces into one program file, as the last step of a build.
lint
A check for code that compiles but is probably a mistake or bad style. Warnings come from lints.
literal
A value written directly in the code: 42, "hello", true.
lock
See mutex.
macro
Code that writes code. A macro call ends in !, as in println!. See chapter 34.
match
The expression that compares a value with a list of patterns and runs the first arm that fits. It must cover every case.
memory leak
Memory that is never freed although nothing uses it any more.
memory safety
The guarantee that a program never reads or writes memory it should not: no dangling pointers, no access past the end of a list, no data races.
method
A function that belongs to a type and is called with a dot: text.len(). Its first parameter is self.
module
A named group of items inside a crate, with its own privacy boundary. See chapter 17.
monomorphisation
The way the compiler handles generics: it makes a separate, specialised copy of the code for every type it is used with.
move
Handing a value over to a new owner. The old variable can no longer be used. See chapter 9.
mutable
Changeable. Asked for with mut.
mutex
A lock that lets only one thread at a time reach the data inside it. See chapter 31.
newtype
A struct with a single field, made to give a value its own type: struct Metres(f64);. See chapter 29.
no_std
A crate that does not use the standard library, so that it can run without an operating system. See chapter 50.
OpenAPI
A standard JSON or YAML schema describing HTTP routes, request bodies, and responses so tools like Swagger UI can generate interactive docs. See chapter 46.
Option
The type for a value that may be missing: Some(value) or None. See chapter 13.
overflow
A calculation whose result does not fit into the type. In a debug build Rust panics, in a release build the number wraps around.
ownership
Rust’s central rule: every value has exactly one owner, and is freed when that owner goes out of scope. See chapter 9.
package
A folder with a Cargo.toml: one or more crates that are built and published together.
panic
The controlled stop of a thread after a bug was detected, with a message and a location. See chapter 18.
parallelism
Doing several things at the same instant, on several processor cores.
parameter
A variable in a function definition that receives an argument.
pattern
A shape that a value is compared with, and that can take it apart: Some(x), (a, b), 1..=5. See chapter 14.
pointer
A value that holds the address of another value in memory.
prelude
The small set of names that every Rust file can use without a use line, such as Vec, Option and String.
procedural macro
A macro written as a Rust function that receives code and returns code. #[derive(…)] macros are of this kind.
profile
A set of compiler settings in Cargo. dev and release are the two that matter most.
profiler
A tool that measures where a running program spends its time.
race condition
A bug where the result depends on which of two threads happens to be faster.
raw pointer
A pointer without any guarantee, *const T or *mut T. It can only be followed in unsafe code. See chapter 35.
Rc
A pointer with a counter that allows several owners of one value in one thread. Arc is the version for several threads.
recursion
A function that calls itself.
reference
A pointer that Rust guarantees to be valid: &T for reading, &mut T for changing. See chapter 10.
release build
The optimised build made by cargo build --release. It is the one to measure and to ship.
Result
The type for an operation that can fail: Ok(value) or Err(error). See chapter 18.
return value
The value that a function hands back to its caller.
run time
The time while the program is running. Also: the support code that a language needs while a program runs. Rust’s is tiny.
runtime (async)
The library that runs async tasks and wakes them when they can continue. Tokio is the usual one.
rustc
The Rust compiler. You normally start it through Cargo.
rustup
The tool that installs and updates Rust itself.
scope
The region of code in which a name is valid, usually up to the closing } of its block.
semantic versioning
The convention for version numbers major.minor.patch: a change that breaks users raises the first number. Short: semver.
Send
The marker trait for types that may be moved to another thread. See chapter 30.
serialisation
Turning Rust values into a format such as JSON, for storing or sending. See chapter 43.
shadowing
Declaring a new variable with the name of an existing one. The old one is hidden from then on.
signature
The first line of a function: its name, its parameters with their types, and its return type.
SIMD
Single instruction, multiple data: CPU vector instructions that operate on several numbers at once in one register. See chapter 52.
slice
A view of a run of elements inside an array, a Vec or a string: &[T] or &str. See chapter 11.
smart pointer
A type that behaves like a pointer and does something more, such as owning the value (Box) or counting owners (Rc).
span
A timed unit of work in structured tracing, tracking everything that happens during one request or operation along with its fields. See chapter 51.
stack
The part of memory for the local variables of the functions that are running. It is fast, and it is tidied up automatically. See chapter 8.
standard library
The library that comes with Rust: collections, text, files, threads and more. A map is in the reference appendix.
statement
A piece of code that does something and produces no value, such as a let. It ends with a semicolon.
static
A value with a fixed place in memory that lives for the whole run of the program.
static dispatch
Choosing which function to call at compile time. It is what generics do, and it costs nothing at run time.
String
Owned, growable text on the heap. Its borrowed relative is the string slice, &str. See chapter 11.
struct
A type that groups several named values into one. See chapter 12.
Sync
The marker trait for types that may be shared between threads by reference.
task
A piece of async work that a runtime runs alongside others. Much cheaper than a thread.
test
A function marked #[test] that checks that code does what it should. cargo test runs them all. See chapter 22.
thread
A separate line of execution inside one program. Several threads can run at the same time on several cores. See chapter 30.
toolchain
The compiler together with its tools: Cargo, the standard library, rustfmt, Clippy.
trait
A set of methods that a type can implement. Traits describe what types have in common. See chapter 20.
trait object
A value used through a trait without knowing its exact type: &dyn Trait or Box<dyn Trait>.
tuple
A fixed group of values that may have different types: (i32, String).
turbofish
The syntax ::<T> for naming a type in a call: "5".parse::<i32>().
type
What kind of value something is: a number, text, a list. It decides how the value is stored and what can be done with it.
type inference
The compiler working out a type from how a value is used, so that you do not have to write it.
undefined behaviour
An operation for which the language promises nothing at all: the program may crash, give wrong results, or seem to work. It can only come from unsafe code. See chapter 35.
unit
The empty tuple (). It is the “result” of code that returns nothing useful.
unit test
A test next to the code it checks, usually in a mod tests at the end of the file.
unsafe
The keyword that marks code whose safety the compiler cannot check, so that the programmer takes over the responsibility. See chapter 35.
UTF-8
The way Rust stores text: every character takes one to four bytes.
variable
A name for a value.
variant
One of the possibilities of an enum.
Vec
A list that can grow, with all elements of one type, stored on the heap. See chapter 15.
WebAssembly
A compact code format that browsers and other hosts can run at near-native speed. Rust compiles to it. Short: Wasm. See chapter 49.
workspace
Several packages that are developed together and share one Cargo.lock and one target folder. See chapter 39.
zero-cost abstraction
A convenient way of writing code that the compiler turns into machine code as fast as the hand-written version. Iterators are the standard example.

No matching term. Try a shorter word.

Reference tables

Tables to keep open while you write code: the words and signs of the language, the formatting codes, the traits you can derive, and a map of the standard library. Every example on this page was compiled and run.

Keywords

A keyword is a word that belongs to the language. You cannot use it as a name.

KeywordMeaningChapter
asconvert between simple types (x as f64); rename in a use29, 17
async, awaitwrite and wait for asynchronous code32
break, continueleave a loop; go to its next round6
consta constant; also const fn and const generics3, 19
cratethe root of the current crate, in paths17
dyna trait object: dyn Trait20
elsethe other branch of if and of let … else6, 13
enumdefine an enum13
externfunctions of another language36
false, truethe two values of bool4
fndefine a function5
for, inloop over an iterator6, 25
ifa decision; also a guard in match6, 14
implmethods for a type, or a trait for a type; impl Trait12, 20
leta new variable3
loop, whilerepeat for ever; repeat while a condition holds6
matchcompare a value with patterns6, 13, 14
moddefine a module17
movea closure takes ownership of what it uses24, 30
mutallow change: let mut, &mut3, 10
pubmake an item visible outside its module17
refbind by reference in a pattern (older style)14
returnleave a function with a value5
self, Selfthe value a method is called on; its type12
statica value that lives for the whole run31
structdefine a struct12
superthe parent module, in paths17
traitdefine a trait20
typea type alias; an associated type29, 28
unsafecode whose safety the compiler cannot check35
usebring a path into scope17
wherebounds on type parameters, after the signature19

A few more words have a meaning only in special places, and can be used as names elsewhere: union, macro_rules, raw, safe, and 'static among the lifetimes.

These words do nothing today, but are reserved for the future, so you cannot use them as names either: abstract, become, box, do, final, gen, macro, override, priv, try, typeof, unsized, virtual, yield.

Using a keyword as a name anyway

Sometimes you need a name that is a keyword: a field called type in data from another program, or a function called try in an old crate. Put r# in front of it. This is called a raw identifier:

Operators and other signs

SignMeaningExample

&& || !and, or, not, for bool values. && and || skip the right side when the left side decidesready && !done
