Which operator goes first

From the tightest binding to the loosest. Operators on the same line are worked out from left to right.

LevelOperators
1method calls, fields: a.b(), a.b
2function calls and indexing: f(x), v[i]
3?
4the one-sided operators: -x, !x, *x, &x, &mut x
5as
6* / %
7+ -
8<< >>
9&
10^
11|
12== != < > <= >= (cannot be chained: a < b < c is an error)
13&&
14||
15.. ..=
16= += and the other assignments
17return, break, closures

Three results that surprise people. When in doubt, add parentheses: they cost nothing.

Working with single bits

An integer is a row of bits (chapter 4). Six operators work on the bits directly. They are used for sets of yes-or-no flags packed into one number, for file formats and network protocols, and for hardware.

For more than a few flags, the crate bitflags gives them a type of their own, so that flags of different kinds cannot be mixed up.

Ways to write a value

You writeYou get
1_000_000an integer; the underscores are only for the reader
0xff, 0o77, 0b1010an integer in base 16, base 8 and base 2
42u8, 7_i64, 1usizean integer of the named type
2.5, 1e3, 2.5f32a float (f64 unless you say f32)
'a', '\n', '\u{1F980}'a char: a letter, a line break, a character by its number
b'a'the byte of an ASCII character: a u8
"text"a &str. \n, \t, \\, \" and \u{…} work inside
r"C:\temp", r#"say "hi""#a raw string: backslashes (and, with #, quotation marks) mean themselves
b"bytes"a byte string: &[u8; 5]
c"text"a C string, with a zero byte at the end: &CStr (chapter 36)
(1, "a"), ()a tuple; the empty tuple, called “unit”
[1, 2, 3], [0; 8]an array; an array of eight zeros

Formatting codes

The codes work in println!, format!, write!, panic!, assert! and all other formatting macros. The general shape is {name:fill align sign # 0 width .precision type}, and every part can be left out.

LineCodeMeaning
1{} and {:?}for people (Display), and for programmers (Debug)
2{:>10} {:<10} {:^10}at least 10 characters wide: aligned right, left, centred. Text goes left unless you say otherwise, numbers go right
3{:*^12} {:->8}the character in front of the alignment sign fills the empty room
4{:6} {:06} {:+}a width for a number; filled with zeros; always with a sign
5{:.2} {:8.3} {:e}digits after the point; width and digits; scientific notation
6{:x} {:X} {:o} {:b}base 16 in small and capital letters, base 8, base 2
7{:#x} {:#b} {:#010b}with the prefix 0x or 0b; the width counts the prefix
8{0} {name} {last}an argument by position; a variable by name; an argument named in the call
9{pi:width$} {pi:.digits$}width and precision taken from variables
10{{ }}a real brace
11{:#?}Debug spread over several lines

{:p} prints the address in a pointer or reference. To make your own type work with {}, implement Display (chapter 20). For {:?}, derive Debug.

Traits you can derive

#[derive(…)] writes the implementation for you. It works when every field of the type already has the trait.

TraitWhat you can do afterwardsNotes
Debugprint with {:?} and dbg!derive it on almost every type
Clonevalue.clone()an explicit copy that may be expensive
Copythe value is copied instead of movedonly for small types without heap data; needs Clone
PartialEq== and !=compares field by field
Eqpromise that equality has no exceptionsneeds PartialEq; not possible with f32 or f64 fields
PartialOrd<, >, <=, >=compares the fields in the order they are written; needs PartialEq
Ordsort(), max(), use as a key in a BTreeMapneeds Eq and PartialOrd
Hashuse as a key in a HashMap or HashSetneeds Eq. Equal values must have equal hashes, which the derived versions guarantee
DefaultType::default() and ..Default::default()numbers become 0, text empty, bool false, Option None. For an enum, mark one variant with #[default]

A common full set for a small value type is #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord, Default)]. Crates add more: Serialize and Deserialize from serde (chapter 43), Error from thiserror (chapter 18), Parser from clap (chapter 44).

Chapter 38 shows these in use.

A map of the standard library

You reach everything with use std::…. The most used items need no use at all: they are in the prelude, which is in scope in every file. It contains Option and Result with their variants, String, Vec, Box, the traits Clone, Copy, Drop, Default, Iterator, From, Into, TryFrom, TryInto, ToString, PartialEq, Ord and their relatives, and the function drop.

ModuleWhat is in itChapter

HTTP status codes

HTTP status codes are part of every web service, and the numbers matter to clients. The ones a Rust web service sends, in practice (chapter 46):

CodeNameMeaningWhen a server sends it
200OKSuccess with a bodyA GET that found something
201CreatedSuccess, something new existsAfter a POST that stored a row; add a Location header
204No ContentSuccess, deliberately no bodyA DELETE, or a PUT whose result the client does not need
301Moved PermanentlyThe resource has a new address for everRedirecting a renamed route in a browser
304Not ModifiedThe client’s cached copy is still goodIf-None-Match matching your ETag
400Bad RequestMalformed: the body is not even parseableBroken JSON, a missing required field
401UnauthorizedI do not know who you areNo session, expired token, bad API key
403ForbiddenI know who you are, and you may notA reader calling an admin route
404Not FoundNo such resource — or none you may know aboutA missing id; also used to hide existence
405Method Not AllowedThe path exists, the method does notDELETE on a read-only route
409ConflictThe request clashes with the current stateA duplicate unique key, an edit of a stale version
413Payload Too LargeThe body exceeds the limitAn upload beyond the configured maximum
415Unsupported Media TypeThe body’s format is not acceptedXML sent to a JSON endpoint
422Unprocessable ContentWell-formed, but fails validationA negative age, a handle with a forbidden character. Older material calls it Unprocessable Entity; the code is the same
429Too Many RequestsRate limitedInclude Retry-After
500Internal Server ErrorThe server’s fault, no detail to the clientAny unexpected error; log it, do not leak it
502Bad GatewayAn upstream answered badlyA proxy could not get a valid answer
503Service UnavailableTemporarily unable to serveStarting up, shutting down, /ready failing
504Gateway TimeoutAn upstream took too longA proxy’s timeout expired

The two that are most often confused are 401 and 403: authentication versus authorisation. The one that is most often wrong is 200 with an error inside the body — a client, a proxy and a monitoring system all read the status code, and none of them reads your JSON.

The full list, with the official definitions, is in RFC 9110.

Authoritative and current sources

This guide aims to explain the ideas and provide a practical route through the ecosystem. It cannot replace the reference for a language guarantee, a crate’s full API, or a target-specific deployment rule. Use primary documentation to verify details before making a production decision:

Zero To Production in RustA production-oriented backend development path and its publicly available examples

For framework and library behavior, start at that project’s official guide or API documentation; examples in this guide are deliberately smaller than those references. Check the version selector, changelog, minimum supported Rust version, feature flags, platform support, license and maintenance status. A link to /latest/ documentation describes what is current when you read it, not necessarily what an older Cargo.lock selected. The ecosystem moves faster than Rust’s stable language guarantees.

C

Compiler errors and how to repair them

The Rust compiler refuses many programs, and it explains itself better than most compilers. This page lists the errors that you will meet most often. Each entry has a small program that produces the error, the real message, the reason, and the usual repairs. Use the search box with the error code, for example E0382.

How to read a message

Every message has the same parts:

  1. The code (E0382) names the kind of error, and the summary says it in one line.
  2. The position: file, line, column.
  3. The lines marked with --- tell the story that led to the error. Read them from top to bottom.
  4. The line marked with ^^^ is where the compiler gave up.
  5. help suggests a change, with +++ under the characters to add. note lines, when present, give background.

A method that works:

  1. Repair the first error first, then compile again. Later errors are often only consequences of the first one.
  2. Read all of it. The ^^^ marks the place where the compiler gave up. The --- marks show the earlier lines that caused the problem, and the real mistake is often there.
  3. Try the help. It is right more often than not. Think for a moment whether it does what you mean: a suggested .clone() compiles, and may still not be what you want.
  4. Ask for the long explanation. rustc --explain E0382 prints a page about that error with examples.
  5. Ask what would go wrong if the compiler accepted the program (chapter 10). The answer usually shows the repair.

Ownership and moves

E0382: use of a moved value

A value has one owner. let moved = names; handed the vector to moved, and names is empty from then on. The same happens when you pass a value to a function that takes ownership, or use it in a for loop without &.

Repairs:

  • Borrow: let view = &names;, or for name in &names.
  • Let the function borrow: change its parameter from Vec<String> to &[String].
  • Clone, if you really need two independent values: names.clone().
  • Use the value for the last time after the other uses.

E0505: moved while it is still borrowed

view still points at text on the last line, so text cannot be given away in between. If it were, view would point at a value that consume has already dropped.

Repairs:

  • Finish using the reference before the move.
  • Pass a reference to the function, or clone.

E0507: cannot move out of a borrow

Through a reference you may look, not take. Moving the String out would leave the team without a leader, and the owner of team would not know. The same error appears for let s = list[0]; with a list of Strings.

Repairs:

  • Borrow the part: let leader = &borrowed.leader;.
  • Clone it: borrowed.leader.clone().
  • If you own the container and want the value out: list.remove(i), list.pop(), option.take() or std::mem::take(&mut team.leader).

Borrowing

E0502: borrowed as mutable while also borrowed as immutable

Many readers or one writer, never both. first reads from the list until the last line, and push wants to change the list in between. Here the danger is real: push may move all elements to a new place.

Repairs:

  • Finish reading before you write: move the println! above the push.
  • Copy out what you need: let first = list[0];.
  • Keep a position, not a reference.
  • Inside a loop over the list: collect the changes and apply them after the loop (chapter 15).

E0499: two mutable borrows at once

Only one &mut to a value can be in use at a time.

Repairs:

  • Use the first reference for the last time before you create the second.
  • For two elements of one list: split_at_mut, swap or get_disjoint_mut (chapter 15).
  • For two fields of a struct: borrow the fields directly, not through a method (chapter 12).

E0596: cannot borrow as mutable

Changing a value needs mut on the variable, or a &mut reference. The same code appears when a function received &T and tries to change the value behind it.

Repairs:

  • let mut list = Vec::new();
  • For a parameter: take &mut Vec<i32>, and pass &mut list.

E0384: assigned twice to an immutable variable

Variables do not change unless you allow it.

Repairs:

  • let mut count = 0;
  • Or create a new variable with the same name: let count = count + 1; (chapter 3).

E0381: used before it has a value

Rust never reads memory that has not been given a value. The error also appears when only some branches of an if assign the variable.

Repairs:

  • Give a value at the declaration, or in every branch before the first use.

Lifetimes

E0597: does not live long enough

word is dropped at the end of the inner block, and longest would still point at it.

Repairs:

  • Declare the value in the outer scope, so that it lives as long as the reference.
  • Store an owned value in place of the reference: longest = word; or word.clone().

E0515: returns a reference to a local variable

text is created inside the function and dropped when the function ends. A reference to it would point at freed memory.

Repairs:

  • Return the owned value: -> String, and return text.
  • A reference may be returned only if it points into something that the caller passed in.

E0106: missing lifetime specifier

The function returns a reference, there are two references among the parameters, and the compiler cannot guess which one the result is tied to.

Repairs:

  • Say it: fn pick<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str (chapter 21).
  • In a struct: struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }, or own the data with a String.
  • If the function creates the value, return an owned type.

E0716: a temporary value is dropped while borrowed

String::from(…) creates a value that belongs to no variable. It lives only until the end of the statement, and trim returns a reference into it.

Repairs:

  • Give the value a name first: let text = String::from(" padded "); let word = text.trim();.

E0373: a closure may outlive the function

The closure borrows name, and a new thread may run longer than the function that started it.

Repairs:

  • move: thread::spawn(move || …) gives the closure ownership.
  • To share with several threads: Arc::clone for each one, then move (chapter 31).
  • To really borrow: thread::scope (chapter 30).

Types and traits

E0308: mismatched types

The most frequent error of all. The compiler shows the type it expected and the type it found. Rust never converts between types silently.

Repairs:

  • Text to number: "5".parse::<u32>() (a Result).
  • Number to number: x as f64, or u64::from(x).
  • &str to String: .to_string(). String to &str: &text.
  • Option<T> where T is expected: handle the None case first (chapter 13).
  • “expected (), found …” at the end of a function: the return type is missing, or a ; after the last expression threw the value away.

E0277: a trait is not implemented

An operation needs a trait that the type does not have. This one code covers many situations, and the summary line tells you which.

Repairs:

  • “doesn’t implement Display”: print with {:?} after #[derive(Debug)], or implement Display (chapter 20).
  • “the ? operator can only be used in a function that returns Result”: give the function (also main) the return type Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>.
  • “cannot add a float to an integer”: convert one side, count as f64 + 2.5.
  • “the trait bound T: … is not satisfied”: add the bound to your generic function (chapter 19).
  • “cannot be sent between threads safely”: an Rc or RefCell crossed a thread. Use Arc and Mutex (chapter 31).
  • “the size … cannot be known at compilation time”: a str or [T] without &, or a dyn Trait without Box.

E0599: no method with this name

The type in front of the dot has no such method. Often the method exists on a neighbour: sum belongs to iterators, not to Vec.

Repairs:

  • Read the help: here it suggests .into_iter() first. numbers.iter().sum() works too, and leaves the list usable.
  • “the trait … is not in scope”: add the use line that the compiler prints.
  • On an Option or Result: get the value out first (?, match, if let).
  • In generic code: the method comes from a trait that is missing in the bounds.

E0369: this operator does not work on this type

Operators are traits: == is PartialEq, < is PartialOrd, + is Add. Your own types have none of them until you say so.

Repairs:

  • #[derive(PartialEq)] for ==, #[derive(PartialOrd)] for <.
  • Implement std::ops::Add for + (chapter 28).
  • In a generic function: add the bound, T: PartialOrd.

E0282: type annotations needed

collect and parse can produce many types, and nothing here says which one you want. (The related codes E0283 and E0284 mean the same thing in slightly different situations.)

Repairs:

  • Annotate the variable: let numbers: Vec<&str> = …. The compiler can fill in the rest: Vec<_>.
  • Or name the type in the call: .collect::<Vec<_>>(), .parse::<i32>().

E0061: wrong number of arguments

Rust has no optional parameters and no default values for them.

Repairs:

  • Pass every argument.
  • For optional settings: an Option<T> parameter, a struct of options with Default, or a builder (chapter 38).

Names, modules and privacy

E0425: cannot find this name

No variable, function or constant with this name is visible here. Usually it is a typing mistake, a name from another scope, or a missing use.

Repairs:

  • Check the spelling: the compiler suggests similar names.
  • A variable declared inside { } is gone after the }.
  • For a function in another module: use crate::module::function;.

E0433: use of an undeclared type or module

The type exists, but this file has not imported it. A wrong path in a use line gives the related code E0432.

Repairs:

  • Add the line from the help: use std::collections::HashMap;.
  • For an external crate: is it in Cargo.toml? cargo add name.

E0616: a private field

Everything in a module is private unless marked pub, and the fields of a pub struct are private one by one. For a private function or type the code is E0603.

Repairs:

  • Make the field public: pub balance: i64.
  • Better, if the field has rules to protect: keep it private and add a method, pub fn balance(&self) -> i64 (chapter 17).

Patterns

E0004: a match that does not cover everything

A match must have an arm for every possible value. The compiler names the missing ones.

Repairs:

  • Add the missing arm.
  • Add a catch-all arm _ => …, if the rest really should be treated alike. For your own enums, prefer to list the variants: then the compiler reminds you when you add one.

E0005: a pattern that might not match, in let

A plain let needs a pattern that always fits. Some(n) does not fit None.

Repairs:

  • let Some(n) = input else { return; };
  • if let Some(n) = input { … }
  • match, or a fallback: input.unwrap_or(0).

Types that the compiler cannot build

E0072: a type of infinite size

A Folder would contain a Folder, which contains a Folder, without end.

Repairs:

  • Put the inner value behind a pointer: Option<Box<Folder>> (chapter 27).

E0038: this trait cannot be used as dyn

Behind a dyn Shape the concrete type is unknown, so a method that returns Self or has type parameters cannot be called through it.

Rust changed the vocabulary here: what older books and forum answers call object safety is now dyn compatibility, and the compiler’s own message uses the new phrase. A trait is dyn compatible when every method can be called through a fat pointer — no Self by value, no generic type parameters, no associated constants, and no associated types without a specified value. Chapter 28 walks through the rules one by one.

Repairs:

  • Add where Self: Sized to that method: it is then left out of the trait object.
  • Return Box<dyn Shape> in place of Self.
  • Or use generics (impl Shape) where you do not need a mixed list (chapter 28).

E0117: a foreign trait for a foreign type

You may implement a trait only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. Otherwise two crates could both do it, in different ways.

Repairs:

  • Wrap the type in a struct of your own: struct Names(Vec<String>);, and implement the trait for that (chapter 28).
  • Or define your own trait and implement it for the foreign type.

Unsafe and async

E0133: an unsafe call outside an unsafe block

The function has requirements that the compiler cannot check, and the caller must take responsibility in writing.

Repairs:

  • unsafe { danger(); }, with a // SAFETY: comment that says why the requirements hold (chapter 35).

E0728: await outside async code

.await works only inside an async fn or an async block, and somebody has to run the future.

Repairs:

  • Make the calling function async.
  • At the top: #[tokio::main] async fn main(), or runtime.block_on(…) (chapter 32).
  • An async function that calls itself gives E0733: put the inner call in Box::pin(…).

Messages without a code

Mistakes in the shape of the code have no number. The most common ones:

MessageUsual cause
expected one of …, found …a missing ;, , or ) on the line before the one that is marked
this file contains an unclosed delimitera {, ( or [ that is never closed. The message shows the candidates: check the indentation there
mismatched closing delimitera ) where a } belongs, or the other way round
unknown start of tokena character that Rust does not know, often curly quotation marks (“ ”) copied from a web page or a document. Type the quotation marks again
expected expression, found …something is missing after an operator or a =
cannot find macro … in this scopea missing ! is not the problem here: the macro is not imported, or misspelled (printn!)
expected ;, found …a statement without its ;

Warnings worth reading

A warning does not stop the build, and it is nearly always right.

WarningWhat it tells you
unused variablea value is computed and never used: a forgotten step, or a typing mistake in a name. Start the name with _ if it is on purpose
variable does not need to be mutableremove the mut
unused Result that must be usedan error is being ignored. Handle it with ?, or write let _ = …; to say that you mean it
function is never used, field is never readdead code: delete it, or it is not finished yet
unused importremove the use line
unreachable patternan earlier arm of the match already catches these values
value assigned … is never readthe variable is overwritten before anyone looks at it
unused comparison, comparison is uselessa test that is always true or always false, such as x >= 0 for an unsigned number

cargo clippy adds several hundred more checks of this kind (chapter 40).

D

Coming from another language

If you already program in another language, most of what you know still holds: variables, functions, loops, collections and tests work as you expect. This page is a translation table for the rest. Find your language, read which Rust feature takes the place of each thing you are used to, and follow the link to the chapter.

The six differences that matter

Whatever language you come from, these are the places where your habits will not work.

In most languagesIn RustChapter
A garbage collector, or free by hand, cleans up memoryEvery value has one owner, and is freed when the owner goes out of scope9
Any number of references can point at an object and change itMany readers or one writer, checked by the compiler10
null, nil or None can turn up anywhereA value that may be missing has the type Option<T>, and you must handle both cases13
Errors are exceptions that fly up the call stackErrors are values of type Result<T, E>, passed on with ?18
Classes inherit from classesStructs hold data, traits describe behaviour, and there is no inheritance20
Variables can be changed, and conversions happen silentlyNothing changes without mut, and nothing is converted unless you write it3, 4

The first weeks feel slow, because the compiler rejects programs that every other language would let you run. Each rejection stands for a bug that you would otherwise have found later, by testing or in production.

PythonRustChapter
list, dict, set, tupleVec<T>, HashMap<K, V>, HashSet<T>, tuples. All elements of a collection have one type15
NoneOption<T>: Some(x) or None13
try / except / raiseResult, match, ?18
class with __init__struct with an impl block and a new function12
__str__, __repr__, __eq__, __lt__, __hash__Display, Debug, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Hash, mostly through #[derive]20

for i, x in enumerate(xs), zip(a, b).iter().enumerate(), .zip()25

pip, venv, pyproject.toml, pytestall in one tool, Cargo: cargo add, Cargo.toml, cargo test39, 22

What will surprise you:

  • Types everywhere, but rarely written. The compiler works most of them out. You write them in function signatures.
  • Integers have a size and can overflow. 7 / 2 is 3, and 7.0 / 2.0 is 3.5. An integer and a float cannot be mixed without as.
  • text[0] does not exist. A string is UTF-8, and a character can take several bytes (chapter 11).
  • No default values for parameters and no keyword arguments. Use Option, a struct of options, or a builder (chapter 38).
  • Speed. A loop in Rust runs at the speed of C. You no longer need a library written in another language for the heavy parts, and you can write such a library for Python yourself with PyO3 (chapter 36).

What will surprise you:

  • await comes after the expression: fetch(url).await. That makes chains readable: client.get(url).send().await?.json().await?.
  • One thread is not the rule. A Tokio program runs tasks on several threads at once, so shared data needs Arc and a lock, and the compiler insists on it.
  • A closure does not keep its surroundings alive. There is no garbage collector, so a closure that outlives its function must own what it uses: move (chapter 24).
  • A struct has exactly the fields it declares. For data of unknown shape there is serde_json::Value.

What will surprise you:

  • There is no base class to put shared code in. See the worked example below.
  • Values are not references by default. A struct sits directly where it is declared, on the stack or inside another struct. A heap allocation is something you ask for, with Box, Vec or String.
  • No run time to start, and nothing to install on the target machine. The result of a build is one program file.
  • Dependency injection frameworks are rare. Pass what a function needs as a parameter, as a trait if tests need a fake (chapter 41).

undefined behaviour anywhereonly inside unsafe blocks35
CMake, Make, vcpkg, ConanCargo39
exceptions, error codesResult. A panic is for bugs, not for expected failures18

What will surprise you:

  • The borrow checker rejects patterns that you know to be correct, such as two pointers into the same structure. Some need a different design (indices in place of pointers), some need Rc<RefCell<T>>, and a few really need unsafe behind a safe interface.
  • Integer overflow is defined: a panic in debug builds, wrapping in release builds. The conversion rules are explicit, with no silent promotion.
  • No copy constructors. A copy that costs something is always visible as .clone().
  • You can keep your C and C++ code. Rust calls it and can be called from it (chapter 36).

What will surprise you:

  • More language to learn, and a slower compiler. In return there is no garbage collector, no nil pointer panic, and enums with data.
  • Async is not built in. You choose a runtime (nearly always Tokio), and a function is either async or not.
  • Unused variables and imports are warnings, not errors.

A class hierarchy, translated

The most common question from object-oriented languages is: where do I put what used to be a base class? A base class does three jobs at once, and Rust has a separate tool for each.

A base class gives youIn Rust
a list of kinds that is known and fixedan enum, and match
a common interface for kinds that others may adda trait, used through generics or dyn
methods written once for all kindsdefault methods in the trait
fields that all kinds sharea struct with those fields, placed inside each kind

Which of the first two to choose? If you know all the kinds, and new operations are added more often than new kinds, take the enum: every match is checked for completeness. If users of your code must be able to add kinds, take the trait.

The other three words of object-oriented programming translate like this:

  • Encapsulation is done by modules, not by classes. Fields are private to the module unless marked pub (chapter 17).
  • Polymorphism has three forms: generics (decided at compile time, fastest), dyn Trait (decided at run time, allows mixed lists), and enums (chapter 20, chapter 28).
  • Inheritance of implementation does not exist. Where you would have overridden one method of a large base class, pass the varying part in: as a closure, or as a value of a trait (chapter 24).

Habits to leave behind, and habits to keep

Leave behindDo this
objects that point at each other in all directionsone owner per value; refer to other values by an index or a key
a null check here and thereOption, handled once, at the place where the value enters
catching every exception at the topreturn Result, add context on the way up, report once in main
a base class “for later”start with plain structs and functions; add a trait when a second kind appears
getters and setters for every fieldpublic fields for plain data; private fields and methods where a rule must hold
cloning or locking everything until it compilesask who should own the data (chapter 38)

Keep: small functions, clear names, tests, code review, and measuring before optimising. Those are the same in every language.
